     CHAPTER 1: DAILY WORK TAKEAWAYS
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    After this chapter, in your daily work you will:
      • Stop writing retry/timeout/TLS code in every microservice
      • Understand why "just add a library" doesn't scale across 7+ services
      • Recognize the 8 problems in your OWN system (every microservices
        architecture has them — you just may not have noticed yet)
      • Be able to explain to your team: "This is why we need a service mesh"
      • Know which service mesh to choose based on your specific needs
      • Understand the proxy/sidecar pattern — the foundation of all meshes
      • Have a mental model: your code handles business logic, the mesh
        handles everything that happens BETWEEN your code

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     CHAPTER 1: ICA EXAM TIPS
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    🎯 ICA EXAM FOCUS — Chapter 1 is FOUNDATIONAL (not directly tested but
       understanding these concepts helps you reason through ALL scenarios):
      • The ICA exam may describe a "cascade failure" scenario — you must
        recognize it and know to apply DestinationRule outlierDetection
      • When a question asks you to "secure service communication," the
        answer is ALWAYS PeerAuthentication with STRICT mTLS
      • "Gradually deploy a new version" = VirtualService with weight field
      • "Prevent one service from overwhelming another" = DestinationRule
        with circuitBreaker / outlierDetection
      • The 8 problems map directly to ICA exam tasks — each problem
        has a specific Istio CRD solution you'll need to apply

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     CHAPTER 1: ICA PRACTICE QUESTIONS (10 Questions)
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    Q1: Your anihpj application has 7 microservices. The auth-service starts
        returning HTTP 503 errors. Without Istio, what is the most likely
        consequence?
    A1: Cascade failure. Every service that calls auth-service will have
        threads blocked waiting. Thread pools exhaust, and the entire
        platform could go down. With Istio circuit breaker (DestinationRule
        outlierDetection), the circuit opens after consecutive errors,
        returning immediate 503 without blocking threads.

    Q2: What is the primary advantage of a service mesh over implementing
        retry/timeout/TLS logic in application code?
    A2: Centralization. A service mesh eliminates code duplication across
        services, ensures consistent behavior, is language-agnostic, and
        allows policy changes via YAML rather than code deployments. Your
        application code focuses on business logic only.

    Q3: Your team is choosing between Istio and Linkerd. You need mTLS,
        canary deployments, circuit breaking, and distributed tracing.
        Which should you choose and why?
    A3: Istio. Linkerd provides mTLS and basic observability but does not
        support circuit breaking or advanced traffic management like canary
        deployments with weighted routing. Istio supports all four requirements.

    Q4: A slow user-service took down the entire anihpj platform. What
        Istio feature specifically prevents this?
    A4: Circuit breaking via DestinationRule's outlierDetection. When Envoy
        detects consecutiveGatewayErrors (e.g., 5), it opens the circuit
        and stops sending to the failing service, returning immediate 503.

    Q5: What is the difference between the "data plane" and "control plane"
        in a service mesh?
    A5: Data plane = all Envoy sidecar proxies handling actual traffic
        (routing, encrypting, retrying). Control plane = istiod, the central
        component that reads CRDs, converts to Envoy config via xDS, and
        pushes config to all proxies. Control plane configures; data plane executes.

    Q6: A developer says: "We don't need Istio — I can add retry logic to
        our Django code." Give three counter-arguments.
    A6: (1) Duplication — 7 services × retry code. (2) Inconsistency — each
        dev implements differently. (3) Language lock-in — adding a Go
        service requires rewriting all Python networking code. Istio applies
        uniformly across all services via YAML.

    Q7: In the Istio architecture, what component issues X.509 certificates
        for mTLS and what standard do they follow?
    A7: Citadel (sub-component of istiod) acts as the CA. It issues SPIFFE-
        compliant X.509 SVID certificates. Format: spiffe://cluster.local/
        ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api-serviceaccount. Certificates auto-rotate
        every 24 hours. (→ explained fully in section 3.2)

    Q8: Which Istio CRD would you use to route only 5% of users to a new
        version of jobpost-api, and what field controls the split?
    A8: VirtualService with the weight field. Two destinations: subset v1
        weight 95, subset v2 weight 5. Subsets defined in DestinationRule
        using pod labels (version: v1, version: v2). Rollback: set v2=0.

    Q9: What is the difference between PERMISSIVE and STRICT mTLS modes?
    A9: PERMISSIVE accepts both plain HTTP and mTLS (migration mode).
        STRICT rejects ALL plain HTTP and requires mTLS for every connection
        (production zero-trust mode). Apply via PeerAuthentication CRD.

    Q10: A compromised pod runs tcpdump on the same node as jobpost-api.
         With Istio STRICT mTLS, what does the attacker see?
    A10: Only encrypted binary data (garbage). All service-to-service traffic
         is TLS-encrypted by Envoy before leaving the pod. Without the private
         key (stored in Envoy memory), captured packets are unreadable.
         This is why STRICT mTLS is critical for zero-trust security.

         - One term has appeared throughout this section without a formal
           definition — worth pinning down before Chapter 2, and worth drawing,
           not just naming:

         - DEFINITION: BLAST RADIUS — the set of services (and users) that end
           up damaged by ONE failing service; it starts at the origin and
           spreads outward through the call graph one hop at a time. A SMALL
           blast radius stays contained at the origin; a LARGE one reaches
           services that never even call the origin directly. Every mechanism
           in this section exists to shrink this radius — none of them fix the
           original failure.

         - The diagram below turns that definition into anihpj's real call
           graph: four concentric rings, innermost is the service that actually
           crashed, outermost is the users who feel it even though they never
           call auth-service directly:

         [BLAST RADIUS — how ONE failure spreads outward through anihpj]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │         RING 3 — WHOLE MESH / END USERS         │
         │ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
         │ │         RING 2 — 2ND-DEGREE CALLER         │  │
         │ │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐   │  │
         │ │  │       RING 1 — DIRECT CALLER        │   │  │
         │ │  │   ┌─────────────────────────────┐   │   │  │
         │ │  │   │  RING 0 — FAILING SERVICE   │   │   │  │
         │ │  │   │ ┌─────────────────────────┐ │   │   │  │
         │ │  │   │ │ auth-service  (CRASHED) │ │   │   │  │
         │ │  │   │ │ root cause: PostgreSQL  │ │   │   │  │
         │ │  │   │ │connection pool exhausted│ │   │   │  │
         │ │  │   │ └─────────────────────────┘ │   │   │  │
         │ │  │   └─────────────────────────────┘   │   │  │
         │ │  │ user-service blocks a worker thread │   │  │
         │ │  │    on every call to auth-service    │   │  │
         │ │  └─────────────────────────────────────┘   │  │
         │ │ jobpost-api blocks waiting on user-service │  │
         │ │    — its own thread pool fills up next     │  │
         │ └────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
         │  skills-service is healthy but now unreachable  │
         │     too — the jobs page needs jobpost-api's     │
         │ response before it can even call skills-service │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Every ring past RING 0 is OPTIONAL — it only happens because nothing
           stops a blocked thread from blocking its OWN caller in turn; Istio's
           entire job in a cascade is to put a hard stop between rings so a
           failure cannot hop outward
         - The five cards below are anihpj's actual resilience toolkit — each
           one defends a different ring, and most production DestinationRules
           combine several of them at once:

         [THE ISTIO RESILIENCE TOOLKIT — 5 ways to shrink the blast radius]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ CARD 1/5 — CIRCUIT BREAKER                                         │
         │ CRD: DestinationRule  →  field: outlierDetection                   │
         ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Ejects an unhealthy endpoint after N consecutive errors. Callers   │
         │ get an instant failure instead of a blocked thread — stops RING 1  │
         │ from ever queuing behind RING 0.                                   │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ CARD 2/5 — RETRIES                                                 │
         │ CRD: VirtualService  →  field: retries (attempts, perTryTimeout)   │
         ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Re-sends a failed request to a different healthy endpoint, masking │
         │ one transient blip before RING 2 ever sees an error — but needs a  │
         │ short perTryTimeout, or retries pile onto the same overloaded      │
         │ service and widen the radius instead of shrinking it.              │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ CARD 3/5 — TIMEOUTS                                                │
         │ CRD: VirtualService  →  field: timeout                             │
         ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Caps how long a caller waits for a reply. Converts "thread blocks  │
         │ forever" — the exact mechanic that powers the whole cascade — into │
         │ "thread blocks for at most 5s," putting a hard ceiling on RING 1's │
         │ exposure.                                                          │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ CARD 4/5 — CONNECTION POOL LIMITS                                  │
         │ CRD: DestinationRule  →  field: connectionPool                     │
         ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Caps concurrent connections/requests per endpoint                  │
         │ (tcp.maxConnections, http.http1MaxPendingRequests). Once the cap   │
         │ is hit, Envoy queues or rejects locally instead of letting a       │
         │ struggling RING 0 consume RING 1's entire thread pool.             │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ CARD 5/5 — FAULT INJECTION                                         │
         │ CRD: VirtualService  →  field: fault (delay / abort)               │
         ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Deliberately injects a delay or abort response in staging so you   │
         │ can watch the blast radius on purpose — proving the other four     │
         │ cards actually contain a failure before a real outage tests them   │
         │ for you.                                                           │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     VISUAL: TWO MORE OFFICIAL TERMS — xDS AND AMBIENT MODE
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

         - This chapter already used two terms without formally defining them:
           xDS (Q5's "converts to Envoy config via xDS") and Ambient mesh
           (1.6's "but Ambient mesh solves this") — both are real istio.io
           vocabulary worth grounding before Part 2 goes deep
         - DEFINITION: xDS — the family of discovery service APIs (Listener,
           Route, Cluster, Endpoint, and Secret Discovery Service) that istiod
           uses to push configuration to every proxy in the data plane over
           gRPC; the sentence to remember: "the control plane speaks xDS to
           the data plane"
         - DEFINITION: AMBIENT MODE — a second data-plane mode Istio supports
           alongside the sidecar mode used throughout this book; it removes the
           per-Pod Envoy sidecar and instead runs one shared per-node proxy
           called "ztunnel" that handles mTLS, identity, and L4 telemetry for
           every Pod on that node, plus an optional per-namespace "waypoint"
           proxy (still Envoy-based) only where a workload needs L7 features
           like HTTP routing or AuthorizationPolicy
         - Per istio.io's official glossary, a service mesh is "an
           infrastructure layer that enables managed, observable and secure
           communication between workload instances" — every DEFINITION box in
           this chapter (sidecar, data plane, control plane) is that same idea
           applied to one specific layer of the mesh
         - anihpj takeaway: this guide teaches sidecar mode because it is the
           original and still the default deployment model; ambient mode
           reaches the same outcome (mTLS, retries, observability) through a
           different data-plane shape — every CRD already introduced here
           (VirtualService, DestinationRule, PeerAuthentication) configures
           BOTH modes identically, so nothing learned in this book is wasted
           if anihpj later adopts ambient mode

         [SIDECAR MODE vs AMBIENT MODE — Istio's two official data-plane modes]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  SIDECAR MODE (this book's default) — one Envoy sidecar per Pod    │
         │                                                                    │
         │    [jobpost-api]◄──Envoy══mTLS══Envoy──►[user-service]             │
         │                                                                    │
         │  AMBIENT MODE (sidecar-less, opt-in per namespace)                 │
         │                                                                    │
         │    [jobpost-api]        [user-service]     no per-Pod proxy        │
         │          │                   │                                     │
         │          └─────────┬─────────┘                                     │
         │                [ztunnel]   per-NODE: L4 mTLS + identity            │
         │                    │   (only if L7 features are needed)            │
         │               [waypoint]   Envoy-based: L7 retries, routing,       │
         │                            VirtualService, AuthorizationPolicy     │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     CHAPTER 1: UNDER THE HOOD — THE MECHANISM BEHIND EVERY CLAIM
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
         Every earlier deep-dive in this chapter (the CASCADE FAILURE
         walkthrough in 1.2, the BLAST RADIUS rings, the 5-card resilience
         toolkit) explained WHAT Istio does and WHY it helps. One question
         remains: HOW does any of this happen without anihpj's Django code
         ever importing anything Istio-related? That mechanical question
         is this chapter's true capstone — it ties 1.4's "zero code
         change" claim, 1.5's sidecar / data-plane / control-plane
         definitions, and Q5/Q7's xDS and Citadel answers into one
         picture:

         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ UNDER THE HOOD — HOW A PLAIN requests.get() BECOMES ENCRYPTED,     │
         │ RETRIED TRAFFIC (the mechanism behind every claim in 1.4-1.7)      │
         │                                                                    │
         │ SCENARIO: jobpost-api's Django code runs one plain line —          │
         │ requests.get("http://user-service/users") — and Istio does the     │
         │ rest, with ZERO code awareness that Istio even exists              │
         │                                                                    │
         │ STEP 1  Django calls plain HTTP on port 80 — no TLS, no retry      │
         │         logic, no Istio import anywhere in views.py                │
         │ STEP 2  iptables rules (written by istio-init at Pod startup, or   │
         │         by the Istio CNI plugin) SILENTLY redirect the outbound    │
         │         packet to 127.0.0.1:15001 — before it leaves the Pod       │
         │ STEP 3  istio-proxy (Envoy) — a second container sharing           │
         │         jobpost-api's network namespace — receives it, matches     │
         │         the "user-service" cluster, and applies whatever your      │
         │         DestinationRule / VirtualService / PeerAuthentication say: │
         │         mTLS? which load-balancing algorithm? retry N times?       │
         │ STEP 4  Envoy opens the REAL connection, now mTLS-encrypted, to    │
         │         user-service's Pod — landing on ANOTHER iptables redirect  │
         │         (inbound this time) pointing at 127.0.0.1:15006            │
         │ STEP 5  user-service's OWN istio-proxy decrypts the mTLS and hands │
         │         plain HTTP to Django on localhost — user-service's code    │
         │         never knew the network in between was ever risky           │
         │ STEP 6  Neither Envoy configured itself: istiod read your CRDs,    │
         │         converted them to Envoy-native config, and pushed both     │
         │         sidecars their rules over xDS (gRPC) — the SAME xDS        │
         │         named back in Q5, now shown doing real work                │
         │                                                                    │
         │ THE INSIGHT: "zero code change" (1.4) is not a slogan — it is two  │
         │ iptables redirects and two Envoys, invisible to jobpost-api's      │
         │ Django process, that make the sidecar and control-plane            │
         │ definitions from 1.5 physically true on every single request       │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     CHAPTER 1: SPEED TIPS
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
         ⚡ When a question says "prevent cascading failures" or "isolate
            a failing service," go straight to DestinationRule
            outlierDetection — don't spend exam minutes considering
            retries or timeouts first.
         ⚡ When a question says "encrypt" or "zero-trust," the answer is
            PeerAuthentication STRICT — no other CRD does mesh-wide mTLS.
         ⚡ Memorize the 1.7 table left-to-right (symptom -> CRD -> field),
            not top-to-bottom — exam questions give you the symptom, never
            the CRD name.
         ⚡ If a scenario mentions BOTH "gradual rollout" AND "specific
            pods," you need TWO objects: a DestinationRule (defines the
            subsets) plus a VirtualService (splits the weight) — never
            just one.
         ⚡ Say "control plane configures, data plane executes" out loud
            once — it's the fastest way to stop istiod and Envoy from
            blurring together under time pressure.
         ⚡ Before touching YAML on any question, ask "which of the 8
            problems is this?" — naming the problem (1.2) picks the CRD
            for you in one step.

         │                      Sept 2026)                                        │
         │    │                                                                   │
         │    ▼                                                                   │

         │    │                                                                   │
         │    ▼                                                                   │
         │ auth-service CRASHES — WITH Istio the blast radius stays 1 -> 1,       │
         │ not 1 -> 7 (1.8) — the whole chapter's promise, proven on a clock      │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         Read top to bottom, this is Chapter 1's entire argument: anihpj
         began as a monolith simple enough to run but too rigid to scale,
         so it split into seven services — and that split, by itself,
         manufactured eight new problems that no amount of individual
         Django code could fix cleanly. The naive attempt (retry/timeout/
         mTLS logic copied into every service) failed under its own
         duplication, which is exactly the gap a service mesh is built to
         close: push retries, encryption, load balancing, and routing into
         a sidecar proxy that sits beside every service and never asks the
         application to change. Istio won the choice among service meshes
         because anihpj needs the full feature set — canary routing,
         circuit breaking, fault injection, and a dashboard-backed
         observability story — not just basic mTLS. The chapter closes by
         proving the whole argument on the clock: the exact same
         auth-service crash that takes down all 7 anihpj services in
         ~60 seconds without Istio stays contained to 1 broken service
         with it, because a circuit breaker's entire job is to shrink
         blast radius, not repair root causes. Every chapter from here
         forward is one CRD, one section, or one command that makes a
         piece of this picture real.

  and how does it work?"
  What you'll build by the end: a precise mental model of Istio's sidecar
  architecture — Envoy, istiod, and the xDS protocol that connects them —
  solid enough to narrate any anihpj request's trip through the mesh from
  memory, before you install a single binary.

  [PART 2 INTRO]
  Part 1 proved you NEED a service mesh — retries, mTLS, timeouts and
  tracing cannot keep living inside jobpost-api's Django views without
  turning anihpj's seven services into a copy-pasted mess. It never said
  which mesh, or how one actually works. Part 2 closes that gap: it is
  the "what is Istio, specifically" chapter, before Part 3 opens the
  hood on Istio's full architecture and later Parts install anything.

  Treat this Part as vocabulary-and-mental-model building, not hands-on
  work yet. By the time Chapter 2 ends you'll know Istio is a
  CNCF-graduated, Envoy-based mesh; that it injects one Envoy "sidecar"
  proxy per Pod instead of routing through a shared load balancer; and
  that a control plane called istiod briefs every one of those sidecars
  over a protocol called xDS. None of that needs a cluster yet — it
  needs a clear picture in your head, because every later chapter
  assumes you already have it.

  Ground it on anihpj/jobpost, this whole guide's running example.
  jobpost-api's call to user-service is the thread Chapter 2 pulls on:
  first a plain, unencrypted Django HTTP call (the Part 1 problem), then
  a call Istio has quietly wrapped in an Envoy on each end, with istiod
  having pushed both Envoys their config before the first packet moved.

  🧠 ANALOGY. Picture jobpost-api and its six sibling services — user-,
  skills-, location-, notification-, auth- and search-service — as
  employees who used to answer their own phone and keep their own call
  log by hand. Istio hires one silent personal assistant (the Envoy
  sidecar) to sit outside every employee's door: every call now passes
  through that assistant first, gets logged and timed, and gets retried
  if unanswered. No employee changed jobs — but now a Head Office
  (istiod) phones every assistant continuously with the current rules:
  who may call whom, how long to wait, where to reroute a failed call.

  which component programs it, and which protocol carries that program.
  Implementation thread: anihpj's jobpost-api Pod goes from "a Django
  container with no network awareness" to "a Django container escorted
  by an Envoy proxy that istiod actively manages."

      kubectl apply -f jobpost-api-deployment.yaml
              │
              ▼
      ┌───────────────────────┐                      ┌──────────────────────┐
      │ Kubernetes API server │   mutating webhook   │ istio-proxy sidecar  │
      │ admits the Pod spec   │  injects a container │ added to jobpost-api │
      └───────────────────────┘                      └──────────────────────┘
                                                                 │  opens xDS (gRPC) stream
                                                                 ▼
                                                    ┌────────────────────────┐
                                                    │ istiod (control plane) │
                                                    │ pushes routes / mTLS / │
                                                    │ certs to that Envoy    │
                                                    └────────────────────────┘
                                                                 │
                                                                 ▼
      jobpost-api ──mTLS──▶ user-service   (the mesh call, now live)

  webhook added a neighbor, and istiod briefs that neighbor over xDS
  for as long as the Pod lives.

Chapter 2: Istio From First Principles
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Chapter 2 only · Difficulty: 🟢 Beginner · Foundational (not a graded ICA domain, but every domain assumes it)
  "If Istio touches zero lines of jobpost-api's Django code, where does all that power actually live?"

  [WHY THIS MATTERS]
  Chapter 1 left anihpj's seven services — jobpost-api, user-service, skills-service, location-service, notification-service, auth-service, search-service — with a real, unsolved problem: every plain HTTP call between them needed its own hand-rolled retries, timeouts, encryption and tracing, hardcoded into Django views service by service, forever drifting out of sync. Chapter 2 does not fix that yet — it builds the mental model every later chapter assumes you already have: what Istio actually is, what physically changes inside a Pod, and which single control-plane component is briefing every proxy in real time. Skip this chapter and later VirtualServices, AuthorizationPolicies, and troubleshooting playbooks all read like disconnected YAML tricks; read it carefully and every later CRD becomes "one more thing istiod compiles for Envoy." Ground every idea here in one thread: jobpost-api's call to user-service, first as a naked Django HTTP request, then wrapped in a mesh neither service had to write a line of code for. By the end of this chapter you can look at `kubectl get pods` showing `2/2 READY` on any anihpj service and know exactly what that second container is doing to every request before your Django code ever sees it.

  [LEARNING OBJECTIVES]
  ✅ Define Istio in one sentence, and name its creators, license, and CNCF status
  ✅ Explain, in your own words, what Kubernetes owns versus what Istio owns in the stack
  ✅ Describe what physically changes inside a Pod after sidecar injection — container count, ports, shared network namespace
  ✅ Trace a single jobpost-api → user-service call through both Envoy sidecars, hop by hop
  ✅ Recite Istio's 9 named capabilities and the CRD that delivers each one
  ✅ Explain how istiod uses xDS to program Envoy, and what keeps working if istiod goes down
  ✅ Distinguish the istio-init and Istio CNI injection paths, and know when each is required

  [EXAM/ICA RELEVANCE]
  Chapter 2 is not itself a graded ICA domain — the official blueprint starts
  grading at Domain 1 (Installation, Upgrade & Configuration). But every one
  of the four graded domains assumes the mental model built here:

    2.1  Istio Defined
         - Istio is an open-source service mesh for Kubernetes
         - Created by Google, IBM, and Lyft in 2017; CNCF graduated 2023
         - It adds a dedicated infrastructure layer on top of Kubernetes Services
         - Works by injecting an Envoy proxy sidecar into every Pod automatically
         - Your Django code at http://user-service/ — Istio intercepts it,
           encrypts it, retries it, traces it, routes it — all without code change
         [CARD: Istio quick facts — version, creator, license, CNCF status]

         [ISTIO QUICK FACTS]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  ★ ISTIO — KEY FACTS                                   │
         │                                                        │
         │  Created by:    Google + IBM + Lyft (2017)             │
         │  Current ver:   Istio 1.22+ (Kubernetes 1.28+)         │
         │  Language:      Go                                     │
         │  License:       Apache 2.0                             │
         │  CNCF Status:   Graduated (2023)                       │
         │  Proxy used:    Envoy (battle-tested at Lyft scale)    │
         │  Core feature:  Automatic mTLS, Traffic Management,    │
         │                 Observability, Security Policies        │
         │  Used by:       Airbnb, Salesforce, Intuit, Red Hat,   │
         │                 eBay, SAP, Cisco                        │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    2.2  What Exactly Does Istio Give You? (The 15-Minute Demo)
         - Automatic mTLS: every HTTP call between anihpj services becomes
           encrypted HTTPS — without adding SSL code in Django
           DEMO: deploy anihpj → check Kiali → see lock icons on all edges
         - Traffic routing: send 90% of traffic to jobpost-api:v1,
           10% to jobpost-api:v2 — gradual canary rollout via YAML
           DEMO: apply VirtualService weight change → watch Kiali update live
         - Retries: "retry this call to user-service 3 times if it fails"
           DEMO: kill user-service pod → see automatic retry in Grafana
         - Timeouts: "give up on auth-service after 5 seconds"
           DEMO: add 10s delay to auth-service → timeout fires at 5s
         - Circuit breaker: "if skills-service fails 5 times, stop calling it"
           DEMO: inject faults into skills-service → circuit opens in Kiali
         - Fault injection: "artificially delay 10% of calls to test resilience"
           DEMO: add 7s delay to 30% of user-service calls → test timeout behavior
         - Metrics: every request is measured — latency, error rate, throughput
           DEMO: open Grafana → see RED metrics for all anihpj services
         - Distributed tracing: follow a request from jobpost-api → user-service
           → auth-service → database, across ALL hops, with timing
           DEMO: open Jaeger → trace a GET /jobs/ request across 5 services
         - Access control: "only jobpost-api is allowed to call user-service"
           DEMO: apply AuthorizationPolicy → curl from skills-service → 403 denied
         [FEATURE WHEEL DIAGRAM: Istio features radiating from center]

         [ISTIO FEATURE WHEEL — all capabilities from one platform]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                                                                  │
         │             🔒 mTLS (auto encrypt)                               │
         │                    │                                             │
         │  🔭 Tracing ───────┤                                             │

    2.3  Istio's Relationship with Kubernetes
         - Istio builds ON TOP of Kubernetes — it does not replace it
         - Kubernetes manages containers (scheduling, restarts, scaling)
         - Istio manages communication BETWEEN those containers
         - Istio uses Kubernetes Custom Resources (CRDs) for its configuration
         - kubectl apply -f virtual-service.yaml → Istio understands it
         [LAYERED DIAGRAM: Hardware → OS → K8s → Istio → Your App]

         [KUBERNETES vs ISTIO — who does what?]
         ┌───────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  KUBERNETES handles:          │  ISTIO handles:                     │
         ├───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  📦 Container scheduling      │  🔀 Traffic routing between services │
         │  🔄 Pod restarts on crash     │  🔒 mTLS between every service pair  │
         │  📈 Horizontal autoscaling    │  🔄 Retry logic for failed calls      │
         │  🌐 Service discovery (DNS)   │  ⏱️  Timeout enforcement             │
         │  💾 Persistent volumes        │  🔌 Circuit breaking                 │
         │  🏗️  Namespace isolation       │  📊 RED metrics per service          │
         │  🔐 RBAC for K8s API          │  🔭 Distributed tracing              │
         │  ⚖️  Resource limits/requests  │  🗺️  Service topology (Kiali)        │
         │  🖥️  Node management          │  🛡️  AuthorizationPolicy (L7 access)  │
         │  📋 ConfigMaps / Secrets      │  🚦 Canary / A-B deployments         │
         │                               │  📤 Egress control to external APIs  │
         ├───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  Uses: Deployment, Service,   │  Uses: VirtualService, Gateway,      │
         │        Pod, Namespace,        │        DestinationRule, PeerAuth,    │
         │        ConfigMap, HPA ...     │        AuthzPolicy, ServiceEntry...  │
         └───────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────┘
         KEY: They complement each other — you need BOTH for a production system

         [THE LAYERED ARCHITECTURE]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                                                        │
