    4.6  Understanding the anihpj Deployment with Istio
         - Complete YAML for all anihpj services with Istio labels
         - Required label: app: jobpost-api version: v1 (Istio uses these)
         - Port naming convention: must name ports "http", "grpc", "tcp"
         - Kubernetes Service selectors and how Istio uses them
         [ANNOTATED YAML: Complete Deployment + Service YAML for jobpost-api]

         [ANNOTATED Deployment YAML for anihpj with Istio]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: apps/v1                                   │
         │  kind: Deployment                                      │
         │  metadata:                                             │
         │    name: jobpost-api                                   │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                   │
         │  spec:                                                 │
         │    replicas: 2                                         │
         │    selector:                                           │
         │      matchLabels:                                      │
         │        app: jobpost-api    # ← Istio uses "app" label │
         │        version: v1         # ← Required for canary!   │
         │    template:                                           │
         │      metadata:                                         │
         │        labels:                                         │
         │          app: jobpost-api                              │
         │          version: v1                                   │
         │      spec:                                             │
         │        containers:                                     │
         │        - name: jobpost                                 │
         │          image: anihpj/jobpost:v1                      │
         │          ports:                                        │
         │          - name: http          # ← Must be "http"!    │
         │            containerPort: 8000 # ← Port naming matters│
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [ANNOTATED Service YAML for jobpost-api — named port "http"]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: v1                                        │
         │  kind: Service                                         │
         │  metadata:                                             │
         │    name: jobpost-api                                   │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                   │
         │  spec:                                                 │
         │    selector:                                           │
         │      app: jobpost-api   # ← matches Deployment label   │
         │    ports:                                              │
         │    - name: http         # ← MUST start with "http"!    │
         │      port: 8000         # ← what callers dial          │
         │      targetPort: 8000   # ← containerPort in the pod   │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         - Replicate the same shape for every anihpj service — only name
           and port change: user-service :8080, skills-service :8090,
           location-service :8070, auth-service, search-service,
           notification-service — ALL with port name "http"
         - If any port name is wrong, Istio treats that service as raw
           TCP: no retries, no canary %, no per-route metrics, no tracing

    4.7  Installation Profiles — Which One for Which Scenario
         - DEFINITION: a profile is a named, pre-configured IstioOperator
           spec shipped inside istioctl — a preset that decides which
           components are installed and how they are tuned

         📖 KEY TERM — Profile: the exam's most-repeated noun in this
           chapter. All 7 built-ins: default, demo, minimal, remote,
           empty, ambient, preview. Exam tell: any ask for "all the
           observability tools" or "Kiali + Jaeger + Prometheus + Grafana
           in one install" always means profile=demo — labs/ICA practice
           ONLY, never production (4.3 has the full component table).
         - Why it matters: the wrong profile either wastes resources
           (demo in production) or strands you without tools (default in
           a lab → "no Kiali pods found" when opening the dashboard)
         - How it works: istioctl install --set profile=<name> loads the
           preset, merges your --set overrides, renders manifests, applies
         - Explore profiles before choosing:
           • istioctl profile list              → names of all 7 profiles
           • istioctl profile dump demo         → full IstioOperator preset
           • istioctl profile diff default demo → exactly what demo adds

         [PROFILE → SCENARIO MAP — all 7 built-in profiles]
         ┌─────────┬──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┐
         │ Profile │ Installs                 │ Use it when...          │
         ├─────────┼──────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
         │ default │ istiod + ingressgateway  │ Production baseline;    │
         │         │                          │ add tools via Helm      │
         ├─────────┼──────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
         │ demo    │ istiod + ingress +       │ Learning, labs, ICA     │
         │         │ egress + Kiali, Jaeger,  │ practice — NEVER prod   │
         │         │ Prometheus, Grafana      │                         │
         ├─────────┼──────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
         │ minimal │ istiod only              │ CI/CD pipeline tests,   │
         │         │                          │ edge/IoT, tight RAM     │
         ├─────────┼──────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
         │ remote  │ injection webhook only   │ Secondary cluster using │
         │         │ (no local istiod)        │ an external istiod      │
         ├─────────┼──────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
         │ empty   │ nothing at all           │ Base for fully custom   │
         │         │                          │ IstioOperator builds    │
         ├─────────┼──────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
         │ ambient │ istiod + ztunnel + CNI   │ Sidecar-free mesh; big  │
         │         │ (no sidecars)            │ RAM savings per pod     │
         ├─────────┼──────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
         │ preview │ default + experimental   │ Testing upcoming        │
         │         │ features enabled         │ features — never prod   │
         └─────────┴──────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────┘
         - Real anihpj scenario: the dev cluster runs demo (all dashboards,
           100% trace sampling); production runs default with Kiali,
           Prometheus and Grafana installed separately via Helm and trace
           sampling dialed down to 1%

    4.8  Deep Dive — What Each Profile REALLY Installs: IstioOperator API and the Helm Pipeline
         - DEFINITION: IstioOperator (install.istio.io/v1alpha1) is the
           CRD that describes a COMPLETE Istio installation — every
           profile is just a pre-filled IstioOperator document
         - Why it matters: every --set flag you pass to istioctl install
           maps 1:1 to an IstioOperator field — understand this CRD and
           you understand ALL installation customization
         - How it works: istioctl merges profile + overrides, renders the
           BUNDLED Helm charts to plain Kubernetes YAML, applies it, then
           waits for readiness — Helm itself is never required
         - GitOps tip: istioctl manifest generate -f op.yaml > all.yaml
           produces the fully rendered YAML to review/commit before apply

         [INSTALL PIPELINE — istioctl → IstioOperator → manifests → pods]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  istioctl install --set profile=demo -y                        │
         │      │                                                         │
         │      ▼ 1. PROFILE RESOLUTION                                   │
         │  loads built-in preset: manifests/profiles/demo.yaml           │
         │      │                                                         │
         │      ▼ 2. MERGE OVERRIDES                                      │
         │  profile + every --set flag → one final IstioOperator spec     │
         │      │                                                         │
         │      ▼ 3. HELM RENDERING (charts bundled inside istioctl)      │
         │  each component (istiod, gateways) = a chart rendered to       │
         │  plain K8s YAML: Deployments, Services, RBAC, webhooks         │
         │      │                                                         │
         │      ▼ 4. CRDs + NAMESPACE                                     │
         │  creates istio-system + ~30 CRDs (VirtualService, Gateway…)    │
         │  + MutatingWebhookConfiguration (the sidecar injector)         │
         │      │                                                         │
         │      ▼ 5. APPLY + PRUNE                                        │
         │  server-side apply of every rendered resource                  │
         │      │                                                         │
         │      ▼ 6. WAIT + VERIFY                                        │
         │  istiod 1/1, gateways 1/1, webhooks answering                  │
         │  → "✔ Installation complete"                                   │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [ANNOTATED IstioOperator YAML — customizing the install]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: install.istio.io/v1alpha1                         │
         │  kind: IstioOperator                                           │
         │  metadata:                                                     │
         │    name: anihpj-istio                                          │
         │    namespace: istio-system                                     │
         │  spec:                                                         │
         │    profile: demo                 # ← starting preset           │
         │    meshConfig:                   # ← global mesh settings      │
         │      accessLogFile: /dev/stdout                                │
         │      enableTracing: true                                       │
         │    components:                                                 │
         │      pilot:                      # ← "pilot" = istiod          │
         │        k8s:                                                    │
         │          replicaCount: 1                                       │
         │          resources:                                            │
         │            requests: {cpu: 500m, memory: 2048Mi}               │
         │      ingressGateways:                                          │
         │      - name: istio-ingressgateway                              │
         │        enabled: true                                           │
         │        k8s:                                                    │
         │          service: {type: LoadBalancer}                         │
         │                                                                │
         │  # Install it:   istioctl install -f operator.yaml -y          │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [PER-PROFILE COMPONENT MATRIX — what actually lands on cluster]
         ┌──────────────────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐
         │ Component        │ def  │ demo │ min  │ rem  │ emp  │ amb  │ pre  │
         ├──────────────────┼──────┼──────┼──────┼──────┼──────┼──────┼──────┤
         │ istiod           │  ✅   │  ✅   │  ✅   │  ❌   │  ❌   │  ✅   │  ✅   │
         │ ingressgateway   │  ✅   │  ✅   │  ❌   │  ❌   │  ❌   │  ❌   │  ✅   │
         │ egressgateway    │  ❌   │  ✅   │  ❌   │  ❌   │  ❌   │  ❌   │  ❌   │
         │ ztunnel + CNI    │  ❌   │  ❌   │  ❌   │  ❌   │  ❌   │  ✅   │  ❌   │
         │ Kiali/Jaeger/    │  ❌   │  ✅   │  ❌   │  ❌   │  ❌   │  ❌   │  ❌   │
         │ Prom/Grafana     │      │      │      │      │      │      │      │
         ├──────────────────┼──────┼──────┼──────┼──────┼──────┼──────┼──────┤
         │ pods installed   │  2   │  7   │  1   │  0   │  0   │ 3+   │  2   │
         │ control-pl. RAM  │ .6Gi │ 2Gi  │ .3Gi │  0   │  0   │ 1Gi  │ .6Gi │
         └──────────────────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘
         - Legend: def=default, min=minimal, rem=remote, emp=empty,
           amb=ambient, pre=preview
         - demo's observability addons ship in the Istio release under
           samples/addons/ — the profile wires them together for the lab

    4.9  Troubleshooting — Common Installation Issues
         - DEFINITION: install troubleshooting = working the stack
           bottom-up: scheduler → control plane → webhook → sidecar →
           config → traffic
         - Why it matters: 90% of "Istio is broken" reports right after
           an install are one of the issues below — each has a 30-second
           check and a one-line fix
         - Golden rule: kubectl describe the failing object FIRST — the
           Events section usually names the cause outright
         - Pre-flight: run istioctl x precheck BEFORE install/upgrade —
           it validates versions, permissions and existing webhooks
           without changing anything on the cluster

         [INSTALL ISSUES — SYMPTOM → CAUSE → FIX]
         ┌───────────────────┬─────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┐
         │ Symptom           │ Root cause          │ Fix                     │
         ├───────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
         │ istio-system pods │ cluster out of CPU/ │ kubectl describe pod →  │
         │ stuck Pending     │ RAM for requests    │ Events; add nodes or    │
         │                   │                     │ use minimal profile     │
         ├───────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
         │ istioctl install  │ API server cannot   │ allow 15017 to istiod;  │
         │ hangs, webhook    │ reach the injection │ istioctl x precheck,    │
         │ timeout           │ webhook (port 15017)│ then retry the install  │
         ├───────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
         │ app pods show 1/1 │ no injection label, │ kubectl label ns anihpj │
         │ instead of 2/2    │ or pods created     │ istio-injection=enabled │
         │                   │ before the label    │ + rollout restart       │
         ├───────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
         │ istioctl analyze  │ bad port names, VS  │ fix the named object;   │
         │ prints warnings   │ subset without DR,  │ re-run analyze until    │
         │                   │ selector mismatch   │ no issues reported      │
         ├───────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
         │ proxy-status is   │ istiod unreachable  │ verify istiod Running,  │
         │ STALE / NOT SENT  │ from pod, port 15012│ NetworkPolicies; then   │
         │                   │                     │ restart the stale pod   │
         └───────────────────┴─────────────────────┴─────────────────────────┘
         🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — why relabeling never catches existing Pods:
           Both "webhook timeout" and "1/1 instead of 2/2" above trace to
           one MutatingWebhookConfiguration watching Pod CREATE on port
           15017: it fires once, before the API server persists the Pod,
           rewriting the spec in-flight to add istio-proxy only if the
           namespace already carries istio-injection=enabled at that exact
           moment — miss the call and the Pod stays exactly as submitted.

         - Nuclear option (labs only): istioctl uninstall --purge -y, then
           delete the istio-system namespace and reinstall from scratch
         - Plaintext-to-STRICT gotcha: a non-mesh pod calling a STRICT-mTLS
           port gets a TCP connection reset — NOT an HTTP 403; if curl says
           "connection reset by peer" right after install, check mTLS mode

    4.10  Installing Istio with Helm — The Alternative to istioctl
         - DEFINITION: Helm is Kubernetes' package manager — it installs,
           upgrades and removes a bundle of Kubernetes manifests (a
           "chart") as ONE tracked release, with helm install / upgrade /
           rollback / uninstall as the lifecycle verbs
         - Why the exam names it separately from istioctl: istioctl
           bundles these SAME charts internally and applies them for you
           (see 4.8) — installing "with Helm" means running helm
           yourself against the charts Istio publishes on its own
           repository, a different day-2 workflow over identical
           underlying manifests
         - Why it matters in production: a Helm release is versioned and
           diffable (helm diff upgrade, helm rollback <rev>) — exactly
           the primitives GitOps controllers like Argo CD and Flux
           reconcile against; istioctl has no release object at all

         🧠 ANALOGY. istioctl install is a couch delivered fully assembled
           on one truck — one delivery, done. Helm's base -> istiod ->
           gateway sequence buys the same living room as three separate
           flat-pack boxes: the frame (base's CRDs) must be bolted down
           before the cushions (istiod) can sit on it, and the side table
           (gateway) is useless without a finished couch beside it — three
           boxes also means three receipts to individually exchange later
           (helm rollback <rev>), unlike the one-truck delivery.
         - How it works: Istio publishes THREE separate charts — install
           them in dependency order:
           • base    → the ~30 Istio CRDs + ClusterRoles ONLY, nothing
             runs yet
           • istiod  → the control plane; needs base's CRDs already on
             the cluster or every VirtualService/Gateway apply fails
           • gateway → a data-plane gateway (e.g. istio-ingress); needs
             istiod already Running to receive its xDS config
         → Install out of order and the next chart's pods CrashLoop on
           "no matches for kind VirtualService", or a gateway pod hangs
           waiting for a control plane that was never installed

         [INSTALLING ISTIO WITH HELM — the three charts, in order]
         ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  # 1. Add the Istio Helm repo and refresh it                      │
         │  helm repo add istio \                                            │
         │      https://istio-release.storage.googleapis.com/charts          │
         │  helm repo update                                                 │
         │                                                                   │
         │  # 2. base chart — CRDs + ClusterRoles only (no pods yet)         │
         │  helm install istio-base istio/base -n istio-system \             │
         │      --create-namespace --set defaultRevision=default             │
         │                                                                   │
         │  # 3. istiod chart — the control plane (wait for Ready)           │
         │  helm install istiod istio/istiod -n istio-system --wait          │
         │                                                                   │
         │  # 4. gateway chart — data-plane ingress gateway, its own ns      │
         │  kubectl create namespace istio-ingress                           │
         │  helm install istio-ingress istio/gateway -n istio-ingress        │
         │                                                                   │
         │  # Order matters: base → istiod → gateway                         │
         │  #   (CRDs first, then control plane, then data plane)            │
         └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Every --set flag maps to a dotted path inside that specific
           chart's values.yaml — --set pilot.resources.requests.cpu=500m
           is IstioOperator's spec.components.pilot.k8s.resources by
           another name, just scoped to the istiod chart alone
         - helm status / helm list replace istioctl's install summary —
           STATUS: deployed is Helm's version of "install complete";
           REVISION climbs by one on every future upgrade

         [CUSTOMIZING THE HELM INSTALL — overrides + verification]
         ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  # Override any chart value at install time with --set            │
         │  # (maps 1:1 to a path in that chart's values.yaml)               │
         │  helm install istiod istio/istiod -n istio-system --wait \        │
         │      --set pilot.resources.requests.cpu=500m \                    │
         │      --set pilot.resources.requests.memory=2048Mi                 │
         │                                                                   │
         │  # Prefer a file once you need more than 1-2 overrides:           │
         │  helm install istiod istio/istiod -n istio-system \               │
         │      --wait -f istiod-values.yaml                                 │
         │                                                                   │
         │  # Verify the release (Helm's equivalent of proxy-status):        │
         │  helm status istiod -n istio-system                               │
         │  STATUS: deployed        REVISION: 1                              │
         │                                                                   │
         │  helm list -n istio-system                                        │
         │  NAME    NAMESPACE     REVISION  STATUS    CHART                  │
         │  istiod  istio-system  1         deployed  istiod-1.22.0          │
         └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [ISTIOCTL vs HELM — which one for which job]
         ┌────────────────────┬─────────────────────┬─────────────────────┐
         │ Scenario           │ istioctl            │ Helm                │
         ├────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
         │ Quick lab / demo   │ fastest: 1 command  │ 3 installs, more    │
         │ profile install    │                     │ setup               │
         ├────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
         │ Production, GitOps │ no release object   │ values.yaml is      │
         │ (Argo CD / Flux)   │ to diff             │ diffable + versioned│
         ├────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
         │ Need a rollback    │ uninstall + re-     │ helm rollback       │
         │                    │ install from scratch│ istiod 1            │
         ├────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
         │ CI/CD smoke test   │ profile=minimal -y  │ 3x helm install     │
         └────────────────────┴─────────────────────┴─────────────────────┘

         - Real anihpj scenario: the dev/lab cluster installs fast with
           istioctl install --set profile=demo -y; the production
           pipeline instead commits istiod-values.yaml to git and lets
           Argo CD run helm upgrade --install on every merge — same
           three charts underneath, a completely different day-2 story
         - 🎯 ICA EXAM NOTE: Installing Istio with istioctl or Helm is a
           named exam topic — you may be asked to install via EITHER
           method, so know both command sequences cold.

    4.11  Installing Istio in Ambient Mode — The Sidecar-Free Exam Topic
         - DEFINITION: sections 4.1-4.9 installed Istio in SIDECAR mode —
           every meshed pod runs its own Envoy container injected next
           to the app (2/2 READY). AMBIENT MODE removes that per-pod
           proxy: a shared ztunnel DaemonSet (one per node) supplies
           mTLS and L4 policy to every ambient pod, with an optional
           per-namespace waypoint proxy added only if L7 features are
           needed. Same mesh, same certificates — a different install.
         - This section covers only the INSTALLATION exam topic: how to
           turn ambient mode on and prove it took effect. → for the full
           ztunnel / waypoint / HBONE architecture, see 16.4-16.6.

         [INSTALLING AMBIENT MODE — install, label, verify]
         ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  # 1. Install control plane + ztunnel + CNI node agent            │
         │  istioctl install --set profile=ambient -y                        │
         │                                                                   │
         │  # 2. Opt anihpj into ambient (NOT istio-injection=enabled!)      │
         │  kubectl label namespace anihpj istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient   │
         │                                                                   │
         │  # Contrast — sidecar mode uses a DIFFERENT namespace label:      │
         │  #   kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled       │
         │                                                                   │
         │  # 3. Verify the ambient data plane (ztunnel, no per-app sidecar) │
         │  kubectl get pods -n istio-system                                 │
         │  NAME                       READY  STATUS   AGE                   │
         │  istiod-7d7f9c7b8c-x4k2z    1/1    Running  3m                    │
         │  istio-cni-node-4d8fk       1/1    Running  3m  ← 1/node          │
         │  istio-cni-node-8k2mz       1/1    Running  3m                    │
         │  ztunnel-4kxpq              1/1    Running  3m  ← 1/node          │
         │  ztunnel-9mvwt              1/1    Running  3m                    │
         │                                                                   │
         │  # 4. Verify anihpj app pods — NO istio-proxy container           │
         │  kubectl get pods -n anihpj                                       │
         │  NAME                          READY  STATUS   RESTARTS           │
         │  jobpost-api-7d4f8b9c-x2k4z    1/1    Running  0                  │
         │  user-service-6c9d8f7b-m3j5y   1/1    Running  0                  │
         │                                ↑ 1/1 is CORRECT here — by design  │
         └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - The two namespace labels are NOT interchangeable — they drive
           TWO DIFFERENT data planes:
           • istio-injection=enabled          → sidecar mode (per-pod Envoy)
           • istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient  → ambient mode (ztunnel only)
         → Applying BOTH labels, or the wrong one, is the single most
           common ambient-install mistake — pick exactly one per namespace

         [WHICH MODE DID THE EXAM ASK FOR?]
         ┌──────────────────────┬─────────────────────┬─────────────────────┐
         │ Signal in the ask    │ Sidecar mode        │ Ambient mode        │
         ├──────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
         │ Pods READY column    │ 2/2 expected        │ 1/1 expected        │
         ├──────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
         │ Namespace label      │ istio-injection=    │ istio.io/dataplane- │
         │ used                 │ enabled             │ mode=ambient        │
         ├──────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
         │ Install flag         │ profile=demo/       │ profile=ambient     │
         │                      │ default             │                     │
         ├──────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
         │ Vocabulary in the    │ "sidecar", "inject",│ "ztunnel",          │
         │ question             │ "istio-proxy"       │ "waypoint", "HBONE" │
         └──────────────────────┴─────────────────────┴─────────────────────┘

         - Real anihpj scenario: notification-service and
           location-service (internal, low-traffic, mTLS-only) go
           ambient with just the dataplane-mode label and no waypoint;
           jobpost-api and skills-service (public, canary weights,
           circuit breakers) stay on sidecar, or move to ambient PLUS a
           waypoint — see 16.6 for the full per-namespace decision guide
         - 🎯 ICA EXAM NOTE: Installing Istio in Sidecar or Ambient Mode
           is a named exam topic — know the install command AND the
           verification signal for each mode.

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     CHAPTER 4: DAILY WORK TAKEAWAYS
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    After this chapter, in your daily work you will:
      • Install Istio on any cluster with a single command
      • Know which profile to use: demo for learning, default for production
      • Enable sidecar injection with one label: kubectl label namespace
      • Verify injection worked: pods show 2/2 containers
      • Check proxy sync: istioctl proxy-status (all must be SYNCED)
      • Validate config: istioctl analyze -n anihpj
      • Open dashboards: istioctl dashboard kiali/grafana/jaeger
      • Know the critical rules: port names must be "http"/"grpc"/"tcp",
        pods need "app" and "version" labels, services need the "app" selector

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     CHAPTER 4: ICA EXAM TIPS & QUESTIONS
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    🎯 ICA EXAM FOCUS (Installation, Upgrade & Config — 20% of exam):
      • "Install Istio with demo profile" = istioctl install --set profile=demo -y
      • "Enable injection for namespace" = kubectl label ns X istio-injection=enabled
      • "Verify injection worked" = kubectl get pods → 2/2 containers
      • "Check Istio config for errors" = istioctl analyze -n <namespace>

    Q1: What command installs Istio with all observability tools included?
    A1: istioctl install --set profile=demo -y

    Q2: How do you verify that a pod has the Istio sidecar injected?
    A2: kubectl get pods → look for 2/2 under READY (app container + istio-proxy)

    Q3: What port naming convention does Istio require for protocol detection?
    A3: Port names must start with the protocol prefix: "http", "grpc", "tcp",
        "tls", etc. Istio uses port names (not port numbers) to determine the protocol.

    Q4: A production cluster gives you only 4 CPUs / 8GB RAM for anihpj's
        7 services. Which profile do you install, and does it fit?
    A4: istioctl install --set profile=default -y
        default = istiod + ingressgateway only (~600Mi vs demo's ~2Gi of
        control-plane RAM). Overhead: istiod 500m/2Gi + 7 sidecars
        700m/896Mi ≈ 1.2 CPU / 2.9Gi → fits, leaving room for the apps.

    Q5: Prepare the anihpj namespace so a future v1→v2 canary of
        jobpost-api will work. What must be in place BEFORE any
        VirtualService is written?
    A5: kubectl create namespace anihpj
        kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled
        Then deploy pods carrying BOTH labels app: jobpost-api and
        version: v1, and name the Service port "http". DestinationRule
        subsets select on the version label — no label, no canary.

    Q6: After installing Istio and deploying anihpj, prove the mesh is
        actually routing traffic — not just that containers run.
    A6: (1) kubectl get pods -n anihpj → all 2/2
        (2) istioctl proxy-status → every proxy SYNCED
        (3) istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj
            → upstream services listed
        (4) kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- curl -s
            user-service:8080/users/ → HTTP 200
        (5) istioctl dashboard kiali → green edge on the graph
        2/2 only proves the sidecar container runs; steps 2-5 prove config
        was pushed and traffic really flows through Envoy.

    Q7: Install the demo profile BUT with istiod requesting 1 CPU / 4Gi
        and access logs on stdout — as one reviewable file.
    A7: Create operator.yaml (kind: IstioOperator, apiVersion:
        install.istio.io/v1alpha1) with spec.profile: demo,
        spec.meshConfig.accessLogFile: /dev/stdout, and
        spec.components.pilot.k8s.resources.requests: {cpu: 1000m,
        memory: 4096Mi} — then: istioctl install -f operator.yaml -y
        A file is reviewable, diffable and GitOps-friendly; every --set
        flag maps to the same IstioOperator fields.

    Q8: Remove Istio COMPLETELY from a cluster (CRDs included) and return
        the anihpj pods to plain Kubernetes.
    A8: istioctl uninstall --purge -y
        kubectl delete namespace istio-system
        kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection-
        kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj
        --purge removes ALL Istio resources including CRDs; the restart
        recreates pods without sidecars (the injection webhook is gone).

    Q9: Before installing on a shared cluster, verify compatibility and
        detect conflicting meshes/webhooks WITHOUT changing anything.
    A9: istioctl x precheck
        It validates the Kubernetes version, required permissions, and
        existing webhooks/installations, printing actionable warnings.
        Read-only — safe to run against production clusters.

    Q10: You labeled anihpj AFTER deploying; pods still show 1/1. Fix it,
         and prove injection now works without redeploying everything.
    A10: kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj
         The webhook fires only at Pod CREATION — labels are never
         retroactive. Proof: kubectl apply --dry-run=server a test pod in
         anihpj and grep the returned YAML for "istio-proxy".

         [SIDECAR VS. AMBIENT — THE SAME ONE NODE, DRAWN TWICE]
         ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                SIDECAR MODE — ONE KUBERNETES NODE                 │
         │                                                                   │
         │ ┌─────────────────────────────┐   ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │
         │ │         jobpost-api         │   │        user-service         │ │
         │ │ ┌───────────┐ ┌───────────┐ │   │ ┌───────────┐ ┌───────────┐ │ │
         │ │ │    app    │ │istio-proxy│ │   │ │    app    │ │istio-proxy│ │ │
         │ │ └───────────┘ └───────────┘ │   │ └───────────┘ └───────────┘ │ │
         │ │          READY 2/2          │   │          READY 2/2          │ │
         │ └─────────────────────────────┘   └─────────────────────────────┘ │
         │                                                                   │
         │  Envoy processes running on THIS node:  2                         │
         │  (1 istio-proxy sidecar per pod → N pods = N Envoys)              │
         └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │              AMBIENT MODE — SAME ONE KUBERNETES NODE              │
         │                                                                   │
         │ ┌─────────────────────────────┐   ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │
         │ │         jobpost-api         │   │        user-service         │ │
         │ │        ┌───────────┐        │   │        ┌───────────┐        │ │
         │ │        │    app    │        │   │        │    app    │        │ │
         │ │        └───────────┘        │   │        └───────────┘        │ │
         │ │          READY 1/1          │   │          READY 1/1          │ │
         │ └─────────────────────────────┘   └─────────────────────────────┘ │
         │                ▼                                 ▼                │
         │      ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
         │      │    ztunnel  (DaemonSet — 1 pod per node, SHARED)    │      │
         │      │  Handles mTLS + L4 authZ + telemetry for both pods  │      │
         │      │                      READY 1/1                      │      │
         │      └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
         │                                                                   │
         │  Envoy-class processes running on THIS node:  1                   │
         │  (ztunnel is shared by ALL ambient pods on the node —             │
         │   N pods still = 1 Envoy-class process, not N)                    │
         └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Same node, same two anihpj pods — the only thing that moved
           is WHERE the Envoy proxy lives: inside every pod (sidecar)
           or on one shared ztunnel DaemonSet pod per node (ambient).
           Scale it out: a 50-pod node runs 50 Envoys under sidecar
           mode and still just 1 ztunnel under ambient mode.
         - The READY column is the tell, but read it carefully — 1/1
           in ambient mode does NOT mean "no mTLS." It means the mTLS
           moved off-pod onto the node's shared ztunnel; the pod
           simply stopped carrying its own copy of Envoy.

         [MIGRATION READINESS CHECK — 4 QUESTIONS BEFORE GOING AMBIENT]
         ┌───────────────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────────────┐
         │ ① L7 FEATURES?                │   │ ② TCP-ONLY / LEGACY?          │
         │ Need retries, circuit-        │   │ Is this route plain TCP or a  │
         │ breaking, or canary traffic   │   │ legacy non-HTTP protocol?     │
         │ splits on this route?         │   │ ----------------------------- │
         │ ----------------------------- │   │ → Ambient L4 (ztunnel)        │
         │ → YES: you still need a       │   │ handles it fine — sidecar L7  │
         │ waypoint proxy — pure L4      │   │ features never applied here   │
         │ ambient alone is not enough   │   │ anyway                        │
         │                               │   │                               │
         └───────────────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────────────┘

         ┌───────────────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────────────┐
         │ ③ CNI INSTALLED?              │   │ ④ TEAM READINESS?             │
         │ Is the Istio CNI plugin       │   │ Comfortable debugging via     │
         │ already installed cluster-    │   │ istioctl/ztunnel logs instead │
         │ wide?                         │   │ of a per-pod sidecar?         │
         │ ----------------------------- │   │ ----------------------------- │
         │ → REQUIRED for ambient,       │   │ → Operational-readiness gate  │
         │ always. No CNI node agent     │   │ — confirm this BEFORE         │
         │ means no ambient data plane,  │   │ cutover, not during an        │
         │ full stop                     │   │ incident                      │
         └───────────────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────────────┘

         - Read the four together: a "no" on ① plus "yes" on ②-④ is
           the green-light profile from 16.6's per-namespace decision
           guide. A "yes" on ① does NOT rule ambient out — it means
           ambient PLUS a waypoint, not pure L4 ambient alone.
         - ③ is the one absolute: ambient mode cannot run at all
           without the Istio CNI plugin already in place (see 4.12) —
           it is not optional the way it can be for sidecar mode.

    4.12  The Istio CNI Plugin — An Install-Time Choice That Removes NET_ADMIN
         - DEFINITION: the Istio CNI plugin replaces the per-pod istio-init
           container with a single privileged istio-cni-node DaemonSet (one
           pod per node, namespace istio-system) that writes the SAME
           traffic-redirect iptables rules from the node instead of from
           inside every application pod
         - Why it matters: without CNI, every user or pipeline deploying to
           a meshed namespace needs Kubernetes RBAC to create containers
           requesting the NET_ADMIN and NET_RAW capabilities — and those
           capabilities are explicitly forbidden under the baseline and
           restricted Pod Security Standards (see 4.13); CNI moves that
           privilege out of application namespaces entirely
         - How it works: CNI is an install-time flag, not a per-pod choice —
           turn it on once for the whole mesh via IstioOperator
           (components.cni.enabled: true) or the istio/cni Helm chart;
           anihpj workloads need zero YAML changes — the init container
           silently disappears from every pod injected afterward
         - Ambient mode ALWAYS installs CNI — it is a required component of
           the ambient data plane (already true in the 4.8 per-profile
           matrix). For SIDECAR mode, CNI is optional and OFF by default;
           turning it on is the prerequisite that unlocks restricted-
           namespace sidecar installs in 4.13

         [CNI OFF vs CNI ON — WHO WRITES THE REDIRECT RULES]
         ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  CNI DISABLED (default sidecar install)                           │
         │    kubectl apply pod → istio-init container runs FIRST            │
         │    istio-init needs NET_ADMIN + NET_RAW → every single pod        │
         │    then istio-proxy + app containers start                        │
         │                                                                   │
         │  CNI ENABLED (components.cni.enabled: true)                       │
         │    kubectl apply pod → NO istio-init container at all             │
         │    istio-cni-node DaemonSet (istio-system, 1/node) already        │
         │    wrote the redirect rule before the pod's containers start      │
         │    app namespace needs ZERO extra capabilities                    │
         └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [ENABLING THE CNI PLUGIN — IstioOperator YAML]
         ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: install.istio.io/v1alpha1                            │
         │  kind: IstioOperator                                              │
         │  metadata:                                                        │
         │    name: anihpj-cni                                               │
         │  spec:                                                            │
         │    profile: default          # any deployment profile             │
         │    components:                                                    │
         │      cni:                                                         │
         │        namespace: istio-system                                    │
         │        enabled: true          ← the only flag that matters        │
         │                                                                   │
         │  # Install it:   istioctl install -f cni.yaml -y                  │
         └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [ENABLING CNI — istioctl vs Helm vs ambient]
         ┌──────────┬────────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────┐
         │ Method   │ Command                                │ Runs in       │
         ├──────────┼────────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────┤
         │ istioctl │ -f cni.yaml, components.cni.enabled:   │ istio-system  │
         │          │ true (see IstioOperator spec below)    │ (DaemonSet)   │
         │ Helm     │ helm install istio-cni istio/cni -n    │ istio-system  │
         │          │ istio-system --wait                    │ (DaemonSet)   │
         │ Ambient  │ automatic: profile=ambient always on   │ always on     │
         └──────────┴────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────┘
         - Real anihpj scenario: the platform team turns CNI on mesh-wide
           the same week they start locking namespaces down with Pod
           Security Admission — enabling it is the prerequisite for 4.13,
           not an alternative to it. Some managed platforms (e.g. GKE)
           restrict the DaemonSet's system-node-critical PriorityClass to
           specific namespaces — check that before picking istio-system

    4.13  Installing Istio Under Pod Security Admission (Restricted Namespaces)
         - DEFINITION: Pod Security Admission (PSA) is Kubernetes' built-in
           admission controller that enforces one of three Pod Security
           Standards — privileged, baseline, restricted — per namespace via
           the pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=<level> label
         - Why it matters: the DEFAULT sidecar install's istio-init
           container requests NET_ADMIN and NET_RAW; baseline explicitly
           forbids added capabilities beyond NET_BIND_SERVICE and
           restricted forbids even more — label an anihpj namespace
           enforce=restricted with default (no-CNI) injection still on and
           every injected pod is REJECTED at admission, not just warned
         - How it works: install Istio with the CNI plugin (4.12) first —
           the elevated capability moves to the istio-cni-node DaemonSet in
           istio-system (which itself must stay enforce=privileged); anihpj
           and every other meshed namespace can then run enforce=restricted
           with zero special capabilities in the app or istio-proxy
           containers. Ambient mode has no init container in the pod at
           all, so it inherits the same shape automatically: istio-system
           stays privileged, application namespaces go restricted
         - restricted also requires seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault on
           every container, in addition to the capability restrictions

         [LABELING NAMESPACES FOR POD SECURITY ADMISSION]
         ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  # anihpj app namespace — restricted, needs CNI already installed │
         │  kubectl label namespace anihpj \                                 │
         │      pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \              │
         │      pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest            │
         │                                                                   │
         │  # istio-system — the CNI DaemonSet needs privileged, always      │
         │  kubectl label namespace istio-system \                           │
         │      pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=privileged                │
         │                                                                   │
         │  # restricted also requires seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault   │
         │  # on every container — set it in the pod spec's securityContext  │
         └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [WHICH PODS GET ADMITTED — PSA level × install mode]
         ┌────────────┬─────────────────────┬───────────────┬────────────────┐
         │ PSA level  │ Sidecar, no CNI     │ Sidecar+CNI   │ Ambient        │
         ├────────────┼─────────────────────┼───────────────┼────────────────┤
         │ privileged │ admitted            │ admitted      │ admitted       │
         │ baseline   │ REJECTED (NET_ADMIN)│ admitted      │ admitted       │
         │ restricted │ REJECTED (NET_ADMIN)│ admitted*     │ admitted*      │
         └────────────┴─────────────────────┴───────────────┴────────────────┘
         - * restricted additionally needs seccompProfile.type set — a
           missing seccompProfile fails admission even with CNI enabled
         - Real anihpj scenario: platform security mandates enforce=
           restricted on every application namespace within one quarter;
           the rollout order is (1) enable CNI cluster-wide, (2) verify
           pods still get 2/2 with no istio-init container, (3) relabel
           namespaces to restricted one at a time, verifying each

    4.14  Platform-Specific Install Profiles — GKE, EKS, OpenShift, k3d, k3s, MicroK8s
         - DEFINITION: platform profiles are a SECOND, separate kind of
           profile from the deployment profiles in 4.3/4.7 — instead of
           choosing WHICH components install, they set the platform-
           specific chart values a given Kubernetes distribution needs
           (values.global.platform=<name>)
         - Why it matters: skip the platform profile on a distribution that
           needs one — OpenShift's SCCs, GKE Autopilot's resource ceilings
           — and the SAME istioctl install --set profile=demo -y that
           works cleanly on kind can fail or half-install with cryptic
           errors that look unrelated to the platform
         - How it works: compose a deployment profile AND a platform
           profile in the SAME install — the platform profile only tunes
           values, it never changes which components a deployment profile
           installs (default still means default, demo still means demo)
         - The 7 built-in platform profiles: gke, eks, openshift, k3d, k3s,
           microk8s, minikube

         [PLATFORM PROFILES — compose with any deployment profile]
         ┌──────────┬─────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ Platform │ platform=   │ What the overlay fixes                   │
         ├──────────┼─────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ GKE      │ gke         │ Autopilot-safe resource requests/limits  │
         │ EKS      │ eks         │ AWS load balancer + IAM-safe defaults    │
         │ OpenShift│ openshift   │ SCC-compatible SecurityContext, UID range│
         │ k3d      │ k3d         │ k3d's embedded networking quirks         │
         │ k3s      │ k3s         │ k3s's lightweight kubelet defaults       │
         │ MicroK8s │ microk8s    │ MicroK8s addon paths + permissions       │
         │ minikube │ minikube    │ Local single-node resource + net tuning  │
         └──────────┴─────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [COMBINING A DEPLOYMENT PROFILE WITH A PLATFORM PROFILE]
         ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  # istioctl: deployment profile + platform profile together       │
         │  istioctl install \                                               │
         │      --set profile=default \                                      │
         │      --set values.global.platform=gke -y                          │
         │                                                                   │
         │  # Ambient on EKS — same pattern, different values                │
         │  istioctl install \                                               │
         │      --set profile=ambient \                                      │
         │      --set values.global.platform=eks -y                          │
         │                                                                   │
         │  # Platform profiles only change VALUES — never which             │
         │  # components a deployment profile installs (see 4.7/4.8)         │
         └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         - Real anihpj scenario: the lab cluster (kind, no platform
           profile needed) runs istioctl install --set profile=demo -y
           unmodified; the staging cluster on GKE runs the exact same
           demo profile plus --set values.global.platform=gke so gateway
           Service annotations and resource ceilings match what Autopilot
           actually allows — same components, platform-correct values

    UNDER THE HOOD 🔧 — THREE INSTALL PATHS, ONE VERIFICATION MENTAL MODEL
    Section 4.8 walked through what happens INSIDE a single istioctl install
    command. This capstone zooms out: no matter which of the three install
    paths you took, the exam (and production) only ever cares about one thing
    afterward — can you prove it worked?

    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ THREE INSTALL PATHS, ONE VERIFICATION MENTAL MODEL                    │
    │                                                                       │
    │   Path A: istioctl install --set profile=demo -y                      │
    │   Path B: helm install (base -> istiod -> gateway), 3 releases        │
    │   Path C: istioctl install --set profile=ambient -y                   │
    │         │                                                             │
    │         ▼                                                             │
    │       All three render the SAME category of objects onto the API      │
    │       server: an istiod Deployment, ~30 CRDs, and either a            │
    │       MutatingWebhookConfiguration (sidecar path) or ztunnel +        │
    │       istio-cni-node DaemonSets (ambient path).                       │
    │         │                                                             │
    │         ▼  Regardless of path, verification is ONE fixed 5-step walk: │
    │                                                                       │
    │     1. kubectl get pods -n istio-system   → control plane Running     │
    │     2. kubectl get pods -n anihpj         → 2/2 (sidecar) or          │
    │                                              1/1 + ztunnel (ambient)  │
    │     3. istioctl proxy-status              → every proxy SYNCED        │
    │     4. istioctl analyze -n anihpj         → no validation issues      │
    │     5. curl jobpost-api -> user-service   → HTTP 200 through Envoy    │
    │                                                                       │
    │   Exam trap: candidates verify step 1 (pods Running) and stop --      │
    │   that only proves containers started, not that traffic flows.        │
    │   anihpj's jobpost-api can show 2/2 Running and STILL 503 if step 4   │
    │   (istioctl analyze) would have caught a bad port name first.         │
    └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    SPEED TIPS
      ⚡ Run istioctl profile diff default demo before installing anything —
         10 seconds tells you exactly which components you're about to add.
      ⚡ Run istioctl analyze -n anihpj BEFORE proxy-status — most
         "SYNCED but broken" reports are actually a bad port name or missing
         subset that analyze catches instantly.
      ⚡ Label the namespace (istio-injection=enabled or
         dataplane-mode=ambient) BEFORE kubectl apply -f anihpj/k8s/ —
         injection is never retroactive, so relabeling after deploy just
         means a second rollout restart.
      ⚡ Memorize the READY-column tell: 2/2 = sidecar working, 1/1 = ambient
         working as designed, 1/1 where you expected 2/2 = broken injection —
         don't debug the wrong problem.
      ⚡ Keep istioctl x precheck in muscle memory for any task that starts
         "before installing on this cluster..." — it's read-only and answers
         the "is it safe" question in one command.
      ⚡ If a scenario mentions "GitOps," "diffable," or "rollback," reach for
         Helm's three charts, not istioctl — the exam is testing whether you
         know WHY the two paths exist, not just that both work.

    COMMANDS CHEAT-CARD
    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ Command                                                               │ What it does / tells you                     │
    ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ INSTALL                                                                                                              │
    ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ istioctl install --set profile=demo -y                                │ Install: learning/lab, all dashboards        │
    │ istioctl install --set profile=default -y                             │ Install: production baseline                 │
    │ istioctl install --set profile=ambient -y                             │ Install: sidecar-free mesh                   │
    │ istioctl install -f operator.yaml -y                                  │ Install from a reviewable IstioOperator file │
    │ INSPECT A PROFILE BEFORE INSTALLING                                                                                  │
    ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ istioctl profile list                                                 │ List all 7 built-in profiles                 │
    │ istioctl profile dump demo                                            │ Show demo's full preset                      │
    │ istioctl profile diff default demo                                    │ Show exactly what demo adds                  │
    │ ENABLE THE DATA PLANE                                                                                                │
    ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ kubectl label ns anihpj istio-injection=enabled                       │ Turn on sidecar injection                    │
    │ kubectl label ns anihpj istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient               │ Turn on ambient mode                         │
    │ VERIFY                                                                                                               │
    ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ kubectl get pods -n istio-system                                      │ Control plane Running?                       │
    │ kubectl get pods -n anihpj                                            │ 2/2 (sidecar) or 1/1 (ambient)?              │
    │ istioctl proxy-status                                                 │ Every proxy SYNCED?                          │
    │ istioctl analyze -n anihpj                                            │ Config internally consistent?                │
    │ istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj            │ Inspect one Envoy's config                   │
    │ HELM (THE ALTERNATIVE TO istioctl)                                                                                   │
    ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ helm install istio-base istio/base -n istio-system --create-namespace │ CRDs only, no pods yet                       │
    │ helm install istiod istio/istiod -n istio-system --wait               │ Control plane release                        │
    │ helm install istio-ingress istio/gateway -n istio-ingress             │ Data-plane gateway release                   │
    │ helm status istiod -n istio-system                                    │ Release status (deployed?)                   │
    │ helm rollback istiod 1                                                │ Undo a bad upgrade                           │
    │ DIAGNOSE / RESET                                                                                                     │
    ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ istioctl x precheck                                                   │ Pre-install compatibility check              │
    │ istioctl dashboard kiali                                              │ Open the service graph                       │
    │ istioctl uninstall --purge -y                                         │ Remove Istio completely                      │
    └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    🧪 PRACTICE DRILL (8 minutes) — Install, Inject, Prove
    On any scratch cluster (kind/minikube/k3d — no platform profile needed):
      1. Install Istio with the demo profile: istioctl install --set
         profile=demo -y, then confirm all 7 pods in istio-system are Running.
      2. Create and label the anihpj namespace for sidecar injection, deploy
         anihpj's manifests (or 2 stand-in Deployments for jobpost-api and
         user-service), and confirm 2/2 READY.
      3. Run the 3-command verification chain: istioctl proxy-status (expect
         SYNCED), istioctl analyze -n anihpj (expect no issues), and a curl
         from one pod to the other (expect HTTP 200).
      4. Break it on purpose: rename one Service port to "web" instead of
         "http", re-run istioctl analyze, and read the exact warning printed.
      5. Clean up: istioctl uninstall --purge -y, then confirm anihpj pods
         return to 1/1 after a rollout restart.
    If you finish steps 1-3 in under 8 minutes with zero lookups, you're at
    exam speed for Domain 1.

    │         │                                                                │

    │   [6] HARDEN FOR PROD         CNI drops NET_ADMIN -> PSA restricted      │

    │   Every arrow above is a graded ICA checkpoint -- skip one and the       │
    │   mesh LOOKS installed while a later chapter's feature silently fails.   │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    Chapter 4 traced one continuous line from an empty Kubernetes cluster to a
    mesh you can defend under audit: choose a profile that matches the
    scenario, install it with istioctl or Helm, label the anihpj namespace for
    the data plane you actually want (sidecar or ambient), watch the data
    plane land as 2/2 pods or a shared ztunnel, and then PROVE — with
    proxy-status, analyze, a real curl, and Kiali — that traffic is actually
    flowing and not just that containers are Running. The CNI plugin and Pod
    Security Admission close the loop by removing the last elevated privilege
    the install needed, and platform profiles make the exact same components
    behave correctly on GKE, EKS, OpenShift, or a laptop's kind cluster. Every
    one of anihpj's seven services rides this same pipeline — installation is
    not a one-time ceremony, it is the foundation every later chapter's
    traffic-shifting, mTLS, and troubleshooting content assumes is already
    solid.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
PART 5: TRAFFIC MANAGEMENT — CONTROLLING HOW SERVICES COMMUNICATE        🟡
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  Chapters 5-8  ·  Difficulty: 🟡 Intermediate  ·  "Who may enter, where
  does it go, how is it delivered, and can it leave the mesh at all?"
  🎯 ICA EXAM FOCUS — Traffic Management is 35% of the exam, the single
  biggest domain (bigger than Observability and Security combined).
  What you'll build by the end: anihpj's jobpost-api open to the public
  internet through a Gateway, canary-split 90/10 and made resilient by a
  VirtualService, load-balanced and circuit-broken by a DestinationRule, and
  able to safely call Stripe and SendGrid via a ServiceEntry.

  [PART 5 INTRO]
  Part 4 leaves anihpj with a working mesh: every pod has a sidecar, and
  every hop between services is already intercepted by Envoy. But nothing
  yet decides who may knock from outside the cluster, where a request should
  go once it is inside, how the chosen destination should actually be
  reached, or whether the mesh may call back out to the rest of the
  internet. Those four questions are exactly the four CRDs this Part
  introduces, one chapter each, in the order a real request experiences
  them.

  This is deliberately the biggest Part in the guide. Traffic Management is
  graded more heavily than any other ICA domain, and it is also where the
  exam's performance-based tasks get compound: write a Gateway from scratch,
  split traffic 90/10 between two subsets, add a 3-attempt retry policy,
  wire up a circuit breaker, and register an external API — often as one
  multi-step scenario instead of four separate questions. Everything you
  build here also becomes the traffic that Part 6 observes in Kiali, Grafana
  and Jaeger, and the traffic that Part 7 locks down with mTLS and
  AuthorizationPolicy, so getting it right now pays off twice.

  🧠 ANALOGY. Think of anihpj's traffic path as an airport. The Gateway is
  the international arrivals terminal — the only door a plane (external
  traffic) may enter through, and it checks the passport and visa (host and
  TLS certificate) before anyone is let off the jet bridge. The
  VirtualService is air traffic control in the tower — it decides which gate
  a given flight taxis to (path and header matching), can send 10% of
  flights to the new gate as a trial run (weighted canary), and enforces
  holding patterns and go-arounds when things go wrong (retries, timeouts,
  fault injection). The DestinationRule is the ground crew's own rulebook
  once a flight is at its gate — which jet bridge to use this time (load
  balancing) and which gate crew gets stood down after five bad turnarounds
  in a row (the circuit breaker). And the ServiceEntry is the bilateral air
  treaty with a foreign country — without it, anihpj's "flights" to
  api.stripe.com are refused a flight plan before they ever take off.

  🐍 OUR RUNNING EXAMPLE — anihpj. Every YAML in Chapters 5-8 is written
  against the same anihpj/jobpost services used throughout this guide —
  jobpost-api, user-service, skills-service, location-service, auth-service,
  search-service, and notification-service — plus the external Stripe and
  SendGrid APIs anihpj already depends on for payments and email. By the end
  of Chapter 8 you will have taken jobpost-api from "reachable only inside
  the cluster" to "publicly routable, canary-released, resilient under
  failure, and safely talking to the outside world," using nothing but the
  four resources in this Part.

  The four chapters build strictly on each other, and skipping the order
  costs real exam time: a VirtualService with no Gateway only routes traffic
  already inside the mesh; a DestinationRule's subsets mean nothing until a
  VirtualService references them by name; and a ServiceEntry solves an
  entirely different direction of traffic (the mesh calling OUT) that
  neither Gateway nor VirtualService touch at all. Read Ch5 → Ch6 → Ch7 →
  Ch8 in sequence — each one assumes the resource before it is already in
  place.

  [HOW THE CHAPTERS FIT — Part 5 map]
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Ch5 GATEWAY ──▶ Ch6 VIRTUALSERVICE ──▶ Ch7 DESTINATIONRULE              │
  │  "who may           "where does it            "how is it                │
  │   enter?"            go once inside?"           delivered?"             │
  │  host/port/TLS       path/weight/header/         LB algorithm/mTLS/     │
  │                      retry/timeout/fault         circuit breaker/pool   │
  │                                                         │               │
  │                                                         ▼               │
  │                   Ch8 SERVICEENTRY — "can it leave the mesh at all?"    │
  │                   register external hosts, route via the egress gateway │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  This is a dependency map, not the request path — the VISUAL above already
  showed a live request's journey through all four resources in order. Read
  this one as "what you must already know before the next chapter makes
  sense": Ch6 assumes Ch5's Gateway exists and is referenced by name; Ch7's
  subsets are meaningless until Ch6's VirtualService routes traffic to them;
  and Ch8 branches off sideways because ServiceEntry governs the opposite
  direction of traffic — the mesh reaching OUT — and does not depend on any
  of the first three.

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE — which of the 4 CRDs solves your problem?
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ If you need to...                                    │ Use...                                       │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Accept HTTPS from the internet for api.anihpj.com    │ Gateway (tls.mode: SIMPLE)                   │
  │ Route /jobs/ to jobpost-api, /users/ to user-service │ VirtualService (http.match.uri.prefix)       │
  │ Split traffic 90/10 between jobpost-api v1 and v2    │ VirtualService (route[].weight)              │
  │ Auto-retry a failed call to user-service             │ VirtualService (retries.attempts: 3)         │
  │ Give up on a slow auth-service call after 5s         │ VirtualService (timeout: 5s)                 │
  │ Chaos-test with injected delays or aborts            │ VirtualService (fault.delay / fault.abort)   │
  │ Define what "subset v1" vs "v2" even means           │ DestinationRule (subsets[].labels)           │
  │ Pick the load-balancing algorithm for search-service │ DestinationRule (trafficPolicy.loadBalancer) │
  │ Stop hammering a crashing skills-service pod         │ DestinationRule (outlierDetection)           │
  │ Cap concurrent connections to a destination          │ DestinationRule (connectionPool)             │
  │ Let jobpost-api call api.stripe.com at all           │ ServiceEntry (location: MESH_EXTERNAL)       │
  │ Force every external call through one audited exit   │ ServiceEntry + Egress Gateway                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  WITHOUT Istio traffic management vs WITH it — why Part 5 exists
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ WITHOUT this Part (anihpj today)          │ WITH Gateway/VS/DR/ServiceEntry             │
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Ingress hand-rolled per team, no shared   │ One Gateway CRD, TLS-terminated,            │
  │   TLS or routing convention               │   the same for every anihpj service         │
  │ Canary = 2 Deployments + a risky script   │ Canary = one weight: field, reversible      │
  │ A/B testing needs custom app middleware   │ VirtualService match.headers, zero code     │
  │ Retry/timeout logic pasted into every     │ retries.attempts / timeout: set once,       │
  │   one of anihpj's 7 services              │   in YAML, outside every service's code     │
  │ kube-proxy round robin only — no other    │ DestinationRule offers 7 load-balancing     │
  │   balancing option available              │   algorithms, picked per destination        │
  │ One bad pod cascades — nothing isolates   │ outlierDetection ejects the bad pod in      │
  │   it (see Part 1's cascading failure)     │   milliseconds; the rest of anihpj stays up │
  │ Calls to Stripe/SendGrid go straight out, │ ServiceEntry registers the host; an Egress  │
  │   unaudited and unencrypted               │   Gateway can force + audit every exit      │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  CAPTION: every row above collapses to the same shape — without this Part,
  jobpost-api's own Django code (or a hand-rolled Ingress config) has to
  implement routing, retries, load balancing and egress control itself, and
  every one of anihpj's other six services must reimplement the same logic
  independently. With a Gateway, VirtualService, DestinationRule and
  ServiceEntry, that logic moves out of application code entirely and into
  four declarative resources Envoy enforces uniformly — a canary release, a
  circuit breaker, or a new external integration becomes one "kubectl
  apply," not a code change and a redeploy.

  [PART 5 SUMMARY + IMPLEMENTATION]
  By the end of this Part you can take any anihpj service from unreachable
  to production-safe using only four resources: a Gateway to open the front
  door, a VirtualService to route and protect individual requests, a
  DestinationRule to load-balance and circuit-break the destinations
  VirtualService chose, and a ServiceEntry to let the mesh reach the handful
  of external systems anihpj genuinely depends on. Implementation thread
  (one continuous story across the four chapters):

      anihpj-gateway  (Ch5)
            │  TLS termination + host match for api.anihpj.com:443
            ▼
      jobpost-api-vs  (Ch6)
            │  match /jobs/* → 90% subset v1 / 10% subset v2,
            │  retries: 3, timeout: 5s
            ▼
      jobpost-api-dr  (Ch7)
            │  subsets v1/v2 defined, loadBalancer: LEAST_CONN,
            │  outlierDetection: consecutiveErrors: 5 (circuit breaker)
            ▼
      stripe-payments ServiceEntry  (Ch8)
            │  location: MESH_EXTERNAL, routed through
            │  istio-egressgateway for a single audited exit
            ▼
      ✅ jobpost-api is public, canary-safe, resilient, and can
         bill a customer through Stripe — all four properties
         earned without touching a single line of Django code
  CAPTION: this is the same request journey the VISUAL at the top of this
  Part already drew end to end — the diagram above is that journey replayed
  as a build order, one resource per chapter, so by Chapter 8 you have
  assembled it yourself instead of just having read it.
