  Read the map top to bottom as the chapter's own argument: first define the
  CRD and prove you can pin traffic to one version, then learn the three
  ways to choose a different route, then make that route survive failure,
  then learn the ordering/scope rules that keep multiple routes from
  fighting each other, and finally layer on the advanced in-flight editing
  and non-HTTP capabilities most exam-takers forget exist.

    6.1  What is a VirtualService?
         - A VirtualService is Istio's routing rules for a service
         - It overrides Kubernetes' default routing (simple round-robin)
         - Defines: WHERE traffic goes, HOW MUCH traffic, WITH WHAT conditions
         - Works for traffic from:
           • External (via Gateway)
           • Internal service-to-service calls within the mesh
         - Attaches to a Kubernetes Service by name
         [VIRTUALSERVICE CONCEPT DIAGRAM: traffic fork based on rules]

         [VIRTUALSERVICE — THE ROUTING BRAIN: hosts → http → match → route]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  VirtualService "jobpost-api-vs"   (namespace: anihpj)               │
         │                                                                      │
         │  hosts:                     ← WHOSE traffic these rules govern       │
         │  - jobpost-api                (the Kubernetes Service name)          │
         │      │                                                               │
         │      ▼                                                               │
         │  http:                      ← ordered rule list, walked TOP → BOTTOM │
         │      │                                                               │
         │      ├─ RULE 1  match: header x-user-type = premium                  │
         │      │          route: → jobpost-api subset v2        (A/B test)     │
         │      │                                                               │
         │      ├─ RULE 2  match: uri prefix /jobs/                             │
         │      │          route: → v1 weight 90 / v2 weight 10  (canary)       │
         │      │                                                               │
         │      └─ RULE 3  (no match block = catch-all default)                 │
         │                 route: → jobpost-api subset v1    (everyone else)    │
         │                                                                      │
         │  A request forks at the FIRST rule whose match succeeds — Envoy      │
         │  stops evaluating right there (first-match-wins, detailed in 6.9)    │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - DEFINITION: a VirtualService is a routing TABLE, not a proxy —
           istiod compiles it into each Envoy's route config, so rules add
           ZERO extra network hops
         - Golden rule: VirtualService = WHERE traffic goes (the GPS route);
           DestinationRule = HOW it behaves once it gets there (Chapter 7)

    6.2  Basic Routing — Send All Traffic to One Version
         - jobpost-api has v1 and v2 deployments running simultaneously
         - By default, Kubernetes alternates between both
         - VirtualService: "Send 100% of traffic to subset: v1"
         - Subset is defined in DestinationRule (covered next)
         [YAML + TRAFFIC FLOW DIAGRAM: all traffic pinned to v1]

         [PIN-TO-V1 YAML — annotated (current API: networking.istio.io/v1)]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1  ← "v1" since Istio 1.22 │
         │  kind: VirtualService                                        │
         │  metadata:                                                   │
         │    name: jobpost-api-vs                                      │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                         │
         │  spec:                                                       │
         │    hosts:                                                    │
         │    - jobpost-api        ← attach to this K8s Service name    │
         │    http:                                                     │
         │    - route:             ← no match block = applies to ALL    │
         │      - destination:                                          │
         │          host: jobpost-api                                   │
         │          subset: v1     ← 100% pinned to v1; the subset is   │
         │                           defined in a DestinationRule (Ch 7)│
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [REQUEST FLOW — before vs after the pin-to-v1 rule]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  BEFORE (plain Kubernetes Service — round-robin over ALL pods):  │
         │                                                                  │
         │   browser ─▶ jobpost-api Service ──┬──▶ v1 pod   (≈50%)          │
         │                                    └──▶ v2 pod   (≈50%)  ⚠️      │
         │   users randomly land on the untested v2                         │
         │                                                                  │
         │  AFTER (VirtualService pins subset v1):                          │
         │                                                                  │
         │   browser ─▶ Envoy sidecar ────────────▶ v1 pod   (100%) ✅      │
         │              v2 pods receive ZERO traffic until YOU flip the rule│
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    6.3  Weight-Based Traffic Splitting (Canary Deployments)
         - Deploy jobpost-api:v2 (new version with better job search)
         - Start with 5% traffic to v2, 95% to v1
         - Gradually shift: 10%→25%→50%→100% as confidence grows
         - Roll back instantly by changing the weight — no downtime
         [YAML WALKTHROUGH + VISUAL: traffic percentage split diagram]

         [WEIGHT-BASED ROUTING — jobpost-api canary for anihpj]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                    │
         │  kind: VirtualService                                  │
         │  metadata:                                             │
         │    name: jobpost-api-vs                                │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                   │
         │  spec:                                                 │
         │    hosts:                                              │
         │    - jobpost-api                                       │
         │    http:                                               │
         │    - route:                                            │
         │      - destination:                                    │
         │          host: jobpost-api                             │
         │          subset: v1    ← DestinationRule defines this  │
         │        weight: 90      ← 90% to stable version        │
         │      - destination:                                    │
         │          host: jobpost-api                             │
         │          subset: v2    ← New version being tested      │
         │        weight: 10      ← 10% canary traffic            │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Weights are RELATIVE — Envoy normalizes them: 90+10, 9+1 and
           900+100 all produce the same 90%/10% split (sum need not be 100)
         - Per request, Envoy draws a random number 0-99: 0-89 → v1,
           90-99 → v2; over 1,000 requests that converges to ≈900/≈100

         🔧 UNDER THE HOOD: that 0-99 draw happens fresh on EVERY request —
            istiod compiles the 90/10 split into Envoy's route config as a
            stateless weighted-cluster choice, so Envoy keeps no memory of
            which subset a caller got last time. Ten calls from the same
            browser can land on v1 nine times and v2 once, or any other
            mix — only Chapter 7's DestinationRule consistentHash setting
            adds a "same user, same pod" guarantee this canary rule lacks.
         - ⚠️ If a route names a subset that no DestinationRule defines,
           ALL traffic to that destination returns 503 — apply the
           DestinationRule first (or in the same kubectl apply -f)

    6.4  Header-Based Routing (A/B Testing)
         - Route specific users to a specific version based on HTTP headers
         - Example: if header x-user-type: premium → send to jobpost-api:v2
         - Example: if header x-canary: true → send to new anihpj UI
         - Useful for: beta testers, internal teams, feature flags
         [YAML + DECISION DIAGRAM: header present → v2, no header → v1]

         [A/B TESTING FLOW — header-based routing decision]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Incoming request to jobpost-api                                   │
         │                    │                                               │
         │          ┌─────────▼──────────┐                                   │
         │          │  Envoy checks:      │                                   │
         │          │  Header present?   │                                   │
         │          │  x-user-type:      │                                   │
         │          │  premium?          │                                   │
         │          └────────┬────────────┘                                   │
         │                   │                                                │
         │          ┌────────┴────────┐                                       │
         │         YES               NO                                       │
         │          │                 │                                       │
         │          ▼                 ▼                                       │
         │  [jobpost-api:v2]   [jobpost-api:v1]                               │
         │  (new UI / features)  (stable production)                          │
         │                                                                    │
         │  YAML that makes this work:                                        │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    http:                                                           │
         │    - match:                                                        │
         │      - headers:                          ← check header           │
         │          x-user-type:                                              │
         │            exact: premium                ← match value             │
         │      route:                                                        │
         │      - destination:                                                │
         │          host: jobpost-api                                         │
         │          subset: v2                      ← premium users → v2     │
         │    - route:                              ← default (no match)     │
         │      - destination:                                                │
         │          host: jobpost-api                                         │
         │          subset: v1                      ← everyone else → v1     │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [A/B TESTING USE CASES for anihpj]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┐
         │  Header / Condition                  │  Route to                   │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┤
         │  x-user-type: premium                │  jobpost-api:v2 (premium UI)│
         │  x-canary: "true"                    │  jobpost-api:v2 (canary)    │
         │  x-internal-user: "1"               │  skills-svc:v2 (beta feats) │
         │  user-agent: contains "Mobile"       │ jobpost-api mobile-optimized│
         │  cookie: session=staging             │  all services:v2 staging    │
         │  Authorization: JWT with role=admin  │  admin-service              │
         └──────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘

    6.5  URI-Based and Path-Based Routing
         - Route /jobs/ → jobpost-api
         - Route /users/ → user-service
         - Route /skills/ → skills-service
         - Single VirtualService can route by prefix, exact, regex
         [YAML: VirtualService routing all anihpj endpoints]

         [PATH-BASED ROUTING — all anihpj services through one VS]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  spec:                                                 │
         │    http:                                               │
         │    - match:                                            │
         │      - uri:                                            │
         │          prefix: /jobs/        → jobpost-api:8000      │
         │    - match:                                            │
         │      - uri:                                            │
         │          prefix: /users/       → user-service:8080     │
         │    - match:                                            │
         │      - uri:                                            │
         │          prefix: /skills/      → skills-service:8090   │
         │    - match:                                            │
         │      - uri:                                            │
         │          prefix: /locations/   → location-service:8070 │
         │    - route:                                            │
         │      - destination:            → default: jobpost-api  │
         │          host: jobpost-api                             │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Rules are checked top → bottom, first match wins: keep the MOST
           specific prefix first and the default (no match) route LAST
         - Strip a prefix before forwarding with rewrite: match prefix
           /api/v2/ + "rewrite: uri: /" delivers /api/v2/users/123 to the
           upstream as /users/123 — the app never sees the version prefix

    6.6  Retries — Automatic Failure Recovery
         - Without Istio: if user-service returns a 503, anihpj fails
         - With Istio VirtualService retries: automatically retry up to 3 times
         - Configure: attempts, perTryTimeout, retryOn (which error codes)
         - Important: retries only safe for idempotent requests (GET, not POST)
         - anihpj use case: retry GET /users/{id}/ if user-service is momentarily down
         [RETRY FLOW DIAGRAM: first call fails → Envoy retries → success]

         [RETRY TIMELINE — how Envoy handles a failing user-service call]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Without retries (default Kubernetes):                             │
         │                                                                    │
         │  T=0ms:   jobpost-api → user-service → ❌ 503 Service Unavailable │
         │  T=1ms:   Envoy returns 503 to Django                             │
         │  T=2ms:   Django returns 500 to user browser                       │
         │  💥 User sees error even though user-service recovers in 200ms    │
         │                                                                    │
         │  With Istio retries (attempts: 3, perTryTimeout: 2s):             │
         │                                                                    │
         │  T=0ms:   jobpost-api → user-service → ❌ 503 (attempt 1)         │
         │  T=100ms: Envoy retries: → user-service → ❌ 503 (attempt 2)      │
         │  T=200ms: Envoy retries: → user-service → ✅ 200 OK (attempt 3)  │
         │  T=201ms: Django receives response normally                        │
         │  ✅ User never sees an error — blip absorbed by retry              │
         │                                                                    │
         │  YAML config that makes this happen:                               │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    http:                                                           │
         │    - retries:                                                      │
         │        attempts: 3           ← try up to 3 times                  │
         │        perTryTimeout: 2s     ← each attempt has 2s timeout        │
         │        retryOn: 5xx,gateway-error,reset  ← what errors to retry  │
         │      route:                                                        │
         │      - destination:                                                │
         │          host: user-service                                        │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Production-grade retryOn set: 5xx,connect-failure,refused-stream,
           reset — covers server errors, TCP connect failures and resets
         - Between tries Envoy inserts a small growing backoff (25ms+), so
           retries are spaced out, not machine-gunned at the failing service

         [VERIFY RETRY CONFIG — ask Envoy what it actually received]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  istioctl proxy-config route deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj \    │
         │    -o json | grep -B2 -A4 retryPolicy                          │
         │  # → "numRetries": 3, "perTryTimeout": "2s",                   │
         │  #   "retryOn": "5xx,gateway-error,reset"                      │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    6.7  Timeouts — Don't Wait Forever
         - Without Istio: your Django code hangs waiting for slow services
         - With Istio: set a global timeout per service (e.g., 5s for skills-svc)
         - Request takes >5s → Envoy returns 408/504, doesn't hang Django
         - anihpj use case: skills-service timeout 3s — fast degradation
         [YAML + TIMELINE DIAGRAM: timeout cut-off visualization]

         [TIMEOUT TIMELINE — how Istio prevents anihpj from hanging]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Without timeout (default):                                        │
         │                                                                    │
         │  T=0s:    jobpost-api → skills-service (slow, database overloaded)│
         │  T=10s:   Still waiting...                                         │
         │  T=30s:   Still waiting... Django thread is BLOCKED                │
         │  T=60s:   Django default timeout → returns error                   │
         │  💥 30-60 seconds of blocked threads = thread pool exhaustion      │
         │                                                                    │
         │  With Istio timeout (timeout: 3s):                                 │
         │                                                                    │
         │  T=0s:    jobpost-api → skills-service                             │
         │  T=3s:    ⏱️ Envoy timeout fires: returns 504 Gateway Timeout     │
         │  T=3.01s: Django gets 504, returns graceful degraded response      │
         │  ✅ Fast failure instead of slow hang — thread pool protected      │
         │                                                                    │
         │  COMBINED retry + timeout pattern for anihpj:                      │
         │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
         │  │  timeout: 10s          ← total budget for the request    │     │
         │  │  retries:                                                 │     │
         │  │    attempts: 3                                            │     │
         │  │    perTryTimeout: 3s   ← 3 tries × 3s = 9s max          │     │
         │  │    retryOn: 5xx                                           │     │
         │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
         │  Math: 3 attempts × 3s each = 9s, under the 10s total timeout ✅  │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    6.8  Fault Injection — Testing Resilience
         - Intentionally inject failures to test how anihpj handles them
         - Two types:
           • Delay: "delay 50% of requests to user-service by 7 seconds"
           • Abort: "return HTTP 500 for 10% of requests to auth-service"
         - WHY: validate that timeouts, retries, circuit breakers work
         - How to inject: add fault block to VirtualService
         [FAULT INJECTION YAML + what it reveals about your system]

         [FAULT INJECTION YAML — testing anihpj resilience]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  # Test 1: Delay 30% of requests to user-service       │
         │  spec:                                                 │
         │    http:                                               │
         │    - fault:                                            │
         │        delay:                                          │
         │          fixedDelay: 7s     # inject 7 second delay   │
         │          percentage:                                   │
         │            value: 30        # affect 30% of requests  │
         │      route:                                            │
         │      - destination:                                    │
         │          host: user-service                            │
         │                                                        │
         │  # Test 2: Abort 10% of requests to auth-service       │
         │  spec:                                                 │
         │    http:                                               │
         │    - fault:                                            │
         │        abort:                                          │
         │          httpStatus: 500    # return 500 error        │
         │          percentage:                                   │
         │            value: 10        # affect 10% of requests  │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Start small (value: 10) and raise gradually — watch p99 latency
           and error-rate dashboards while the fault is live
         - Expected result for anihpj: with the 7s delay active, the 3s
           timeout from 6.7 fires first and Django degrades gracefully
           instead of hanging — if it does NOT, you found a real bug cheaply
         - ⚠️ Fault injection and retries/timeout CAN be defined on the same
           route — but per the official docs, timeouts or retries will NOT
           be enabled when faults are enabled on that route; keep a
           separate fault-only VS for test days (see 6.11)
         - 🎯 ICA EXAM NOTE: "Using Fault Injection" is its own NAMED exam
           subtopic under Traffic Management (35%) — it is graded
           separately from resilience features (retries/timeouts/circuit
           breaking), even though you use it to TEST them

         [FAULT INJECTION TESTING WORKFLOW — a real resilience test day]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  STEP 1: baseline — capture normal Grafana numbers first        │
         │    847 req/s, 2.1% errors, p99 234ms  (write these down)        │
         │                                                                  │
         │  STEP 2: apply a SMALL fault (delay: 3s @ value: 10) on a       │
         │    fault-only VirtualService, NOT the production one             │
         │                                                                  │
         │  STEP 3: watch — does the CALLER'S timeout/retry/circuit        │
         │    breaker absorb it? p99 should rise but stay < timeout,       │
         │    error rate should stay near 2.1% (retries hide the delay)    │
         │                                                                  │
         │  STEP 4: raise the fault (delay: 7s @ value: 30, or             │
         │    abort: 500 @ value: 10) — this is where real bugs show:      │
         │    • p99 exceeds the timeout → caller hangs (missing timeout)   │
         │    • error rate spikes 1:1 with abort % → no retries configured │
         │    • ALL callers fail together → no circuit breaker isolating   │
         │      the bad subset                                             │
         │                                                                  │
         │  STEP 5: remove the fault-only VS — never leave fault injection │
         │    active outside a test window                                 │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    6.9  Route Matching Precedence — How Envoy Chooses Routes
         - DEFINITION: when a VirtualService lists several http rules, Envoy
           walks them TOP → BOTTOM and uses the FIRST rule whose match
           succeeds — then STOPS. There is no "best match", only first match
         - Why it matters: the #1 VirtualService bug is a catch-all route
           placed ABOVE a specific route — the specific rule becomes dead
           code that never fires
         - The three uri match styles, most → least precise:
           • exact:  /healthz         → matches ONLY /healthz
           • prefix: /api/v1/         → matches /api/v1/jobs, /api/v1/users…
           • regex:  ^/api/v[12]/.*   → pattern match (CPU-costly, use last)
         - AND vs OR: conditions inside ONE match entry are ANDed; separate
           entries in the match list (or separate rules) are ORed
         - Ordering recipe: exact matches first → longer prefixes before
           shorter → regex → the catch-all default (no match block) LAST

         [FIRST-MATCH-WINS TRAP — why "my route isn't working"]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  REQUEST: GET /api/v1/users/123        (no special headers)        │
         │                                                                    │
         │  ❌ BROKEN ORDER — catch-all placed first:                         │
         │     RULE 1: (no match = catch-all)          → v1  ◀ swallows ALL   │
         │     RULE 2: prefix /api/v1/ + x-canary hdr  → v2  ◀ NEVER reached  │
         │     symptom: canary testers keep landing on v1 "for no reason"     │
         │                                                                    │
         │  ✅ CORRECT ORDER — specific first, general last:                  │
         │     RULE 1: uri exact /healthz              → health handler       │
         │     RULE 2: prefix /api/v1/ + x-canary hdr  → v2                   │
         │     RULE 3: prefix /api/v1/                 → v1 90% / v2 10%      │
         │     RULE 4: (no match = catch-all)          → v1                   │
         │                                                                    │
         │  the request above, walked through the CORRECT order:              │
         │     RULE 1: /api/v1/users/123 ≠ /healthz           → skip          │
         │     RULE 2: prefix ✓ but x-canary header missing   → skip          │
         │     RULE 3: prefix ✓ and no extra condition        → MATCH, STOP   │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [MATCH TYPES — everything a VirtualService rule can match on]
         ┌───────────────┬──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
         │  Match on     │  YAML example            │  Typical use         │
         ├───────────────┼──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
         │  uri exact    │  exact: /healthz         │  health, metrics     │
         │  uri prefix   │  prefix: /jobs/          │  path/API routing    │
         │  uri regex    │  regex: ^/api/v[12]/.*   │  variable patterns   │
         │  headers      │  x-canary: {exact: "1"}  │  A/B, canary users   │
         │  queryParams  │  version: {exact: v2}    │  ?version=v2 switch  │
         │  method       │  method: {exact: POST}   │  verb-based routing  │
         │  sourceLabels │  app: jobpost-api        │  route by CALLER     │
         │  port         │  port: 8000              │  multi-port services │
         └───────────────┴──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘

         [COPY-PASTE PATTERNS — the five VirtualService moves you reuse]
         ┌──────────────────┬───────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┐
         │  Pattern         │  Use case             │  Key fields                 │
         ├──────────────────┼───────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────┤
         │  Weighted canary │  90% v1 / 10% v2      │  weight: 90 + weight: 10    │
         │  Header A/B test │  premium users → v2   │  headers: x-user-type:      │
         │                  │                       │    exact: premium           │
         │  Path routing    │  /jobs/ → jobpost-api │  match: uri: prefix: /jobs/ │
         │  Fault injection │  chaos / resilience   │  fault: delay: | abort:     │
         │  Retry + timeout │  absorb 5xx blips     │  retries: {attempts: 3}     │
         │                  │                       │  + timeout: 5s              │
         └──────────────────┴───────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────┘

    6.10  Sidecar CRD — Controlling Proxy Scope and Performance
         - DEFINITION: the Sidecar resource (networking.istio.io/v1) limits
           WHICH services an Envoy proxy is told about — its egress scope
         - Default behavior: EVERY sidecar receives config for EVERY service
           in the mesh — 500 services = 500 clusters inside EACH Envoy
         - jobpost-api actually calls only user-service, skills-service and
           auth-service; carrying the other 497 is pure memory + push waste

         🧠 ANALOGY: an unscoped sidecar is like handing a brand-new hire
            the entire company phone directory on day one — thousands of
            numbers they will never dial. The Sidecar CRD instead hands
            jobpost-api's Envoy a business-card holder with exactly the
            three contacts it actually calls: user-service, skills-service,
            and auth-service — nothing more.
         - A Sidecar with no workloadSelector applies to ALL workloads in
           its namespace; config pushes get smaller AND faster
         - Not a security control by itself — it trims what the proxy KNOWS,
           it does not authenticate anything (pair with AuthorizationPolicy)
         - Exam cue: "reduce per-sidecar memory" or "limit reachable
           services" → the answer is the Sidecar CRD, not NetworkPolicy

         [SIDECAR EGRESS SCOPING — trim jobpost-api's view of the mesh]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                                │
         │  kind: Sidecar                                                     │
         │  metadata:                                                         │
         │    name: default          ← convention for namespace-wide scope    │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                               │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    egress:                                                         │
         │    - hosts:                                                        │
         │      - "./user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"    ← only the     │
         │      - "./skills-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"  ← services     │
         │      - "./auth-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"    ← truly used   │
         │      - "istio-system/*"   ← keep mesh infrastructure reachable     │
         │  # "./x" = service x in THIS namespace; "ns/*" = all of ns         │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [MEMORY BEFORE / AFTER — Sidecar scoping on a 500-service mesh]
         ┌───────────────────────────┬─────────────┬──────────────────────┐
         │  Per-sidecar metric       │  Without    │  With Sidecar        │
         ├───────────────────────────┼─────────────┼──────────────────────┤
         │  Clusters in Envoy config │  500+       │  ~10                 │
         │  Envoy memory (RSS)       │  ~300 MB    │  ~50 MB              │
         │  Pushed config size       │  100%       │  ~10% (90% smaller)  │
         │  Push time per change     │  seconds    │  milliseconds        │
         │  Config blast radius      │  whole mesh │  3 declared services │
         └───────────────────────────┴─────────────┴──────────────────────┘

         [VERIFY THE SHRINK — count clusters Envoy knows about]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj \  │
         │    | wc -l        # before: 500+ clusters → after: ~15         │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    6.11  Application vs Mesh-Level Failure Recovery — Avoiding Conflicts
         - Your Django code AND Istio both recover from failures — and they
           do it INDEPENDENTLY: neither layer knows the other exists
         - Classic conflict: Django's requests.get(..., timeout=2) gives up
           at 2s, BEFORE Istio's 3s timeout — Envoy's retry helps nobody
         - Golden rule: app timeout ≥ (Istio attempts + 1) × perTryTimeout
           plus a buffer — or delete the app timeout and let Istio own it
         - Retry multiplication: app retries 3× × Envoy retries 3× = up to
           9 hits on an already-struggling user-service (a retry storm)
         - Decide ONE owner per concern: timeouts/retries in the mesh
           (visible, tunable without redeploys); business fallbacks (cached
           skills list, "try later" page) stay in Django

         [TIMEOUT CONFLICT — Django timeout=2s vs Istio timeout=3s]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Django view (application layer):                                  │
         │    requests.get("http://user-service:8080/users/",                 │
         │                 timeout=2)           ← app gives up after 2s       │
         │                                                                    │
         │  VirtualService (mesh layer):                                      │
         │    timeout: 3s                       ← Envoy's total budget        │
         │    retries:                                                        │
         │      attempts: 1                                                   │
         │      perTryTimeout: 2s               ← the retry needs ~2s more    │
         │                                                                    │
         │  What ACTUALLY happens when user-service stalls:                   │
         │  T=0.0s  Django sends request → its sidecar forwards it            │
         │  T=2.0s  Django's OWN timeout fires → Timeout exception 💥         │
         │          Envoy is still mid-attempt; its retry is now pointless    │
         │  T=3.0s  Envoy's timeout fires… into a connection Django closed    │
         │                                                                    │
         │  FIX (pick ONE owner for the timeout):                             │
         │    requests.get(..., timeout=5)      ← ≥ (1+1)×2s + buffer ✅      │
         │    …or remove Django's timeout and let the mesh enforce 3s         │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [FAULT INJECTION vs RETRY/TIMEOUT — a documented limitation]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  ❌ IGNORED — fault + retries/timeout in ONE VirtualService:        │
         │     http:                                                          │
         │     - fault:   {delay: …}      injected faults IGNORE the retry    │
         │       retries: {attempts: 3}   and timeout policy sitting next     │
         │       timeout: 5s              to them — they will not "absorb"    │
         │                                your own injected failure           │
         │                                                                    │
         │  ✅ WORKING PATTERN — two VirtualServices, swapped on demand:      │
         │     user-service-prod.yaml  → retries + timeout   (production)     │
         │     user-service-test.yaml  → fault block only    (chaos test)     │
         │     kubectl delete -f prod.yaml && kubectl apply -f test.yaml      │
         │     …run the experiment, then swap back                            │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    6.12  Deep Dive — Retry Budget Math: Why Your Timeouts Fail
         - The #1 resilience misconfiguration: retry settings that can
           never finish inside the total timeout budget
         - Formula to memorize:  timeout ≥ (attempts + 1) × perTryTimeout
         - The "+1" is the INITIAL try — the attempts field counts only the
           RETRIES stacked on top of it, and nearly everyone forgets that
         - Envoy also inserts a small growing backoff (25ms+) between tries
           — leave headroom rather than budgeting to the exact second
         - Symptom of a blown budget: 504s plus FEWER retries in the metrics
           than you configured — the last tries were cut off mid-flight

         [RETRY BUDGET WORKSHEET — attempts: 2, perTryTimeout: 1s]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  FORMULA   timeout ≥ (attempts + 1) × perTryTimeout                │
         │            needed here: (2 + 1) × 1s = 3s                          │
         │                                                                    │
         │  ❌ timeout: 2s — watch the budget blow up:                        │
         │  T=0.0s  try 1   starts ── stalls ── perTryTimeout at T=1.0s       │
         │  T=1.0s  retry 1 starts ── stalls ── perTryTimeout at T=2.0s       │
         │  T=2.0s  GLOBAL timeout fires → 504.  Retry 2 NEVER RUNS 💥        │
         │          ("attempts: 2" silently behaved like "attempts: 1")       │
         │                                                                    │
         │  ✅ timeout: 4s — every try fits (3s needed ≤ 4s budget):          │
         │  T=0.0s  try 1   ── fails at 1.0s                                  │
         │  T=1.0s  retry 1 ── fails at 2.0s                                  │
         │  T=2.0s  retry 2 ── succeeds at 2.4s → 200 OK ✅                   │
         │                                                                    │
         │  anihpj audit — the 6.7 combo (timeout: 10s, attempts: 3,          │
         │  perTryTimeout: 3s) passes the naive 3×3s = 9s check, but the      │
         │  strict formula needs (3+1)×3s = 12s > 10s ⚠️ → the last retry     │
         │  can get cut short.  Fix: perTryTimeout: 2s, because               │
         │  (3+1)×2s = 8s ≤ 10s ✅                                            │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [ICA EXAM TRAP — spot the broken budget in seconds]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Given:   attempts: 3, perTryTimeout: 2s, timeout: 5s              │
         │  Math:    (3 + 1) × 2s = 8s needed, only 5s budget → ❌ broken     │
         │  Fixes:   raise timeout to ≥ 8s   OR   drop attempts to 1          │
         │           ((1 + 1) × 2s = 4s ≤ 5s ✅)                              │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘


    6.13  Header Manipulation — Rewriting Requests and Responses In Flight
         - DEFINITION: the headers field on an HTTPRoute adds, overwrites,
           or strips HTTP headers — headers.request (edits BEFORE the call
           reaches the upstream) and headers.response (edits BEFORE the
           reply reaches the caller); each has set / add / remove
         - set: map key → value, overwrites or creates the header
         - add: map key → value, appends WITHOUT removing an existing one
           (can produce duplicate header lines — use set unless duplicates
           are wanted, e.g. multi-value headers)
         - remove: a plain list of header names, deleted outright
         - WHY: inject/strip headers mesh-wide with zero app code changes —
           stamp a trace hint, hide an internal debug header from callers,
           add a security header every service forgot

         [HEADER REWRITE — anihpj hides an internal header, adds a trace tag]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                            │
         │  kind: VirtualService                                          │
         │  metadata:                                                     │
         │    name: user-service-vs                                       │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                           │
         │  spec:                                                         │
         │    hosts:                                                      │
         │    - user-service                                              │
         │    http:                                                       │
         │    - headers:                                                  │
         │        request:                                                │
         │          set:                                                  │
         │            x-request-source: mesh   ← stamped on every call    │
         │          remove:                                               │
         │          - x-internal-debug-token    ← app header, drop it     │
         │        response:                                               │
         │          remove:                                               │
         │          - x-powered-by              ← don't leak stack info   │
         │      route:                                                    │
         │      - destination:                                            │
         │          host: user-service                                    │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [REQUEST/RESPONSE HEADER EDITING — where each operation applies]
         ┌──────────────────────┬─────────────────────┬──────────────┐
         │  headers.* field     │  Direction          │  Applied by  │
         ├──────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────┤
         │  request.set / add   │  caller → upstream  │  outbound    │
         │  request.remove      │  before delivery    │  outbound    │
         │  response.set / add  │  upstream → caller  │  inbound     │
         │  response.remove     │  before return      │  inbound     │
         └──────────────────────┴─────────────────────┴──────────────┘

         - Same headers block can sit next to a match, so different rules
           stamp different headers per route (e.g. only the /jobs/ prefix
           rule adds x-cache-tier: hot)
         - ⚠️ Header manipulation still runs even on a request a match
           rejects for OTHER reasons — it's per-ROUTE, not conditional on
           the rest of that route's outcome

    6.14  CORS Policy — Browser Cross-Origin Access Control
         - DEFINITION: corsPolicy on an HTTPRoute makes Envoy answer
           Cross-Origin Resource Sharing preflight (OPTIONS) requests and
           stamp CORS headers on real responses — on the caller's BEHALF,
           no app code involved
         - Key fields: allowOrigins (list of exact/prefix/regex string
           matches), allowMethods, allowHeaders, exposeHeaders, maxAge,
           allowCredentials
         - WHY: anihpj's SPA frontend lives on a different origin
           (app.anihpj.example) than the API (api.anihpj.example) — the
           BROWSER blocks the fetch() unless the API's response carries
           Access-Control-Allow-Origin — Django would otherwise need
           django-cors-headers wired into every service separately

         [CORS PREFLIGHT — browser asks permission before the real request]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  1. Browser JS on app.anihpj.example calls:                    │
         │     fetch("https://api.anihpj.example/jobs/")                  │
         │                                                                │
         │  2. Browser sends OPTIONS preflight FIRST (not the real GET):  │
         │     OPTIONS /jobs/  Origin: https://app.anihpj.example         │
         │                                                                │
         │  3. Envoy answers using corsPolicy — NEVER reaches jobpost-api:│
         │     200 OK                                                     │
         │     Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.anihpj.example    │
         │     Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST                    │
         │     Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400                              │
         │                                                                │
         │  4. Browser is satisfied → sends the REAL GET /jobs/ request,  │
         │     which now reaches jobpost-api normally                     │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [CORS POLICY YAML — anihpj SPA calling the jobpost-api origin]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                            │
         │  kind: VirtualService                                          │
         │  metadata:                                                     │
         │    name: jobpost-api-vs                                        │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                           │
         │  spec:                                                         │
         │    hosts:                                                      │
         │    - jobpost-api                                               │
         │    http:                                                       │
         │    - corsPolicy:                                               │
         │        allowOrigins:                                           │
         │        - exact: https://app.anihpj.example                     │
         │        allowMethods: ["GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE"]          │
         │        allowHeaders: ["authorization", "content-type"]         │
         │        maxAge: "24h"        ← cache the preflight, skip retest │
         │        allowCredentials: true  ← cookies/auth headers allowed  │
         │      route:                                                    │
         │      - destination:                                            │
         │          host: jobpost-api                                     │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - ⚠️ allowOrigins with exact: "*" is NOT the same as allowing
           credentials from anywhere — browsers reject a wildcard origin
           combined with allowCredentials: true; be explicit per origin
         - Exam cue: "the API works with curl but the SPA's browser fetch
           fails with a CORS error" → check corsPolicy, not AuthorizationPolicy

    6.15  TCP and TLS Route Blocks — Routing Beyond HTTP
         - DEFINITION: besides http:, a VirtualService can carry tcp: and
           tls: blocks — tcp: routes raw L4 connections by port/source,
           with NO awareness of what's inside them; tls: routes by the
           SNI hostname of a TLS handshake WITHOUT decrypting the traffic
         - WHY: not everything in the anihpj mesh is HTTP — a raw Postgres
           connection, a Redis connection, or a plain-TLS legacy endpoint
           the sidecar should route but never terminate
         - tcp: match fields: destinationSubnets, port, sourceLabels,
           sourceNamespace, gateways (no uri/headers — there's no HTTP
           request to inspect)
         - tls: match fields: sniHosts (required), destinationSubnets,
           port, sourceLabels, sourceNamespace, gateways — Envoy peeks at
           the unencrypted SNI field of the ClientHello, then forwards the
           still-encrypted bytes untouched

         [BLOCK SELECTION — how Envoy picks http: vs tcp: vs tls:]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  New connection arrives at the sidecar                         │
         │            │                                                   │
         │            ▼                                                   │
         │  Is the payload HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, or gRPC?                     │
         │     YES ──────────────────────────▶ use the  http:  block      │
         │     NO, but it's a TLS ClientHello ─▶ use the  tls:  block     │
         │            (routes on SNI, payload stays encrypted)            │
         │     NO, plain TCP ──────────────────▶ use the  tcp:  block     │
         │            (routes on port / source only, opaque bytes)        │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [TCP ROUTE — anihpj's Postgres connection, routed by port]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                            │
         │  kind: VirtualService                                          │
         │  metadata:                                                     │
         │    name: postgres-vs                                           │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                           │
         │  spec:                                                         │
         │    hosts:                                                      │
         │    - postgres-primary                                          │
         │    tcp:                                                        │
         │    - match:                                                    │
         │      - port: 5432                                              │
         │      route:                                                    │
         │      - destination:                                            │
         │          host: postgres-primary                                │
         │          port:                                                 │
         │            number: 5432                                        │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [TLS ROUTE — split by SNI without decrypting the handshake]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  spec:                                                         │
         │    hosts:                                                      │
         │    - "*"                                                       │
         │    tls:                                                        │
         │    - match:                                                    │
         │      - port: 443                                               │
         │        sniHosts:                                               │
         │        - legacy.anihpj.example    ← routes by SNI only         │
         │      route:                                                    │
         │      - destination:                                            │
         │          host: legacy-tls-service                              │
         │          port:                                                 │
         │            number: 443                                         │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [HTTP vs TCP vs TLS — what each block type can and cannot do]
         ┌────────────────────┬─────────┬────────┬──────────────────┐
         │  Capability        │  http:  │  tcp:  │  tls:            │
         ├────────────────────┼─────────┼────────┼──────────────────┤
         │  uri/header match  │  yes    │  no    │  no              │
         │  sniHosts match    │  no     │  no    │  yes             │
         │  weighted routing  │  yes    │  yes   │  yes             │
         │  retries/timeout   │  yes    │  no    │  no              │
         │  fault injection   │  yes    │  no    │  no              │
         │  corsPolicy        │  yes    │  no    │  no              │
         │  sees payload      │  yes    │  no    │  no (encrypted)  │
         └────────────────────┴─────────┴────────┴──────────────────┘

         - ⚠️ A VirtualService's hosts: for a tls: block is usually "*" —
           the SNI value in sniHosts does the real routing, not hosts:
         - Route precedence rule from 6.9 (first-match-wins, top→bottom)
           applies independently WITHIN each block — http:, tcp:, and
           tls: are evaluated as separate rule lists, not merged together

  [CHAPTER 6 UNDER THE HOOD 🔧 — Precedence + Weight + Retry + Timeout, Together]
  6.12 already showed the retry-budget formula in isolation; this closing
  deep dive shows what happens when precedence (6.9), weight (6.3), retries
  (6.6) and timeout (6.7) all fire together for ONE real request, because in
  production they never fire alone.

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ONE REQUEST, ONE RULE'S BUNDLE — jobpost-api-vs has 3 http rules:        │
  │                                                                          │
  │   RULE 1  match: header x-user-type=premium                              │
  │           route: subset v2 | retries: 2, perTryTimeout 1s | timeout 3s   │
  │   RULE 2  match: uri prefix /jobs/                                       │
  │           route: 90% v1 / 10% v2 | retries: 3, perTryTimeout 2s |        │
  │                  timeout 10s                                             │
  │   RULE 3  (catch-all, no match block)                                    │
  │           route: subset v1 | (no retries/timeout block set)              │
  │                                                                          │
  │ REQUEST A: GET /jobs/42, header x-user-type: premium                     │
  │   step 1  Envoy walks rules top -> bottom (6.9 precedence)               │
  │   step 2  RULE 1's header match succeeds -> STOP. RULE 2 and RULE 3      │
  │           are never evaluated for this request at all                    │
  │   step 3  destination is a single subset (v2) -- no weight draw needed,  │
  │           RULE 2's 90/10 split is 100% irrelevant here                   │
  │   step 4  RULE 1's OWN resilience bundle arms: up to 2 retries, 1s per   │
  │           try, 3s total -- RULE 2's numbers (3 / 2s / 10s) never apply   │
  │                                                                          │
  │ REQUEST B: GET /jobs/42, no special headers                              │
  │   step 1  RULE 1 match fails (header absent) -> skip                     │
  │   step 2  RULE 2's uri prefix matches -> STOP                            │
  │   step 3  NOW the weight draw runs: random 0-99, 0-89 -> v1, 90-99 -> v2 │
  │   step 4  RULE 2's OWN bundle arms: up to 3 retries, 2s per try, 10s     │
  │           total -- a completely different budget than REQUEST A got      │
  │                                                                          │
  │ THE SYNTHESIS: match, weight, retries and timeout are NOT independent    │
  │ mesh-wide settings that blend together -- they are all bolted onto the   │
  │ SAME winning rule and travel as one bundle. A request inherits exactly   │
  │ one rule's whole bundle, never a mix of two rules' numbers. Misreading   │
  │ this (assuming 'the' timeout for a VirtualService) is the #1 reason a    │
  │ person debugging jobpost-api reads the wrong retries/timeout pair.       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  [CHAPTER 6 SPEED TIPS ⚡]
  ⚡ Weights don't need to sum to 100 — Envoy normalizes any ratio (9:1 is
     the same split as 90:10), so pick numbers that are easy to reason about
     under exam pressure, not numbers that merely add up cleanly
  ⚡ Memorize 6.12's formula cold: timeout ≥ (attempts + 1) × perTryTimeout —
     the exam will hand you numbers that look fine at a glance and fail it
  ⚡ Before debugging "my route never fires," check order first — a
     catch-all (no match: block) sitting above a specific rule is the #1
     cause, not a typo inside the match condition itself
  ⚡ fault: and retries:/timeout: on the SAME route silently disable each
     other per the docs — if you need both, use two VirtualServices, not one
  ⚡ Delete an app-level timeout (or size it generously above the mesh's)
     before trusting Istio's retries — a tighter app timeout races the mesh
     and wins before Envoy's retry ever gets a chance to help
  ⚡ Run istioctl analyze before kubectl apply — an undefined subset
     (missing DestinationRule) is a free catch that saves real exam minutes

  [CHAPTER 6 COMMANDS CHEAT-CARD]
  Every command below already appeared earlier in this chapter — grouped
  here as one reference:

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ COMMAND                                              WHAT IT DOES  SEC  │
  │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
  │ kubectl apply -f jobpost-api-vs.yaml -n anihpj       create/update  6.2 │
  │ kubectl get vs -n anihpj                             list VS (vs=  6.1  │
  │                                                       short name)       │
  │ kubectl describe vs jobpost-api-vs -n anihpj         see routes,   6.3  │
  │                                                       matches, wts      │
  │ kubectl delete -f jobpost-api-vs.yaml                remove a VS   6.11 │
  │                                                       (fault swap)      │
  │ istioctl analyze -n anihpj                           validate      6.3  │
  │                                                       before apply      │
  │ istioctl proxy-config route deploy/jobpost-api \     confirm the   6.6  │
  │   -n anihpj -o json | grep -A4 retryPolicy            live retries      │
  │ istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api \    count what   6.10 │
  │   -n anihpj | wc -l                                   this Envoy        │
  │                                                        can reach        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  [CHAPTER 6 PRACTICE DRILL 🧪 — 8 minutes, hands-on, live cluster]
  🧪 Build and verify a real jobpost-api-vs, right now:
  1. Write a VirtualService that sends 90% of jobpost-api traffic to subset
     v1 and 10% to subset v2 (reuse 6.3's YAML as your starting point)
  2. Add a header-based rule ABOVE the weighted rule: requests carrying
     x-user-type: premium always go to v2 — and confirm your rule ORDER
     follows 6.9 (the specific match sits before the weighted catch-all)
  3. Attach retries (attempts: 3, perTryTimeout: 2s, retryOn: 5xx) and a
     timeout to the weighted rule, then run 6.12's formula against your own
     numbers: does (attempts + 1) × perTryTimeout fit inside your timeout?
  4. kubectl apply -f jobpost-api-vs.yaml -n anihpj, then run istioctl
     proxy-config route deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -o json | grep -A4
     retryPolicy and confirm Envoy actually holds the numbers you wrote
  5. Break it on purpose — move the catch-all rule to the top — and watch
     your premium-header rule stop firing, then put the order back

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ CHAPTER 6 END-TO-END — one anihpj request's whole VirtualService life  │
  │                                                                        │
  │   REQUEST arrives for jobpost-api (VS already applied, 6.1-6.2)        │
  │           │                                                            │
  │           ▼                                                            │
  │   MATCH RULES walked top -> bottom, FIRST match wins (6.9)             │
  │      ├─ header x-user-type: premium?  -> subset v2  (A/B test, 6.4)    │
  │      ├─ uri prefix /jobs/ + weight draw -> 90% v1 / 10% v2 (6.3, 6.5)  │
  │      └─ no match -> catch-all v1                                       │
  │           │                                                            │
  │           ▼                                                            │
  │   THE WINNING RULE'S OWN resilience bundle arms (6.6, 6.7, 6.11, 6.12) │
  │      retries: N attempts @ perTryTimeout  |  timeout: total budget     │
  │      (a fault: block on this route disables retries/timeout instead,   │
  │       6.8 -- test faults on a SEPARATE VirtualService, never prod)     │
  │           │                                                            │
  │           ▼                                                            │
  │   HEADERS rewritten in flight (6.13); CORS preflight answered if the   │
  │   caller is a browser on another origin (6.14)                         │
  │           │                                                            │
  │           ▼                                                            │
  │   Envoy delivers to the chosen pod -- non-HTTP traffic (Postgres, a    │
  │   raw TLS endpoint) skips ALL of the above and uses the separate       │
  │   tcp:/tls: rule lists instead, matched by port or SNI only (6.15)     │
  │                                                                        │
  │   (running underneath everything: the Sidecar CRD, 6.10, already       │
  │    decided which destinations THIS Envoy was even told about)          │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  CAPTION: every arrow above is a decision this chapter taught you to make
  deliberately instead of by accident. A request is matched exactly once
  (6.1, 6.9), routed by weight, header, or path depending on which rule wins
  (6.2-6.5), handed the winning rule's OWN retry/timeout bundle rather than
  some mesh-wide default (6.6-6.7, 6.11-6.12), spared from testing tools
  bleeding into production traffic (6.8), optionally rewritten and
  CORS-annotated in flight (6.13-6.14), and — for traffic that was never
  HTTP to begin with — handled by a completely separate tcp:/tls: pipeline
  that ignores everything else in this list (6.15). Chapter 7 picks up
  exactly where this diagram's last arrow lands: once Envoy knows WHERE a
  request goes, DestinationRule decides HOW it actually gets there.

Chapter 7: DestinationRule — Traffic Policies and Load Balancing
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    Chapter 7 of 5-8 (Part 5: Traffic Management)  ·  Difficulty: 🟡 Intermediate
    ·  "VirtualService already picked subset: v2 — how does that chosen
    destination actually get reached, load-balanced, and protected?"
    🎯 ICA EXAM FOCUS — Traffic Management is 35% of the ICA exam (the
    single biggest domain); DestinationRule is one of its four named CRDs,
    graded on subsets, load balancing, circuit breaking, and connection pools.

    [WHY THIS MATTERS]
         Chapter 6's VirtualService can say "send 90% of /jobs/ traffic to
         subset: v1" all day, but that instruction means nothing until
         something defines what "subset: v1" actually IS and decides how a
         request reaches it once chosen — that something is this chapter's
         DestinationRule. Without it, jobpost-api's canary split has no pods
         to land on, user-service has no sticky-session guarantee for its
         per-user cache, and — most importantly — a single misbehaving
         auth-service pod has nothing stopping it from doing exactly what
         Chapter 1's cascade failure showed: blocking every caller's threads
         until all of anihpj goes down with it. DestinationRule's
         outlierDetection is the one setting in this entire guide that turns
         "one slow dependency takes down the whole system" into "one bad pod
         gets ejected in milliseconds while the rest of anihpj keeps
         serving." Every canary you will ever ship, and every circuit
         breaker anihpj ever trips in production, is configured right here.

    [LEARNING OBJECTIVES]
         ✅ Write a DestinationRule that defines subsets by Pod label,
            matching the names a VirtualService already routes to (7.1, 7.2)
         ✅ Choose the correct load-balancing algorithm — from all 7 real
            options, not just ROUND_ROBIN — for each anihpj service (7.3, 7.8)
         ✅ Configure outlierDetection so a failing pod is ejected, cooled
            off, and re-admitted automatically: CLOSED → OPEN → HALF-OPEN
            (7.4, 7.7)
         ✅ Size a connectionPool's TCP and HTTP limits to protect a slow
            service like skills-service from being overwhelmed (7.5, 7.10)
         ✅ Apply per-port and per-subset trafficPolicy overrides without
            silently losing your circuit breaker on one port (7.11, 7.12)
         ✅ Configure consistentHash session affinity by header, cookie, or
            source IP for services like user-service (7.13)
         ✅ Scope a DestinationRule to a single namespace with exportTo so
            an aggressive canary tuning never leaks mesh-wide (7.15)

    [EXAM / ICA RELEVANCE] 🎯
         DestinationRule is one of exactly four CRDs the Linux Foundation
         names by title under Domain 2 — Traffic Management (35% of the ICA
         exam, the single biggest domain): "Defining Traffic Policies with
         Destination Rules." The performance-based exam does not stop at
         "write one DestinationRule" — it grades whether you can also wire
         up a circuit breaker, pick the right load-balancing algorithm, and
         size a connection pool, often inside the SAME multi-step task that
         also touches Chapter 6's VirtualService.

         ┌───────────────────────────────────┬───────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┐
