    7.1  What is a DestinationRule?
         - DestinationRule defines POLICIES for traffic going to a specific service
         - Works AFTER VirtualService routing decides WHERE to send traffic
         - VirtualService = the "GPS route" (which road to take)
         - DestinationRule = the "driving rules" (speed limit, lane choice)
         - Defines: load balancing algorithm, connection pool size, circuit breaker,
           TLS mode, and named subsets (for canary routing)
         [VS + DR RELATIONSHIP DIAGRAM]

         [VIRTUALSERVICE + DESTINATIONRULE — how they work together]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                                                                    │
         │  REQUEST: GET /jobs/                                               │
         │            │                                                       │
         │            ▼                                                       │
         │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐                 │
         │  │  VirtualService: "WHERE should this go?"     │                 │
         │  │  → match /jobs/* → destination: jobpost-api  │                 │
         │  │  → weight: 90% → subset: v1                  │                 │
         │  │  → weight: 10% → subset: v2                  │                 │
         │  └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────┘                 │
         │                             │  "I chose subset: v1"               │
         │                             ▼                                      │
         │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐                 │
         │  │  DestinationRule: "HOW should we send it?"   │                 │
         │  │  → subset v1 = pods with version: v1 label   │                 │
         │  │  → loadBalancer: LEAST_CONN                  │                 │
         │  │  → tls: mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL                   │                 │
         │  │  → outlierDetection (circuit breaker):       │                 │
         │  │      consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5             │                 │
         │  └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────┘                 │
         │                             │                                      │
         │                ┌────────────┼──────────────┐                      │
         │                ▼            ▼              ▼                       │
         │          [pod:v1-1]   [pod:v1-2]   [pod:v1-3]                     │
         │          (least conn picks the one with fewest active connections) │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    7.2  Defining Subsets (Required for Canary)
         - Subsets link labels on Pods to route targets in VirtualService
         - subset: v1 → select Pods with label version: v1
         - subset: v2 → select Pods with label version: v2
         - VirtualService uses "subset: v1" names → DestinationRule resolves them

         🔧 UNDER THE HOOD: a subset doesn't create new Pods or new network
         paths — Istiod is already watching the Kubernetes Endpoints behind
         the jobpost-api Service. A subset's label selector is applied on
         top of that existing endpoint list, and the filtered result is
         pushed to every Envoy sidecar as an EDS (Endpoint Discovery
         Service) update. No pods match the label → EDS pushes an empty
         list to Envoy — which is exactly why the COMMON MISTAKE above
         produces 503s instead of a config error.
         [LABEL → SUBSET → VIRTUALSERVICE connection diagram]

         [SUBSET RESOLUTION — how labels on Pods connect to routing]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                                                                    │
         │  YOUR PODS:                        DESTINATIONRULE:               │
         │                                                                    │
         │  Pod jobpost-v1-abc   ──────────▶  subsets:                       │
         │    labels:                         - name: v1                     │
         │      app: jobpost-api               labels:                       │
         │      version: v1     ◀─ matches ──   version: v1                  │
         │                                                                    │
         │  Pod jobpost-v2-xyz   ──────────▶  - name: v2                     │
         │    labels:                           labels:                      │
         │      app: jobpost-api                  version: v2                 │
         │      version: v2     ◀─ matches ──                                │
         │                                                                    │
         │  VIRTUALSERVICE uses:              RESULT:                        │
         │    destination:                    Envoy sends to pods matching   │
         │      host: jobpost-api             the label selector for the     │
         │      subset: v1      ─────────────▶ chosen subset ✅              │
         │                                                                    │
         │  ⚠️  COMMON MISTAKE: If pods are missing the version label,       │
         │     the subset resolves to ZERO endpoints → 503 errors!           │
         │     Always add: labels: version: v1 to all your Deployments       │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    7.3  Load Balancing Algorithms
         - Default: ROUND_ROBIN (Kubernetes default, Envoy default)
         - LEAST_CONN: send to the pod with fewest active connections
         - RANDOM: random pod selection (surprisingly effective)
         - PASSTHROUGH: bypass Envoy load balancing
         - CONSISTENT_HASH: stick same user to same pod (session affinity)
           → anihpj use case: user-service sticky sessions by user ID header
         [ALGORITHM VISUALIZATION: traffic distribution comparison]

         [LOAD BALANCING ALGORITHMS — visual comparison]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  3 pods of user-service: [Pod A] [Pod B] [Pod C]                  │
         │  10 incoming requests numbered 1-10                                │
         │                                                                    │
         │  ROUND_ROBIN (default):                                            │
         │  1→A  2→B  3→C  4→A  5→B  6→C  7→A  8→B  9→C  10→A              │
         │  Each pod: ~3-4 requests. Fair, but ignores pod health/load       │
         │                                                                    │
         │  LEAST_CONN (recommended for anihpj):                             │
         │  Pod A: 2 active, Pod B: 0 active, Pod C: 5 active                │
         │  Next request → Pod B (fewest active connections)                  │
         │  Best for: variable-duration requests (some Django views are slow) │
         │                                                                    │
         │  RANDOM:                                                           │
         │  1→C  2→A  3→A  4→B  5→C  6→A  7→B  8→C  9→B  10→A              │
         │  Statistically uniform at scale. Simplest. Works well in practice │
         │                                                                    │
         │  CONSISTENT_HASH (by header):                                     │
         │  User 42 → always → Pod A (same session, warm cache)              │
         │  User 99 → always → Pod B                                         │
         │  User 7  → always → Pod C                                         │
         │  Best for: user-service with per-user caches                      │
         │                                                                    │
         │  CONSISTENT_HASH YAML for user-service:                           │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    trafficPolicy:                                                  │
         │      loadBalancer:                                                 │
         │        consistentHash:                                             │
         │          httpHeaderName: x-user-id  ← route by this header       │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [WHEN TO USE WHICH ALGORITHM — decision guide for anihpj]
         ┌────────────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
         │  Service           │  Algorithm    │  Why                         │
         ├────────────────────┼───────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤
         │  jobpost-api       │  LEAST_CONN   │  Mix of fast/slow views      │
         │  user-service      │  CONSISTENT   │  Per-user cache warmth       │
         │  skills-service    │  ROUND_ROBIN  │  Uniform stateless queries   │
         │  auth-service      │  RANDOM       │  Very fast, stateless        │
         │  search-service    │  LEAST_CONN   │  Variable search complexity  │
         └────────────────────┴───────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘

         - NAMING UPDATE: LEAST_CONN above is the legacy alias — modern
           Istio calls the same algorithm LEAST_REQUEST, and
           LEAST_REQUEST (not ROUND_ROBIN) is Istio's ACTUAL default
           when you configure no loadBalancer at all — istio.io
           documented this default by Istio 1.17, well before the v1
           API GA'd at Istio 1.22
         - Envoy's own default is ROUND_ROBIN — that is why older docs
           (and the first bullet above) call it "the default"; Istio
           overrides it per-cluster
         - Sticky sessions at scale get two extra algorithm choices,
           RING_HASH and MAGLEV → full 7-algorithm tour in section 7.8

    7.4  Circuit Breaking (Outlier Detection)
         - What is a circuit breaker? (borrowed from electrical engineering)
         - CLOSED: requests flow normally
         - OPEN: service is failing → Envoy STOPS sending requests to it
         - HALF-OPEN: after a pause, try again — if OK, close circuit
         - Configuration in DestinationRule: outlierDetection
           • consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5 → after 5 errors, eject host
           • interval: 30s → check every 30 seconds
           • baseEjectionTime: 30s → keep ejected for 30 seconds
           • maxEjectionPercent: 50 → never eject more than 50% of hosts
         - anihpj use case: if auth-service returns 5 consecutive 503s →
           stop sending requests, return error immediately, spare the service
         [CIRCUIT BREAKER STATE MACHINE DIAGRAM: Closed → Open → Half-Open]

         [CIRCUIT BREAKER STATE MACHINE]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                                                        │
         │  ┌─────────────┐   5 errors    ┌─────────────────┐    │
         │  │   CLOSED    │ ─────────────▶│     OPEN        │    │
         │  │             │               │                 │    │
         │  │  Requests   │               │ Requests fail   │    │
         │  │  flow ✅    │               │ immediately ❌  │    │
         │  │  Success    │               │ (saves service) │    │
         │  └─────────────┘               └────────┬────────┘    │
         │         ▲                               │              │
         │         │ test request             baseEjectionTime   │
         │         │ succeeds                      │              │
         │         │                     ┌─────────┴────────┐    │
         │         └─────────────────────│   HALF-OPEN      │    │
         │                               │                  │    │
         │                               │ Allow 1 test     │    │
         │                               │ request through  │    │
         │                               └──────────────────┘    │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    7.5  Connection Pool Settings
         - Control how many concurrent connections Envoy allows per service
         - HTTP settings: http1MaxPendingRequests, http2MaxRequests
         - TCP settings: maxConnections, connectTimeout
         - anihpj use case: limit skills-service to 100 concurrent connections
           (protect a slow service from being overwhelmed)

         🧠 ANALOGY. Think of skills-service's connection pool like a small
         coffee shop: maxConnections is the number of tables inside (a hard
         cap on how many customers are served at once), and
         http1MaxPendingRequests is the line forming outside the door. As
         long as there's room in that line, new customers wait their turn
         — but once the line itself is full, the shop turns people away at
         the door (a fast 503) instead of making them stand outside
         forever while skills-service quietly falls over.
         [YAML + DIAGRAM: connection pool as a queue with a max size]

         [CONNECTION POOL — visualizing request queuing]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  skills-service connection pool config:                            │
         │    connectionPool:                                                 │
         │      http:                                                         │
         │        http1MaxPendingRequests: 100   ← queue max                 │
         │        http2MaxRequests: 200           ← concurrent max           │
         │                                                                    │
         │  VISUAL:                                                           │
         │                                                                    │
         │  Incoming requests ──▶ [=====QUEUE=====|100 max|] ──▶ skills-svc  │
         │                                                                    │
         │  Scenario A (normal):  50 requests → queue at 50% — ✅ OK        │
         │  Scenario B (busy):   100 requests → queue FULL → 503 returned   │
         │  Scenario C (spike):  200 requests → 100 queued, 100 rejected    │
         │                                                                    │
         │  WHY THIS HELPS: Without limit, 1000 requests queue up in Envoy  │
         │  consuming memory until skills-svc falls over entirely.            │
         │  With limit: 100 get served, rest get fast 503 → caller can retry │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    7.7  Deep Dive — Circuit Breaker States: CLOSED → OPEN → HALF-OPEN
         - DEFINITION: a circuit breaker is a per-pod health switch inside
           Envoy — it counts failures for every backend pod and "trips"
           (stops sending that pod traffic) once failures cross a threshold

         📖 KEY TERM
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ outlierDetection = Istio's config field name for what        │
         │ this chapter calls a "circuit breaker." Same mechanism,      │
         │ two names: docs say circuit breaker, the YAML field is       │
         │ outlierDetection — the ICA exam expects you to know both.    │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         - Why it matters: without one, every caller keeps hammering a
           dying pod → requests queue behind it → caller threads block →
           the failure CASCADES upstream:
           • one sick auth-service pod → jobpost-api workers stuck waiting
           • jobpost-api runs out of workers → ALL of anihpj goes down
         - How it works: Envoy's outlierDetection analysis runs every
           interval (30s here), ejects pods that crossed the error
           threshold, and re-admits them after a cooling-off period — the
           classic CLOSED → OPEN → HALF-OPEN breaker pattern
         - The canonical anihpj parameters — identical in EVERY example in
           this chapter, memorize them once:
           • consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5 → trip after 5 straight failures
           • interval: 30s → the error-analysis sweep runs every 30 seconds
           • baseEjectionTime: 30s → the first ejection lasts 30 seconds
           • maxEjectionPercent: 50 → at most half the pool ejected at once
         - Repeat offenders sit out longer: ejection time =
           baseEjectionTime × times-ejected (30s → 60s → 90s → ...)
         - Envoy reality check: there is no literal probe request — in
           HALF-OPEN the pod simply rejoins the pool and the next few REAL
           requests are the probe; 5 more errors send it straight back

         [CIRCUIT BREAKER STATE MACHINE — transitions & canonical params]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  STATE 1: CLOSED   (normal — pod is in the load-balancing pool)    │
         │    • every request is forwarded; Envoy counts errors per pod       │
         │    • consecutive-error counter: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 = threshold!     │
         │    • any single success resets the counter back to 0               │
         │             │                                                      │
         │             │  TRIP CONDITION: consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5         │
         │             │  (5 straight 502/503/504 or TCP connect failures)    │
         │             ▼                                                      │
         │  STATE 2: OPEN     (tripped — pod EJECTED from the pool)           │
         │    • Envoy sends this pod NOTHING; remaining pods take over        │
         │    • callers never block on the sick pod → no cascade upstream     │
         │    • guard rail: maxEjectionPercent: 50 → with 4 pods, at most     │
         │      2 are ever OPEN at once — 2 always keep serving               │
         │             │                                                      │
         │             │  COOL-OFF: baseEjectionTime: 30s expires             │
         │             │  (2nd ejection waits 60s, 3rd waits 90s, ...)        │
         │             ▼                                                      │
         │  STATE 3: HALF-OPEN (probation — pod quietly re-admitted)          │
         │    • pod rejoins the pool; live traffic is the probe               │
         │    • requests succeed → error count stays 0 → back to CLOSED ✅     │
         │    • 5 more failures → re-ejected → back to OPEN, for longer ❌     │
         │                                                                    │
         │  Sweep cadence: the outlier analysis runs every interval: 30s      │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [OUTLIER DETECTION TUNING TABLE — meaning, defaults, symptoms]
         ┌────────────────────┬────────────────────┬──────┬───────────────────┐
         │ Field              │ Meaning            │ Safe │ Symptom if wrong  │
         ├────────────────────┼────────────────────┼──────┼───────────────────┤
         │ consecutiveGateway │ 502/503/504 + TCP  │ 5    │ 1-2: pods flap on │
         │ Errors             │ connect failures   │      │ one blip; 50: it  │
         │                    │ count toward trip  │      │ never trips at all│
         ├────────────────────┼────────────────────┼──────┼───────────────────┤
         │ consecutive5xx     │ app 5xx only; TCP  │ (off)│ conn-refused pod  │
         │ Errors             │ failures are NOT   │      │ is never ejected  │
         │                    │ counted            │      │                   │
         ├────────────────────┼────────────────────┼──────┼───────────────────┤
         │ interval           │ how often the      │ 30s  │ 300s: a sick pod  │
         │                    │ ejection analysis  │      │ serves errors for │
         │                    │ sweep runs         │      │ 5 whole minutes   │
         ├────────────────────┼────────────────────┼──────┼───────────────────┤
         │ baseEjectionTime   │ length of the 1st  │ 30s  │ 1h: capacity stays│
         │                    │ ejection (x2, x3   │      │ down long after   │
         │                    │ ... on repeats)    │      │ the pod recovers  │
         ├────────────────────┼────────────────────┼──────┼───────────────────┤
         │ maxEjectionPercent │ cap on % of pool   │ 50   │ 100: breaker can  │
         │                    │ ejected at the     │      │ eject EVERY pod = │
         │                    │ same time          │      │ self-made outage  │
         ├────────────────────┼────────────────────┼──────┼───────────────────┤
         │ minHealthPercent   │ below this healthy │ 0    │ set high on small │
         │                    │ %, ejection is     │ (off)│ pools: ejection   │
         │                    │ suspended entirely │      │ quietly disables  │
         └────────────────────┴────────────────────┴──────┴───────────────────┘

         [REAL SCENARIO TIMELINE — skills-service bad deploy vs the breaker]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Fleet: 4 skills-service pods behind :8090; mesh baseline          │
         │  847 req/s, 2.1% errors, p99 234ms. Pod 3 ships a bad deploy.      │
         │                                                                    │
         │  T=0s     pod 3 starts timing out; service-wide numbers hit        │
         │           8.1% errors / p99 1240ms — dashboards go red             │
         │  T=4s     pod 3 returns its 5th consecutive 503                    │
         │           → circuit OPENS: pod 3 ejected (1/4 = 25% ≤ 50% cap)     │
         │  T=4-34s  3 healthy pods absorb the load; caller-visible           │
         │           errors drop back under 1%                                │
         │  T=34s    baseEjectionTime: 30s expires → HALF-OPEN:               │
         │           pod 3 re-admitted, live requests probe it                │
         │  T=35s    still broken → 5 fast failures → OPEN again              │
         │           (2nd ejection = 60s this time)                           │
         │  T=95s    the bad deploy is rolled back; pod 3 restarts clean      │
         │  T=97s    probes succeed → CLOSED ★ users never saw an outage      │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    7.8  Load Balancing — All 7 Algorithms and the Decision Guide
         - DEFINITION: the load-balancing algorithm is the rule Envoy uses
           to pick WHICH pod gets each request, AFTER VirtualService
           routing and DestinationRule subset selection narrowed the pool
         - Why it matters: the right algorithm hides slow pods, keeps
           caches warm, and survives scaling events; the wrong one sends
           your longest Django queries to the busiest pod
         - Naming update: LEAST_CONN is a DEPRECATED alias — the current
           name is LEAST_REQUEST, and LEAST_REQUEST (not ROUND_ROBIN) is
           Istio's ACTUAL default when nothing is set — istio.io
           documented this default by Istio 1.17, well before the v1
           API GA'd at Istio 1.22
         - How LEAST_REQUEST picks: "power of two choices" — sample 2
           random pods, send to the one with fewer active requests;
           near-optimal spread at a fraction of the bookkeeping cost
         - RING_HASH and MAGLEV are not standalone simple: values — they
           are the two hash implementations selectable UNDER
           consistentHash (ketama ring vs Google's Maglev lookup table)

         [ALL 7 LOAD BALANCING ALGORITHMS — the complete Istio menu]
         ┌─────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┬────────────┐
         │ Algorithm       │ How it picks the pod                │ Sticky?    │
         ├─────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
         │ ROUND_ROBIN     │ each pod in turn: 1 → 2 → 3 → 1 ... │ no         │
         ├─────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
         │ LEAST_REQUEST   │ P2C: sample 2 random pods, send to  │ no         │
         │ (THE DEFAULT)   │ the one with fewer active requests  │            │
         ├─────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
         │ RANDOM          │ any pod, uniformly at random        │ no         │
         ├─────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
         │ PASSTHROUGH     │ no LB — connect to the original IP  │ n/a        │
         │                 │ the client itself resolved          │            │
         ├─────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
         │ CONSISTENT_HASH │ hash a request key (header, cookie, │ YES        │
         │                 │ source IP, query param) → same pod  │            │
         ├─────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
         │ RING_HASH       │ consistent-hash impl #1: ketama     │ YES        │
         │ (under c-hash)  │ ring; ~1/N keys move on scaling     │            │
         ├─────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
         │ MAGLEV          │ consistent-hash impl #2: O(1) table │ YES        │
         │ (under c-hash)  │ lookup; evenest spread, big pools   │            │
         └─────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────┴────────────┘

         [LB DECISION TREE — pick your algorithm in 4 questions]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Q1: Must the same user/key always land on the same pod?           │
         │      YES → CONSISTENT_HASH on a key (header/cookie/source IP)      │
         │            • medium pool, minimal churn on scale → RING_HASH       │
         │            • large pool, fastest + evenest spread → MAGLEV         │
         │      NO ↓                                                          │
         │  Q2: Do request durations vary a lot? (slow Django views,          │
         │      complex searches mixed with quick lookups)                    │
         │      YES → LEAST_REQUEST — the default; you may set nothing        │
         │      NO ↓                                                          │
         │  Q3: Uniform + stateless, want strict predictable fairness?        │
         │      YES → ROUND_ROBIN        NO → RANDOM (cheapest of all)        │
         │  Q4: Client does its own load balancing (smart gRPC client)?       │
         │      YES → PASSTHROUGH — Envoy steps aside entirely                │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [ANIHPJ LB GUIDE — service-by-service, reaffirming the 7.3 picks]
         ┌───────────────────────┬─────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
         │ Service               │ Algorithm       │ Why                      │
         ├───────────────────────┼─────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
         │ jobpost-api :8000     │ LEAST_REQUEST   │ fast + slow Django views │
         │ user-service :8080    │ CONSISTENT_HASH │ per-user cache warmth —  │
         │                       │ (x-user-id)     │ same user → same pod     │
         │ skills-service :8090  │ ROUND_ROBIN     │ uniform stateless reads  │
         │ location-service :8070│ ROUND_ROBIN     │ uniform geo lookups      │
         │ auth-service          │ RANDOM          │ tiny, fast, stateless    │
         │ search-service        │ LEAST_REQUEST   │ query cost varies wildly │
         │ notification-service  │ ROUND_ROBIN     │ fire-and-forget fan-out  │
         └───────────────────────┴─────────────────┴──────────────────────────┘

         - Same picks as section 7.3 — only the spelling is modern:
           LEAST_CONN (legacy alias) → LEAST_REQUEST (current name)

         [ANNOTATED YAML — modern LB config, apiVersion v1 (Istio 1.22+)]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1    ← v1 since Istio 1.22       │
         │  kind: DestinationRule                                             │
         │  metadata:                                                         │
         │    name: search-service-lb                                         │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                               │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    host: search-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local                   │
         │    trafficPolicy:                                                  │
         │      loadBalancer:                                                 │
         │        simple: LEAST_REQUEST      ← modern name for LEAST_CONN     │
         │  ---                                                               │
         │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                                │
         │  kind: DestinationRule                                             │
         │  metadata:                                                         │
         │    name: user-service-lb                                           │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                               │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    host: user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local                     │
         │    trafficPolicy:                                                  │
         │      loadBalancer:                                                 │
         │        consistentHash:                                             │
         │          httpHeaderName: x-user-id   ← the hash key                │
         │          maglev:                                                   │
         │            tableSize: 65537   ← prime; bigger = smoother spread    │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [VERIFY — which algorithm is Envoy really using?]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  $ istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj \    │
         │      --fqdn user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local -o json \        │
         │      | grep -i lbPolicy                                            │
         │  "lbPolicy": "MAGLEV"     ← the DestinationRule took effect ✅      │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    7.9  Deep Dive — Locality Load Balancing: Region → Zone → Sub-Zone Failover
         - DEFINITION: locality load balancing makes Envoy prefer backend
           pods that are topologically CLOSE to the caller (same zone) and
           spill over to farther pods only when the close ones fail
         - Why it matters (milliseconds AND money): every major cloud
           bills cross-zone traffic, and a same-zone hop is far faster
           than a cross-zone one — at anihpj's 847 req/s peak that is both
           a latency win and a real invoice line
         - Where the location comes from: Kubernetes NODE labels — Istiod
           reads them and stamps every endpoint with a locality string
           "region/zone/subzone"
         - Two modes inside localityLbSetting (mutually exclusive):
           • distribute → YOU set the traffic split per origin locality
           • failover   → Envoy keeps 100% in-zone until pods fail, then
             walks outward: sub-zone → zone → region → anywhere
         - HARD REQUIREMENT ⚠️: locality LB only activates when the same
           DestinationRule ALSO configures outlierDetection — with no
           health signal Envoy cannot know when to fail over, and Istio
           silently ignores your locality settings

         [TOPOLOGY LABEL HIERARCHY — how a pod learns where it lives]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  NODE labels (set by the cloud provider or cluster admin):         │
         │                                                                    │
         │  topology.kubernetes.io/region: eu-west-1        ← REGION          │
         │     │    "which geography" (Dublin)                                │
         │     └──▶ topology.kubernetes.io/zone: eu-west-1a ← ZONE            │
         │             │    "which datacenter building"                       │
         │             └──▶ topology.istio.io/subzone: rack7 ← SUB-ZONE       │
         │                     "which rack/cell" — Istio-only, optional       │
         │                                                                    │
         │  → Istiod stamps every endpoint: "eu-west-1/eu-west-1a/rack7"      │
         │                                                                    │
         │  PREFERENCE ORDER for a caller in eu-west-1/eu-west-1a/rack7:      │
         │  1. same sub-zone  eu-west-1/eu-west-1a/rack7  (fastest, free)     │
         │  2. same zone      eu-west-1/eu-west-1a/*                          │
         │  3. same region    eu-west-1/*                 ($ cross-zone)      │
         │  4. anywhere       *                           ($$ cross-region)   │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [ANNOTATED YAML — localityLbSetting.distribute for skills-service]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                                │
         │  kind: DestinationRule                                             │
         │  metadata:                                                         │
         │    name: skills-service-locality                                   │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                               │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    host: skills-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local                   │
         │    trafficPolicy:                                                  │
         │      loadBalancer:                                                 │
         │        simple: ROUND_ROBIN        ← 7.3 / 7.8 choice kept          │
         │        localityLbSetting:                                          │
         │          enabled: true                                             │
         │          distribute:              ← weighted-spread mode           │
         │          - from: eu-west-1/eu-west-1a/*  ← callers in zone 1a      │
         │            to:                                                     │
         │              "eu-west-1/eu-west-1a/*": 70  ← keep 70% in-zone      │
         │              "eu-west-1/eu-west-1b/*": 20                          │
         │              "eu-west-1/eu-west-1c/*": 10                          │
         │      outlierDetection:            ← REQUIRED — without this        │
         │        consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5     block, the locality         │
         │        interval: 30s                   settings are silently       │
         │        baseEjectionTime: 30s           IGNORED by Istio            │
         │        maxEjectionPercent: 50                                      │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [THE SILENT TRAP — no outlierDetection means NO failover]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Setup: skills-service pods in 3 zones; callers in eu-west-1a.     │
         │  At T=0 every skills-service pod in zone 1a crashes.               │
         │                                                                    │
         │  WITH outlierDetection (correct config):                           │
         │  T=0s    1a pods begin failing — 8.1% errors, p99 1240ms           │
         │  T=~5s   5 consecutive gateway errors → 1a pods ejected            │
         │  T=5s+   locality failover: traffic shifts to 1b / 1c pods ✅       │
         │  T=35s   HALF-OPEN probes keep checking zone 1a for recovery       │
         │                                                                    │
         │  WITHOUT outlierDetection (the trap):                              │
         │  T=0s    1a pods begin failing                                     │
         │  T=∞     Envoy has NO health signal → keeps preferring the         │
         │          local, DEAD zone → hard errors until a human acts ❌       │
         │                                                                    │
         │  RULE: every DestinationRule that enables localityLbSetting        │
         │  MUST also carry the canonical outlierDetection block (7.4).       │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Rollout tip: start with failover mode (nothing to maintain),
           switch to distribute only when you need cost-shaping
           percentages per zone


    7.10  Connection Pool — The Complete Field Reference
         - DEFINITION: connectionPool has exactly two sub-blocks — tcp
           (TCPSettings) and http (HTTPSettings) — 7.5 introduced only 4
           of the real 13 fields; this section completes the reference
         - Why it matters: the fields 7.5 skipped are exactly the ones
           that bite in production — maxRequestsPerConnection controls
           HTTP keep-alive recycling, idleTimeout silently closes
           connections Envoy thinks are dead, h2UpgradePolicy decides
           whether Envoy-to-backend traffic gets promoted to HTTP/2
         - How it works: every field you don't set falls back to its own
           Istio/Envoy default below — connectionPool ships permissive
           (near-unlimited) until you deliberately tighten it

         [CAPTION: TCPSettings — the complete field list]
         ┌──────────────────────┬────────┬────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ Field                │ Default│ What it controls                   │
         ├──────────────────────┼────────┼────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ maxConnections       │ 2^32-1 │ hard cap on HTTP/1.1 + TCP conns   │
         │ connectTimeout       │ 10s    │ TCP handshake timeout to backend   │
         │ tcpKeepalive         │ (unset)│ SO_KEEPALIVE: probes/time/interval │
         │ maxConnectionDuration│ (unset)│ force-close a conn after this long │
         │ idleTimeout          │ 1 hour │ close idle conn; 0s = disabled     │
         └──────────────────────┴────────┴────────────────────────────────────┘

         [CAPTION: HTTPSettings — the complete field list]
         ┌──────────────────────────┬─────────────┬───────────────────────────┐
         │ Field                    │ Default     │ What it controls          │
         ├──────────────────────────┼─────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
         │ http1MaxPendingRequests  │ 2^32-1      │ pending-req queue depth   │
         │ http2MaxRequests         │ 2^32-1      │ max active HTTP/2 reqs    │
         │ maxRequestsPerConnection │ 0 (max 2^29)│ reqs/conn before recycle  │
         │ maxRetries               │ 2^32-1      │ max retries in flight     │
         │ idleTimeout              │ 1 hour      │ idle conn-pool timeout    │
         │ h2UpgradePolicy          │ DEFAULT     │ h1→h2 upgrade policy      │
         │ useClientProtocol        │ false       │ mirrors client protocol   │
         │ maxConcurrentStreams     │ 2^31-1      │ HTTP/2 streams per conn   │
         └──────────────────────────┴─────────────┴───────────────────────────┘

         - maxRequestsPerConnection: 1 is the one field that fully
           DISABLES HTTP keep-alive — every request gets a brand-new TCP
           connection; only worth it for legacy backends that can't
           multiplex, expensive (extra handshakes) everywhere else
         - tcpKeepalive has its own probes/time/interval sub-fields; when
           left unset, Envoy inherits whatever the OS-level socket
           defaults are (commonly probes: 9, time: 7200s, interval: 75s
           on Linux) — set it explicitly to detect a dead backend faster
           than a 2-hour OS default

    7.11  portLevelSettings — Per-Port Traffic Policy Overrides
         - DEFINITION: portLevelSettings lets ONE DestinationRule apply
           different loadBalancer / connectionPool / outlierDetection /
           tls settings to different ports on the SAME host — the
           top-level trafficPolicy becomes the fallback for any port not
           explicitly listed
         - Why it matters: a real anihpj service often exposes more than
           one port — search-service serves REST on :8080 and an
           internal gRPC API on :9090; those two ports have completely
           different traffic shapes and deserve different tuning, not
           one-size-fits-all
         - How it works — the CRITICAL gotcha: unlike subset-level
           trafficPolicy (7.12), portLevelSettings does NOT inherit from
           the destination-level trafficPolicy — it is a full replacement.
           Any field you omit on a port falls back to Istio's own default,
           NOT to the value you set at the top level

         [CAPTION: portLevelSettings — per-port override, and the trap]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                                │
         │  kind: DestinationRule                                             │
         │  metadata:                                                         │
         │    name: search-service-ports                                      │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                               │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    host: search-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local                   │
         │    trafficPolicy:                    ← fallback for any port below │
         │      loadBalancer:                                                 │
         │        simple: LEAST_REQUEST                                       │
         │      outlierDetection:                                             │
         │        consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5                                 │
         │        interval: 30s                                               │
         │        baseEjectionTime: 30s                                       │
         │        maxEjectionPercent: 50                                      │
         │      portLevelSettings:                                            │
         │      - port:                                                       │
         │          number: 8080             ← REST API port                  │
         │        loadBalancer:                                               │
         │          simple: ROUND_ROBIN      ← overrides the fallback above   │
         │        connectionPool:                                             │
         │          http:                                                     │
         │            http1MaxPendingRequests: 50                             │
         │        # ⚠ outlierDetection is NOT inherited by ports below —      │
         │        #   reverts to OFF (Istio default) for port 8080            │
         │      - port:                                                       │
         │          number: 9090             ← internal gRPC port             │
         │        connectionPool:                                             │
         │          http:                                                     │
         │            h2UpgradePolicy: UPGRADE                                │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [CAPTION: inheritance rules — portLevelSettings vs subset trafficPolicy]
         ┌─────────────────────┬──────────────────┬───────────────────────────┐
         │ Scope               │ Inherits parent? │ Gotcha                    │
         ├─────────────────────┼──────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
         │ subset trafficPolicy│ YES - field merge│ only sets it overrides    │
         │ portLevelSettings   │ NO - full replace│ omitted = Istio default   │
         └─────────────────────┴──────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘

         - Rule of thumb: if you add portLevelSettings for ONE field
           (say, just loadBalancer), copy the rest of the top-level
           trafficPolicy block into it too — otherwise you silently lose
           your circuit breaker and connection pool limits on that port

    7.12  Subset-Level trafficPolicy — Per-Subset Overrides
         - DEFINITION: a subset (7.2) can carry its OWN trafficPolicy
           block; subsets INHERIT the destination-level trafficPolicy and
           the subset's own fields MERGE over it, overriding only what
           they explicitly set — the opposite inheritance model from
           portLevelSettings (7.11)
         - Why it matters: an untested v2 canary should not get the same
           trust as the stable v1 — a canary deserves a smaller
           connection pool (limit its blast radius) and a faster-tripping
           circuit breaker (its own bugs shouldn't need 5 strikes to
           notice)
         - How it works: Envoy builds one cluster per subset; each
           cluster starts from the destination-level trafficPolicy, then
           applies the subset's trafficPolicy fields on top

         [CAPTION: subset trafficPolicy — v1 inherits, v2 overrides]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                                │
         │  kind: DestinationRule                                             │
         │  metadata:                                                         │
         │    name: jobpost-api-dr                                            │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                               │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    host: jobpost-api                                               │
         │    trafficPolicy:                ← baseline, applies to ALL subsets│
         │      loadBalancer:                                                 │
         │        simple: LEAST_REQUEST                                       │
         │      outlierDetection:                                             │
         │        consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5                                 │
         │        interval: 30s                                               │
         │        baseEjectionTime: 30s                                       │
         │        maxEjectionPercent: 50                                      │
         │    subsets:                                                        │
         │    - name: v1                                                      │
         │      labels:                                                       │
         │        version: v1              ← no override: uses baseline as-is │
         │    - name: v2                                                      │
         │      labels:                                                       │
         │        version: v2                                                 │
         │      trafficPolicy:                ← MERGES over the baseline above│
         │        connectionPool:                                             │
         │          http:                                                     │
         │            http1MaxPendingRequests: 10  ← canary: throttle harder  │
         │        outlierDetection:                                           │
         │          consecutiveGatewayErrors: 2    ← canary: trip 5x faster   │
         │          interval: 10s                                             │
         │          baseEjectionTime: 30s                                     │
         │          maxEjectionPercent: 100      ← ok to eject all of a canary│
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - v2's outlierDetection block above replaces the baseline
           outlierDetection wholesale (all 4 fields must be re-specified
           together) — Istio merges at the FIELD level between
           trafficPolicy blocks, not by mixing individual sibling values
           from two different outlierDetection objects

    7.13  consistentHash — The Complete Field Reference
         - DEFINITION: every field below lives under
           trafficPolicy.loadBalancer.consistentHash (or its nested
           ringHash / maglev sub-message) — 7.3 and 7.8 showed
           httpHeaderName and maglev.tableSize; four more real fields
           exist and are exam-relevant
         - Why it matters: httpHeaderName only works when the CALLER
           already sends a stable header — for browser traffic with no
           custom headers, httpCookie or useSourceIp are the practical
           choices for the same sticky-session outcome
         - How it works: whichever key field you set (header, cookie,
           source IP, or query param) is fed into the SAME ring-hash or
           Maglev table selected by consistentHash's ringHash/maglev
           sub-message — the key source and the hash algorithm are
           independent choices

         [CAPTION: ConsistentHashLB — every field]
         ┌──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┬──────────┐
         │ Field                    │ Meaning                      │ Default  │
         ├──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┼──────────┤
         │ httpHeaderName           │ hash one HTTP header value   │ -        │
         │ httpCookie               │ mint/read a session cookie   │ -        │
         │ useSourceIp              │ hash the caller's source IP  │ false    │
         │ httpQueryParameterName   │ hash one URL query param     │ -        │
         │ ringHash.minimumRingSize │ ketama ring size             │ 1024     │
         │ maglev.tableSize         │ lookup table size (prime)    │ 65537    │
         └──────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┴──────────┘

         [CAPTION: httpCookie — session affinity with no custom header]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                                │
         │  kind: DestinationRule                                             │
         │  metadata:                                                         │
         │    name: user-service-cookie-affinity                              │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                               │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    host: user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local                     │
         │    trafficPolicy:                                                  │
         │      loadBalancer:                                                 │
         │        consistentHash:                                             │
         │          httpCookie:                                               │
         │            name: anihpj-session   ← Envoy MINTS this if not present│
         │            path: /                                                 │
         │            ttl: 3600s             ← cookie lifetime = 1 hour       │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Unlike httpHeaderName (which only reads a header the client
           already sends), httpCookie is special: if the browser has no
           cookie yet, ENVOY ITSELF sets one on the response — the very
           next request from that browser is then sticky, no client
           changes required

    7.14  TunnelSettings — Tunneling TCP/TLS Through a Proxy
         - DEFINITION: trafficPolicy.tunnel wraps outbound TCP or TLS
           traffic inside an HTTP CONNECT (or POST) tunnel toward an
           intermediate proxy before it reaches the real destination —
           an advanced, low-frequency field but a real, documented part
           of DestinationRule
         - Why it matters: some anihpj partner integrations only accept
           connections that arrive through a corporate forward proxy
           (firewall allow-listing, audit logging at the proxy) — tunnel
           lets Envoy speak to that proxy without the application ever
           knowing a proxy is involved
         - How it works: Envoy opens a connection to targetHost:targetPort
           (the intermediate proxy), issues an HTTP CONNECT (or POST) to
           establish the tunnel, then relays the original TCP/TLS bytes
           through it — usable ONLY on TCP or TLS routes, never on HTTP
           routes

         [CAPTION: tunnel — routing through an intermediate proxy]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                                │
         │  kind: DestinationRule                                             │
         │  metadata:                                                         │
         │    name: legacy-proxy-tunnel                                       │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                               │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    host: legacy-mainframe.partner.internal                         │
         │    trafficPolicy:                                                  │
         │      tunnel:                                                       │
         │        protocol: CONNECT       ← wrap traffic in an HTTP CONNECT   │
         │        targetHost: proxy.partner.internal                          │
         │        targetPort: 3128        ← the intermediate proxy's port     │
         │                                                                    │
         │    # tunnel: valid on TCP/TLS routes only — not usable for HTTP    │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - protocol accepts CONNECT (the standard HTTP proxy tunnel
           method) or POST (for proxies that only forward POST bodies);
           targetHost and targetPort are both required — they identify
           the intermediate proxy itself, not the final backend

    7.15  exportTo — Scoping a DestinationRule Across Namespaces
         - DEFINITION: exportTo controls which namespaces can SEE and USE
           this DestinationRule; the default (when omitted) is "*" —
           exported to every namespace in the mesh, exactly like the
           exportTo behavior already introduced for ServiceEntry (8.1+)
         - Why it matters: in a multi-team anihpj-style cluster, a
           DestinationRule with aggressive tuning (say, a canary's
           throttled connectionPool from 7.12) written for one team's
           testing should not silently apply everywhere that host is
           reachable from — exportTo is the fix
         - How it works: Istiod filters which proxies receive this
           DestinationRule's config based on exportTo — proxies outside
           the allowed namespaces never see it, so their traffic to the
           same host falls back to Istio's defaults

         [CAPTION: exportTo — keep a DestinationRule private to anihpj]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                                │
         │  kind: DestinationRule                                             │
         │  metadata:                                                         │
         │    name: jobpost-api-dr                                            │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                               │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    host: jobpost-api                                               │
         │    exportTo:                                                       │
         │    - "."                      ← visible ONLY inside anihpj         │
         │    trafficPolicy:                                                  │
         │      loadBalancer:                                                 │
         │        simple: LEAST_REQUEST                                       │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [CAPTION: exportTo values — who can see this DestinationRule]
         ┌─────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ exportTo value          │ Visible from                             │
         ├─────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ "*"  (the default)      │ every namespace in the mesh              │
         │ "."                     │ only the DR's own namespace              │
         │ ["team-a","team-b"]     │ only the namespaces listed               │
         └─────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Same rule applies to VirtualService and ServiceEntry — exportTo
           is a mesh-wide visibility mechanism, not a DestinationRule-only
           feature; anihpj's convention is exportTo: ["."] on every
           team-owned DestinationRule unless cross-namespace sharing is a
           deliberate, documented decision

    [UNDER THE HOOD 🔧 — One Request, Three Resources Cooperating]
         7.7 walked through the circuit breaker alone; 7.9 walked through
         locality failover alone. In production, anihpj's resources never
         act alone — a single request routinely exercises a VirtualService's
         subset choice, a DestinationRule's label resolution, AND a
         completely different service's circuit breaker, all in the same
         few milliseconds. Here is what that looks like end to end.

         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ ONE REQUEST, THREE RESOURCES — POST /jobs/42/apply under partial failure│
         │                                                                         │
         │ (1) VirtualService jobpost-api-vs (Ch6) matches POST /jobs/*/apply,     │
         │     rolls the canary weight, and this time picks subset: v2 (10% slice) │
         │              │                                                          │
         │              ▼                                                          │
         │ (2) DestinationRule jobpost-api-dr (7.2) resolves subset v2 = pods      │
         │     labeled version: v2, then loadBalancer: LEAST_REQUEST (7.3/7.8)     │
         │     picks pod jobpost-api-v2-7f8 out of that pool                       │
         │              │                                                          │
         │              ▼                                                          │
         │ (3) jobpost-api-v2-7f8's own code calls auth-service to check the       │
         │     caller's session token — a second, independent Envoy hop            │
         │              │                                                          │
         │              ▼                                                          │
         │ (4) auth-service's DestinationRule already tripped ITS OWN              │
         │     outlierDetection 40s ago: pod auth-3 hit consecutiveGatewayErrors:  │
         │     5 and sits EJECTED / OPEN (7.4, 7.7) — auth-3 is NOT in the pool    │
         │              │                                                          │
         │              ▼                                                          │
         │ (5) LEAST_REQUEST can only choose among the 3 healthy auth-service      │
         │     pods — request lands on auth-1, succeeds in 40ms                    │
         │              │                                                          │
         │              ▼                                                          │
         │ (6) jobpost-api-v2-7f8 returns 201 Created. The caller never learns     │
         │     auth-3 exists, is unhealthy, or was ever a candidate at all         │
         │                                                                         │
         │ WHAT JUST COOPERATED: VirtualService chose a subset by NAME, the        │
         │ DestinationRule turned that name into real PODS and picked one, and a   │
         │ completely separate DestinationRule's circuit breaker had already       │
         │ pre-filtered a THIRD service's pool before this request ever arrived.   │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ WITHOUT outlierDetection on auth-service │ WITH outlierDetection (this chapter's config) │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ auth-3 stays in the LB pool while sick   │ auth-3 ejected after 5 gateway errors (7.4)   │
         │ ~1-in-4 requests still routed to auth-3  │ 0-in-4 requests routed to auth-3              │
         │ caller blocks for connectTimeout (7.10)  │ caller never notices auth-3 exists            │
         │ VS retry (Ch6) doubles latency, or fails │ p99 latency unaffected by the sick pod        │
         │ enough pile-up reproduces Ch1's cascade  │ rest of anihpj stays fully served             │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    [SPEED TIPS ⚡]
         ⚡ Name subsets identically to how VirtualService references them —
            a typo'd subset: v2 vs subset: V2 resolves to zero endpoints,
            not an error message
         ⚡ Start outlierDetection with the canonical anihpj values (5 / 30s /
            30s / 50%) from 7.4 and only tune from there — inventing numbers
            under exam time pressure wastes minutes
         ⚡ Remember portLevelSettings does NOT inherit (7.11) — if you add
            it for one field, copy the whole trafficPolicy block in with it
         ⚡ On the exam, istioctl analyze catches a broken subset label
            reference before you waste time debugging a 503 by hand
         ⚡ Reach for LEAST_REQUEST by doing nothing — it is Istio's real
            default (7.8); only write loadBalancer when you need something
            else
         ⚡ If locality LB (7.9) "isn't working," check outlierDetection
            first — without it, Istio silently ignores localityLbSetting

    [COMMANDS CHEAT-CARD 🔑]
         ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ Command                                                           │ What it shows / does                                       │
         ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ kubectl apply -f jobpost-api-dr.yaml -n anihpj                    │ create/update the DestinationRule                          │
         │ kubectl get destinationrule -n anihpj                             │ list every DestinationRule in the namespace                │
         │ kubectl describe destinationrule jobpost-api-dr -n anihpj         │ resolved subsets, trafficPolicy, Istiod events             │
         │ kubectl get pods -n anihpj --show-labels                          │ confirm pods carry version: v1/v2 (7.2's #1 mistake)       │
         │ istioctl analyze -n anihpj                                        │ catch a broken subset reference before you apply it        │
         │ istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj \      │                                                            │
         │     --fqdn user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local -o json \        │                                                            │
         │     | grep -i lbPolicy                                            │ confirm which LB algorithm Envoy is really running (7.8)   │
         │ kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/jobpost-api -c istio-proxy -- \     │                                                            │
         │     pilot-agent request GET clusters | grep -A1 outlier_detection │ live ejection counters for the circuit breaker (7.4/7.7)   │
         │ istioctl proxy-status                                             │ confirm the DestinationRule reached every sidecar (SYNCED) │
         └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    🧪 PRACTICE DRILL (7-10 min) — Circuit-Break auth-service
         1. kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=auth-service --show-labels —
            confirm you have real version: labels to work with
         2. Write auth-service-dr.yaml: host: auth-service, outlierDetection
            with the canonical values from 7.4 (consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5,
            interval: 30s, baseEjectionTime: 30s, maxEjectionPercent: 50)
         3. kubectl apply -f auth-service-dr.yaml -n anihpj
         4. kubectl describe destinationrule auth-service-dr -n anihpj —
            confirm the outlierDetection block is present and no Istiod
            warnings appear
         5. kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/jobpost-api -c istio-proxy -- \
            pilot-agent request GET clusters | grep -A1 outlier_detection —
            confirm the ejection counters exist and read 0 (healthy baseline)

    [VISUAL SUMMARY]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ CHAPTER 7 VISUAL SUMMARY — DestinationRule end to end                    │
         │                                                                          │
         │ 7.1/7.2  DEFINE          subsets: v1 (version: v1), v2 (version: v2)     │
         │                                     │                                    │
         │                                     ▼                                    │
         │ 7.3/7.8  LOAD BALANCE    pick ONE of 7 algorithms per anihpj service     │
         │                          (LEAST_REQUEST, CONSISTENT_HASH, ROUND_ROBIN...)│
         │                                     │                                    │
         │                                     ▼                                    │
         │ 7.4/7.7  CIRCUIT BREAK   outlierDetection: 5 errors → EJECT (OPEN) →     │
         │                          30s cool-off → HALF-OPEN probe → CLOSED         │
         │                                     │                                    │
         │                                     ▼                                    │
         │ 7.5/7.10 CONNECTION POOL cap concurrent tcp/http load per destination    │
         │                                     │                                    │
         │                                     ▼                                    │
         │ 7.9      LOCALITY LB     prefer same-zone pods, failover outward —       │
         │                          REQUIRES outlierDetection to be set at all      │
         │                                     │                                    │
         │                                     ▼                                    │
         │ 7.11-7.14 OVERRIDES      portLevelSettings (per port, no inherit) /      │
         │                          subset trafficPolicy (per subset, merges) /     │
         │                          consistentHash fields / tunnel (proxy egress)   │
         │                                     │                                    │
         │                                     ▼                                    │
         │ 7.15     exportTo        keep tuning private to anihpj unless shared     │
         │                                     │                                    │
         │                                     ▼                                    │
         │ RESULT: jobpost-api-dr.yaml (7.6) — one CRD carrying subsets, load       │
         │ balancing, circuit breaking, pooling, and visibility — anihpj's single   │
         │ biggest defense against the cascade failure that opened this guide       │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         Chapter 7 took anihpj from "VirtualService knows WHERE to send
         traffic" to "DestinationRule knows HOW to deliver it and survive
         when it fails": 7.1-7.2 defined subsets so a canary split has real
         pods to land on; 7.3-7.4-7.5 picked a load-balancing algorithm,
         wired up the CLOSED → OPEN → HALF-OPEN circuit breaker, and capped
         connection pools; 7.6 combined all three into one production-ready
         YAML; 7.7-7.9 went deep on the breaker's internals and on
         zone-aware failover; and 7.10-7.15 supplied the complete field
         reference — per-port overrides, per-subset overrides, every
         consistentHash field, proxy tunneling, and cross-namespace scoping
         — for every one of those settings. The result, jobpost-api-dr.yaml,
         is anihpj's single biggest structural defense against the exact
         cascade failure that opened this guide back in Chapter 1.

Chapter 8: ServiceEntry — Connecting to External Services
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    Chapter 8 of 5-8  ·  Difficulty: 🟡 Intermediate  ·  🎯 Traffic
    Management — 35% of the ICA exam (the biggest domain)
    "Ch5-7 got traffic INTO and AROUND the mesh — can the mesh leave
     itself at all?"

    WHY THIS MATTERS
         Chapters 5-7 solved three questions about traffic already inside
         the anihpj mesh — who may enter (Gateway), where it goes
         (VirtualService), and how it's delivered (DestinationRule) — but
         none of them can get jobpost-api's payment call to
         api.stripe.com out the door, because that traffic is trying to
         leave the mesh entirely. By default, Istio's REGISTRY_ONLY
         posture treats api.stripe.com exactly like a mistyped hostname:
         unknown to the registry, blackholed, 502. ServiceEntry is the
         one CRD in this Part that answers the direction none of the
         other three touch — can the mesh leave itself at all, and if
         so, through which door and under whose audit? Register the
         host and every tool you already trust from Chapters 5-7 —
         retries, timeouts, TLS, circuit breakers — becomes available
         for the call to Stripe too, not just the call to user-service.
         Skip this chapter and anihpj is stuck between two bad
         defaults: REGISTRY_ONLY silently kills every payment and
         password-reset email, or ALLOW_ANY ships every outbound call
         unaudited and in the clear. Chapter 8 is the shortest chapter
         in Part 5, but it is the only one that faces outward — get it
         wrong and a perfectly-configured mesh still can't collect a
         single payment.

    LEARNING OBJECTIVES — by the end of Chapter 8 you can:
         ✅ Explain why REGISTRY_ONLY blackholes api.stripe.com by
            default, and what changes under ALLOW_ANY vs a mandatory
            Egress Gateway (8.1)
         ✅ Write a complete ServiceEntry that registers an external
            host with hosts, ports, location: MESH_EXTERNAL, and
            resolution (8.2)
         ✅ Wire the mandatory Gateway + two-match VirtualService pair
            that detours traffic through istio-egressgateway, and name
            the one resource that stays optional (8.3, 8.5)
         ✅ Stack REGISTRY_ONLY + egress gateway + AuthorizationPolicy
            into the three-layer egress defense pattern PCI auditors
            expect (8.4)
         ✅ Pick the correct resolution mode — NONE, STATIC, DNS,
            DNS_ROUND_ROBIN, or DYNAMIC_DNS — for a given external
            dependency (8.7)
         ✅ Choose endpoints vs workloadSelector for a MESH_INTERNAL
            ServiceEntry, and scope its visibility with exportTo
            (8.8, 8.9)
         ✅ Pin an external server's certificate identity with
            subjectAltNames and prove traffic is really detouring
            through the egress gateway instead of bypassing it
            (8.5, 8.10)

    ICA EXAM RELEVANCE
         🎯 ServiceEntry sits inside Traffic Management, the
         35%-weighted domain that decides more exam points than any
         other single topic — and within that 35%, egress is graded as
         concretely as ingress. Expect a live cluster, a real external
         host, and a scoring check for whether traffic actually left
         through the door you built, not just whether your YAML parses:

         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┐
         │ Graded skill                                    │ Where Chapter 8 teaches it │
         ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
         │ Register an external host with the right fields │ 8.2                        │
         │ Pick hosts/ports/location/resolution correctly  │ 8.2, 8.7                   │
         │ Force traffic through an audited egress gateway │ 8.3, 8.5                   │
         │ Originate TLS at the gateway edge               │ 8.5                        │
         │ Layer identity-based egress authorization       │ 8.4, 8.10                  │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────┘

         Note the split from 8.4's audit table: registering and routing
         the ServiceEntry is graded here under Traffic Management,
         while the AuthorizationPolicy that pins api.stripe.com to one
         ServiceAccount is graded under the separate Securing Workloads
         domain (25%), and reading the egress gateway's access log to
         PROVE the detour worked is a Troubleshooting-domain skill
         (20%) — one feature, three exam domains, all worth points.

    8.1  The Problem: Calling External APIs from Within the Mesh
         - By default, Istio (in REGISTRY_ONLY mode) blocks all external traffic
         - anihpj needs to call: external payment gateway, email service (SendGrid),
           S3 for media files, third-party job board API
         - Without ServiceEntry: HTTP 502 when calling external-api.com
         - 🎯 ICA EXAM NOTE: "Connecting In-Mesh Workloads to External
           Workloads and Services" covers BOTH directions — this chapter
           teaches mesh → external (ServiceEntry, below); for the reverse
           direction, an external VM joining the mesh via WorkloadEntry,
           see 16.2
         [BLOCKED TRAFFIC DIAGRAM: egress blocked without ServiceEntry]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  REGISTRY_ONLY mode, NO ServiceEntry for api.stripe.com yet:       │
         │                                                                    │
         │  [jobpost-api Pod]                                                 │
         │   app ── "POST https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges" ──▶ (sidecar)    │
         │                                                                    │
         │   [Envoy sidecar] looks up its cluster table:                      │
         │     outbound|443||api.stripe.com ............ NOT FOUND ❌          │
         │     → the request falls into Envoy's BlackHoleCluster              │
         │                                                                    │
         │   plain HTTP call → Envoy answers 502 Bad Gateway                  │
         │   HTTPS/TCP call  → connection dropped — no bytes leave the pod    │
         │                                                                    │
         │   api.stripe.com ......... never contacted (mesh = walled garden)  │
         │                                                                    │
         │  FIX: apply a ServiceEntry → istiod pushes a new Envoy cluster     │
         │       via xDS → the very same call now reaches Stripe ✅            │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🔧 UNDER THE HOOD. BlackHoleCluster isn't a made-up error state —
           it's a real, statically-configured Envoy cluster every sidecar
           ships with. REGISTRY_ONLY routes any unmatched host straight
           into it, and its handler is deliberately minimal: HTTP gets an
           immediate 502, raw TCP/TLS just gets reset — no upstream
           connection is ever attempted. That's why 8.2's fix works
           instantly: istiod's next xDS push simply swaps the host onto a
           real cluster instead of this dead-end one.

         [ISTIO OUTBOUND TRAFFIC MODES — three choices]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                                                                    │
         │  Mode 1: ALLOW_ANY (still the default in current Istio)            │
         │  ─────────────────                                                 │
         │  All external traffic passes through uncontrolled                  │
         │  No policies applied to external calls                             │
         │  Easy to set up, less secure                                       │
         │                                                                    │
         │  Mode 2: REGISTRY_ONLY (recommended for production)               │
         │  ──────────────────────                                            │
         │  Only registered ServiceEntry hosts allowed out                   │
         │  Unknown external calls: BLOCKED with 502                         │
         │  Forces explicit declaration of all external dependencies          │
         │                                                                    │
         │  Mode 3: Egress Gateway (most controlled)                         │
         │  ─────────────────────                                             │
         │  ALL external traffic forced through one egress Pod               │
         │  Central audit point for all outbound traffic                     │
         │  Required for strict compliance environments                       │
         │                                                                    │
         │  For anihpj:                                                       │
         │  Use REGISTRY_ONLY + ServiceEntry for each external API           │
         │  Add Egress Gateway for payment APIs (PCI compliance)             │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🧠 ANALOGY. Picture anihpj's outbound traffic as a warehouse with
           a dozen loading-dock doors. ALLOW_ANY is every door propped
           open — trucks roll out whichever way is closest, unlogged.
