        ejection still leaves 2 healthy pods serving. Don't disable
        outlierDetection: with it off, a truly dead pod keeps receiving live
        traffic and users see 100% of THEIR requests fail instead of a
        bounded, self-healing 50%.

    Q22: Ops configures localityLbSetting.distribute on skills-service to keep
        70% of eu-west-1a traffic in-zone, and ships the DestinationRule
        WITHOUT an outlierDetection block ("we'll add circuit breaking
        later"). All eu-west-1a pods later crash together. What happens to
        eu-west-1a callers, and what's the one-block fix?
    A22: Nothing fails over — Istio silently IGNORES localityLbSetting on any
        DestinationRule that lacks outlierDetection (7.9's hard requirement:
        no health signal means Envoy has no trigger to spill traffic outward),
        so eu-west-1a callers keep getting routed to the dead local pods
        forever, with zero automatic recovery. Fix: add the canonical breaker
        block to the SAME DestinationRule:
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  outlierDetection:                                                  │
        │    consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5                                      │
        │    interval: 30s                                                    │
        │    baseEjectionTime: 30s                                            │
        │    maxEjectionPercent: 50                                           │
        └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        Once present, the 5-error trip ejects the dead 1a pods and Envoy
        walks the locality preference outward to 1b/1c automatically.

    Q23: notification-service opens long-lived connections to an internal
        Redis cache on port 6379. The Service port is defined as
        {port: 6379, name: "redis"} with no appProtocol set. Under load, some
        connections hang for several seconds before finally going through;
        packet captures show Envoy waiting before forwarding the first bytes.
        Explain the cause and fix it.
    A23: Protocol selection (8.6) fell through to auto-detection because the
        port name carries no recognized prefix (http-, grpc-, tcp-, tls-,
        https-), and Redis's RESP protocol is neither HTTP/1.1 nor HTTP/2 —
        Envoy's sniffer waits for CLIENT bytes to decide, and that wait is
        exactly the hang. It's the same failure mode as 8.6's psql
        server-first-protocol trap, just for Redis. Fix — name the port so
        Envoy skips sniffing entirely: ports: [{port: 6379, name: tcp-redis}]
        (or set appProtocol: tcp, which outranks the name if both are
        present) — either turns an auto-detect gamble into a guarantee.

    Q24: notification-service currently calls SendGrid directly over plain
        HTTP. Compliance now requires ALL of that traffic to exit through
        istio-egressgateway, upgraded to HTTPS at the gateway (TLS
        origination) instead of staying plaintext end-to-end. The SendGrid
        ServiceEntry from 8.2 already exists (hosts: [api.sendgrid.com], port
        443 HTTPS). Write every ADDITIONAL resource needed, and name which one
        actually performs the HTTP→HTTPS upgrade.
    A24: Three more resources — an egress Gateway, a two-match VirtualService,
        and the DestinationRule that does the real work:
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                                 │
        │  kind: Gateway                                                      │
        │  metadata: {name: egress-sendgrid, namespace: istio-system}         │
        │  spec:                                                              │
        │    selector: {istio: egressgateway}                                 │
        │    servers:                                                         │
        │    - port: {number: 80, name: http, protocol: HTTP}                 │
        │      hosts: ["api.sendgrid.com"]                                    │
        │  ---                                                                │
        │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                                 │
        │  kind: VirtualService                                               │
        │  metadata: {name: sendgrid-through-egress, namespace: anihpj}       │
        │  spec:                                                              │
        │    hosts: [api.sendgrid.com]                                        │
        │    gateways: [mesh, istio-system/egress-sendgrid]                   │
        │    http:                                                            │
        │    - match: [{gateways: [mesh], port: 80}]     ← BLOCK 1: app→gw    │
        │      route:                                                         │
        │      - destination:                                                 │
        │          host: istio-egressgateway.istio-system.svc.cluster.local   │
        │          port: {number: 80}                                         │
        │    - match:                                    ← BLOCK 2: gw→net    │
        │      - gateways: [istio-system/egress-sendgrid]                     │
        │        port: 80                                                     │
        │      route:                                                         │
        │      - destination:                                                 │
        │          host: api.sendgrid.com                                     │
        │          port: {number: 443}      ← DR below originates TLS here    │
        │  ---                                                                │
        │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                                 │
        │  kind: DestinationRule                                              │
        │  metadata: {name: sendgrid-originate-tls, namespace: istio-system}  │
        │  spec:                                                              │
        │    host: api.sendgrid.com                                           │
        │    trafficPolicy:                                                   │
        │      portLevelSettings:                                             │
        │      - port: {number: 443}                                          │
        │        tls:                                                         │
        │          mode: SIMPLE   ← THIS is what upgrades HTTP to HTTPS       │
        └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        The Gateway only opens the door and the VirtualService only steers
        traffic through it — neither touches encryption. The
        DestinationRule's tls.mode: SIMPLE is the one field that makes the
        egress gateway originate a real TLS handshake toward SendGrid on the
        way out (same 8.5 pattern used for Stripe, reused here for a plain-
        HTTP caller instead of a PASSTHROUGH one).

    UNDER THE HOOD 🔧 — the capstone synthesis for Chapter 8

         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ 🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — THE FULL OUTBOUND-CALL DECISION MODEL                │
         │                                                                          │
         │ SCENARIO: jobpost-api calls https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges. Five      │
         │ gates decide exactly what happens to that call — this is the model       │
         │ 8.5-8.10 built piece by piece; here it is as ONE decision path.          │
         │                                                                          │
         │ GATE 1 — IS THE HOST REGISTERED? (8.1, 8.2)                              │
         │   no ServiceEntry  → outboundTrafficPolicy decides: ALLOW_ANY passes     │
         │                       it through blind; REGISTRY_ONLY → 502, done        │
         │   ServiceEntry exists → continue to Gate 2                               │
         │                                                                          │
         │ GATE 2 — HOW DOES ENVOY FIND THE IP? (8.7, 8.8)                          │
         │   resolution: DNS            → re-resolves periodically (Stripe's case)  │
         │   resolution: STATIC         → fixed endpoints/workloadSelector (8.8)    │
         │   resolution: NONE           → wildcard passthrough, already-resolved IP │
         │   resolution: DNS_ROUND_ROBIN/DYNAMIC_DNS → CDN- or ambient-specific     │
         │                                                                          │
         │ GATE 3 — DIRECT EXIT OR THROUGH THE EGRESS GATEWAY? (8.3, 8.5)           │
         │   no egress Gateway/VS wired → sidecar dials api.stripe.com directly     │
         │                                 (registered, but unaudited)              │
         │   Gateway + 2-match VS wired → 4-hop detour: app → sidecar →             │
         │                                 istio-egressgateway → api.stripe.com     │
         │                                                                          │
         │ GATE 4 — TLS: PASSTHROUGH OR ORIGINATED AT THE EDGE? (8.5)               │
         │   app already speaks HTTPS → Gateway tls.mode: PASSTHROUGH (Stripe)      │
         │   app speaks plain HTTP    → DestinationRule tls.mode: SIMPLE            │
         │                               originates TLS at the gateway (SendGrid)   │
         │                                                                          │
         │ GATE 5 — WHO ELSE MAY SEE OR TRUST THIS HOST? (8.4, 8.9, 8.10)           │
         │   AuthorizationPolicy on the egress gateway → pins the caller's SA       │
         │   exportTo                                  → scopes which namespaces    │
         │                                                may reference the host    │
         │   subjectAltNames                           → pins the exact cert        │
         │                                                identity Envoy accepts    │
         │                                                                          │
         │ RESULT for jobpost-api → api.stripe.com: registered (DNS) → routed       │
         │ via egress gateway → TLS PASSTHROUGH → AuthorizationPolicy allows        │
         │ only jobpost-api's ServiceAccount → subjectAltNames pins Stripe's        │
         │ certificate identity. Five gates, one line in an exam scenario:          │
         │ "make this external call, and prove it's controlled."                    │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    SPEED TIPS
         ⚡ MESH_EXTERNAL is for real external hosts (Stripe, SendGrid);
            MESH_INTERNAL is only for VM-mesh-expansion ServiceEntries
            backed by WorkloadEntry — mixing them up makes a
            ServiceEntry silently do nothing
         ⚡ Before wiring an egress gateway, check
            outboundTrafficPolicy first — you can't tell REGISTRY_ONLY
            from ALLOW_ANY by staring at ServiceEntry YAML alone
         ⚡ An empty istio-egressgateway access log after a
            "successful" call means traffic bypassed your detour, not
            that nothing happened — always check the log before
            trusting the demo
         ⚡ Wildcard hosts (*.amazonaws.com) can't use resolution: DNS
            or DNS_ROUND_ROBIN — reach for NONE (or DYNAMIC_DNS in
            ambient mode) or the ServiceEntry won't apply at all
         ⚡ A STATIC endpoint with no ports map just inherits the
            ServiceEntry's own port numbers — no need to repeat them
            for the common case
         ⚡ On exam day, verify with istioctl proxy-config cluster
            BEFORE curl-ing — a missing cluster proves the ServiceEntry
            never reached Envoy; a failed curl could mean five
            different things

    COMMANDS CHEAT-CARD

         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ CHAPTER 8 COMMANDS CHEAT-CARD                                       │
         │                                                                     │
         │ # check ALLOW_ANY vs REGISTRY_ONLY (8.1)                            │
         │ kubectl get configmap istio -n istio-system -o yaml \               │
         │     | grep -A1 outboundTrafficPolicy                                │
         │                                                                     │
         │ # switch outbound mode mesh-wide (8.1)                              │
         │ istioctl install --set \                                            │
         │     meshConfig.outboundTrafficPolicy.mode=REGISTRY_ONLY -y          │
         │                                                                     │
         │ # register an external host, then confirm it landed (8.2)           │
         │ kubectl apply -f stripe-serviceentry.yaml                           │
         │ kubectl get serviceentry -n anihpj                                  │
         │                                                                     │
         │ # confirm Envoy actually received the new cluster (8.2)             │
         │ istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj \        │
         │     | grep stripe                                                   │
         │                                                                     │
         │ # prove a real call leaves the mesh (8.2)                           │
         │ kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- curl -s \              │
         │     -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://api.stripe.com/v1        │
         │                                                                     │
         │ # install the egress gateway, then confirm the Pod is Running (8.3) │
         │ istioctl install -y \                                               │
         │     --set components.egressGateways[0].enabled=true                 │
         │ kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=egressgateway             │
         │                                                                     │
         │ # emergency kill switch for ALL routed egress (8.3)                 │
         │ kubectl scale deploy/istio-egressgateway -n istio-system \          │
         │     --replicas=0                                                    │
         │                                                                     │
         │ # prove the detour worked, not just that the call succeeded (8.5)   │
         │ kubectl logs -n istio-system -l istio=egressgateway --tail=3 \      │
         │     | grep stripe                                                   │
         │                                                                     │
         │ # confirm real SAN values BEFORE hardcoding subjectAltNames (8.10)  │
         │ openssl s_client -connect api.stripe.com:443 2>/dev/null \          │
         │     | openssl x509 -noout -ext subjectAltName                       │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    PRACTICE DRILL 🧪 (7 minutes) — Register and audit a new external
    dependency
         Scenario: anihpj is integrating a fictional background-check
         API, api.checkr.com, for auth-service. Do this now, on a real
         (or kind) cluster with Istio installed:
         1. (2 min) Write and apply a ServiceEntry named checkr-verify
            in anihpj: hosts: [api.checkr.com], port 443 HTTPS,
            location: MESH_EXTERNAL, resolution: DNS.
         2. (1 min) Confirm it landed: kubectl get serviceentry
            -n anihpj, then istioctl proxy-config cluster
            deploy/auth-service -n anihpj | grep checkr.
         3. (2 min) Write an egress Gateway (selector istio:
            egressgateway) plus the two-match VirtualService that
            detours auth-service's calls to api.checkr.com through
            istio-egressgateway.
         4. (1 min) Generate one real call from auth-service and
            confirm it appears in the egress gateway's access log — an
            empty log means the detour didn't work.
         5. (1 min) Add exportTo: ["."] to checkr-verify so only anihpj
            can reference it, and say out loud what error a different
            namespace would now see.

    VISUAL SUMMARY

         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ CHAPTER 8 IN ONE PICTURE — FROM BLOCKED CALL TO AUDITED EGRESS   │
         │                                                                  │
         │ 8.1 THE PROBLEM: jobpost-api → api.stripe.com → ❌ 502            │
         │     (REGISTRY_ONLY, no ServiceEntry yet)                         │
         │         │                                                        │
         │         ▼                                                        │
         │ 8.2 REGISTER: ServiceEntry(api.stripe.com, MESH_EXTERNAL, DNS)   │
         │     → istiod → new Envoy cluster pushed mesh-wide                │
         │         │                                                        │
         │         ▼                                                        │
         │ 8.3 ROUTE: Gateway + 2-match VirtualService → detour through     │
         │     istio-egressgateway                                          │
         │         │                                                        │
         │         ▼                                                        │
         │ 8.4 SECURE: REGISTRY_ONLY + egress gateway + AuthorizationPolicy │
         │     (jobpost-api ServiceAccount only)                            │
         │         │                                                        │
         │         ▼                                                        │
         │ 8.5-8.10 THE INTERNALS: traffic path · DNS/protocol · 5          │
         │     resolution modes · WorkloadEntry YAML · exportTo scoping ·   │
         │     subjectAltNames pinning                                      │
         │         │                                                        │
         │         ▼                                                        │
         │ RESULT: jobpost-api → egress gateway → api.stripe.com —          │
         │ registered, routed, audited, and pinned to one certificate       │
         │ identity ✅                                                       │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         Chapter 8 took jobpost-api from a hard-blocked 502 against
         api.stripe.com to a fully governed outbound call: 8.1 showed
         why REGISTRY_ONLY blocks unknown hosts by default, 8.2
         registered Stripe (and SendGrid, and S3) as a ServiceEntry so
         Envoy would even consider the call, 8.3 added an egress
         gateway as the one audited door external traffic must use,
         and 8.4 stacked REGISTRY_ONLY, the gateway, and an
         AuthorizationPolicy into the three-layer defense PCI auditors
         expect. The six deep dives in 8.5-8.10 filled in exactly how
         that machinery works — the 4-hop egress path, DNS proxying
         and protocol selection, all five resolution modes, the real
         YAML behind endpoints and workloadSelector, exportTo's
         namespace-list form, and subjectAltNames pinning — so that by
         the end of this chapter you can not only make anihpj call the
         outside world, but prove, log, and lock down exactly how it
         does.

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     PART 6 COVER — OBSERVABILITY (CHAPTERS 9-11)
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    Difficulty: 🟡 Intermediate          Chapters: 9-11 (3 chapters)
    Covers: Metrics (Ch9) · Distributed Tracing (Ch10) · Kiali (Ch11)

    ⚠️ Honest framing: Observability is NOT its own graded ICA exam domain —
    there is no "Observability" line on the official blueprint (see Section
    0's Domain Coverage Audit). It is the TOOLING you use to score points in
    Troubleshooting (Domain 4, 20%). Every skill in Ch9-11 exists for one
    reason: so that on exam day, when a VirtualService misroutes traffic or
    a DestinationRule ejects a healthy Pod, you can find the broken piece in
    minutes instead of guessing. Treat this Part as a toolbox for Domain 4,
    never as a separate 15-20% bucket of its own.

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     PART 6 INTRO — WHY THIS PART EXISTS
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    Part 4 (Traffic Management) taught the anihpj mesh to route, retry, and
    load-balance every request, and Part 5 (Security) taught it to encrypt
    and authorize every call — both landed with zero Django code changes.
    But smarter is not the same as visible: right now, if jobpost-api's p99
    latency quietly climbs from its 234ms baseline toward 1,240ms at 3 AM,
    you have no way to know it happened, let alone which of the seven
    anihpj services — jobpost-api, user-service, skills-service,
    location-service, notification-service, auth-service, search-service —
    is responsible.

    That is the gap Part 6 closes. Every production incident really asks
    three questions: WHAT is wrong (a number moved — error rate, latency,
    request volume), WHERE is it wrong (which one hop, out of five or more,
    is slow), and WHY is it wrong (a missing DB index, a retry storm, a bad
    deploy). Chapter 9 answers WHAT with metrics, Chapter 10 answers WHERE
    with distributed tracing, and Chapter 11 (Kiali) turns both into one
    graph you can read in seconds instead of a wall of numbers.

    🧠 ANALOGY: Part 6 is the difference between a car with no dashboard
    and one with a full instrument cluster. Drive without gauges and you
    only learn the engine is overheating when it stalls on the highway. The
    temperature gauge (metrics, Ch9) tells you WHAT is wrong before it is
    fatal. A mechanic's diagnostic trace of exactly which cylinder misfired
    (tracing, Ch10) tells you WHERE. A dashboard light that turns red and
    points at the engine bay (Kiali, Ch11) is the at-a-glance view that
    sends you to the right page instead of popping the hood and guessing.

    None of this costs a line of Django code, same as Parts 4-5. The Envoy
    sidecar already sits in front of every anihpj Pod and already sees
    every request — Ch9 just points Prometheus at metrics Envoy already
    records, Ch10 turns on trace headers Envoy already knows how to
    propagate, and Ch11 reads both plus live Kubernetes/Istio config into
    one picture. You write YAML and open dashboards; you never instrument
    application code.

    💡 RUNNING EXAMPLE: every chapter is demonstrated on the same
    anihpj/jobpost mesh used throughout this guide — the same jobpost-api,
    user-service, skills-service, location-service, notification-service,
    auth-service, and search-service Pods you have already deployed,
    secured, and load-balanced. The baseline reused across all three
    chapters is jobpost-api at 847 req/s, 2.1% errors, p99 234ms — and the
    canonical incident is skills-service degrading to 8.1% errors at a
    1,240ms p99, the scenario Chapter 9's RED-metrics walkthrough (9.2)
    flags first and Chapters 10-11 each re-solve with a different tool. By
    the end of Part 6 you will not need to SSH into a Pod and grep logs to
    guess what is slow — Chapter 9 starts with the one number every later
    chapter builds on: the request.

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     HOW THE CHAPTERS FIT — CH9 → CH10 → CH11
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ CHAPTER 9: METRICS  🟢               Answers: "WHAT is wrong?"          │
    │   Envoy counts every request -> Prometheus scrapes -> Grafana graphs it │
    │   -> jobpost-api baseline: 847 req/s, 2.1% errors, p99 234ms            │
    │   -> skills-service flagged: 8.1% errors, p99 1240ms  <- the clue       │
    │       │  metrics name ONE suspect service -- now find WHERE it hurts    │
    │       ▼                                                                 │
    │ CHAPTER 10: DISTRIBUTED TRACING  🟡  Answers: "WHERE is it slow?"       │
    │   Envoy propagates trace headers across every hop -> Jaeger renders it  │
    │   -> jobpost-api -> user-service -> auth-service : fast (fine)          │
    │   -> jobpost-api -> skills-service : 195ms of the 342ms trace  <- HERE  │
    │       │  a trace pinpoints ONE hop -- but reading raw traces all day    │
    │       │  doesn't scale past a handful of incidents                      │
    │       ▼                                                                 │
    │ CHAPTER 11: KIALI  🔴                Answers: "SHOW ME"                 │
    │   Merges Ch9's Prometheus metrics + Ch10's Jaeger traces + live         │
    │   Kubernetes/Istio config into one clickable service graph              │
    │   -> red edge: jobpost-api -> skills-service, 8.1% errors, 1240ms       │
    │   -> green everywhere else -- the whole mesh's health in one screen     │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

    walk through on the SAME incidents, using only istioctl dashboards and
    zero application code changes.

Chapter 9: Metrics — Measuring Every Request
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     CHAPTER 9 AT A GLANCE
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    Chapter 9 of 9-11 · Difficulty: 🟢 · Tooling for Troubleshooting (20% of
    the ICA exam) — not its own graded domain
    "What is wrong, right now?"

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     WHY THIS MATTERS
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    Right now, somewhere in the anihpj mesh, a number is moving — and until
    this chapter, you have no way to see it. jobpost-api's healthy baseline
    is 847 req/s, 2.1% errors, p99 234ms; if skills-service quietly drifts
    to 8.1% errors and a 1,240ms p99, nothing in Django's own code and no
    "kubectl get pods" output will tell you. Metrics are the FIRST of the
    three observability pillars this Part introduces (9.1) — the layer that
    catches the drift the instant it happens, using only three numbers per
    service: rate, errors, duration (the RED metrics of 9.2). Chapter 10's
    traces can only tell you WHERE a slow request lost its time once you
    already suspect skills-service, and Chapter 11's Kiali graph can only
    light up red once metrics and traces both exist to feed it — everything
    downstream of this chapter starts here. None of it costs a line of
    Django code: Envoy's sidecar already counts every request in and out of
    all seven anihpj services, and Prometheus is already scraping it. By
    the end of this chapter you can look at one Grafana panel, or write one
    PromQL query, and say with confidence exactly which service is unwell —
    before a single user opens a support ticket.

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
      ✅ Name the three observability pillars (metrics, traces, logs) and
         state which parts of each Istio gives you automatically.
      ✅ Define RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) and read it straight off a
         Grafana panel for any anihpj service.
      ✅ Trace one request's metrics from Envoy's raw :15090 stats through
         the merged :15020 scrape endpoint into a Prometheus time series.
      ✅ Pick the correct PromQL function for a counter, a gauge, or a
         histogram — rate()/increase(), raw/avg_over_time(),
         histogram_quantile() — without guessing.
      ✅ Add a low-cardinality custom dimension to istio_requests_total with
         a Telemetry resource, and explain why a user_id dimension would
         melt Prometheus.
      ✅ Read a default Envoy access-log line field by field and pull a
         request's trace ID out of it.
      ✅ Tell proxy-level, service-level, and control-plane metrics apart,
         and name the one istiod metric that means "a proxy just rejected
         a config push."

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     ICA EXAM RELEVANCE
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    Metrics have no line item of their own on the official ICA blueprint —
    Observability sits outside all four graded domains (see Section 0's
    Domain Coverage Audit and Part 6's honest framing above). What IS
    graded is 🎯 Troubleshooting (Domain 4, 20%), and almost every
    troubleshooting scenario opens with a symptom phrased in exactly this
    chapter's vocabulary: "users report an elevated error rate," "p99
    latency spiked," "a service stopped receiving traffic." The exam will
    never literally say "run this PromQL query" — it expects the reflex:
    reach for istioctl dashboard prometheus/grafana, spot the RED-metric
    anomaly in seconds, and use it to decide which config object
    (VirtualService, DestinationRule, PeerAuthentication) is worth
    inspecting next. Skip this chapter and you lose no single graded
    question directly — you lose the minutes every Domain 4 task assumes
    you already have.

     SECTION MAP — how 9.1-9.12 fit together
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

    │   9.6 access logs catch the ONE request metrics averaged away               │
    │                                                                             │
    │                               ▼                                             │
    │                                                                             │
    │ GROUP 3 -- BEYOND THE HTTP DEFAULT (9.7, 9.10)   "what does RED miss?"      │

    CAPTION: read top to bottom as one story — Group 1's vocabulary and 3
    free numbers travel, in Group 2, from Envoy to a screen you can read,
    then Group 3 covers the two places that HTTP-shaped picture does not
    reach (istiod itself, and raw TCP), and Group 4 is the reference shelf
    you return to once you already know why each field exists.

    9.1  The Observability Pillars: Metrics, Traces, Logs
         - Metrics: numbers over time (e.g., requests/sec, error rate, latency p99)
         - Traces: follow a single request across multiple services
         - Logs: human-readable events from each service
         - Istio provides Metrics + Traces automatically — zero code change!
         [OBSERVABILITY PILLARS DIAGRAM — three overlapping circles]

         │    • skills-service logs: "SLOW QUERY: SELECT * FROM skills       │

    9.2  RED Metrics — What Istio Measures Automatically
         - R: Rate — how many requests per second is jobpost-api receiving?
         - E: Errors — what percentage are failing (HTTP 4xx/5xx)?
         - D: Duration — how long do requests take (p50, p95, p99 latency)?
         - Istio's Envoy proxy measures these for EVERY service, EVERY request
         - No Prometheus instrumentation needed in your Django code

         🧠 ANALOGY. RED is a nurse's triage vitals check, not a full
            diagnosis: a pulse (rate), a fever reading (errors), and a
            blood-pressure cuff (duration) take seconds and flag that
            skills-service is unwell — they don't say WHY. That "why"
            needs Chapter 10's trace (the MRI) or this chapter's own
            access logs (the lab report, 9.6) — RED only tells you which
            patient to look at next.
         [RED METRICS DASHBOARD MOCKUP for anihpj services]

         [RED METRICS — what Istio gives you for FREE]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  SERVICE: jobpost-api               LAST 5 MINUTES     │
         │                                                        │
         │  Rate (Requests/sec):   ████████████████ 847 req/s     │
         │  Error Rate:            ██░░░░░░░░░░░░░░  2.1%        │
         │  Duration (p99):        ████░░░░░░░░░░░░  234ms        │
         │                                                        │
         │  SERVICE: user-service              LAST 5 MINUTES     │

         │  SERVICE: skills-service            LAST 5 MINUTES     │

         │                     ↑ This service needs attention!   │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    9.3  Prometheus + Istio — How Metrics Are Collected
         - Istio configures Envoy to emit metrics in Prometheus format
         - Prometheus scrapes metrics from every Envoy proxy
         - Key metrics exposed: istio_requests_total, istio_request_duration_milliseconds
         - Configuring scraping interval, retention, alerting rules
         [PROMETHEUS SCRAPING FLOW: Envoy → /metrics → Prometheus → Grafana]

         [METRICS PIPELINE — from request to dashboard]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                                                                    │
         │  1. REQUEST HAPPENS                                                │
         │     User hits GET /jobs/ → jobpost-api                            │
         │                                                                    │
         │  2. ENVOY RECORDS METRICS (automatically, per request)            │
         │     istio_requests_total{source_workload="jobpost-api",           │
         │      destination_service="user-service", response_code="200"} += 1│
         │     istio_request_duration_milliseconds{...} = 87ms               │
         │                                                                    │
         │  3. PROMETHEUS SCRAPES (every 15s by default)                     │
         │     GET http://jobpost-api-pod:15090/metrics                       │
         │     GET http://user-service-pod:15090/metrics                      │
         │     ... (scrapes ALL pods in mesh)                                 │
         │                                                                    │
         │  4. GRAFANA QUERIES PROMETHEUS                                     │
         │     PromQL: rate(istio_requests_total[5m])                         │
         │     PromQL: histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(                         │
         │       istio_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket[5m]))             │
         │                                                                    │
         │  5. DASHBOARD SHOWS                                                │
         │     jobpost-api: 847 req/s, 2.1% errors, p99=234ms               │
         │                                                                    │
         │  KEY ISTIO METRICS TO KNOW:                                        │
         │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
         │  │  istio_requests_total          ← request count              │  │
         │  │  istio_request_duration_milliseconds ← latency histogram    │  │
         │  │  istio_request_bytes           ← request body size          │  │
         │  │  istio_response_bytes          ← response body size         │  │
         │  │  istio_tcp_connections_opened_total  ← TCP connection count │  │
         │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - ⚠️ Scrape-port clarification (exam-accurate): Prometheus does
           NOT scrape Envoy directly by default — it scrapes the
           istio-agent on :15020, which serves MERGED app + Envoy metrics
           • :15020/stats/prometheus → istio-agent, the DEFAULT scrape
             target (injected pods carry prometheus.io/port: "15020")
           • :15090/stats/prometheus → the RAW Envoy stats endpoint,
             served by the Envoy process itself — Envoy metrics ONLY
         - DEFINITION: metrics merging — the istio-agent fetches the
           Django app's own /metrics output AND Envoy's :15090 stats,
           then serves BOTH in one response on :15020 → a single scrape
           per pod collects application + mesh metrics together
         - → when a diagram (like the one above) says "Prometheus scrapes
           :15090", read it as "the Envoy metrics ORIGINATE at :15090" —
           the scrape itself lands on the agent's merged :15020 endpoint

         [SIDECAR METRICS PORTS — :15020 (merged) vs :15090 (raw Envoy)]
         ┌────────────────┬──────────────────┬────────────────────────────┐
         │  PORT          │  SERVED BY       │  WHAT YOU GET              │
         ├────────────────┼──────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
         │  :15020        │  istio-agent     │  MERGED app + Envoy stats  │
         │                │  (pilot-agent)   │  ✅ DEFAULT scrape target   │
         ├────────────────┼──────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
         │  :15090        │  Envoy process   │  RAW Envoy stats only      │
         │                │  directly        │  (debugging, no app data)  │
         ├────────────────┼──────────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
         │  :8000         │  Django app      │  app's own custom metrics  │
         │                │  (your code)     │  (merged INTO :15020)      │
         └────────────────┴──────────────────┴────────────────────────────┘

         [MERGE FLOW — how one scrape collects everything]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Django app :8000/metrics ──────┐                              │
         │                                 ├──► istio-agent :15020        │
         │  Envoy :15090/stats/prometheus ─┘         │  (one merged page) │
         │                                           ▼                    │
         │                             Prometheus scrape (every 15s)      │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
