    11.5  The Observability Debug Flow — From Alert to Root Cause
         - DEFINITION: the debug flow is a fixed four-step route through
           the observability stack: Grafana → Kiali → Jaeger → logs
         - Why it matters: without a fixed route you tab-hop between
           dashboards for an hour; with it, most anihpj incidents go
           from alert to root cause in minutes
         - How it works — each tool answers exactly ONE question:
           • Grafana answers WHAT is wrong (which metric crossed a line)
           • Kiali answers WHERE it lives (which service/edge is red)
           • Jaeger answers WHY it is slow (which span eats the time)
           • Logs answer HOW to fix it (the exact application error)
         - Never skip a step: jumping straight to logs means grepping
           seven services blind instead of one service, one timestamp

         [OBSERVABILITY DEBUG FLOW — 4 steps from alert to root cause]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │   ALERT: "anihpj p99 latency > 500ms for 5 minutes"                │
         │      │                                                             │
         │      ▼                                                             │
         │   STEP 1  GRAFANA — WHAT is wrong?                                 │
         │           Istio Service Dashboard → skills-service p99 = 1240ms    │
         │      │                                                             │
         │      ▼                                                             │
         │   STEP 2  KIALI — WHERE is it?                                     │
         │           Graph → red edge jobpost-api → skills-service, 8.1%      │
         │      │                                                             │
         │      ▼                                                             │
         │   STEP 3  JAEGER — WHY is it slow?                                 │
         │           Widest span: skills-service PostgreSQL query = 1,100ms   │
         │      │                                                             │
         │      ▼                                                             │
         │   STEP 4  LOGS — HOW to fix it?                                    │
         │           psql EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan → missing index     │
         │                                                                    │
         │   Each step narrows the search: mesh → service → span → SQL line   │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [WORKED INCIDENT — anihpj p99 alert, from page to fix]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  T+0min : PagerDuty fires: "anihpj p99 > 500ms for 5 minutes"      │
         │  T+1min : GRAFANA — jobpost-api p99 = 234ms ✅ ... but             │
         │           skills-service p99 = 1240ms 🔴 → suspect found           │
         │  T+2min : KIALI — edge jobpost-api → skills-service is red:        │
         │           89 req/s at 8.1% errors (rest of the mesh green)         │
         │  T+4min : JAEGER — sort by duration, open top trace (1,340ms):     │
         │           span "SELECT ... FROM skills WHERE user_id" = 1,100ms    │
         │  T+6min : LOGS — kubectl logs deploy/skills-service -n anihpj      │
         │           shows the slow query; psql EXPLAIN: Seq Scan on          │
         │           skills — there is no index on user_id                    │
         │  T+9min : FIX — psql: CREATE INDEX idx_skills_user_id              │
         │                       ON skills(user_id);                          │
         │  T+12min: VERIFY — Grafana p99 falls 1240ms → 87ms; the Kiali      │
         │           edge turns green; incident closed in 12 minutes          │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    11.6  Deep Dive — How Kiali Builds the Service Graph
         - DEFINITION: the service graph is COMPUTED, never configured —
           Kiali assembles it on every refresh from three live sources
         - Why it matters: when the graph looks wrong, fix the SOURCE:
           • empty graph      → Prometheus is down or not scraping
           • versions missing → pods lack app/version labels
           • no config badges → Kiali cannot reach the Istio config
         - How it works — three sources merged on every refresh:
           • Prometheus     → istio_requests_total counters become EDGES
             (source_workload → destination_workload label pairs)
           • Kubernetes API → pods/services/deployments become NODES,
             with readiness feeding node health
           • Istio config   → VS/DR/Gateway objects add badges and the
             validation results from 11.3
         - Health scoring: a node's color combines request error rate
           AND pod readiness — traffic can look clean while pods
           crash-loop, and Kiali still flags the workload
         - anihpj gotcha: a service with zero traffic shows GRAY (idle),
           not green — edges come from Prometheus counters, so no
           requests means no edges, even when pods are perfectly fine

         [KIALI GRAPH ASSEMBLY — three sources, one picture]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  SOURCE 1  PROMETHEUS      → EDGES   istio_requests_total pairs,   │
         │            (telemetry)               req/s, error %, p99 per edge  │
         │  SOURCE 2  KUBERNETES API  → NODES   pods, services, versions,     │
         │            (state)                   readiness → node health       │
         │  SOURCE 3  ISTIO CONFIG    → BADGES  VS/DR/Gateway icons plus      │
         │            (CRDs)                    validation errors (see 11.3)  │
         │                                                                    │
         │                    merged on every refresh (15s)                   │
         │                              │                                     │
         │                              ▼                                     │
         │              ┌───────────────────────────────┐                     │
         │              │      KIALI GRAPH ENGINE       │                     │
         │              │  1. edges  ← telemetry pairs  │                     │
         │              │  2. nodes  ← Kubernetes state │                     │
         │              │  3. badges ← Istio CRDs       │                     │
         │              │  4. colors ← health scoring   │                     │
         │              └───────────────────────────────┘                     │
         │                              │                                     │
         │                              ▼                                     │
         │               colored, clickable service graph                     │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [KIALI HEALTH LEGEND — one legend for nodes AND edges]
         ┌───────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Color    │  Meaning — one legend for nodes and edges              │
         ├───────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  🟢 green │  healthy — errors under threshold, pods ready          │
         │  🟠 orange│  degraded — error rate above 10% of requests           │
         │  🔴 red   │  failing — no healthy pods, or requests failing        │
         │  ⚪ gray  │  idle — no traffic in the selected time window         │
         ├───────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  Edge extras: thickness = request volume, 🔒 = mTLS on that hop    │
         │  Thresholds are tunable in Kiali's health config — anihpj sets     │
         │  "failing" at 5% errors, which is why skills-service (8.1%)        │
         │  shows RED in this chapter's graphs                                │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    11.7  Installing Kiali — Demo Add-on vs Production-Ready Setup
         - Kiali is NOT a core Istio control-plane component — it is an
           optional observability integration that ships and is
           installed separately from istiod and the data plane
         - DEFINITION: three real install paths exist for Kiali; only
           two of them are supported for anything beyond a demo cluster
         - Why it matters: the anihpj kind cluster you study on and a
           real anihpj production cluster should almost never use the
           same install method — the quick-start YAML is not hardened
         - How it works — pick the path that matches the cluster:
           • Sample add-on (kubectl apply -f samples/addons/kiali.yaml)
             → Istio's own docs call this install "for demonstration
             only, and not tuned for performance or security"
           • kiali-operator → a Kubernetes Operator that reconciles a
             Kiali custom resource; this is the Kiali project's own
             recommended path for a supported, day-2-managed install
           • Helm chart (kiali/kiali-server) → for teams that already
             manage every other Istio addon (Prometheus, Grafana,
             Jaeger) through Helm and want one consistent toolchain
         - If you expose the sample install without anonymous auth,
           update the `signing_key` value in Kiali's ConfigMap first —
           every sample install ships with the identical default key

         🔧 UNDER THE HOOD. The signing_key is not an Istio or mTLS
         certificate — it is a secret Kiali's own web server uses to
         sign the session cookie your browser gets after login, fully
         separate from anything in the data plane. Because every
         sample install ships the identical key, anyone who copies it
         can forge a valid Kiali session against a cluster they never
         ran kubectl against — rotating it (11.7) secures only the web
         console's front door, not mesh traffic or mTLS certificates.
         - anihpj note: istioctl dashboard kiali behaves the same
           regardless of which path installed it — the command just
           port-forwards to whatever Service named kiali it finds, so
           this is not a decision you need to relearn for the exam

         [KIALI INSTALL PATHS — sample add-on vs kiali-operator vs Helm]
         ┌─────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ Install Path            │ Production-ready?  /  anihpj uses it for       │
         ├─────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ samples/addons/         │ ❌ Demo only — Istio's own docs call this       │
         │ kiali.yaml              │ "not tuned for performance or security"        │
         │ (kubectl apply)         │ → anihpj: local kind cluster, exam study       │
         ├─────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ kiali-operator          │ ✅ Production-ready — the Kiali project's       │
         │ (Kubernetes Operator)   │ own recommended install path                   │
         │                         │ → anihpj: staging + production clusters        │
         ├─────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Helm chart              │ ✅ Production-ready — fits teams already        │
         │ kiali/kiali-server      │ managing every Istio addon via Helm            │
         │                         │ → anihpj: same lifecycle as the rest           │
         └─────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    11.8  Kiali's Validation Categories — What Gets Checked Beyond VS/DR
         - 11.3 showed three real errors, but VirtualService/DestinationRule
           mistakes are only two of roughly a dozen categories Kiali
           validates on every refresh
         - DEFINITION: every Istio object kind Kiali understands has its
           own set of checks, each with a severity (❌ error, ⚠️ warning,
           or an informational note) and its own code prefix

         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  📖 KEY TERM — VALIDATION CATEGORY                                 │
         │  A group of checks for ONE Istio object kind (Gateway,             │
         │  Sidecar, PeerAuthentication...), sharing a code prefix            │
         │  (KIA0xxx-KIA12xx) and severity; 11.3's two errors came            │
         │  from just ONE category out of roughly a dozen.                    │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         - Why it matters: exam and real-world misconfigurations don't
           only hide in VirtualServices — a missing ServiceAccount on an
           AuthorizationPolicy, an unnamed Service port, or a stale
           Sidecar egress host are just as common, and each lives on a
           different tab than the "Istio Config" list you already know
         - How it works: open a namespace → Istio Config → the object
           list groups warnings by kind; click any row to jump straight
           to the offending line, same as the VS/DR examples in 11.3

         [KIALI VALIDATION CATEGORIES — a representative check per kind]
         ┌──────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────┐
         │ Category             │ Example check Kiali runs                          │ Severity     │
         ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
         │ AuthorizationPolicy  │ KIA0106 — rule's ServiceAccount principal not     │              │
         │                      │ found anywhere in the mesh                        │ ❌ error      │
         ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
         │ DestinationRule      │ KIA0203 — subset selector labels match zero       │              │
         │                      │ live pods (a typo'd version: label)               │ ❌ error      │
         ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
         │ Gateway              │ KIA0302 — selector matches no workload in         │              │
         │                      │ this namespace (see 11.3's corrected example)     │ ❌ error      │
         ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
         │ PeerAuthentication   │ KIA0501 — namespace sets STRICT mTLS but no       │              │
         │                      │ DestinationRule enables ISTIO_MUTUAL to match     │ ⚠️ warning   │
         ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
         │ Ports                │ KIA0601 — Service port name skips the required    │              │
         │                      │ protocol prefix (http-, grpc-, tcp-…)             │ ⚠️ warning   │
         ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
         │ Services             │ KIA0701 — a Deployment has no Service exposing    │              │
         │                      │ a matching containerPort                          │ ⚠️ warning   │
         ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
         │ Sidecar              │ KIA1004 — an egress host in a Sidecar resource    │              │
         │                      │ has no match in the service registry              │ ⚠️ warning   │
         ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
         │ VirtualService       │ KIA1105 — the same host+subset pair is targeted   │              │
         │                      │ by two different route rules                      │ ⚠️ warning   │
         ├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────┤
         │ ServiceEntry         │ KIA1211 — two ServiceEntries define the exact     │              │
         │                      │ same host+port combination                        │ ⚠️ warning   │
         └──────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────┘

         - anihpj gotcha: skills-service's container port was named
           "8090" instead of "http-skills" — Istio's protocol sniffing
           depends on the http-/grpc-/tcp- prefix convention, not the
           number, so requests were silently treated as raw TCP (no
           retries, no HTTP-aware routing) until KIA0601 flagged it

    11.9  Graph Types & Traffic Animation — Reading the Graph Correctly
         - DEFINITION: the Service Graph shown in 11.2 is only ONE of
           four graph types Kiali can render — Graph Settings lets you
           change the "altitude" of the picture without leaving the page
         - Why it matters: picking the wrong graph type can hide the
           answer — an App Graph merges v1 and v2 into a single node, so
           a canary regression that only affects v2 traffic is invisible
           until you switch to the Versioned App Graph
         - How it works — the four graph types, from most to least
           granular:
           • Workload Graph      → one node per Kubernetes workload
             (Deployment/StatefulSet), the most granular view
           • Versioned App Graph → one node per app VERSION (v1 and v2
             drawn separately)
           • App Graph           → one node per app, ALL versions merged
           • Service Graph       → one node per Kubernetes Service, the
             highest-altitude view (this is what 11.2 uses)

         [KIALI GRAPH TYPES — pick the right altitude for the question]
         ┌────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ Graph Type         │ One node =                │ Best anihpj use case                    │
         ├────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ App Graph          │ one app, all versions     │ daily morning health scan               │
         │                    │ merged into one node      │ (fewest nodes, fastest read)            │
         ├────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Versioned App      │ one app VERSION (v1,      │ confirming a canary's v2 slice is       │
         │ Graph              │ v2 shown separately)      │ healthy before shifting to 100%         │
         ├────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Workload Graph     │ one Kubernetes workload   │ a specific pod is crash-looping —       │
         │                    │ (Deployment/StatefulSet)  │ 1:1 with kubectl get deploy             │
         ├────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Service Graph      │ one Kubernetes Service    │ the default 11.2 topology view;         │
         │                    │ (highest altitude)        │ ideal for onboarding a new engineer     │
         └────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Traffic animation: Graph Settings → Traffic Animation overlays
           moving dots on every edge so you can watch requests flow
           without clicking anything
         - How it works: dot density approximates request volume, a dot
           that stutters or pauses mid-edge flags a latency spike on
           that exact hop, and dot color always matches the edge's
           health color from 11.6's legend

         [TRAFFIC ANIMATION — reading the dots on a live edge]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Graph Settings → ✅ Traffic Animation                              │
         │                                                                    │
         │  [jobpost-api]  ··●···●····●··  [skills-service]                   │
         │                 dots = live requests flowing right now             │
         │                                                                    │
         │  Dot spacing → requests/sec (dense dots = high volume)             │
         │  Dot stutter → this hop's edge latency just spiked                 │
         │  Dot color   → matches the edge health color (11.6's legend)       │
         │                                                                    │
         │  anihpj tip: turn animation OFF on a >20-service graph — the       │
         │  redraw cost makes the whole tab lag; turn it back on only         │
         │  for the one edge you are actively debugging                       │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     CHAPTERS 9-11: DAILY WORK TAKEAWAYS (Observability)
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    After these chapters, in your daily work you will:
      • Check Grafana every morning: RED metrics for all anihpj services
      • Know which service is slowest, which has most errors, at a glance
      • Use Jaeger to trace a slow request across ALL services in one view
      • Find bottlenecks: "skills-service DB query takes 1,100ms → add index"
      • Use Kiali service graph as your daily dashboard — see live topology
      • Validate Istio config with istioctl analyze before applying
      • Kiali can catch: missing subsets, port mismatches, VS without DR
      • Remember: metrics = WHAT, traces = WHY, logs = DETAILS
      • Propagate Istio tracing headers in your Django code (x-b3-* headers)
      • Set tracing sampling: 100% in dev, 1-5% in production

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     CHAPTERS 9-11: ICA EXAM TIPS & QUESTIONS (Observability — feeds Troubleshooting 20%)
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    🎯 ICA EXAM FOCUS — Observability is not its own graded domain; it is
       how you FIND the root cause tested by Troubleshooting (20%, see
       17.9-17.11). Skipping this chapter cluster costs you there instead:
      • "Check RED metrics for a service" = Grafana Istio dashboards
      • "Find why a request is slow across services" = Jaeger distributed tracing
      • "See live service topology" = Kiali service graph
      • "Validate Istio config" = istioctl analyze -n <namespace>

    Q1: How do you open the Kiali dashboard?
    A1: istioctl dashboard kiali

    Q2: What are the three RED metrics Istio captures automatically?
    A2: Rate (requests/sec), Errors (4xx/5xx %), Duration (latency p50/p95/p99)

    Q3: How does Istio enable distributed tracing without code changes?
    A3: Envoy automatically injects tracing headers (x-b3-traceid, x-b3-spanid)
        into every request. Your app just needs to propagate these headers.

    Q4: Jaeger shows ZERO traces for the anihpj namespace. Walk the debug
        chain that finds the cause.
    A4: Check, cheapest first:
        1) Generate traffic — traces only exist for sampled requests:
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ for i in $(seq 1 100); do                                │
        │   curl -s -o /dev/null http://$GATEWAY_IP/api/jobs/      │
        │ done                                                     │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        2) Sampling too low? kubectl get telemetry -A — at the default
           1% you need ~100 requests to see a single trace
        3) Tracing provider configured? Check meshConfig
           extensionProviders + a Telemetry resource that references it
        4) App dropping headers? Verify x-b3-* propagation (see Q10).
        Why: no sampling, no provider, or dropped headers all produce an
        empty Jaeger — this order tests them fastest.

    Q5: EXAM TASK: set trace sampling to 100% for the anihpj namespace
        only, leaving the mesh-wide default untouched.
    A5: Apply a namespace-scoped Telemetry resource:
        ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1          │
        │ kind: Telemetry                            │
        │ metadata:                                  │
        │   name: full-sampling                      │
        │   namespace: anihpj   # ← scope = this ns  │
        │ spec:                                      │
        │   tracing:                                 │
        │   - randomSamplingPercentage: 100          │
        └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        Why: a Telemetry object in a workload namespace overrides the
        mesh default only there — dev debugging gets every trace while
        production namespaces keep their cheap 1-5%.

    Q6: EXAM TASK: add a "request_host" label to istio_requests_total
        for anihpj workloads, without touching application code.
    A6: Use the Telemetry API's tagOverrides:
        ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1                  │
        │ kind: Telemetry                                    │
        │ metadata:                                          │
        │   name: custom-labels                              │
        │   namespace: anihpj                                │
        │ spec:                                              │
        │   metrics:                                         │
        │   - providers:                                     │
        │     - name: prometheus                             │
        │     overrides:                                     │
        │     - match:                                       │
        │         metric: REQUEST_COUNT  # requests_total    │
        │       tagOverrides:                                │
        │         request_host:                              │
        │           value: request.host  # CEL expression    │
        └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        Why: Envoy stamps the new label on every sample; Prometheus picks
        it up from the merged metrics endpoint (istio-agent :15020) on
        the next scrape — zero app redeploys.

    Q7: EXAM TASK: enable Envoy access logs for the anihpj namespace
        only, then read jobpost-api's access log.
    A7: Apply namespace-scoped access logging:
        ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1          │
        │ kind: Telemetry                            │
        │ metadata:                                  │
        │   name: access-logs                        │
        │   namespace: anihpj                        │
        │ spec:                                      │
        │   accessLogging:                           │
        │   - providers:                             │
        │     - name: envoy                          │
        └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        Then read the log:
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ kubectl logs deploy/jobpost-api -c istio-proxy -n anihpj │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        Why: a namespace-scoped Telemetry beats mesh-wide
        meshConfig.accessLogFile — you pay the log volume only in the
        namespace you are debugging.

    Q8: Kiali shows a red edge from jobpost-api to skills-service. Give
        the triage sequence.
    A8: 1) Click the edge → per-hop RED metrics: 89 req/s, 8.1% errors,
           p99 1240ms
        2) Check OTHER inbound edges to skills-service — all red means a
           callee (skills-service) problem; only this one red means a
           caller (jobpost-api) problem
        3) Edge panel → "View Traces" → Jaeger opens pre-filtered on
           this hop; open the widest span
        4) Confirm in the proxy log:
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ kubectl logs deploy/skills-service -c istio-proxy \      │
        │   -n anihpj | grep " 503 "                               │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        Why: edge → traces → logs narrows topology → request → cause
        without ever guessing.

    Q9: Alert: "istiod config push latency high, proxies STALE." What do
        you check, in order?
    A9: 1) Grafana → Istio Control Plane Dashboard: istiod CPU/memory,
           push latency, connected proxy count
        2) istioctl proxy-status — any proxy not SYNCED for
           CDS/LDS/EDS/RDS is running on stale routing config
        3) kubectl top pod -n istio-system -l app=istiod (at its limit?)
        4) Fix — scale out or raise limits:
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ kubectl scale deploy/istiod -n istio-system --replicas=2 │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        Why: STALE proxies silently ignore new VirtualServices — a
        routing change that "does nothing" is often an istiod push
        problem, not a YAML problem.

    Q10: Jaeger shows every anihpj service as its own one-span trace
         instead of one connected chain. Fix it in the Django code.
    A10: The apps are dropping trace context between inbound and
         outbound calls. Propagate the B3 headers:
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ # anihpj/tracing.py                                        │
         │ TRACE_HEADERS = ["x-request-id", "x-b3-traceid",           │
         │     "x-b3-spanid", "x-b3-parentspanid",                    │
         │     "x-b3-sampled", "x-b3-flags"]                          │
         │                                                            │
         │ def trace_headers(request):                                │
         │     return {h: request.headers[h]                          │
         │             for h in TRACE_HEADERS                         │
         │             if h in request.headers}                       │
         │                                                            │
         │ # jobpost/views.py — pass context downstream               │
         │ requests.get(                                              │
         │     "http://skills-service:8090/api/skills/",              │
         │     headers=trace_headers(request))                        │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         Why: Envoy creates a span per hop, but only the APP can link an
         inbound request to its outbound calls — forwarding x-b3-* joins
         the per-hop spans into one end-to-end trace.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ 🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — PART 6'S HIDDEN THREAD: THE COORDINATES THAT     │
         │ CARRY ONE INCIDENT ACROSS THREE TOOLS (Ch9 → Ch10 → Ch11 → fixed)    │
         │                                                                      │
         │ Ch9-11 look like three unrelated tools, but the skills-service       │
         │ incident only closes in 12 minutes (11.5) because ONE small set of   │
         │ coordinates travels with you from screen to screen. Lose one and a   │
         │ 12-minute fix becomes an hour of blind tab-hopping.                  │
         │                                                                      │
         │ ① GRAFANA (Ch9) narrows the whole mesh to ONE coordinate:            │
         │    service=skills-service, window=last 15 min, p99=1240ms. That is   │
         │    the only thing you carry forward — a name and a time window, not  │
         │    a saved query.                                                    │
         │                                                                      │
         │ ② KIALI (Ch11) takes that coordinate as a namespace filter and       │
         │    instantly adds a SECOND coordinate Grafana never had: the exact   │
         │    CALLER. Grafana graphed skills-service alone; Kiali's graph shows │
         │    the red edge is specifically jobpost-api -> skills-service, 8.1%  │
         │    errors — every other inbound edge to skills-service is still      │
         │    green, which rules out a mesh-wide problem in one glance.         │
         │                                                                      │
         │ ③ JAEGER (Ch10) receives both coordinates (the edge, the window) as  │
         │    a service+operation search and returns a THIRD coordinate: the    │
         │    exact span — SELECT ... FROM skills WHERE user_id, 1,100ms.       │
         │                                                                      │
         │ ④ THE WIRE BETWEEN ② AND ③: Kiali's edge panel has a "View Traces"   │
         │    button (11.5, step 2->3) that pre-fills Jaeger's search with the  │
         │    coordinates Kiali already holds — you never retype a namespace or │
         │    a service name by hand.                                           │
         │                                                                      │
         │ ⑤ THE FIX (psql CREATE INDEX) happens OUTSIDE all three tools — but  │
         │    it is CONFIRMED inside Kiali, because Kiali is the only one of    │
         │    the three that redraws itself every 15 seconds (11.6) without you │
         │    re-running anything: the SAME red edge from step ② turns green,   │
         │    closing the loop back to Grafana's p99 panel from step ①.         │
         │                                                                      │
         │ THE INSIGHT: Ch9-11 are not three skills to memorize separately —    │
         │ they are one coordinate system (service -> edge -> span) that gets   │
         │ more precise at each stop, and Kiali is both the SECOND stop (finds  │
         │ the edge) and the LAST stop (confirms the fix). That dual role is    │
         │ why Kiali closes Part 6 instead of just extending it.                │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
         ⚡ Scan for red first: on a graph with 20+ nodes, ignore every
           green and gray node and jump straight to the one red edge —
           Kiali's whole value is that you read ONE broken connection,
           not all seven anihpj services.
         ⚡ Trust the wizard over hand-typed YAML: a wizard-generated
           subset can never typo a version: label because it reads that
           label off LIVE pods (11.4) — reserve hand-written
           VirtualServices for the cases a wizard does not cover.
         ⚡ Read ⚠️ warnings differently from ❌ errors: a KIA1106 "two
           VirtualServices, same host" warning is often an intentional
           in-progress migration, not a bug — only ❌ errors reliably
           block traffic, so do not burn exam-clock minutes chasing
           every icon.
         ⚡ Run istioctl analyze -n anihpj before opening Kiali: it is
           scriptable and instant, so you already know whether a problem
           is CONFIG (analyze catches it) or RUNTIME (analyze will not)
           before the graph even loads.
         ⚡ Default to the App Graph for a fast morning scan (fewest
           nodes, fastest read) and switch to the Versioned App Graph
           only when you need to isolate one canary version's traffic
           (11.9).
         ⚡ Turn Traffic Animation off on any graph bigger than ~20
           services and back on only for the one edge you are actively
           debugging (11.9) — it is a nice-to-have that costs render
           time mid-incident.

PART 7: SECURITY — ZERO-TRUST WITH ISTIO                                 🟡
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  Chapters 12-13  ·  Difficulty: 🟡 core (🔴 in 12.13, 13.8)  ·  25%
  of the ICA exam — official domain "Securing Workloads"
  What you'll build by the end: a zero-trust anihpj mesh where every hop is
  encrypted (mTLS) AND explicitly authorized (AuthorizationPolicy) — nothing
  reachable by default.

  [PART 7 INTRO]
  Parts 5 and 6 made anihpj's traffic fast and visible — canary releases,
  retries, Kiali, Jaeger — but every one of those hops still travels as plain,
  unauthenticated HTTP. Any pod that learns a Service's DNS name can call it
  and read the response, and nothing downstream can prove who actually sent
  the request. Part 7 is where anihpj stops trusting the network and starts
  verifying every call.

  Like Part 1, this Part starts by making you uncomfortable: 12.1 walks a
  rogue pod through sniffing JWTs, impersonating user-service, and reading
  anihpj's Postgres credentials off the wire — all without Istio in the way.
  That threat model earns Chapter 12's mTLS and Chapter 13's
  AuthorizationPolicy their keep — by the end of Chapter 13, every one of
  those attacks is blocked by two CRDs applied once per service, not a line of
  Django code.

  🧠 ANALOGY. Picture anihpj's mesh before Part 7 as an office building with a
  locked front door and nothing else: a visitor badges in at reception (the
  ingress gateway), but every internal door — payroll (user-service), the
  server room (postgres), the CEO's suite (auth-service) — stands unlocked
  once you're inside. mTLS is the building issuing every employee an
  unforgeable badge that's CHECKED at every internal door, not just the front
  one. AuthorizationPolicy is the building deciding WHICH badges open WHICH
  doors — the payroll badge doesn't open the server room, even though both are
  equally real badges. Identity answers "who are you?"; authorization answers
  "are you allowed in HERE?" — a building needs both, in that order, or the
  badge system is theater.

  🐍 OUR RUNNING EXAMPLE — anihpj. Every manifest and diagram below targets the
  same anihpj namespace and the same seven services used since Part 1 —
  jobpost-api, user-service, skills-service, location-service, notification-
  service, auth-service, and search-service — plus the postgres database they
  all share. Part 7 adds no new services; it adds RULES for how the existing
  ones may talk to each other.

  [HOW THE CHAPTERS FIT — Part 7 map]
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 12.1-12.4 identity ──▶ 12.5-12.13 hardening & internals              │
  │  every anihpj pod        secure naming, policy hierarchy, auto       │
  │  gets a SPIFFE cert      mTLS, TTL/rotation internals                │
  │        │                                            │                │
  │        └────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘                │
  │                             ▼                                        │
  │        13.1-13.4  deny-all → explicit ALLOW → JWT via RequestAuth    │
  │                             │                                        │
  │                             ▼                                        │
  │        13.5-13.12  exclusions · TCP ports · dry-run · AUDIT/CUSTOM · │
  │                    the complete evaluation order                     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Read it top to bottom: 12.1-12.4 give every pod a verifiable identity and
  turn on encryption; 12.5-12.13 harden and explain that identity (secure
  naming, policy hierarchy, auto mTLS, rotation internals) without changing
  the mental model; then 13.1-13.4 spend that identity on a separate decision
  — who's ALLOWED to call whom — before 13.5-13.12 close out the exam's
  remaining edge cases.

  🧭 DECISION GUIDE — which security control do you reach for?
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ If you...                                         │ Then...                                          │
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ need to encrypt all service-to-service traffic    │ PeerAuthentication mode: STRICT (12.3)           │
  │ must migrate a live mesh to mTLS, zero downtime   │ PERMISSIVE first, then STRICT (12.3-12.4)        │
  │ need to restrict which service may call which     │ AuthorizationPolicy ALLOW/DENY rules (13.2-13.3) │
  │ must validate a JWT from auth-service in the mesh │ RequestAuthentication (13.4)                     │
  │ need to protect a non-HTTP port (postgres:5432)   │ AuthorizationPolicy + to.operation.ports (13.6)  │
  │ want to test a risky policy before it goes live   │ istio.io/dry-run: "true" annotation (13.8)       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  WITHOUT vs WITH Part 7 — why zero-trust isn't optional
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ WITHOUT Part 7 (mTLS off, no AuthzPolicy)     │ WITH Part 7 done (zero-trust anihpj)          │
  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Traffic between services is plaintext HTTP    │ Every hop is mTLS-encrypted, automatically    │
  │ Any service can call any other service        │ AuthorizationPolicy denies by default         │
  │ Service identity is just an IP — easy to fake │ SPIFFE X.509 cert — cryptographically real    │
  │ One compromised pod can reach the whole mesh  │ Blast radius = only what that identity allows │
  │ Security is enforced only at the ingress edge │ Zero-trust — enforced on every internal hop   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  CAPTION: none of the WITH column requires touching jobpost-api, user-
  service, or any other Django app's code — every row is a property of the
  mesh, configured once as Istio CRDs and enforced by every Envoy sidecar from
  then on.

  [PART 7 SUMMARY + IMPLEMENTATION]
  By the end of Part 7, anihpj runs as a genuine zero-trust mesh: every one of
  the seven services (plus postgres) speaks mTLS only, nothing is reachable by
  default, and each ALLOW rule documents exactly who may call whom and how.
  Implementation thread:

      anihpj mesh, PeerAuthentication mode: PERMISSIVE (Week 1)
            │  apply PeerAuthentication mode: STRICT, ns: anihpj
            ▼
      every hop now mTLS-encrypted — plaintext callers rejected (12.3)
            │  apply AuthorizationPolicy deny-all, ns: anihpj
            ▼
      🚨 everything 403s — by design, nothing is ALLOWed yet
            │  apply 6 ALLOW policies (ingressgw→jobpost-api,
            │  jobpost-api→{user,skills,location}-service, user-
            │  service→auth-service, prometheus→all :metrics)
            │  + RequestAuthentication jwt-auth
            ▼
      ✅ anihpj is zero-trust — encrypted (Ch12) AND authorized (Ch13)

  CAPTION: the deny-all step sits AFTER the STRICT switch and BEFORE the ALLOW
  policies above for teaching clarity — 13.3's real rollout reverses steps 2
  and 3 (ALLOWs first, deny-all last, ideally behind a dry-run) so production
  traffic never sees a live 403 storm.

Chapter 12: Mutual TLS (mTLS) — Encrypting Everything
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Chapter 12 of 12-13  ·  Difficulty: 🟡 (🔴 in 12.10-12.13)  ·  🎯 Securing
  Workloads — 25% of the ICA exam
  "Every anihpj pod says 'trust me' over the wire — who, cryptographically,
  is actually calling?"

  [WHY THIS MATTERS]
  Parts 5 and 6 made anihpj's traffic fast and visible — Gateways, canary
  VirtualServices, circuit-breaking DestinationRules, Kiali graphs, Jaeger
  traces — but every one of those beautifully instrumented hops still
  travels as plain, unauthenticated HTTP between pods. jobpost-api still
  shouts "GET /users/42" across the wire in the clear, complete with the
  caller's JWT and session cookie, and any pod that lands on the same node
  can tcpdump the lot. Chapter 12 is the first time anihpj gets a REAL
  identity: not a Pod name, not an IP, but an unforgeable SPIFFE X.509
  certificate that says exactly which ServiceAccount issued this request,
  minted and rotated by istiod without touching a line of Django. By 12.13
  every one of jobpost-api, user-service, skills-service, location-service,
  notification-service, auth-service, and search-service will hold — and
  prove — its own cryptographic identity on every single hop. Chapter 13
  then spends that identity to decide who may call whom; none of that is
  possible until Chapter 12 establishes WHO everyone is.

  [LEARNING OBJECTIVES]
  ✅ Explain why plaintext service-to-service HTTP is a sniffing,
     impersonation, and lateral-movement risk — even "internal" traffic
  ✅ Configure PeerAuthentication in PERMISSIVE, STRICT, DISABLE, and UNSET
     modes at mesh, namespace, and workload scope, and predict which one
     wins when scopes overlap
  ✅ Trace the full certificate lifecycle: CSR at pod startup, istiod
     (Citadel CA) issuance, SDS delivery to Envoy, and grace-period-ratio
     rotation around the 12-hour mark
  ✅ Read a SPIFFE ID (spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api) and
     name which segment is the trust domain, namespace, and ServiceAccount
  ✅ Tell an mTLS failure (TCP reset, no HTTP code at all) apart from an
     AuthorizationPolicy failure (HTTP 403 RBAC) using istioctl x describe
     pod and istioctl proxy-config secret
  ✅ Explain the DestinationRule/PeerAuthentication TLS contract and why a
     stale tls.mode: DISABLE causes 503s the moment STRICT is enabled
  ✅ Describe auto mTLS (Istio 1.5+) and identify when an external CA
     (plug-in certs, SPIRE, cert-manager) should replace istiod's built-in CA

  [EXAM RELEVANCE]
  Chapter 12 lives inside "Securing Workloads," the ICA's official domain
  worth 25% of the exam — tied with Traffic Management for the single
  heaviest weighting. Roughly half of that 25% is graded on material
  covered in THIS chapter alone (the other half is Chapter 13's
  AuthorizationPolicy):

  [EXAM RELEVANCE -- Chapter 12's slice of Securing Workloads, 25%]
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────┐
  │ ICA-graded skill                      │ Where it's covered │
  ├───────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────┤
  │ Configure PeerAuthentication modes    │ 12.3, 12.6, 12.10  │
  │ Explain cert issuance and rotation    │ 12.4, 12.13        │

  └───────────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────┘

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

  Read top to bottom: 12.1-12.2 name the problem and the concept, 12.3-12.4
  turn mTLS on and explain how its certificates are born, 12.5-12.7 harden
  that identity against impersonation and teach you to troubleshoot it, and
  12.8-12.13 go under the hood on everything left — the DR/PA contract,
  external CAs, the UNSET mode, SPIFFE anatomy, auto mTLS, and rotation
  timing.

    12.1 The Security Problem Without mTLS
         - Inside a Kubernetes cluster: traffic is plain HTTP by default
         - Any compromised pod can sniff traffic from other services
         - Anyone with access to the network can read jobpost DB passwords,
           user tokens, session data passing between anihpj services
         - Traditional solution: implement TLS in every service → complex
         [THREAT DIAGRAM: rogue pod sniffing plain HTTP between services]

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     VISUAL: SECURITY THREAT MODEL — BEFORE vs AFTER ISTIO
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  WITHOUT ISTIO — 3 ATTACK VECTORS OPEN                              │

         │                                                                     │

         │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │

         │  │  "GET /users/42/payment-info"                            │      │
         │  │                                                          │      │
         │  │  ❌ Any service can call any other service               │      │
         │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
         │                                                                     │
         │  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════    │
         │                                                                     │
         │  WITH ISTIO — ALL 3 ATTACKS BLOCKED                                 │
         │                                                                     │
         │  DEFENSE 1: mTLS Encryption (PeerAuthentication)                    │
         │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
         │  │                                                          │      │
         │  │  [jobpost-api] ──🔒 mTLS tunnel ──▶ [user-service]      │      │

         │  │       │         │ ENCRYPTED    │     │  Decrypts with    │      │

         │                                                                     │

         │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐      │
         │  │                                                          │      │
         │  │  [jobpost-api] ──mTLS──▶ [😈 fake-user-svc]             │      │

         │  │                "Show me your SPIFFE certificate!"        │      │
         │  │                              │                           │      │
         │  │                fake-svc presents: NO VALID CERT ❌       │      │
         │  │                (or presents: spiffe://.../ns/hack/sa/x)  │      │
         │  │                                                          │      │
         │  │  ✅ Envoy REJECTS — certificate not from anihpj/user-svc │      │
         │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
         │                                                                     │

         │  │           ❌ 403 Forbidden — BLOCKED! ✅                 │      │
         │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘      │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [THREAT MODEL — QUICK RECAP]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  ATTACK 1: Network Sniffing (Man-in-the-Middle)                    │
         │                                                                    │
         │  [jobpost-api] ──HTTP──▶ [user-service]                           │
         │                    │                                               │

         │               "password=SuperSecret123"            ← DATA EXPOSED  │
         │                                                                    │
         │  ATTACK 2: Service Impersonation                                   │
         │                                                                    │
         │  [jobpost-api] ──HTTP──▶ [😈 fake-user-service]                   │
         │                          (attacker deployed a pod                  │
         │                           named "user-service" in a                │
         │                           different namespace)                     │
         │                          "I'm the real user-service — trust me!"  │
         │                          → Returns fake user data                  │
         │                                                                    │
         │  ATTACK 3: Lateral Movement                                        │
