         │  [😈 compromised skills-svc] ──HTTP──▶ [user-service]            │
         │  "Please give me all users' personal data..."                      │
         │  → No AuthorizationPolicy = request ALLOWED!                      │
         │  → All user data exfiltrated                                       │
         │                                                                    │
         │  WITH ISTIO mTLS + AuthorizationPolicy:                            │
         │  ✅ Attack 1 blocked: all traffic is encrypted                     │
         │  ✅ Attack 2 blocked: fake service has no valid SPIFFE cert        │
         │  ✅ Attack 3 blocked: AuthzPolicy denies skills-svc→user-svc call  │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Bundle those gaps together and a single foothold on the
           node/network — with mTLS off — buys an attacker four
           separate capabilities, side by side:

         [ATTACKER'S TOOLKIT — 4 THINGS A FOOTHOLD BUYS YOU WITHOUT mTLS]
         ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐
         │ 1. 🔍 Sniffing  │  │ 2. 🎭 Fake Svc  │  │ 3. 😈 MITM      │  │ 4. 🚪 Lateral   │
         │ tcpdump reads   │  │ fake pod claims │  │ intercept +     │  │ foothold =      │
         │ plaintext body  │  │ "user-service"  │  │ modify traffic  │  │ full mesh reach │
         │ + creds ❌       │  │ no ID check ❌   │  │ undetected ❌    │  │ no extra ID ❌   │
         └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘

         - The real question is scope: how far does ONE compromised pod's
           damage spread? Compare anihpj's blast radius before Istio's
           STRICT mTLS is on vs after:

         [BLAST RADIUS — ONE COMPROMISED POD, BEFORE vs AFTER STRICT mTLS]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ SCENARIO: attacker gets remote code execution inside the skills-service │
         │ pod (e.g. a vulnerable dependency) — the SAME compromised pod in both   │
         │ panels below                                                            │
         │                                                                         │
         │ BEFORE — no PeerAuthentication STRICT mode (blast radius = WHOLE mesh)  │
         │                                                                         │
         │   😈 skills-service (compromised)                                       │
         │        │   plaintext HTTP, zero identity check on any hop               │
         │        ├──▶ jobpost-api    ✅ reachable — traffic readable & spoofable   │
         │        ├──▶ user-service   ✅ reachable — traffic readable & spoofable   │
         │        └──▶ postgres       ✅ reachable — DB creds sniffed in cleartext  │
         │                                                                         │
         │   BLAST RADIUS: every anihpj service the attacker can now read or spoof │
         │                                                                         │
         │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
         │                                                                         │
         │ AFTER — PeerAuthentication mode: STRICT (blast radius = ONE identity)   │
         │                                                                         │
         │   😈 skills-service (compromised)                                       │
         │        │   every hop now demands mTLS + a valid SPIFFE certificate      │
         │        ├──▶ jobpost-api    ✅ its own, already-allowed call — unchanged  │
         │        ├──▶ user-service   ✅ its own, already-allowed call — unchanged  │
         │        └──▶ postgres       ❌ tries "I am jobpost-api" — but its Envoy   │
         │             can only present ONE cert: spiffe://.../ns/anihpj/sa/       │
         │             skills-service (SDS-issued, can't be faked). AuthzPolicy:   │
         │             ALLOW postgres callers = jobpost-api ONLY → ❌ 403 REJECTED  │
         │                                                                         │
         │   BLAST RADIUS: only what skills-service's own identity could already   │
         │   reach — it can never borrow jobpost-api's or user-service's identity  │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    12.2 What is Mutual TLS (mTLS)?
         - Regular TLS: server proves identity to client (HTTPS website)
         - Mutual TLS: BOTH sides prove identity to each other
         - Istio issues X.509 SVID certificates (SPIFFE standard) to every workload
         - Certificate contains: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api
         - This certificate identifies the service, not just the node/IP
         - Rotation: certificates expire and rotate every 24 hours automatically
         [mTLS HANDSHAKE DIAGRAM: jobpost-api ↔ user-service certificate exchange]

         [mTLS HANDSHAKE LADDER — jobpost-api ↔ user-service, step by step]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │   Envoy @ jobpost-api                 Envoy @ user-service      │
         │       │                                         │               │
         │       │ ① ClientHello — TLS 1.3, ALPN "istio"   │               │
         │       │────────────────────────────────────────▶│               │
         │       │                                         │               │
         │       │ ② ServerHello + server SVID certificate │               │
         │       │◀────────────────────────────────────────│               │
         │       │      spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/  │               │
         │       │      sa/user-service                    │               │
         │       │                                         │               │
         │       │ ③ client verifies the server cert:      │               │
         │       │    • signed by the mesh root CA?        │               │
         │       │    • SAN = the SPIFFE ID istiod says    │               │
         │       │      user-service must have? (→ 12.5)   │               │
         │       │    • not expired?  → all checks ✅       │               │
         │       │                                         │               │
         │       │ ④ client sends its OWN SVID certificate │               │
         │       │────────────────────────────────────────▶│               │
         │       │      spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/  │               │
         │       │      sa/jobpost-api                     │               │
         │       │                                         │               │
         │       │ ⑤ server verifies chain + records the   │               │
         │       │    caller principal for AuthzPolicy     │               │
         │       │                                         │               │
         │       │ ⑥ 🔒 encrypted tunnel established        │               │
         │       │◀═══════════════════════════════════════▶│               │
         │       │    "GET /users/42" now travels encrypted│               │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [mTLS EXPLAINED — what happens in each handshake]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  WITHOUT mTLS (plain HTTP):                            │
         │  jobpost-api ──────────────────────────▶ user-service  │
         │               "GET /users/42 HTTP/1.1"                 │
         │               (anyone can read this!)                  │
         │                                                        │
         │  WITH mTLS (Istio automatic):                          │
         │                                                        │
         │  ① Envoy(jobpost) → "Hello, I am jobpost-api"         │
         │                    presents certificate (SVID)         │
         │  ② Envoy(user)   → "I am user-service"                │
         │                    presents certificate (SVID)         │
         │  ③ BOTH verify each other's certificates with istiod   │
         │  ④ Encrypted tunnel established                        │
         │  ⑤ "GET /users/42" sent through encrypted tunnel      │
         │                                                        │
         │  ✅ No code change in Django to get mTLS!              │
         │  ✅ Certificates auto-issued and rotated by istiod     │
         │  ✅ SPIFFE identity — tied to service, not IP          │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    12.3 PeerAuthentication — Configuring mTLS Mode
         - PeerAuthentication is the Istio CRD that controls mTLS
         - Three modes:
           • PERMISSIVE: accept both plain HTTP and mTLS (migration mode)
           • STRICT: reject all plain HTTP — enforce mTLS everywhere
           • DISABLE: turn off mTLS (for debugging only)
         - Apply per namespace or per workload
         - anihpj: start with PERMISSIVE during migration, then STRICT
         [YAML: PeerAuthentication for anihpj namespace in STRICT mode]

         [PeerAuthentication YAML — enforce mTLS for anihpj]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1                      │
         │  kind: PeerAuthentication                              │
         │  metadata:                                             │
         │    name: default                                       │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                   │
         │  spec:                                                 │
         │    mtls:                                               │
         │      mode: STRICT   # ALL traffic must use mTLS       │
         │                     # Plain HTTP will be rejected      │
         │                                                        │
         │  # Alternative: per-workload only                      │
         │  spec:                                                 │
         │    selector:                                           │
         │      matchLabels:                                      │
         │        app: user-service   # Only for user-service     │
         │    mtls:                                               │
         │      mode: STRICT                                      │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    12.4 Certificate Lifecycle — How istiod Issues Certs
         - Every Pod gets an X.509 certificate at startup via istiod CA
         - Certificate Authority is built into istiod (no external CA needed)
         - SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Document (SVID) format
         - Rotation: 24-hour default TTL; istio-agent requests renewal
           once the default grace-period ratio (0.5) of that lifetime
           has elapsed — around the 12-hour mark, not moments before
           expiry (see 12.13 for the full mechanics)
         - Plugging in external CAs (AWS ACM, Vault, Cert-Manager)

         🔧 UNDER THE HOOD. Certificate delivery (T=0.6s below) rides
           SDS (Secret Discovery Service) — a gRPC streaming API
           istio-agent exposes to its own sidecar over a local Unix
           Domain Socket, not a file istiod writes to disk. Envoy
           holds the cert and private key in memory only, and SDS
           PUSHES the replacement the instant istio-agent gets a new
           one — which is why 12.13's rotation is a live swap, zero
           pod restart required.
         [CERT ISSUANCE FLOW DIAGRAM: Pod starts → istiod issues cert → mTLS ready]

         [CERTIFICATE LIFECYCLE — full flow for anihpj]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  T=0s:   kubectl apply deploys jobpost-api Pod                     │
         │  T=0.1s: Istio Mutating Webhook INJECTS istio-proxy sidecar       │
         │  T=0.2s: Pod starts — istio-proxy starts alongside Django          │
         │  T=0.3s: istio-proxy sends CSR to istiod via port 15012           │
         │          CSR contains: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/          │
         │                        sa/jobpost-api-serviceaccount               │
         │  T=0.5s: istiod (Citadel CA) validates ServiceAccount identity    │
         │          istiod signs X.509 cert with 24h expiry                  │
         │  T=0.6s: Certificate delivered to istio-proxy (in-memory)         │
         │  T=0.7s: mTLS ready! All outbound calls from this pod now use     │
         │          the certificate to authenticate                           │
         │                                                                    │
         │  T=~12h:   grace-period ratio 0.5 reached → rotation begins        │
         │  T=~12h+j: new CSR sent → new cert issued → old cert replaced      │
         │  T=24h:    original cert's validity ends — already rotated         │
         │                                                                    │
         │  CERT ANATOMY:                                                     │
         │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
         │  │  Subject:  spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/             │     │
         │  │            sa/jobpost-api-serviceaccount                  │     │
         │  │  Issuer:   istiod (cluster.local root CA)                │     │
         │  │  Valid:    24 hours                                       │     │
         │  │  SANs:     URI:spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/...      │     │
         │  │  Uses:     mTLS authentication only                      │     │
         │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [PERMISSIVE vs STRICT mTLS — migration path for anihpj]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  WEEK 1: Add Istio, keep PERMISSIVE mode                          │
         │  ────────────────────────────────────                             │
         │  • Sidecars injected, no traffic disruption                       │
         │  • Existing services still use plain HTTP internally              │
         │  • Kiali shows: some connections encrypted, some plain            │
         │  • Validate: all services working → check Kiali graph             │
         │                                                                    │
         │  WEEK 2: Switch to STRICT mode per namespace                      │
         │  ────────────────────────────────────────────                     │
         │  • kubectl apply PeerAuthentication with mode: STRICT             │
         │  • Any non-sidecar service → 403 errors start appearing           │
         │  • Fix: ensure ALL consumers have Istio sidecars injected         │
         │  • Validate: no plain HTTP in Kiali → all edges show lock icon    │
         │                                                                    │
         │  RESULT: Every service-to-service call in anihpj is encrypted     │
         │  without a single line of Django code changed ✅                  │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    12.5  Secure Naming — Preventing Service Impersonation
         - DEFINITION: secure naming is istiod's built-in mapping of
           "service name → the SPIFFE identities allowed to SERVE it";
           client Envoys enforce it on every mTLS handshake
         - Why it matters: a VALID certificate alone only proves mesh
           membership, not the right to answer as user-service — without
           secure naming, ANY workload's cert could front any service
         - How it works:
           • istiod watches Services and the ServiceAccounts behind them
           • it compiles the map and pushes it to every client Envoy (xDS)
           • in the handshake, the client compares the presented SVID
             against the identities registered for the service it dialed
           → mismatch = handshake aborted before any app data is sent
         - Network tricks are useless against it: stolen ClusterIPs,
           poisoned DNS and spoofed IPs all fail the cryptographic check

         [IMPERSONATION ATTACK — stolen ClusterIP, defeated by secure naming]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  GOAL: attacker wants to receive jobpost-api → user-service     │
         │  traffic (sessions, JWTs, PII)                                  │
         │                                                                 │
         │  STEP 1  compromise the "test-team" ServiceAccount              │
         │          → attacker now owns a VALID mesh certificate:          │
         │            spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/test-team        │
         │  STEP 2  deploy a fake pod and hijack user-service's            │
         │          ClusterIP (or poison DNS) to redirect traffic          │
         │  STEP 3  jobpost-api dials "user-service:8080"                  │
         │          → packets land on the fake pod — the NETWORK           │
         │            layer has been fooled successfully 😈                 │
         │  STEP 4  mTLS handshake — fake pod presents its SVID:           │
         │            …/ns/anihpj/sa/test-team  (valid! trusted CA!)       │
         │                                                                 │
         │  WITHOUT secure naming:                                         │
         │  cert is valid + chains to the mesh root → accepted             │
         │  → live anihpj traffic flows to the attacker ❌                  │
         │                                                                 │
         │  WITH secure naming (Istio default, always on):                 │
         │  client Envoy consults the istiod-pushed map:                   │
         │    "user-service" ⇒ only …/ns/anihpj/sa/user-service            │
         │  presented …/sa/test-team ⇒ MISMATCH                            │
         │  → handshake ABORTED at STEP 4 — the TCP connection is          │
         │    torn down before a single application byte is sent ✅         │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [SECURE NAMING MAP — pushed by istiod to every client Envoy]
         ┌───────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
         │ Service being dialed          │ authorized server identity      │
         ├───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
         │ user-service.anihpj:8080      │ …/ns/anihpj/sa/user-service ✅   │
         │ jobpost-api.anihpj:8000       │ …/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api ✅    │
         │ skills-service.anihpj:8090    │ …/ns/anihpj/sa/skills-service ✅ │
         │ user-service.anihpj:8080      │ …/sa/test-team ❌ NOT AUTHORIZED │
         └───────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘

    12.6  PeerAuthentication Policy Hierarchy — Mesh → Namespace → Workload
         - DEFINITION: PeerAuthentication can be declared at three scopes:
           mesh-wide (root namespace istio-system, no selector),
           namespace-wide (any namespace, no selector), and
           workload-specific (spec.selector.matchLabels set)
         - Why it matters: production meshes layer all three — a mesh-wide
           PERMISSIVE fallback, STRICT per hardened namespace, plus the
           odd workload exemption; you must predict which one applies
         - The rule: the NARROWEST match wins — workload beats namespace,
           namespace beats mesh (think CSS specificity, but for mTLS)
         - Only ONE mesh-wide and ONE namespace-wide policy take effect
           (convention: name them "default") — if duplicates exist, the
           OLDEST wins and newer ones are silently ignored
         - Several workload policies may exist; if two select the same
           pod, again the OLDEST wins — delete stale ones to avoid
           mystery behaviour

         [POLICY PRECEDENCE — narrowest match wins]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Pod: user-service-6b9c…  (app: user-service, ns: anihpj)       │
         │                                                                 │
         │  candidate policies:                            mode            │
         │  ① MESH-WIDE   istio-system, no selector       PERMISSIVE       │
         │  ② NAMESPACE   anihpj, no selector             STRICT           │
         │  ③ WORKLOAD    selector app: user-service      DISABLE          │
         │                (legacy port exemption)                          │
         │                                                                 │
         │  precedence:  ③ beats ② beats ①                                 │
         │  → effective mode for THIS pod:  DISABLE   (from ③)             │
         │  → every other anihpj pod:       STRICT    (from ②)             │
         │  → pods in other namespaces:     PERMISSIVE (from ①)            │
         │                                                                 │
         │  delete ③ → pod falls back to ②  (STRICT)                       │
         │  delete ② → namespace falls back to ①  (PERMISSIVE)             │
         │  delete ① → Istio built-in default:  PERMISSIVE                 │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [THE 3 SCOPES — YAML differences at a glance]
         ┌──────────────┬─────────────────┬─────────────────┬──────────────┐
         │ Scope        │ namespace:      │ selector:       │ priority     │
         ├──────────────┼─────────────────┼─────────────────┼──────────────┤
         │ Mesh-wide    │ istio-system    │ (none)          │ LOWEST       │
         │              │ (the root ns)   │                 │ (fallback)   │
         ├──────────────┼─────────────────┼─────────────────┼──────────────┤
         │ Namespace    │ anihpj          │ (none)          │ MIDDLE       │
         ├──────────────┼─────────────────┼─────────────────┼──────────────┤
         │ Workload     │ anihpj          │ matchLabels:    │ HIGHEST      │
         │              │                 │   app: user-svc │              │
         └──────────────┴─────────────────┴─────────────────┴──────────────┘

         [3-SCOPE YAML — same CRD, three different reaches]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1   # v1 GA since Istio 1.22    │
         │  kind: PeerAuthentication                                       │
         │  metadata:                                                      │
         │    name: default                                                │
         │    namespace: istio-system    ← root namespace = MESH-WIDE      │
         │  spec:                                                          │
         │    mtls:                                                        │
         │      mode: PERMISSIVE         # mesh-level fallback             │
         │  ---                                                            │
         │  apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1                               │
         │  kind: PeerAuthentication                                       │
         │  metadata:                                                      │
         │    name: default                                                │
         │    namespace: anihpj          ← no selector = NAMESPACE-WIDE    │
         │  spec:                                                          │
         │    mtls:                                                        │
         │      mode: STRICT             # all of anihpj must use mTLS     │
         │  ---                                                            │
         │  apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1                               │
         │  kind: PeerAuthentication                                       │
         │  metadata:                                                      │
         │    name: legacy-batch-exempt                                    │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                            │
         │  spec:                                                          │
         │    selector:                                                    │
         │      matchLabels:                                               │
         │        app: legacy-batch      ← selector = WORKLOAD scope       │
         │    mtls:                                                        │
         │      mode: PERMISSIVE         # this ONE app may still get      │
         │                               # plaintext (overrides STRICT)    │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    12.7  mTLS Troubleshooting — Common Scenarios and Solutions
         - Golden rule 1: STRICT rejects plaintext at the TCP layer — the
           caller sees "connection reset by peer", NEVER an HTTP 403
           → if you see 403 "RBAC: access denied", the problem is an
             AuthorizationPolicy (Chapter 13), not mTLS
         - Golden rule 2: 503 (response flag UC) minutes after enabling
           STRICT almost always means a stale DestinationRule still says
           tls.mode: DISABLE on the client side (deep dive in 12.8)
         - Golden rule 3: measure before guessing — four modern probes:
           istioctl x describe pod, istioctl proxy-config secret, the
           Kiali lock icons, and a raw openssl s_client handshake

         [mTLS TROUBLESHOOTING MATRIX — symptom → root cause → fix]
         ┌─────────────────────┬─────────────────────┬─────────────────────┐
         │ SYMPTOM             │ ROOT CAUSE          │ FIX                 │
         ├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
         │ 503 (flag UC) right │ stale Destination-  │ set tls.mode:       │
         │ after enabling      │ Rule with tls.mode: │ ISTIO_MUTUAL or     │
         │ STRICT              │ DISABLE (client)    │ delete the tls      │
         │                     │                     │ block entirely      │
         ├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
         │ curl: "connection   │ plaintext hit a     │ inject sidecar into │
         │ reset by peer" —    │ STRICT port — mTLS  │ the caller pod; or  │
         │ NOT an HTTP 403!    │ rejects at the TCP  │ PERMISSIVE while    │
         │                     │ layer               │ migrating           │
         ├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
         │ sidecar-less pod    │ STRICT demands a    │ label namespace     │
         │ can't reach anihpj  │ client SVID cert    │ istio-injection=    │
         │ services            │ it does not have    │ enabled + rollout   │
         │                     │                     │ restart             │
         ├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
         │ calls OK from ns A, │ PA scope differs    │ align PeerAuthN;    │
         │ fail from ns B      │ between namespaces  │ check istioctl x    │
         │                     │                     │ describe pod        │
         ├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
         │ HTTP 403 "RBAC:     │ NOT mTLS! An        │ fix the Authz-      │
         │ access denied"      │ AuthorizationPolicy │ Policy (Ch 13)      │
         │                     │ denied the caller   │                     │
         ├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
         │ TLS handshake       │ istiod down >24h —  │ restore istiod;     │
         │ fails, cert expired │ no CSR renewals     │ restart pod for a   │
         │                     │ happened            │ fresh CSR + cert    │
         └─────────────────────┴─────────────────────┴─────────────────────┘

         [mTLS VERIFICATION TOOLBOX — modern commands only]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  # 1 — one-shot mTLS posture of a pod (BEST first move)         │
         │  istioctl x describe pod jobpost-api-7d9f4b-x2v4c -n anihpj     │
         │  #   → prints effective PeerAuthentication + DR TLS mode        │
         │                                                                 │
         │  # 2 — inspect the live SPIFFE cert Envoy holds in memory       │
         │  istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj      │
         │  #   → shows "default" cert + ROOTCA, ~24h validity window      │
         │                                                                 │
         │  # 3 — Kiali:  Graph → Display → Security                       │
         │  #   → every encrypted edge shows a 🔒 padlock icon              │
         │                                                                 │
         │  # 4 — raw probe: openssl against the service port              │
         │  openssl s_client -connect user-service.anihpj:8080             │
         │  #   → shows the presented chain; SAN = SPIFFE URI              │
         │                                                                 │
         │  ⚠️  "istioctl authn tls-check" was REMOVED long ago —          │
         │      if a runbook still mentions it, use #1/#2 instead          │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    12.8  Deep Dive — The DR/PA TLS Contract (Why 503s Happen)
         - DEFINITION: mTLS is a CONTRACT between two independent configs:
           • DestinationRule trafficPolicy.tls.mode → what the CLIENT
             Envoy sends (ISTIO_MUTUAL, MUTUAL, SIMPLE, DISABLE)
           • PeerAuthentication mtls.mode → what the SERVER Envoy
             accepts (STRICT, PERMISSIVE, DISABLE)
         - 503s are born when the two sides disagree — the client-side
           Envoy fails to open the upstream connection and synthesizes
           a 503 (flag UC); the server never even logs a request
         - Best practice: write NO tls block in DRs at all — sidecar-to-
           sidecar traffic then auto-negotiates mTLS ("auto mTLS") and
           tracks the PA mode with zero extra configuration

         [DR × PA TLS MATRIX — client mode vs server mode]
         ┌─────────────────┬───────────────┬───────────────┬───────────────┐
         │ DR tls.mode     │ PA: STRICT    │ PA: PERMISSIVE│ PA: DISABLE   │
         ├─────────────────┼───────────────┼───────────────┼───────────────┤
         │ ISTIO_MUTUAL    │ ✅ mTLS 🔒      │ ✅ mTLS 🔒      │ ❌ handshake   │
         │ (mesh certs)    │               │               │ fails         │
         ├─────────────────┼───────────────┼───────────────┼───────────────┤
         │ DISABLE         │ ❌ TCP reset   │ ✅ works       │ ✅ works       │
         │ (plaintext)     │ client: 503   │ ⚠️ UNENCRYPTED│ ⚠️ UNENCRYPTED│
         ├─────────────────┼───────────────┼───────────────┼───────────────┤
         │ (no tls block)  │ ✅ auto-mTLS   │ ✅ auto-mTLS   │ ✅ plaintext   │
         │ = safest DR     │               │               │               │
         └─────────────────┴───────────────┴───────────────┴───────────────┘

         [THE 3 CLASSIC TRAPS — memorize these before the exam]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  TRAP 1 — the invisible DISABLE:                                │
         │  a DR written pre-Istio with tls.mode: DISABLE sits             │
         │  harmless under PERMISSIVE for months… the day PA flips         │
         │  to STRICT, every call through it dies with 503 UC              │
         │  → audit BEFORE enabling STRICT:                                │
         │    kubectl get destinationrules -A -o yaml | grep -B5 \         │
         │      "mode: DISABLE"                                            │
         │                                                                 │
         │  TRAP 2 — ISTIO_MUTUAL ≠ MUTUAL:                                │
         │  ISTIO_MUTUAL = mesh's auto-issued SPIFFE certs (normal)        │
         │  MUTUAL       = certs YOU mount yourself (external TLS)         │
         │  picking MUTUAL without providing certs = broken handshake      │
         │                                                                 │
         │  TRAP 3 — blaming the server:                                   │
         │  the 503 is generated CLIENT-side (Envoy could not open         │
         │  the upstream TLS connection) — the server never saw the        │
         │  request; its access log stays empty. Read the CALLER's         │
         │  logs and response flags (UC/UF) first                          │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    12.9  Deep Dive — External CAs: SPIRE Integration and Plug-in CA Certificates
         - By default istiod IS the CA: it creates a self-signed root at
           install and signs every workload cert in-process — perfect
           for anihpj-sized shops, zero configuration required
         - When security/PKI teams demand more, three upgrade paths:
           • PLUG-IN CA CERTS — istiod keeps signing, but with YOUR
             enterprise root/intermediate (the "cacerts" secret)
           • SPIRE — the CNCF SPIFFE Runtime Environment takes over
             cert issuance entirely (HSM backends, FIPS 140-2,
             identity federation across clusters and clouds)
           • CERT-MANAGER (istio-csr) — istiod becomes a Registration
             Authority and forwards CSRs to cert-manager, which signs
             via Vault, Venafi, or a private ACME CA
         - Exam signals that point here: "FIPS compliance", "use our
           existing PKI", "HSM integration", "trust-domain federation"

         [SPIRE INTEGRATION FLOW — external SPIFFE CA replaces istiod CA]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  ① SPIRE Agent (DaemonSet — one per node) ATTESTS each          │
         │     workload: k8s ServiceAccount? namespace? pod labels?        │
         │  ② SPIRE Server checks the attestation against its              │
         │     registration entries                                        │
         │       entry: spiffe://anihpj.com/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api       │
         │  ③ SPIRE Server signs an X.509 SVID — the signing key can       │
         │     live in an HSM or Vault (FIPS 140-2 territory)              │
         │  ④ SVID is pushed down to the node's SPIRE Agent, which         │
         │     exposes it on a Unix Domain Socket (UDS)                    │
         │  ⑤ istio-proxy fetches the SVID via SDS from that socket        │
         │     (istiod no longer issues certs — SPIRE owns rotation)       │
         │  ⑥ mTLS handshakes work EXACTLY as before — Envoy only          │
         │     cares that the cert chains to the trusted root 🔒            │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         - Note the trust domain changes: SPIRE SVIDs carry your
           registered domain (spiffe://anihpj.com/…), not cluster.local

         [PLUG-IN CA CERTIFICATES — the cacerts secret, step by step]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  # STEP 1 — generate a root CA (keep root-key.pem OFFLINE)      │
         │  make -f tools/certs/Makefile.selfsigned.mk root-ca             │
         │                                                                 │
         │  # STEP 2 — generate this cluster's intermediate CA             │
         │  make -f tools/certs/Makefile.selfsigned.mk \                   │
         │    cluster1-cacerts                                             │
         │                                                                 │
         │  # STEP 3 — create the magic secret; name MUST be               │
         │  #          "cacerts", namespace MUST be istio-system           │
         │  kubectl create secret generic cacerts -n istio-system \        │
         │    --from-file=cluster1/ca-cert.pem \                           │
         │    --from-file=cluster1/ca-key.pem \                            │
         │    --from-file=cluster1/root-cert.pem \                         │
         │    --from-file=cluster1/cert-chain.pem                          │
         │                                                                 │
         │  # STEP 4 — (re)install Istio — istiod auto-detects it          │
         │  istioctl install --set profile=default -y                      │
         │                                                                 │
         │  # STEP 5 — restart workloads to pick up new certs              │
         │  kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj                   │
         │                                                                 │
         │  RESULT: istiod still issues + rotates 24h workload             │
         │  certs, but every cert now chains to YOUR root ✅                │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         - cert-manager route in one line: install istio-csr, point
           istiod at it, and every CSR flows to cert-manager's issuer
           → certificates audited and managed like the rest of your PKI

         [CA HIERARCHY — one offline root, per-cluster intermediates]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │              ROOT CA — offline, HSM-protected                   │
         │                          │ signs                                │
         │          ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐                      │
         │          ▼               ▼               ▼                      │
         │   Intermediate CA Intermediate CA Intermediate CA               │
         │     (cluster1)      (cluster2)      (cluster3)                  │
         │          │               │               │                      │
         │      istiod #1       istiod #2       istiod #3                  │
         │                                                                 │
         │   each istiod signs 24h workload SVIDs that chain to            │
         │   the SAME root → cross-cluster mTLS with one trust             │
         │   domain 🔒                                                      │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘


    12.10  The Fourth Mode — UNSET and PeerAuthentication Inheritance
         - DEFINITION: mtls.mode actually has FOUR legal values, not three
           — STRICT, PERMISSIVE, DISABLE, and UNSET. UNSET is the
           implicit default whenever a PeerAuthentication (or a single
           portLevelMtls entry) omits mode entirely
         - Why it matters: 12.6 already showed workload beats namespace
           beats mesh — UNSET is the MECHANISM that makes that hierarchy
           possible. A policy that is UNSET does not mean "no mTLS
           setting" — it means "look at my parent scope and copy it"
         - How it works:
           • UNSET at workload scope → inherit the namespace-wide policy
           • UNSET at namespace scope → inherit the mesh-wide policy
           • UNSET at mesh scope (or no mesh-wide policy exists at all)
             → Istio's hard-coded fallback is PERMISSIVE
           • portLevelMtls entries follow the SAME rule at port
             granularity: an UNSET port inherits the workload's own
             mtls.mode instead of the namespace/mesh chain

         [THE 4 MODES — official semantics, straight from the CRD]
         ┌───────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ Mode      │ Meaning                                    │
         ├───────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ UNSET     │ inherit from parent scope; if there is no  │
         │           │ parent (mesh-wide policy itself is UNSET), │
         │           │ treated as PERMISSIVE                      │
         ├───────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ DISABLE   │ connection is not tunneled — plaintext only│
         ├───────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ PERMISSIVE│ connection can be EITHER plaintext or mTLS │
         ├───────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ STRICT    │ connection MUST be an mTLS tunnel — client │
         │           │ cert required, plaintext rejected          │
         └───────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [WHY portLevelMtls: UNSET IS USEFUL — one legacy port on an
          otherwise STRICT anihpj workload]
         ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1                             │
         │  kind: PeerAuthentication                                     │
         │  metadata:                                                    │
         │    name: jobpost-api-mixed                                    │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                          │
         │  spec:                                                        │
         │    selector:                                                  │
         │      matchLabels:                                             │
         │        app: jobpost-api                                       │
         │    mtls:                                                      │
         │      mode: STRICT        # workload default: STRICT           │
         │    portLevelMtls:                                             │
         │      8888:                                                    │
         │        mode: UNSET       # port 8888 (health probe) instead   │
         │                           # inherits anihpj's namespace policy│
         └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         - portLevelMtls only applies once a workload selector is set,
           and the port number is the CONTAINER port, not the Kubernetes
           Service port — a common exam trap
         - Deletion cascade recap (ties back to 12.6): delete the
           workload policy → its pods fall to UNSET → they now inherit
           namespace; delete that too → namespace falls to UNSET → mesh;
           delete the mesh-wide policy too → Istio's built-in UNSET
           fallback is PERMISSIVE, never STRICT — "secure by default"
           is something YOU configure, not something Istio assumes

    12.11  SPIFFE Identity Anatomy — Reading a Cert Like the Exam Wants
         - DEFINITION: every workload identity in the mesh is a SPIFFE
           ID with exactly four parts:
             spiffe://<trust-domain>/ns/<namespace>/sa/<service-account>
         - Why it matters: SPIFFE IDs are the noun every other security
           feature operates on — secure naming (12.5) matches against
           them, AuthorizationPolicy source.principals (Chapter 13)
           filters on them, and istioctl/Kiali display them verbatim
         📖 KEY TERM. SPIFFE ID vs. SVID — the ID is the URI STRING
           itself (e.g. spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-
           api); the SVID is the signed X.509 CERTIFICATE that
           carries that ID inside its SAN field. The exam uses both
           words on purpose — one is a name, the other is the
           document that proves it.

         - How it works — anatomy of a real anihpj identity:

         [SPIFFE ID ANATOMY — spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api]
         ┌────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ Component      │ Meaning                                 │
         ├────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ spiffe://      │ fixed scheme — always this literal      │
         │ cluster.local  │ TRUST DOMAIN — the mesh's identity root │
         │                │ (default "cluster.local"; your own      │
         │                │ domain under SPIRE federation, see 12.9)│
         │ /ns/anihpj     │ literal "/ns/" + the Kubernetes         │
         │                │ NAMESPACE the workload runs in          │
         │ /sa/jobpost-api│ literal "/sa/" + the Kubernetes         │
         │                │ ServiceAccount the Pod runs as — THIS   │
         │                │ is the actual "who", not the Pod name   │
         └────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [EVERY anihpj SERVICE — SPIFFE ID cheat sheet]
         ┌─────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ Service             │ SPIFFE ID                              │
         ├─────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ jobpost-api         │ spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/   │
         │                     │ jobpost-api                            │
         ├─────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ user-service        │ spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/   │
         │                     │ user-service                           │
         ├─────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ skills-service      │ spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/   │
         │                     │ skills-service                         │
         ├─────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ istio-ingressgateway│ spiffe://cluster.local/ns/istio-system/│
         │ (mesh-wide, not     │ sa/istio-ingressgateway-service-account│
         │ anihpj-owned)       │                                        │
         └─────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────┘
         - The identity is bound to the ServiceAccount, NOT the Pod name,
           NOT the IP, NOT the Deployment — scale jobpost-api to 20 pods
           and every single one presents the IDENTICAL SPIFFE ID, because
           they all run under the same ServiceAccount
         - Two anihpj Pods can therefore never be told apart by identity
           alone if they share a ServiceAccount — if you need per-Pod
           granularity in an AuthorizationPolicy, you need a DIFFERENT
           ServiceAccount per workload, not just a different Pod
         - Where you will SEE this string in real tooling:
           • istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj
             lists the "default" workload cert + "ROOTCA" by name — to
             read the SPIFFE URI itself, decode the cert bytes (openssl,
             below) or check istioctl x describe pod's identity output
           • openssl s_client -connect ... | openssl x509 -noout -text
             → under X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: URI:spiffe://...
           • Kiali → click an edge → "mTLS" panel shows both principals
           • AuthorizationPolicy source.principals (Chapter 13) is a
             list of these exact strings

    12.12  Auto mTLS — Zero-Config Client-Side TLS Since Istio 1.5
         - DEFINITION: Auto mTLS is the Pilot feature (default ON, has
           been since Istio 1.5) that automatically sets the CLIENT
           Envoy's TLS behavior to match what the destination can
           accept — WITHOUT you writing a DestinationRule tls block

         🧠 ANALOGY. Auto mTLS is a car's automatic transmission:
           Django just says "go" — a plain http:// call — and Pilot,
           like the transmission, silently picks the right gear
           (ISTIO_MUTUAL or plaintext) by reading road conditions
           (does the destination's Envoy have a sidecar?). A manual
           DestinationRule tls block is shifting gears by hand — it
           works, but forgetting to update it when PeerAuthentication
           moves to STRICT is exactly how 12.8's 503s get born.
         - Why it matters: before 1.5, every mesh needed a hand-written
           ISTIO_MUTUAL DestinationRule per hardened service; forget one
           and that service silently kept sending/receiving plaintext
           even though PeerAuthentication said STRICT. Auto mTLS removes
           that entire failure mode for standard in-mesh traffic
         - How it works:
           • every sidecar-injected Pod's Endpoint carries an internal
             label recording that it has a sidecar
           • istiod's Pilot component reads that label through service
             discovery and knows, for each destination, "has a sidecar"
             or "does not have a sidecar"
           • when building the CLIENT'S Envoy config, if the caller did
             NOT write an explicit tls block in a DestinationRule, Pilot
             fills one in FOR them: ISTIO_MUTUAL if the destination has
             a sidecar, plaintext (no TLS origination) if it does not
           • an explicit tls block in a DestinationRule ALWAYS overrides
             auto mTLS — this is TRAP 1 from 12.8 in reverse: auto mTLS
             is the safe default, a leftover explicit block is the trap

         [AUTO mTLS DECISION — what Pilot fills in when a DR has no
          tls block at all]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  jobpost-api Envoy about to call user-service.anihpj:8080   │
         │  DestinationRule for user-service: NO tls block             │
         │                                                             │
         │       Does user-service's endpoint have a sidecar?          │
         │              │                          │                   │
         │            YES                          NO                  │
         │              │                          │                   │
         │              ▼                          ▼                   │
         │   Pilot injects:                Pilot injects:              │
         │   tls.mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL        (nothing — plaintext origin)│
         │   → 🔒 mTLS automatically         → talks plaintext to a    │
         │                                    non-mesh / VM / legacy   │
         │                                    endpoint, e.g. a payment │
         │                                    gateway outside anihpj   │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Auto mTLS is a MESH-WIDE MeshConfig toggle, on by default:

         [MESHCONFIG — disabling auto mTLS (rare, mostly for legacy
          egress audits that want an explicit fail-closed DR everywhere)]
         ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: install.istio.io/v1alpha1        │
         │  kind: IstioOperator                          │
         │  spec:                                        │
         │    meshConfig:                                │
         │      enableAutoMtls: false   # default is true│
         └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         - Turning it off does NOT turn off mTLS itself — PeerAuthn
           STRICT still rejects plaintext on the SERVER side. It only
           means every DestinationRule now needs an explicit tls block,
           because Pilot stops filling one in automatically
         - Exam framing: "why does jobpost-api get mTLS to user-service
           with ZERO DestinationRule anywhere in anihpj?" → auto mTLS,
           not magic — Pilot saw both sidecars and wired ISTIO_MUTUAL in

    12.13  Certificate TTL and Rotation Internals — the Real Numbers
         - DEFINITION: two DIFFERENT certificates live in an Istio mesh,
           with two very different lifetimes — the WORKLOAD cert (what
           12.4 covers) and the ROOT/intermediate CA cert that signs it
         - Why it matters: the exam expects you to know rotation is NOT
           "wait until 5 minutes before expiry" — it happens much
           earlier, and mixing up workload-cert TTL with root-cert TTL
           is a common wrong answer on certificate-lifetime questions
         - How it works:

         [TWO CLOCKS — workload cert vs the CA that signs it]
         ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  WORKLOAD CERT (per-Pod SVID, what Envoy presents in a        │
         │  handshake)                                                   │
         │    • default TTL: 24 hours                                    │
         │    • istio-agent requests a renewal once the default grace-   │
         │      period ratio (0.5) of that lifetime has elapsed — i.e.   │
         │      around the 12-HOUR mark for a 24h cert, not moments      │
         │      before expiry                                            │
         │    • since Istio 1.24, a small random jitter (default ratio   │
         │      0.01, roughly ± 15 minutes) is added on top so that      │
         │      hundreds of jobpost-api replicas started together do NOT │
         │      all hit istiod for renewal in the same instant           │
         │    • old cert keeps working right up to its own real expiry — │
         │      the swap is seamless, no dropped connections             │
         ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  ROOT / INTERMEDIATE CA CERT (signs every workload cert)      │
         │    • default self-signed root TTL: 10 years                   │
         │    • lives in the istio-ca-secret in istio-system, NOT rotated│
         │      on the same schedule as workload certs                   │
         │    • root rotation is a deliberate, rare, operator-driven     │
         │      procedure (old root and new root are trusted side-by-side│
         │      during the transition window) — not something anihpj     │
         │      pods trigger automatically                               │
         └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [CORRECTED ROTATION TIMELINE — replaces "5 minutes before
          expiry" with the real ~50% grace-period-ratio trigger]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  T=0h:      cert issued, 24h validity window opens             │
         │  T≈12h:     grace-period ratio (0.5) reached — istio-agent     │
         │             requests a NEW cert (± ~15 min jitter since 1.24)  │
         │  T≈12h+j:   new CSR signed by istiod → new cert swapped into   │
         │             Envoy via SDS → OLD cert is simply discarded early,│
         │             it was still technically valid                     │
         │  T=24h:     original cert's validity window would have ended — │
         │             irrelevant, it was replaced 12 hours earlier       │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         - Both numbers are configurable on istiod, but the exam only
           expects you to know the DEFAULTS and the RELATIONSHIP: workload
           certs rotate WAY before they expire (roughly the halfway
           point), the root CA cert does not rotate on any per-Pod
           schedule at all
         - If istiod is down for more than the workload cert's TTL (24h
           by default), NO renewals can happen — existing certs expire,
           handshakes start failing mesh-wide until istiod is restored
           (this is 12.7's Golden Rule 3 scenario, "cert expired")

  [UNDER THE HOOD -- ONE anihpj CALL, START TO FINISH: jobpost-api -> user-service]
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ PHASE 1 - IDENTITY IS BORN (pod boot -- ties the pieces from 12.4 together) │
  │   T=0.0s  jobpost-api Pod scheduled; istio-proxy sidecar injected           │
  │   T=0.3s  sidecar sends a CSR to istiod: "I am sa/jobpost-api, ns/anihpj"   │
  │   T=0.5s  istiod (Citadel CA) verifies the ServiceAccount token, signs a    │
  │           24h X.509 SVID: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api   │
  │   T=0.7s  cert lands in Envoy via SDS -- jobpost-api can now PROVE itself   │
  │                                                                             │
  │ PHASE 2 - THE CALL (hours later, e.g. T=6h -- well inside the 24h cert)     │
  │   ①  Django calls http://user-service:8080/users/42 -- the app has NO       │
  │      idea mTLS exists (12.12: auto mTLS wires this up silently)             │
  │   ②  jobpost-api's Envoy checks secure naming (12.5): the istiod-pushed     │
  │      map says only .../sa/user-service may answer for user-service:8080     │
  │   ③  TLS 1.3 ClientHello sent; user-service's Envoy answers with ITS SVID:  │
  │      spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/user-service                       │
  │   ④  jobpost-api's Envoy verifies: signed by the mesh root? SAN matches     │
  │      the secure-naming map from step 2? not expired? -- all checks pass     │
  │   ⑤  jobpost-api's Envoy presents ITS OWN SVID in return -- this is the     │
  │      "mutual" in mTLS; user-service now knows the caller's identity too     │
  │   ⑥  user-service's Envoy checks its OWN effective PeerAuthentication       │
  │      mode (12.6/12.10): namespace anihpj = STRICT -- a valid client cert    │
  │      is mandatory, this one qualifies -- tunnel accepted                    │
  │   ⑦  encrypted tunnel established; "GET /users/42" travels inside it;       │
  │      user-service's access log records the caller's principal for           │
  │      Chapter 13's AuthorizationPolicy to filter on next                     │
  │                                                                             │
  │ RESULT: one HTTP call, zero Django code touched -- yet it crossed FOUR      │
  │ independent gates (a live cert from Phase 1, a secure-naming check, a       │
  │ two-way identity exchange, and a PeerAuthentication mode gate) and every    │
  │ single one had to say yes before byte one of /users/42 could move.          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  [SPEED TIPS]
  ⚡ Migrate PERMISSIVE → STRICT namespace-by-namespace, never mesh-wide in
     one shot — flip the namespace-wide PeerAuthentication only after Kiali
     shows every inbound edge already locked
  ⚡ 503 (flag UC) right after flipping STRICT is 9 times out of 10 a stale
     DestinationRule with tls.mode: DISABLE — grep for it BEFORE you flip
  ⚡ TCP reset with no HTTP code = mTLS problem; HTTP 403 "RBAC: access
     denied" = AuthorizationPolicy problem (Ch13) — never debug the wrong CRD
  ⚡ istioctl x describe pod is your first command, not proxy-config secret
     — it prints the EFFECTIVE PA mode + DR TLS mode in one shot
  ⚡ To read a cert fast: pipe openssl s_client into openssl x509 -noout
     -text and jump straight to "Subject Alternative Name" — that URI IS
     the identity, ignore the Subject/Issuer CN noise
  ⚡ "istioctl authn tls-check" is gone — if a runbook mentions it, mentally
     substitute istioctl x describe pod

  [COMMANDS CHEAT-CARD -- the mTLS command set from this chapter]
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Command                                                            │ What it tells you / does                                  │
  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ kubectl apply -f peerauth.yaml                                     │ sets PA mode: PERMISSIVE/STRICT/DISABLE (12.3, 12.6)      │
  │ istioctl x describe pod <pod> -n anihpj                            │ effective PA mode + DR TLS mode, ONE call (12.7)          │
  │ istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/<name> -n anihpj               │ live SPIFFE cert + ROOTCA in Envoy's memory (12.7, 12.11) │
  │ openssl s_client -connect <svc>.anihpj:<port>                      │ raw handshake; prints the presented cert chain (12.7)     │
  │ openssl x509 -noout -text                                          │ decode a cert; read the SPIFFE URI under SAN (12.11)      │
  │ kubectl get destinationrules -A -o yaml | grep -B5 "mode: DISABLE" │ find stale DRs before flipping to STRICT (12.8)           │
  │ kubectl create secret generic cacerts -n istio-system ...          │ install your own root/intermediate CA (12.9)              │
  │ kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj                       │ force pods to re-CSR after a CA or PA change (12.9)       │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  [PRACTICE DRILL]
  🧪 5-10 MIN DRILL — flip anihpj from PERMISSIVE to STRICT and prove it
    1. kubectl get peerauthentication -n anihpj -o yaml — confirm today's
       mode (likely PERMISSIVE from the Week-1 migration in 12.4)
    2. Apply a namespace-wide PeerAuthentication with mtls.mode: STRICT
       for the anihpj namespace (the YAML in 12.3 is ready to reuse)
    3. istioctl x describe pod on a jobpost-api pod — confirm the
       EFFECTIVE mode now reads STRICT, not just "applied"
    4. From a NON-sidecar pod (or curl --http1.1 with no mesh identity),
       hit user-service:8080 — expect "connection reset by peer," not a
       403 — that confirms you're seeing mTLS enforcement, not AuthzPolicy
    5. Open Kiali's graph, enable the Security display — every anihpj
       edge should now show a 🔒 padlock; any edge without one is a
       sidecar-less straggler to fix before calling this done

  [VISUAL SUMMARY -- Chapter 12's arc, plaintext to provable identity]
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ PLAINTEXT anihpj (12.1)                                                   │
  │   │  any rogue pod can sniff, impersonate, or move laterally              │
  │   ▼                                                                       │
  │ mTLS THE CONCEPT (12.2) -- BOTH sides present a SPIFFE cert, not just one │
  │   │                                                                       │
  │   ▼                                                                       │
  │ PeerAuthentication (12.3) -- PERMISSIVE → STRICT switches enforcement on  │
  │   │                                                                       │
  │   ▼                                                                       │
  │ Certificate Lifecycle (12.4) -- istiod issues + rotates 24h SVIDs         │
  │   │                                                                       │
  │   ▼                                                                       │
  │ Secure Naming (12.5) -- a VALID cert alone isn't enough; the NAME must    │
  │   │  match too, or the handshake aborts before app data moves             │
  │   ▼                                                                       │
  │ Policy Hierarchy (12.6) -- workload beats namespace beats mesh            │
  │   │                                                                       │
  │   ▼                                                                       │
  │ Troubleshooting (12.7) -- TCP reset = mTLS; HTTP 403 RBAC = AuthzPolicy   │
  │   │                                                                       │
  │   ▼                                                                       │
  │ Deep Dives (12.8-12.9) -- the DR/PA contract behind 503s; external CAs    │
  │   │                                                                       │
  │   ▼                                                                       │
  │ UNSET + Inheritance (12.10) -- the MECHANISM behind the 12.6 hierarchy    │
  │   │                                                                       │
  │   ▼                                                                       │
  │ SPIFFE Anatomy (12.11) -- reading spiffe://.../ns/.../sa/... on demand    │
  │   │                                                                       │
  │   ▼                                                                       │
  │ Auto mTLS (12.12) -- Pilot wires ISTIO_MUTUAL with zero DestinationRules  │
  │   │                                                                       │
  │   ▼                                                                       │
  │ TTL & Rotation (12.13) -- ~12h renewal, never "5 minutes before expiry"   │
  │   │                                                                       │
  │   ▼                                                                       │
  │ ==> Chapter 13: AuthorizationPolicy decides WHO may call WHOM             │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Chapter 12 took anihpj from every hop being plaintext and every identity
  being an easily-spoofed IP, to every one of jobpost-api, user-service,
  skills-service, location-service, notification-service, auth-service,
  and search-service holding an unforgeable SPIFFE certificate that is
  issued at boot, checked on every handshake, hardened against
  impersonation, and silently rotated roughly every 12 hours — all without
  a single Django code change. What Chapter 12 deliberately does NOT do is
  decide who is ALLOWED to call whom once identity is proven; that
  authorization decision, layered on top of the identity this chapter
  builds, is exactly where Chapter 13's AuthorizationPolicy picks up.

Chapter 13: Authorization Policies — Who Can Call What
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    Chapter 13 of 12-13  ·  Difficulty: 🟡 (🔴 in 13.8-13.12)  ·  🎯 Securing
    Workloads — 25% of the ICA exam  ·  "who is allowed in HERE?"

    WHY THIS MATTERS
    Chapter 12 spent thirteen sections proving WHO is calling — every anihpj
    pod now carries an unforgeable SPIFFE certificate and every hop is
    encrypted end to end. But identity alone is a dead end: with only mTLS
    switched on, a compromised skills-service still authenticates perfectly
    AS skills-service, then walks straight into user-service and dumps every
    row of PII — the request was 100% encrypted and 100% authenticated the
    whole way, and nothing stopped it. That is exactly the trap Part 7's own
    analogy warns about: a badge system that only checks whether the badge
    is real, never whether THIS badge should open THIS door, is theater —
    cryptographically perfect, and useless. Chapter 13 is where anihpj closes
    that gap: AuthorizationPolicy is the doorman who actually reads the
    badge and decides. By 13.11 you will trace one real request through
    FOUR simultaneous decision layers — CUSTOM, AUDIT, DENY, ALLOW — the
    single most exam-critical sequence in the whole Securing Workloads
    domain, because getting the order wrong either 403s legitimate traffic
    or silently lets an attacker straight through.

    LEARNING OBJECTIVES
    By the end of this chapter you will be able to:
      ✅ Explain why mTLS (identity) and AuthorizationPolicy (authorization)
         are two separate controls, and why anihpj needs BOTH
      ✅ Write a deny-all AuthorizationPolicy and layer explicit ALLOW rules
         on top of it without causing a traffic outage
      ✅ Wire RequestAuthentication + requestPrincipals together so a
         MISSING JWT, not just an invalid one, becomes a real 403
      ✅ Use exclusion fields (notPaths, notPrincipals) to carve out an
         exception like /healthz without weakening the rest of a policy
      ✅ Lock down a non-HTTP TCP port (postgres:5432) with a ports-only
         ALLOW rule, and explain why paths/methods can never match there
      ✅ Rehearse a risky policy with istio.io/dry-run before enforcing it,
         and read the shadow verdict across logs, metrics, and traces
      ✅ Trace one request through the full CUSTOM -> DENY -> ALLOW order
         (with AUDIT as a non-blocking side-channel) and predict the verdict

    EXAM/ICA RELEVANCE

    13.1 The Need for Service-Level Authorization
         - mTLS proves identity but doesn't restrict what is allowed
         - Without AuthorizationPolicy: any service can call any other service
         - anihpj threat: a compromised skills-service could call user-service
           and read all user data — even though it has no business doing so
         - Zero-trust principle: deny everything by default, allow explicitly
         [THREAT DIAGRAM: overly permissive mesh vs zero-trust mesh]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  WITHOUT AuthorizationPolicy — mTLS-only 'permissive' mesh:        │
         │                                                                    │
         │   😈 compromised skills-service (attacker inside the pod)           │
         │      ├──✅──▶ user-service      GET /api/users/*  → dumps user PII  │
         │      ├──✅──▶ auth-service      probes /validate  → forges sessions │
         │      └──✅──▶ location-service  maps the internal network           │
         │                                                                    │
         │   mTLS happily says: 'this really IS skills-service' — then lets   │
         │   every call through. Identity ✅  Encryption 🔒  Permissions ❌      │
         │                                                                    │
         │  WITH zero-trust (deny-all + explicit ALLOW policies):             │
         │                                                                    │
         │   😈 compromised skills-service                                     │
         │      ├──❌──▶ user-service      403 RBAC: access denied             │
         │      ├──❌──▶ auth-service      403 (not on the allow-list)         │
         │      └──❌──▶ location-service  403                                 │
         │                                                                    │
         │   jobpost-api ──✅──▶ skills-service  (explicitly allowed, GET)     │
         │                                                                    │
         │   Blast radius of one hacked pod: EVERYTHING → almost nothing      │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    13.2 AuthorizationPolicy — The Istio Firewall
         - AuthorizationPolicy is Istio's access control CRD
         - Works at L7 (HTTP): can allow/deny based on:
           • Source service identity (SPIFFE certificate)
           • HTTP method (GET, POST, DELETE)
           • HTTP path (/jobs/, /admin/)
           • HTTP headers (Authorization, x-user-id)
           • Source namespace
         - Default behavior: ALLOW ALL (if no policy exists)
         🔧 UNDER THE HOOD. Applying this YAML doesn't make kube-apiserver
            start checking requests — istiod (the control plane from Part 3)
            compiles the AuthorizationPolicy's rules into an Envoy RBAC
            filter and pushes it to every matching sidecar over xDS, the
            same channel that already delivers listeners, routes, and
            certs. The ALLOW/DENY check then runs entirely inside each
            pod's own Envoy sidecar, request by request — no round trip
            back to istiod or the API server is ever made.

         - With a DENY-ALL policy: must explicitly allow each path

         [AUTHORIZATIONPOLICY EVALUATION — how Istio decides ALLOW or DENY]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Incoming request: skills-service → GET /users/42 → user-service  │
         │                                                                    │
         │  EVALUATION ORDER:                                                 │
         │                                                                    │
         │  1. Is there a CUSTOM policy (action: CUSTOM) for user-service?   │
         │     • YES → evaluate it first; if it rejects → DENY               │
         │     • NO  → continue                                               │
         │                                                                    │
         │  2. Is there a DENY policy matching this request?                  │
         │     • YES, DENY all traffic to user-service?                      │
         │       • Does it match source: skills-service? YES → DENY ❌        │
         │     • NO matching DENY → continue                                  │
         │                                                                    │
         │  3. Is there an ALLOW policy for user-service?                     │
         │     • YES, ALLOW from: jobpost-api only                           │
         │       • Does skills-service match? NO → implicit DENY ❌           │
         │                                                                    │
         │  4. No matching ALLOW found → DENY (when any policy exists)       │
         │                                                                    │
         │  RESULT: skills-service → user-service = ❌ DENIED (403)          │
         │                                                                    │
         │  KEY RULE: If ANY AuthorizationPolicy targets a workload,         │
         │  then all requests NOT explicitly ALLOWED are DENIED.             │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [COMPLETE AUTHORIZATIONPOLICY YAML — deny-all then allow-list]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  # Step 1: Deny ALL traffic in anihpj namespace                   │
         │  apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1                                 │
         │  kind: AuthorizationPolicy                                        │
         │  metadata:                                                        │
         │    name: deny-all                                                 │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                              │
         │  spec: {}   ← empty spec = deny everything                       │
         │  ---                                                               │
         │  # Step 2: Allow ingress gateway → jobpost-api                    │
         │  kind: AuthorizationPolicy                                        │
         │  metadata:                                                        │
         │    name: allow-ingress-to-jobpost                                 │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                              │
         │  spec:                                                            │
         │    selector:                                                      │
         │      matchLabels: {app: jobpost-api}    ← applies to jobpost-api  │
         │    action: ALLOW                                                   │
         │    rules:                                                         │
         │    - from:                                                        │
         │      - source:                                                    │
         │          principals:                                              │
         │          - "cluster.local/ns/istio-system/sa/istio-ingressgateway"│
         │      to:                                                          │
         │      - operation:                                                 │
         │          methods: ["GET", "POST"]  ← only GET and POST           │
         │  ---                                                               │
         │  # Step 3: Allow jobpost-api → user-service (GET only)            │
         │  kind: AuthorizationPolicy                                        │
         │  metadata:                                                        │
         │    name: allow-jobpost-to-users                                   │
         │  spec:                                                            │
         │    selector:                                                      │
         │      matchLabels: {app: user-service}                             │
         │    action: ALLOW                                                   │
         │    rules:                                                         │
         │    - from:                                                        │
         │      - source:                                                    │
         │          principals:                                              │
         │          - "cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api"              │
         │      to:                                                          │
         │      - operation:                                                 │
         │          methods: ["GET"]                                         │
         │          paths: ["/api/users/*"]   ← restrict to specific paths  │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    13.3 Building a Zero-Trust Policy for anihpj
         [COMPLETE POLICY WALKTHROUGH]
         - Step 1: Deny everything in the anihpj namespace
         - Step 2: Allow external traffic in via ingressgateway only
         - Step 3: Allow jobpost-api to call user-service (GET only)
         - Step 4: Allow jobpost-api to call skills-service (GET only)
         - Step 5: Allow user-service to call auth-service (GET/POST)
         - Step 6: Allow NO cross-calls that aren't explicitly needed
         - Step 7: Allow metrics scraping (Prometheus to all services)
         [POLICY MATRIX DIAGRAM: who is allowed to call what]

         [ZERO-TRUST POLICY MATRIX for anihpj]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  SOURCE        │  TARGET          │  ALLOWED METHODS  │
         │  ──────────────│──────────────────│──────────────────  │
         │  ingressgw     │  jobpost-api     │  GET, POST        │
         │  jobpost-api   │  user-service    │  GET only         │
         │  jobpost-api   │  skills-service  │  GET only         │
         │  jobpost-api   │  location-svc    │  GET only         │
         │  user-service  │  auth-service    │  GET, POST        │
         │  prometheus    │  ALL services    │  GET /metrics     │
         │  ANY OTHER     │  ANY             │  ❌ DENIED        │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Rollout order matters: apply the ALLOW policies FIRST, the
           deny-all LAST (or shadow it with dry-run, see 13.8) —
           applying deny-all before the ALLOWs exist will 403 every
           live call for a few seconds
         - Each ALLOW policy lives next to its TARGET service: the
           policy selecting user-service governs traffic INTO
           user-service, not traffic it sends out

         [ROLLOUT & VERIFY — applying the matrix without an outage]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  # 1. Apply every ALLOW policy from the matrix (rows above)        │
         │  $ kubectl apply -f authz/ -n anihpj      # 6 ALLOW policies       │
         │                                                                    │
         │  # 2. Apply deny-all in DRY-RUN mode first (see 13.8)              │
