         │  #    metadata.annotations: "istio.io/dry-run": "true"             │
         │  $ kubectl apply -f deny-all-dryrun.yaml                           │
         │                                                                    │
         │  # 3. Watch shadow-denies across live traffic (847 req/s)          │
         │  #    → zero legitimate flows would be denied? proceed             │
         │                                                                    │
         │  # 4. Enforce: remove the dry-run annotation                       │
         │  $ kubectl annotate authorizationpolicy/deny-all -n anihpj \       │
         │      istio.io/dry-run-                                             │
         │                                                                    │
         │  # 5. Verify one allowed and one denied path                       │
         │  $ kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- \                  │
         │      curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' \                      │
         │      http://user-service:8080/api/users/42        → 200 ✅          │
         │  $ kubectl exec deploy/skills-service -n anihpj -- \               │
         │      curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' \                      │
         │      http://user-service:8080/api/users/42        → 403 ❌          │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    13.4 RequestAuthentication — JWT Verification
         - RequestAuthentication: validate incoming JWT tokens at the mesh level
         - Verify JWTs from your auth-service without code in every Django service
         - Extract JWT claims for use in AuthorizationPolicy conditions
         - anihpj use case: only requests with valid JWT issued by auth-service
           can reach user-service or jobpost-api
         [YAML: RequestAuthentication + AuthorizationPolicy using JWT claims]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  # Step 1: teach the mesh how to VALIDATE anihpj JWTs              │
         │  apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1                                  │
         │  kind: RequestAuthentication                                       │
         │  metadata:                                                         │
         │    name: jwt-auth                                                  │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                               │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    selector:                                                       │
         │      matchLabels: {app: jobpost-api}  ← guard the public API pods  │
         │    jwtRules:                                                       │
         │    - issuer: "https://auth.anihpj.com"   ← must equal iss claim    │
         │      jwksUri: "https://auth.anihpj.com/.well-known/jwks.json"      │
         │                ↑ public signing keys Envoy fetches to verify JWTs  │
         │  ---                                                               │
         │  # Step 2: REQUIRE the JWT — RequestAuthentication alone does NOT  │
         │  # block requests that simply OMIT the token!                      │
         │  apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1                                  │
         │  kind: AuthorizationPolicy                                         │
         │  metadata:                                                         │
         │    name: require-jwt                                               │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                               │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    selector:                                                       │
         │      matchLabels: {app: jobpost-api}                               │
         │    action: ALLOW                                                   │
         │    rules:                                                          │
         │    - from:                                                         │
         │      - source:                                                     │
         │          requestPrincipals: ["https://auth.anihpj.com/*"]          │
         │            ↑ "issuer/subject" — only set when a VALID JWT exists   │
         │      when:                                                         │
         │      - key: request.auth.claims[role]     ← claim-based condition  │
         │        values: ["admin", "recruiter"]  ← Django roles in the JWT   │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [JWT ENFORCEMENT MATRIX — 401 vs 403 vs silent pass-through]
         ┌────────────────┬────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
         │  TOKEN STATE   │ RequestAuthN alone     │ + AuthZ (reqPrincipals)  │
         ├────────────────┼────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┤
         │  valid JWT     │ ✅ pass, claims set     │ ✅ 200 (principal set)    │
         │  INVALID JWT   │ ❌ 401 rejected HERE    │ (never reaches AuthZ)    │
         │  NO token      │ ⚠️  passes through!     │ ❌ 403 (no principal)     │
         ├────────────────┴────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────┤
         │  KEY EXAM FACT: RequestAuthentication only rejects requests that   │
         │  PRESENT a broken/expired/wrong-issuer token (→ 401). A request    │
         │  with NO token sails straight past it — only an AuthorizationPolicy│
         │  demanding requestPrincipals turns "missing token" into a 403.     │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [VERIFY END-TO-END — three curls, three different verdicts]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  # 1. valid admin JWT → allowed                                    │
         │  $ TOKEN=$(curl -s https://auth.anihpj.com/token)   # demo helper  │
         │  $ curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \                        │
         │      http://jobpost-api.anihpj:8000/api/jobs/       → 200 OK ✅     │
         │                                                                    │
         │  # 2. malformed token → RequestAuthentication rejects it           │
         │  $ curl -H "Authorization: Bearer not.a.jwt" \                     │
         │      http://jobpost-api.anihpj:8000/api/jobs/                      │
         │      → 401 Jwt is not in the form of Header.Payload.Signature ❌    │
         │                                                                    │
         │  # 3. NO token → passes RequestAuthN, blocked by AuthZ policy      │
         │  $ curl http://jobpost-api.anihpj:8000/api/jobs/                   │
         │      → 403 RBAC: access denied ❌                                   │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    13.5  Exclusion Matching — NOT Conditions in AuthorizationPolicy
         - DEFINITION: exclusion matching lets a rule apply to everything
           EXCEPT the listed values — every positive match field has a
           negated "not" twin (paths → notPaths, principals →
           notPrincipals, and so on)
         - Why it matters: real policies always need carve-outs —
           "require a JWT on every path EXCEPT /healthz" cannot be
           expressed with positive matches alone
         - How it works: a request matches the rule only if it does NOT
           match any excluded value; exclusions sit inside the same
           from/to/when blocks and combine with positive fields
         - anihpj war story: the day require-jwt went live, kubelet
           liveness probes (which carry no JWT) started failing →
           jobpost-api pods restart-looped until /healthz was exempted
           with notPaths — the fix shown below

         [EXCLUSION FIELD REFERENCE — the "not" twin of each match field]
         ┌──────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  FIELD               │  RULE MATCHES WHEN ...                      │
         ├──────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  notPrincipals       │  caller SPIFFE identity is NOT in the list  │
         │  notNamespaces       │  caller namespace is NOT in the list        │
         │  notIpBlocks         │  source IP is NOT inside these CIDRs        │
         │  notMethods          │  HTTP method is NOT one of these            │
         │  notPaths            │  URL path is NOT one of these               │
         │  notHosts            │  Host header is NOT one of these            │
         ├──────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  Also available: notPorts, notRequestPrincipals (JWT identity),    │
         │  and notValues (inside when: conditions)                           │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [HEALTH-CHECK EXEMPTION — JWT required everywhere EXCEPT probes]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1                                  │
         │  kind: AuthorizationPolicy                                         │
         │  metadata:                                                         │
         │    name: require-jwt-except-health                                 │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                               │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    selector:                                                       │
         │      matchLabels: {app: jobpost-api}                               │
         │    action: ALLOW                                                   │
         │    rules:                                                          │
         │    - from:                          # rule 1: JWT holders only     │
         │      - source:                                                     │
         │          requestPrincipals: ["https://auth.anihpj.com/*"]          │
         │      to:                                                           │
         │      - operation:                                                  │
         │          notPaths: ["/healthz", "/ready"] ← every path BUT these   │
         │    - to:                            # rule 2: probes stay open     │
         │      - operation:                                                  │
         │          paths: ["/healthz", "/ready"]  ← no from: = anyone        │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    13.6  TCP Authorization — Protecting Non-HTTP Workloads
         - DEFINITION: AuthorizationPolicy also protects plain TCP
           servers (PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka) — but only with the
           TCP-valid fields: ports, principals, namespaces, ipBlocks
         - Why it matters: anihpj's PostgreSQL at postgres.anihpj:5432
           holds every user and job row; only jobpost-api and
           user-service have any business opening a connection to it
         - Identity still works on TCP: principals come from the mTLS
           SPIFFE certificate exchanged in the TLS handshake — Istio's
           auto-mTLS upgrades sidecar-to-sidecar traffic to mTLS by
           default even under PERMISSIVE, so principals populate
           without needing STRICT; STRICT only matters to reject
           non-mesh plaintext callers outright (under PERMISSIVE such
           a caller is simply let through with no principal set,
           silently failing any principals-based ALLOW rule)
         - ⚠️ HTTP-only fields (methods, paths, hosts,
           requestPrincipals) can NEVER match TCP traffic:
           → in an ALLOW rule, Istio ignores the whole rule — it can
             never match, so the traffic you meant to allow is DENIED
           → in a DENY rule, Istio drops only the HTTP-only fields and
             enforces the rest — the policy may DENY MORE than written

         🧠 ANALOGY. A TCP-only checkpoint is a parking-garage gate arm: it
            reads your access card and answers GO or NO-GO, full stop — it
            cannot ask "which floor" or "what's your business here" the way
            an HTTP-aware policy's staffed lobby desk can (paths, methods,
            headers). Taping paths: ["/admin/*"] onto a postgres:5432 rule
            is like stickering "floor 4 only" on a gate arm that can't read
            floors — it changes nothing; you still only get GO or NO-GO.

         [TCP AUTHORIZATIONPOLICY — lock PostgreSQL :5432 to two callers]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1                                  │
         │  kind: AuthorizationPolicy                                         │
         │  metadata:                                                         │
         │    name: postgres-allow                                            │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                               │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    selector:                                                       │
         │      matchLabels: {app: postgres}   ← the PostgreSQL StatefulSet   │
         │    action: ALLOW                                                   │
         │    rules:                                                          │
         │    - from:                                                         │
         │      - source:                                                     │
         │          principals:                                               │
         │          - "cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api"                │
         │          - "cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/user-service"               │
         │      to:                                                           │
         │      - operation:                                                  │
         │          ports: ["5432"]      ← the ONLY operation field valid     │
         │                                  for TCP — no paths, no methods!   │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [VERIFY WITH psql — allowed pod connects, others get RESET]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  # From jobpost-api (on the allow-list) → works                    │
         │  $ kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- \                  │
         │      psql "host=postgres.anihpj port=5432 dbname=jobpost \         │
         │            user=anihpj" -c "SELECT count(*) FROM jobs;"            │
         │     count                                                          │
         │    -------                                                         │
         │      1847                           ✅ query returns                │
         │                                                                    │
         │  # From skills-service (NOT on the list) → TCP reset               │
         │  $ kubectl exec deploy/skills-service -n anihpj -- \               │
         │      psql "host=postgres.anihpj port=5432 dbname=jobpost" \        │
         │      -c "SELECT 1;"                                                │
         │  psql: error: connection to server ... failed: server closed       │
         │        the connection unexpectedly    ❌ reset, NOT an HTTP 403     │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    13.7  Deep Dive — Policy Evaluation with Real Requests
         - DEFINITION: for every request, the target's sidecar evaluates
           policies in a FIXED order: CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW → default
         - The two defaults you must memorize:
           → NO ALLOW policy targets the workload = allow-by-default
             (the mesh behaves as if authorization does not exist)
           → ANY ALLOW policy targets it = implicit deny — everything
             not explicitly matched by an ALLOW rule gets 403
         - DENY always beats ALLOW: a matching DENY ends evaluation
           immediately; no ALLOW further down can rescue the request
         - Policies in force below: deny-skills (DENY skills-service →
           user-service) and allow-jobpost (ALLOW jobpost-api GET
           /api/users/* → user-service)

         [EVALUATION WALKTHROUGH — three live anihpj requests]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  REQUEST 1: jobpost-api → GET /api/users/42 → user-service         │
         │    1. CUSTOM?  none → continue                                     │
         │    2. DENY?    deny-skills: source = skills-service? NO → continue │
         │    3. ALLOW?   allow-jobpost: source ✅ method ✅ path ✅             │
         │    RESULT: ✅ ALLOW → 200 OK (ALL conditions in one rule true)      │
         │  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
         │  REQUEST 2: skills-service → GET /api/users/42 → user-service      │
         │    1. CUSTOM?  none                                                │
         │    2. DENY?    deny-skills: source = skills-service? YES → ❌ DENY  │
         │    RESULT: 403 — evaluation STOPS; ALLOW is never even consulted   │
         │  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
         │  REQUEST 3: notification-service → GET /api/users/9 → user-service │
         │    1. CUSTOM?  none        2. DENY? no match → continue            │
         │    3. ALLOW?   allow-jobpost exists but source ≠ jobpost-api       │
         │    RESULT: ❌ 403 IMPLICIT deny — an ALLOW policy targets           │
         │            user-service, so anything unmatched is rejected         │
         │            (with ZERO ALLOW policies this would have been 200)     │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    13.8  Deep Dive — Dry-Run Authorization: Test Policies Without Breaking Traffic
         - DEFINITION: annotating a policy with istio.io/dry-run: "true"
           makes Envoy SHADOW-evaluate it — recording what WOULD be
           allowed or denied while enforcing nothing
         - Why it matters: the first ALLOW policy flips a workload to
           implicit-deny; one missing rule 403s real users. Dry-run
           rehearses the change against live traffic (anihpj's
           847 req/s) with zero user impact
         - Workflow: apply annotated policy → watch shadow results in
           logs/metrics/traces → fix rule gaps → remove the annotation
           (or set "false") → policy is now enforced

         [DRY-RUN AUTHORIZATIONPOLICY — annotated YAML]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1                                  │
         │  kind: AuthorizationPolicy                                         │
         │  metadata:                                                         │
         │    name: deny-admin-paths                                          │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                               │
         │    annotations:                                                    │
         │      "istio.io/dry-run": "true"  ← shadow mode: log, don't block   │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    selector:                                                       │
         │      matchLabels: {app: jobpost-api}                               │
         │    action: DENY                                                    │
         │    rules:                                                          │
         │    - to:                                                           │
         │      - operation:                                                  │
         │          paths: ["/admin/*"]   ← would block /admin — only logged  │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [WHERE DRY-RUN RESULTS APPEAR — three output channels]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  1. PROXY LOGS (raise RBAC logging first):                         │
         │     $ istioctl proxy-config log deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj \     │
         │         --level rbac:debug                                         │
         │     → "shadow denied, matched policy                               │
         │        ns[anihpj]-policy[deny-admin-paths]-rule[0]"                │
         │                                                                    │
         │  2. METRICS (Prometheus scrapes merged stats from istio-agent      │
         │     :15020; graph in Prometheus or Kiali BEFORE enforcing):        │
         │     envoy_http_inbound_0_0_0_0_8000_rbac{                          │
         │       authz_dry_run_action="deny",                                 │
         │       authz_dry_run_result="denied"}  ← count of would-be blocks   │
         │                                                                    │
         │  3. TRACE TAGS (Zipkin/Jaeger span attributes):                    │
         │     istio.authorization.dry_run.deny_policy.name:                  │
         │       ns[anihpj]-policy[deny-admin-paths]-rule[0]                  │
         │     istio.authorization.dry_run.deny_policy.result: denied         │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Limitations (exam-relevant):
           • only ALLOW and DENY actions are shadowed — CUSTOM is not
           • ALLOW and DENY dry-run results are reported separately —
             check BOTH before promoting a deny-all + allow-list pair
           • shadow log lines appear only at rbac:debug proxy log level
           • experimental annotation — re-verify after Istio upgrades
           • enforcement begins ONLY when the annotation is removed or
             set to "false" — a forgotten annotation = toothless policy

         - Putting the mechanic in a picture: one request hits BOTH
           policies at the same instant, but only the REAL policy's
           verdict is ever allowed to touch the connection

         [DRY-RUN PARALLEL EVALUATION — one request, two policies, one verdict]
                        ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
                        │ Incoming request to jobpost-api  │
                        │ (evaluated by the Envoy sidecar) │
                        └──────────────────────────────────┘
                                          │
                     Envoy evaluates BOTH policies on the SAME
                      request, at the SAME time — in parallel
                                          │
                        ┌─────────────────┴─────────────────┐
                        │                                   │
                        ▼                                   ▼
         ┌────────────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────────────┐
         │ REAL POLICY (enforcing)    │      │ DRY-RUN POLICY (shadow)    │
         │ name: allow-jobpost-read   │      │ name: deny-admin-paths     │
         │ action: ALLOW              │      │ istio.io/dry-run: "true"   │
         │                            │      │                            │
         │ -> REAL verdict:           │      │ -> SHADOW verdict:         │
         │    ALLOW or DENY           │      │    ALLOW or DENY           │
         └────────────────────────────┘      └────────────────────────────┘
                        │                                   │
                ENFORCED on the                    RECORDED to logs,
                real connection                  metrics & traces only
                        │                                   │
                        ▼                                   ▼
         ┌────────────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────────────┐
         │ Request ALLOWED/DENIED     │      │ Nothing is enforced —      │
         │ — strictly per the REAL    │      │ just a "would-have"        │
         │ policy's verdict           │      │ record for review          │
         └────────────────────────────┘      └────────────────────────────┘
                        │                                   │
                        └─────────────────┬─────────────────┘
                                          │
                                          ▼
                      ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
                      │  Request proceeds based ONLY on the │
                      │ REAL policy's verdict — the dry-run │
                      │   result NEVER wins, NEVER blocks   │
                      └─────────────────────────────────────┘

         - The dry-run lane never feeds back into the real lane — a bug
           in the shadow policy's YAML cannot cause a real outage; the
           worst it can do is write a noisy line to the three channels
           below

         [QUICK-REFERENCE: the three output channels, side by side]
         ┌────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┐
         │ CHANNEL            │ WHAT TO LOOK FOR                  │ WHY IT MATTERS                    │
         ├────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Envoy access /     │ rbac:debug log line: "shadow      │ names the EXACT rule that         │
         │ proxy logs         │ denied/allowed, matched policy    │ would fire — best for pinpointing │
         │                    │ ns[anihpj]-policy[NAME]-rule[N]"  │ which rule needs a fix            │
         │ Prometheus         │ rbac filter's dry-run-labeled     │ aggregate, mesh-wide view —       │
         │ metrics            │ counters (authz_dry_run_action /  │ spot a spike in would-be          │
         │                    │ authz_dry_run_result) per verdict │ denies before it ships live       │
         │ Distributed traces │ istio.authorization.dry_run.      │ ties ONE shadow verdict to ONE    │
         │ (Zipkin/Jaeger)    │ deny_policy.name/.result span     │ exact request — correlate with    │
         │                    │ tags on that request's span       │ a specific user's report          │
         └────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┘

         - Cross-check all three during a rollout: the trace tag says
           WHICH request would have been hit, the metric says HOW OFTEN,
           and the log line says WHICH RULE matched — three angles on
           one shadow verdict

         [SAFE ROLLOUT SEQUENCE — ship a stricter policy with zero risk first]
         ┌──────────────────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────────┐
         │ STEP 1: DEPLOY DRY-RUN       │────▶│ STEP 2: WATCH & VERIFY       │────▶│ STEP 3: FLIP TO ENFORCE      │
         │ add istio.io/dry-run:        │     │ logs + metrics + traces,     │     │ remove the annotation (or    │
         │   "true" to the new policy   │     │ one full traffic cycle       │     │   set it to "false")         │
         │ risk: ZERO (observe only)    │     │ confirm no surprise DENYs    │     │ now enforced with confidence │
         └──────────────────────────────┘     └──────────────────────────────┘     └──────────────────────────────┘

         - This sequence is the Workflow bullet above, split into three
           concrete steps — Step 2 is where the real decision gets made:
           unexpected DENYs in the shadow verdict send you back to fix
           the rule and repeat Step 1, before the annotation ever comes off
         - anihpj takeaway: every new deny-heavy AuthorizationPolicy for
           jobpost-api ships through this exact sequence — dry-run is the
           difference between "we think this rule is safe" and "we
           watched 847 req/s prove it"


    13.9  The AUDIT Action — Logging Requests Without Blocking Them
         - DEFINITION: AUDIT is a fourth AuthorizationPolicy action
           alongside ALLOW, DENY, and CUSTOM — it logs a request that
           matches its rules but never changes whether the request is
           allowed or denied; the docs are explicit: "AUDIT policies
           do not affect whether requests are allowed or denied to
           the workload. Requests will be allowed or denied based
           solely on CUSTOM, DENY and ALLOW actions"
         - Why it matters: anihpj's compliance team wants a paper
           trail of every hit on /admin/* with zero risk of an
           outage on the admin console — AUDIT gives visibility with
           no enforcement, the opposite trade-off from dry-run (13.8),
           which rehearses enforcement that IS about to go live
         - How it works: a request matching an AUDIT rule is only
           "internally marked" as auditable — producing an actual log
           line requires "a separate plugin... configured and enabled
           to actually fulfill the audit decision"; with none wired
           up, the mark is set but nothing observable happens
         - anihpj rollout: audit-admin-access ships as a standing
           policy (not a one-time rehearsal like dry-run) and stays
           in place indefinitely, even after a real DENY or ALLOW
           policy is later added for the same path

         [AUDIT AT A GLANCE — the four action types side by side]
         ┌──────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  ACTION  │  WHAT IT DOES TO THE REQUEST                               │
         ├──────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  ALLOW   │  Permits the request if it matches the rules               │
         │  DENY    │  Rejects the request if it matches any rule                │
         │  CUSTOM  │  Delegates the verdict to an external authorizer;          │
         │          │  its answer is ANDed with DENY/ALLOW, never overrides them │
         │  AUDIT   │  Logs a match for visibility only                          │
         │          │  never allows or denies anything by itself                 │
         └──────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [ANIHPJ AUDIT POLICY — watch /admin/* before a DENY exists]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1                                  │
         │  kind: AuthorizationPolicy                                         │
         │  metadata:                                                         │
         │    name: audit-admin-access                                        │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                               │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    selector:                                                       │
         │      matchLabels: {app: jobpost-api}                               │
         │    action: AUDIT      ← logs matches, never blocks anything        │
         │    rules:                                                          │
         │    - to:                                                           │
         │      - operation:                                                  │
         │          paths: ["/admin/*"]   ← every hit on /admin/* gets logged │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [AUDIT vs DRY-RUN — easy to confuse, mechanically different]
         ┌──────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  ASPECT          │  AUDIT (action: AUDIT)                                 │
         ├──────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  What it is      │  A 4th, independent action type on its own policy      │
         │  Needs a plugin? │  YES - a logging plugin must be enabled or             │
         │                  │  nothing observable happens (docs: request is only     │
         │                  │  'internally marked')                                  │
         │  Attaches to     │  Its own standing AuthorizationPolicy + rules          │
         │  Typical use     │  Ongoing compliance trail: 'who touched /admin'        │
         └──────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         ┌──────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  ASPECT          │  DRY-RUN (istio.io/dry-run: "true")                    │
         ├──────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  What it is      │  An annotation on an existing ALLOW/DENY policy        │
         │  Needs a plugin? │  NO - proxy logs, Prometheus metrics and trace         │
         │                  │  tags work out of the box (see 13.8)                   │
         │  Attaches to     │  The SAME rules the real ALLOW/DENY would enforce      │
         │  Typical use     │  One-time rehearsal before flipping a NEW policy live  │
         └──────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - KEY EXAM FACT: AUDIT sits OUTSIDE the CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW
           pipeline entirely — it is evaluated independently and never
           gates a response. Don't confuse it with dry-run, which
           shadow-tests a REAL ALLOW/DENY policy that's about to be
           enforced; AUDIT is a standing, separate action type with no
           enforcement intent at all.

    13.10  CUSTOM Action — External Authorization with ext-authz
         - DEFINITION: action: CUSTOM delegates the allow/deny decision
           to an external authorizer over Envoy's ext_authz protocol
           (HTTP or gRPC). The docs are explicit that the extension
           "cannot bypass the authorization decision made by ALLOW and
           DENY action" — a request is allowed if and only if CUSTOM
           and every ALLOW/DENY policy all agree to allow it
         - Why it matters: some checks are too dynamic for a static
           AuthorizationPolicy field — anihpj's fraud-check service
           scores every POST /api/jobs/ against account age, posting
           velocity, and an ML risk model; none of that fits into
           principals/paths/when-conditions alone
         - How it works: two-step wiring — (1) register the authorizer
           as a MeshConfig extensionProvider (envoyExtAuthzHttp or
           envoyExtAuthzGrpc) naming its Kubernetes service and port,
           (2) point an AuthorizationPolicy's action: CUSTOM +
           provider.name at that name, scoping which requests are sent
           to it with rules
         - anihpj detail: only POST /api/jobs/* is routed to
           fraud-check — GET calls and every other path skip the
           external hop entirely, keeping the fast path fast

         [MESHCONFIG EXTENSIONPROVIDER — register fraud-check]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  # patch istiod's MeshConfig (istioctl install or "kubectl edit cm       │
         │  #   istio -n istio-system") to register the external authorizer         │
         │  apiVersion: v1                                                          │
         │  kind: ConfigMap                                                         │
         │  metadata:                                                               │
         │    name: istio                                                           │
         │    namespace: istio-system                                               │
         │  data:                                                                   │
         │    mesh: |-                                                              │
         │      extensionProviders:                                                 │
         │      - name: fraud-check      ← this name is what CUSTOM policies cite   │
         │        envoyExtAuthzHttp:                                                │
         │          service: "fraud-check.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"                 │
         │          port: "9000"                                                    │
         │          timeout: "2s"       ← default is 600s, far too slow in prod     │
         │          includeRequestHeadersInCheck: ["authorization", "x-user-id"]    │
         │          headersToUpstreamOnAllow: ["x-fraud-score"]                     │
         │          headersToDownstreamOnDeny: ["content-type"]                     │
         │          failOpen: false      ← default; see the table below             │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [AUTHORIZATIONPOLICY — action: CUSTOM referencing fraud-check]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1                                  │
         │  kind: AuthorizationPolicy                                         │
         │  metadata:                                                         │
         │    name: fraud-check-on-post                                       │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                               │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    selector:                                                       │
         │      matchLabels: {app: jobpost-api}                               │
         │    action: CUSTOM                                                  │
         │    provider:                                                       │
         │      name: fraud-check   ← must match extensionProviders[].name    │
         │    rules:                                                          │
         │    - to:                 # only these requests go to fraud-check;  │
         │      - operation:         # everything else skips it entirely      │
         │          methods: ["POST"]                                         │
         │          paths: ["/api/jobs/*"]                                    │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [EXTENSION PROVIDER FIELD REFERENCE — envoyExtAuthzHttp]
         ┌────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  FIELD                         │  MEANING                               │
         ├────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  service                       │  K8s DNS name of the authorizer        │
         │  port                          │  port the authorizer listens on        │
         │  timeout                       │  max wait for a verdict (def. 600s)    │
         │  includeRequestHeadersInCheck  │  headers copied INTO the check call    │
         │  headersToUpstreamOnAllow      │  authorizer headers forwarded on       │
         │                                │  to the real backend on ALLOW          │
         │  headersToDownstreamOnAllow    │  authorizer headers returned to        │
         │                                │  the caller on ALLOW                   │
         │  headersToDownstreamOnDeny     │  authorizer headers returned to        │
         │                                │  the caller on DENY                    │
         │  failOpen                      │  true = allow through on error;        │
         │                                │  false (default) = deny on error       │
         │  statusOnError                 │  HTTP status sent to the caller if     │
         │                                │  the authorizer itself is unreachable  │
         └────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [FAIL-OPEN vs FAIL-CLOSED — what happens when fraud-check is down]
         ┌──────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  SETTING         │  WHEN fraud-check.anihpj TIMES OUT OR ERRORS         │
         ├──────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  failOpen: false │  403 returned immediately - jobpost-api's            │
         │  (the default)   │  business logic never runs. Safe default for         │
         │                  │  a money-moving path: an outage never silently       │
         │                  │  disables fraud protection.                          │
         │  failOpen: true  │  Request proceeds AS IF fraud-check said             │
         │                  │  ALLOW. Only pick this for non-critical checks       │
         │                  │  where availability beats strict enforcement.        │
         └──────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Limitations (exam-relevant): at most ONE extension provider
           is allowed per workload — different workloads may each use
           a different provider, but you cannot stack two on one; a
           CUSTOM policy is NEVER shadow-evaluated by dry-run (13.8);
           CUSTOM always runs BEFORE DENY and ALLOW on every request
           that reaches the sidecar, regardless of policy creation
           order (this is the mechanism behind Q16)
         - KEY EXAM FACT: failOpen defaults to false — if
           fraud-check.anihpj is unreachable, jobpost-api fails
           CLOSED (403), not open; that default must be changed
           explicitly per-provider if a check is meant to be
           best-effort rather than mandatory.

    13.11  The Complete Evaluation Order — CUSTOM, AUDIT, DENY, and ALLOW Together
         - DEFINITION: with all four action types now covered
           individually, the full per-request pipeline is: CUSTOM
           decides first (and can only ever end in a deny — it cannot
           rescue a request DENY/ALLOW would otherwise reject) → DENY
           → ALLOW → workload default, while AUDIT runs the entire
           time as a side-channel that only writes log/metric/trace
           evidence and never participates in the allow/deny decision
         - Why it matters: real anihpj workloads carry more than one
           action type at once — 13.7's deny-skills and allow-jobpost,
           now joined by fraud-check's CUSTOM policy and
           audit-admin-access's AUDIT policy — and the exam tests
           whether you can trace ONE request through all four layers
           without losing the order
         - How it works: see the numbered steps below; step 0 (AUDIT)
           is drawn separately because it never gates steps 1-4

         [FULL EVALUATION ORDER — one anihpj request, all four actions]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Incoming request → jobpost-api sidecar                              │
         │                                                                      │
         │  0. AUDIT runs INDEPENDENTLY, the whole time, in parallel -          │
         │     audit-admin-access logs a hit if the path is /admin/* -          │
         │     this NEVER changes the outcome of steps 1-4 below                │
         │                                                                      │
         │  1. CUSTOM   fraud-check fires first, only for POST /api/jobs/*      │
         │       authorizer says DENY  → STOP here → 403 (steps 2-3 skipped)    │
         │       authorizer says ALLOW → continue to step 2                     │
         │                                                                      │
         │  2. DENY     deny-skills: source == skills-service?                  │
         │       YES → STOP here → 403 (step 3 never runs)                      │
         │       NO  → continue to step 3                                       │
         │                                                                      │
         │  3. ALLOW    allow-jobpost: source + method + path all match?        │
         │       YES → 200 OK                                                   │
         │       NO  → 403 (an ALLOW policy targets this workload, so           │
         │              anything unmatched is implicit-denied)                  │
         │                                                                      │
         │  4. If NO ALLOW policy targets the workload at all -> allow by       │
         │     default (CUSTOM and DENY above still apply either way)           │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [THREE-REQUEST WALKTHROUGH — CUSTOM, AUDIT, DENY, ALLOW together]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  REQUEST A: jobpost-api's own retry → POST /api/jobs/ (from a        │
         │             legit caller, not skills-service)                        │
         │    0. AUDIT: path isn't /admin/* → no log entry                      │
         │    1. CUSTOM: fraud-check called, returns ALLOW → continue           │
         │    3. ALLOW: allow-jobpost matches → 200 OK                          │
         │  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────    │
         │  REQUEST B: skills-service → POST /api/jobs/ (should never reach     │
         │             business logic - it's on the deny list)                  │
         │    0. AUDIT: path isn't /admin/* → no log entry                      │
         │    1. CUSTOM: fraud-check STILL runs and is billed/logged for        │
         │       this call - CUSTOM cannot be skipped by a later DENY           │
         │    2. DENY: deny-skills matches → STOP → 403                         │
         │    (this is Q16's lesson: scope the CUSTOM policy's own              │
         │     selector/from to exclude callers you already know are denied)    │
         │  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────    │
         │  REQUEST C: notification-service → GET /admin/reports (never         │
         │             explicitly allowed anywhere)                             │
         │    0. AUDIT: path IS /admin/* → audit-admin-access LOGS the hit      │
         │    1. CUSTOM: rule only matches POST /api/jobs/* → skipped           │
         │    2. DENY: deny-skills source doesn't match → continue              │
         │    3. ALLOW: allow-jobpost exists but source doesn't match → 403     │
         │    RESULT: request is BOTH logged by AUDIT and rejected by           │
         │    implicit-deny - AUDIT firing changes nothing about the 403        │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - KEY EXAM FACT: reordering YAML, reapplying policies in a
           different sequence, or renaming resources never changes
           this order — the ACTION TYPE alone fixes the phase (CUSTOM,
           then DENY, then ALLOW), and AUDIT is not a phase at all,
           just a parallel observer that never blocks anything.

    13.12  The Complete `when` Condition Key Reference
         - DEFINITION: every when: entry needs a key drawn from a
           fixed, documented vocabulary plus either values or
           notValues — 13.4 already used one of these keys
           (request.auth.claims[role]); this section is the full list
         - Why it matters: exam questions routinely swap in a
           DIFFERENT key from this same family — request.auth.principal
           instead of requestPrincipals, source.ip instead of
           source.principal, connection.sni for a TLS-passthrough
           Gateway — confusing them is the trap
         - How it works: each key is scoped to HTTP-only or HTTP+TCP,
           and several require mTLS or TLS to even be populated
           (source.namespace, source.principal, connection.sni)

         [COMPLETE WHEN CONDITION KEY REFERENCE]
         ┌────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  KEY                       │  MATCHES / SCOPE                                   │
         ├────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  source.ip                 │  source workload IP, single IP or CIDR (HTTP+TCP)  │
         │  source.namespace          │  caller's namespace, needs mTLS (HTTP+TCP)         │
         │  source.principal          │  caller's SPIFFE identity, needs mTLS (HTTP+TCP)   │
         │  remote.ip                 │  original client IP via X-Forwarded-For or         │
         │                            │  PROXY protocol (HTTP+TCP)                         │
         │  destination.ip            │  target workload IP (HTTP+TCP)                     │
         │  destination.port          │  target port, 0-65535 (HTTP+TCP)                   │
         │  connection.sni            │  SNI from the TLS handshake, needs TLS (HTTP+TCP)  │
         │  request.headers[x]        │  any HTTP request header (HTTP only)               │
         │  request.auth.principal    │  JWT "iss/sub" once RequestAuthN validates         │
         │                            │  it (HTTP only)                                    │
         │  request.auth.audiences    │  JWT "aud" claim (HTTP only)                       │
         │  request.auth.presenter    │  JWT "azp" claim (HTTP only)                       │
         │  request.auth.claims[x]    │  any raw JWT claim, e.g. claims[role]              │
         │                            │  (HTTP only)                                       │
         └────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [ANIHPJ when: EXAMPLES — four conditions, four use cases]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  # 1. geofence the admin console to the corp VPN egress range        │
         │    when:                                                             │
         │    - key: remote.ip                                                  │
         │      values: ["203.0.113.0/24"]                                      │
         │                                                                      │
         │  # 2. scope a rule to only the Prometheus scrape port                │
         │    when:                                                             │
         │    - key: destination.port                                           │
         │      values: ["15020"]                                               │
         │                                                                      │
         │  # 3. TLS-passthrough gateway: only accept anihpj's real domain      │
         │    when:                                                             │
         │    - key: connection.sni                                             │
         │      values: ["jobs.anihpj.com"]                                     │
         │                                                                      │
         │  # 4. require a canary marker header on the canary subset            │
         │    when:                                                             │
         │    - key: request.headers[x-canary]                                  │
         │      values: ["true"]                                                │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Also available: notValues inside any when: block negates
           the match (the condition-level sibling of the notPaths/
           notPrincipals family already introduced in 13.5); an
           experimental experimental.envoy.filters.* key also exists
           for raw Envoy filter metadata but carries no backward-
           compatibility guarantee — treat it as non-exam material.

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     CHAPTERS 12-13: DAILY WORK TAKEAWAYS (Security)
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    After these chapters, in your daily work you will:
      • Enable STRICT mTLS: every service call encrypted, zero code changes
      • Know that SPIFFE certs auto-rotate every 24h — no manual renewal
      • Build a deny-all AuthorizationPolicy → then allow specific paths
      • Create a zero-trust policy matrix: which service can call which
      • Validate JWT tokens at the mesh level — no auth code in services
      • Migrate safely: PERMISSIVE mode first → verify → then STRICT
      • Check certs: openssl s_client to verify mTLS between pods
      • Remember: mTLS = identity (WHO), AuthzPolicy = permissions (WHAT)
      • Know that without AuthzPolicy, ANY service can call ANY service
        even with mTLS enabled — mTLS alone is NOT access control!
      • Exempt /healthz probes with notPaths — never disable JWT auth
      • Lock PostgreSQL :5432 with a ports-based ALLOW (verify via psql)
      • Rehearse risky policies with istio.io/dry-run: "true" — read
        shadow results in proxy logs, Prometheus metrics and Kiali

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     CHAPTERS 12-13: ICA EXAM TIPS & QUESTIONS (Securing Workloads — 25%)
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    🎯 ICA EXAM FOCUS — This is 25% of the exam (official domain name:
       "Securing Workloads" — Authorization, Authentication, and Edge TLS):
      • "Encrypt all service traffic" = PeerAuthentication mode: STRICT
      • "Restrict which service can call which" = AuthorizationPolicy
      • "Validate JWT tokens at mesh level" = RequestAuthentication
      • "Protect a database/TCP port" = AuthorizationPolicy with
        to.operation.ports — HTTP-only fields NEVER match TCP traffic
      • "Test a policy safely first" = istio.io/dry-run: "true"
      • Evaluation order = CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW; the FIRST ALLOW
        policy on a workload flips its default to implicit deny

    Q1: How do you enforce STRICT mTLS for the anihpj namespace?
    A1: Create a PeerAuthentication resource with spec.mtls.mode: STRICT in the anihpj namespace.

    Q2: What AuthorizationPolicy would allow ONLY jobpost-api to GET /api/users/* on user-service?
    A2: selector: {app: user-service}, action: ALLOW, rules: [{from: [{source:
        {principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api"]}}], to:
        [{operation: {methods: ["GET"], paths: ["/api/users/*"]}}]}]

    Q3: Why is mTLS alone not sufficient for security?
    A3: mTLS provides identity (WHO is calling) but not authorization (WHAT are
        they allowed to do). Without AuthorizationPolicy, ANY authenticated
        service can call ANY other service. You need BOTH.

    Q4: anihpj still has two legacy Deployments without sidecars. How do you
        reach STRICT mTLS without an outage?
    A4: Stage it: apply PeerAuthentication mode: PERMISSIVE to anihpj first
        (accepts BOTH plaintext and mTLS), confirm every edge shows locks in
        Kiali and istioctl x describe pod reports mTLS, inject sidecars into
        the two stragglers, then edit the same resource to mode: STRICT.

    Q5: Task: only istio-ingressgateway may call jobpost-api; everything else
        in anihpj is blocked. Which two AuthorizationPolicies do you apply?
    A5: (1) deny-all: namespace anihpj, spec: {} — empty spec denies all.
        (2) ALLOW: selector {app: jobpost-api}, action: ALLOW, from.source.
        principals: ["cluster.local/ns/istio-system/sa/istio-ingressgateway"].
        The deny-all flips the default; the ALLOW re-opens exactly one path.

    Q6: Only JWTs carrying role=admin may POST /api/jobs/. What do you build?
    A6: A RequestAuthentication (issuer https://auth.anihpj.com, jwksUri
        https://auth.anihpj.com/.well-known/jwks.json) plus an ALLOW
        AuthorizationPolicy: from.source.requestPrincipals
        ["https://auth.anihpj.com/*"], to.operation {methods: ["POST"],
        paths: ["/api/jobs/*"]}, when request.auth.claims[role] = admin.
        RA validates the signature; the claim check lives in the AuthZ policy.

    Q7: After turning on STRICT mTLS, every call to user-service returns 503
        (upstream connect error). A DestinationRule for user-service exists.
        Diagnose.
    A7: The DestinationRule likely sets trafficPolicy.tls.mode: DISABLE, so
        client sidecars send plaintext that the STRICT server resets. Confirm
        with istioctl x describe pod <user-service-pod> (it flags the PA/DR
        conflict), then set tls.mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL or delete the stale rule.

    Q8: Restrict PostgreSQL at postgres.anihpj:5432 so only jobpost-api and
        user-service can connect. Write and verify the policy.
    A8: ALLOW policy: selector {app: postgres}, from.source.principals
        [".../sa/jobpost-api", ".../sa/user-service"], to.operation.ports
        ["5432"]. Use ONLY ports — methods/paths never match TCP and would
        make the ALLOW rule unmatchable (traffic denied). Verify with psql:
        allowed pods run SELECT 1; blocked pods get a connection reset.

    Q9: You must land a deny policy on jobpost-api mid-day with zero risk.
        How do you test it live, and where do you read the results?
    A9: Annotate it "istio.io/dry-run": "true" — traffic keeps flowing while
        Envoy shadow-evaluates. Read results in: proxy logs ("shadow denied",
        after istioctl proxy-config log ... --level rbac:debug), the rbac
        metric with authz_dry_run_result="denied" in Prometheus/Kiali, and
        dry-run span tags in tracing. Remove the annotation to enforce.

    Q10: Kubelet probes to /healthz return 403 after you required JWTs on
         jobpost-api. Fix it without weakening auth on the real endpoints.
    A10: Use exclusion matching in the require-jwt ALLOW policy: on the JWT
         rule set to.operation.notPaths ["/healthz", "/ready"], and add a
         second rule with paths ["/healthz", "/ready"] and no from: block.
         Probes (no JWT) now pass; every other path still demands a token.

    Q11: anihpj's namespace-wide PeerAuthentication is STRICT, yet a debug
         pod's plain curl to notification-service returns 200 OK instead
         of a connection reset. kubectl get peerauthentication -n anihpj
         lists a second object, notification-legacy (selector app:
         notification-service, mode: PERMISSIVE), left over from a
         debugging session. Explain why plaintext still works, and fix
         it without touching the namespace-wide default.
    A11: PeerAuthentication precedence is narrowest-scope-wins, not
         creation order or "namespace beats workload": the workload-
         scoped notification-legacy (selector matches notification-
         service, mode PERMISSIVE) beats the namespace-wide default
         (STRICT) for that one workload only, so notification-service
         still accepts plaintext. Fix: kubectl delete peerauthentication
         notification-legacy -n anihpj — the pod then inherits the
         namespace default (STRICT). Confirm with istioctl x describe
         pod <notification-service-pod> -n anihpj (should now report
         STRICT), then re-curl plaintext and expect "connection reset by
         peer", not 200.

    Q12: istiod was accidentally scaled to 0 for about 30 hours during a
         botched Helm upgrade; the data plane kept routing on cached
         config the whole time. Now that istiod is back, calls between
         jobpost-api and user-service fail with a hard TLS handshake
         error — not a 503, not a 403. How do you confirm this is a
         cert-expiry problem, and fix it?
    A12: SVID certs are valid only 24h, and with istiod unreachable for
         over a day neither pod could renew before expiry — a plain
         PA/DR mismatch produces a 503, not a handshake failure, so
         suspect expired crypto material instead. Confirm with istioctl
         proxy-config secret deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj (the default
         cert's "Not After" timestamp is in the past) or openssl
         s_client -connect user-service.anihpj:8080 ("certificate has
         expired"). Fix: verify istiod is healthy (kubectl get pods -n
         istio-system), then force fresh CSRs with kubectl rollout
         restart deployment jobpost-api user-service -n anihpj — expired
         certs do not renew themselves without a restart.

    Q13: Security mandates that every anihpj mesh certificate chain to
         the company's existing enterprise root CA instead of istiod's
         self-signed root — but wants the least invasive change: istiod
         should keep issuing and auto-rotating the 24h workload certs,
         just under the new root. Which upgrade path do you pick, and
         what are the exact steps?
    A13: Plug-in CA certs — istiod keeps signing and rotating SVIDs,
         only the root changes (SPIRE and cert-manager/istio-csr both
         take issuance away from istiod entirely, more invasive than
         asked). Steps: (1) generate an intermediate CA under the
         enterprise root, producing ca-cert.pem, ca-key.pem, root-
         cert.pem, cert-chain.pem; (2) kubectl create secret generic
         cacerts -n istio-system --from-file=ca-cert.pem --from-file=
         ca-key.pem --from-file=root-cert.pem --from-file=cert-
         chain.pem — name MUST be cacerts, namespace MUST be istio-
         system; (3) istioctl install --set profile=default -y so
         istiod picks up the new root; (4) kubectl rollout restart
         deployment -n anihpj so every workload requests a fresh CSR
         under the new chain. Verify: istioctl proxy-config secret
         deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj should show the enterprise
         intermediate as ROOTCA, not istiod's old self-signed default.

    Q14: The test-team ServiceAccount (cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/test-
         team) was compromised in a credential-stuffing incident and
         must be blocked from calling search-service immediately — but
         every other caller in anihpj (jobpost-api, user-service,
         skills-service, and any service added later) must keep working
         without you hand-listing every legitimate principal. Write the
         policy.
    A14: Use notPrincipals so the rule matches everyone except the
         compromised identity, instead of enumerating every legitimate
         caller: selector {app: search-service}, action: ALLOW, rules:
         [{from: [{source: {notPrincipals:
         ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/test-team"]}}]}]. Any principal
         other than test-team satisfies the rule and is allowed; test-
         team fails the match and — because this ALLOW policy now
         targets search-service — falls through to implicit deny (403).
         Belt-and-suspenders option: add a companion action: DENY rule
         with from.source.principals:
         ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/test-team"] so the block survives
         even if the ALLOW policy is later removed.

    Q15: anihpj adds a Kafka broker at kafka.anihpj:9092; only
         notification-service and search-service should publish to it.
         A teammate tries to scope a DENY policy narrowly — blocking
         skills-service only when it hits an "/admin" path — with
         rules: [{from: [{source: {principals:
         ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/skills-service"]}}], to:
         [{operation: {ports: ["9092"], paths: ["/admin"]}}]}]. After
         applying it, ALL of skills-service's Kafka traffic is blocked,
         not just calls to "/admin". Explain the bug and give the
         corrected policy.
    A15: Kafka on 9092 is raw TCP, and paths is an HTTP-only match
         field — Istio silently drops it from a DENY rule instead of
         rejecting the policy, leaving only ports: ["9092"] plus the
         principal to enforce. The rule actually reads "DENY skills-
         service on port 9092, full stop," denying MORE than intended —
         exactly the TCP DENY trap. TCP has no concept of a path, so
         there is no way to scope a TCP DENY by URL. Correct policy:
         drop the paths field and own the fact this is an all-or-
         nothing TCP block — action: DENY, rules: [{from: [{source:
         {principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/skills-service"]}}],
         to: [{operation: {ports: ["9092"]}}]}]. If skills-service
         genuinely needs partial access, split it onto a separate port
         or topic-level ACL — AuthorizationPolicy cannot inspect L7
         semantics inside a raw TCP stream.

    Q16: anihpj wires an external fraud-detection CUSTOM
         AuthorizationPolicy in front of jobpost-api's POST
         /api/jobs/, calling out to fraud-check.anihpj:9000 on every
         request. A separate DENY policy permanently blocks
         skills-service from reaching jobpost-api. During a load test,
         fraud-check.anihpj's logs show it being invoked for requests
         FROM skills-service — traffic that should never reach business
         logic. Is this a bug, and does moving the DENY policy ahead of
         the CUSTOM one fix it?
    A16: Not a bug — it is the fixed Istio evaluation order: CUSTOM
         always runs first, before DENY and before ALLOW, for every
         request that reaches the sidecar, and this order cannot be
         changed by editing YAML or by policy creation order — the
         action type dictates the phase, not application sequence. So
         the fraud-check CUSTOM provider fires even for skills-service
         traffic the DENY policy will reject moments later; reordering
         the DENY policy ahead of it is not possible, and would not
         help if it were. To cut wasted external calls, filter cheaper
         callers out before CUSTOM ever runs — for example, scope the
         CUSTOM policy's own selector/from.source.notPrincipals to
         exclude skills-service directly, so a caller that is denied
         anyway never triggers the external fraud-check round trip.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — Tracing a Disguised Request Through All Four Actions
    13.7 walked three separate requests, each tripping only ONE layer.
    13.11 then laid out the clean four-step pipeline. Here is the messy,
    realistic case the exam loves: a single request that LOOKS like it
    should hit every layer, but doesn't — because "CUSTOM runs first"
    only means CUSTOM runs first for requests its OWN rule actually scopes
    in, not for every request that reaches the sidecar.

    Scenario: skills-service (already on deny-skills' block list) tries to
    dodge the fraud-check CUSTOM policy — scoped only to POST /api/jobs/*
    — by posting to an admin-side import path instead: POST
    /admin/api/jobs/bulk-import on jobpost-api.

              ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
              │ REQUEST: skills-service -> POST /admin/api/jobs/bulk-import        │
              │ -> jobpost-api sidecar (a disguised lateral-movement attempt)      │
              └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                           │
         AUDIT runs independently the whole time — the CUSTOM/DENY/ALLOW
         trunk on the right is evaluated separately, in the same pass
                                           │
                      ┌────────────────────┴────────────────────┐
                      │                                         │
                      ▼                                         ▼
          ┌────────────────────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
          │ AUDIT (audit-admin-access)         │      │ STEP 1 - CUSTOM (fraud-check)      │
          │ path matches /admin/* ?  YES       │      │ rule matches POST /api/jobs/*?     │
          │ -> LOG the hit, right now          │      │ NO - path is /admin/api/jobs/*     │
          │                                    │      │ -> SCOPED OUT: does not run;       │
          │                                    │      │    "runs first" never fires here   │
          └────────────────────────────────────┘      └────────────────────────────────────┘
                                                    │
                                                    ▼
          ┌────────────────────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
          │ AUDIT VERDICT                      │      │ STEP 2 - DENY (deny-skills)        │
          │ logged to proxy log, metrics,      │      │ source == skills-service ?         │
          │ and trace tags — this NEVER        │      │ YES -> STOP HERE -> 403            │
          │ changes the ALLOW/DENY outcome     │      │ (step 3, ALLOW, never reached)     │
          └────────────────────────────────────┘      └────────────────────────────────────┘
          │                                         │
                      └────────────────────┬────────────────────┘
                                           │
                                           ▼
              ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
              │ RESULT: 403, reason = DENY (deny-skills)                       │
              │ PLUS one AUDIT log line recorded for /admin/*                  │
              │ — two independent outcomes from one request                    │
              └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    The lesson: disguising the path did not help the attacker (deny-skills
    still catches the source identity regardless of URL), but it DID prove
    that CUSTOM's "runs first" guarantee is conditional on its own rule
    actually matching — a request can sail past a CUSTOM policy entirely
    and still be judged, and logged, by the layers behind it.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
      ⚡ Apply every ALLOW policy for a workload BEFORE its deny-all goes
         live (or dry-run the deny-all first) — flipping deny-all before the
         ALLOWs exist 403s all live traffic for as long as the gap lasts
      ⚡ A sudden wave of 403s right after ONE new AuthorizationPolicy lands?
         Check whether it is the FIRST ALLOW targeting that workload — that
         alone flips the default from allow-by-default to implicit-deny
      ⚡ 401 vs 403 is a free diagnostic: 401 = RequestAuthentication
         rejected a present-but-broken JWT; 403 = AuthorizationPolicy
         rejected it (including "no token at all" once requestPrincipals
         is required)
      ⚡ Dry-run every new ALLOW/DENY before enforcing it and read all three
         channels (rbac:debug proxy logs, Prometheus authz_dry_run_* metrics,
         trace tags) — CUSTOM can never be dry-run, so stage those against a
         canary path instead
      ⚡ One phrase covers every ordering question the exam can ask: "CUSTOM
         can only say no, DENY always wins, ALLOW is the last word, AUDIT
         never speaks"
      ⚡ TCP workload (postgres, kafka)? Only ports/principals/namespaces/
         ipBlocks are valid match fields — paths or methods showing up in a
         TCP-target policy is the bug, not a feature

    COMMANDS CHEAT-CARD
    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ COMMAND                                                                           │ WHAT IT DOES                              │
    ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ kubectl apply -f authz/ -n anihpj                                                 │ apply the anihpj ALLOW policy set         │
    │ kubectl get authorizationpolicy -n anihpj                                         │ list every policy in the namespace        │
    │ kubectl describe authorizationpolicy <name> -n anihpj                             │ show one policy's full rule set           │
    │ kubectl annotate authorizationpolicy/<name> -n anihpj istio.io/dry-run-           │ remove dry-run -> start enforcing         │
    │ istioctl proxy-config log deploy/<svc> -n anihpj --level rbac:debug               │ raise RBAC log level, see shadow verdicts │
    │ kubectl exec deploy/<svc> -n anihpj -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w %{http_code} <url> │ quick allow/deny smoke test               │
    │ psql "host=postgres.anihpj port=5432 ..." -c "SELECT 1;"                          │ verify TCP ALLOW: reset=blocked, rows=OK  │
    └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┘

    🧪 PRACTICE DRILL (8 minutes) — Ship deny-all + one ALLOW, zero outage
      1. Apply a deny-all AuthorizationPolicy in anihpj, but annotate it
         istio.io/dry-run: "true" first — nothing is enforced yet
      2. curl jobpost-api -> user-service from inside the mesh right now and
         confirm it still returns 200 (dry-run enforces nothing)
      3. Run istioctl proxy-config log deploy/user-service -n anihpj
         --level rbac:debug, then watch for "shadow denied" lines
      4. Write and apply one real ALLOW policy on user-service permitting
         only jobpost-api, GET, /api/users/*
      5. Remove the dry-run annotation (istio.io/dry-run-) and re-run both
         curls: jobpost-api -> 200, skills-service -> 403

    In prose: Chapter 13 starts from a single gap — mTLS proves identity but
    enforces nothing — and closes it in stages, first with a blunt deny-all
    plus a hand-built allow-list for anihpj, then with JWT-based identity
    checks, then with the carve-outs real production traffic always needs
    (health probes, TCP databases), then with the tooling to change any of
    it safely (dry-run), and finally with the complete four-action mental
    model — CUSTOM, DENY, ALLOW, and the log-only AUDIT side-channel —
    that the ICA exam expects you to trace for any single request without
    hesitation.

  [PART 8 INTRO]
  By the end of Part 7 the anihpj mesh is installed, every hop between
  jobpost-api, user-service, skills-service, location-service,
  notification-service, auth-service and search-service is routed on
  purpose and encrypted by default, and AuthorizationPolicy decides who may
  call whom. That is a mesh that behaves correctly. It says nothing yet
  about two questions every production team eventually asks: how do I
  change this system without breaking it, and how do I grow it without it
  breaking me. Part 8 answers both — which is why it is not a new exam
  domain, it is Traffic Management and Installation, Upgrade & Config
  pushed to their production edge.

  Chapter 14 answers the first question. A VirtualService weight field
  turns "ship jobpost-api v2" from an all-or-nothing kubectl rollout into a
  dial: mirror the traffic first, then send it 5%, 25%, 50%, 100%, with a
  2-second YAML edit to pull back to zero at any stage. Canary, shadow/
  mirror and blue-green are three settings on that same dial, chosen by how
  much blast radius you can tolerate.

  Chapter 15 answers a question Chapter 14 does not: what stops one caller
  — a retry storm from search-service, a misbehaving batch job, a scraper
  hammering jobpost-api's /api/jobs/ — from taking it down even after v2 is
  fully rolled out and healthy? Local and global rate limiting cap abusive
  traffic at the Envoy layer before it ever reaches Django. And when a
  limiter, a header rewrite or a custom check has no matching Istio CRD,
  EnvoyFilter and WasmPlugin let you extend Envoy itself — the same proxy
  already sitting in front of every anihpj pod — without waiting on an
  Istio release.

  Chapter 16 answers the second question — growth. A single cluster with a
  sidecar in every pod is not how anihpj runs forever: EU/US latency needs
  push it toward multiple clusters with locality-aware failover, resource
  pressure at scale pushes some namespaces from sidecars toward the
  ztunnel-based ambient mode, and a legacy PostgreSQL VM that can never be
  containerized still needs to join the mesh as a WorkloadEntry. None of
  this changes what you built in Chapters 1-13 — it changes how far it can
  stretch.

  🧠 ANALOGY: think of Chapters 1-13 as building a car that works — engine,
  brakes, steering. Part 8 is everything a car needs AFTER it works: a way
  to swap the engine while driving without anyone noticing (canary/blue-
  green), a speed limiter so one reckless driver doesn't total the fleet
  (rate limiting), and the ability to run the same model on two continents
  — some fully equipped, some stripped to a lighter chassis (multi-cluster/
  ambient).

  Every YAML, weight and threshold in this Part is drawn from the anihpj/
  jobpost example used throughout this guide — the jobpost-api canary of
  14.1, the same seven services already stress-tested in Part 5's circuit
  breakers, now reappearing across an EU/US multi-cluster topology in 16.1.
