Chapter 14: Canary Deployments — Safe Feature Releases
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    Chapter 14 of 14-16  ·  Difficulty: 🔴 Advanced  ·  No graded domain of
    its own — extends Traffic Management (35%) and Installation, Upgrade &
    Config (20%)  ·  "how do I ship a change without betting everything on it?"

    WHY THIS MATTERS
    jobpost-api's matching-logic rewrite (v2) is exactly the kind of change
    anihpj cannot afford to ship blind — get it wrong and every job search
    on the platform breaks at once. Chapter 6 already gave you the two YAML
    fields this entire chapter runs on: a VirtualService's weight field,
    which splits traffic by percentage, and its mirror field, which copies
    traffic without ever touching the response a real user sees. Chapter 14
    adds no new CRD at all — it asks a harder question about those same two
    fields: in what SEQUENCE, gated by what SIGNAL, with what ROLLBACK PLAN,
    do you move weight from 0 to 100? Canary (14.1), shadow/mirror testing
    (14.2), and blue-green (14.3) are three disciplined answers to that one
    question, not three different technologies — and 14.4's decision matrix
    exists because picking the wrong one for a given anihpj change (a schema
    migration flipped like a canary, or a one-line patch flipped like
    blue-green) is its own kind of outage. By 14.7 you can also tell apart
    "canary" applied to jobpost-api (an application decision, yours to make)
    from "canary" applied to istiod itself (a mesh-operator decision, covered
    fully in Chapter 17) — two ideas the exam tests as separate questions.

    LEARNING OBJECTIVES
    By the end of this chapter you will be able to:
      ✅ Run jobpost-api-v2 through a full canary ramp — mirror → 5% → 25%
         → 50% → 100% — using only VirtualService weight edits, with a
         same-second rollback available at every single step
      ✅ Configure mirror + mirrorPercentage so jobpost-api-v2 sees real
         production traffic while its responses are silently discarded, and
         explain why a mirrored write still lands in PostgreSQL
      ✅ Execute an instant blue-green cut-over (and rollback) for a service
         like user-service, and name the shared-database compatibility trap
         that comes bundled with it
      ✅ Use the risk/rollback/cost decision matrix (14.4) to pick canary,
         blue-green, rolling, or shadow for any anihpj scenario in under
         30 seconds
      ✅ Describe how a metrics-gated automated canary (Flagger, Argo
         Rollouts) promotes or rolls back jobpost-api v2 without a human
         staring at Grafana for five days
      ✅ Ramp mirrorPercentage independently of route weight (1% → 10% →
         50% → 100%) and configure a multi-destination mirrors[] rule
      ✅ Tell an APPLICATION canary (jobpost-api v1/v2 via VirtualService
         weight) apart from a CONTROL-PLANE canary (istiod stable/canary
         via istioctl revision) without hesitating

    EXAM/ICA RELEVANCE
    Chapter 14 carries no line item of its own on the ICA blueprint — Part 8
    exists to extend Traffic Management (35%) and Installation, Upgrade &
    Config (20%) to production scale, not to add a ninth domain. In practice
    this means the exam almost never says "canary deployment" outright; it
    says "roll out a change gradually," "test a new version without risking
    real users," or "release with an instant rollback," and expects you to
    reach for the exact VirtualService weight/mirror pattern Chapter 6
    already taught. The one place this chapter draws a hard,
    independently-graded line is 14.7: a scenario about safely upgrading
    Istio itself belongs to Chapter 17's Installation/Upgrade domain and is
    answered with istioctl revisions, not VirtualService weights — confusing
    the two is a guaranteed wrong answer, not a partial-credit one.

    Read it top to bottom: 14.1-14.3 hand you three disciplined ways to move
    traffic from v1 to v2 (gradual, shadowed, or instant), 14.4 turns "which
    one" into a lookup instead of a debate, and 14.5-14.7 go deeper on those
    same three patterns — automating the gate, shrinking the mirror's blast
    radius, and drawing the one hard line the exam grades separately.

    14.1 The Full Canary Deployment Workflow
         - Phase 1: Deploy jobpost-api:v2 with replicas: 0 (shadow deployment)
         - Phase 2: Route 5% traffic to v2, watch error rate in Kiali
         - Phase 3: Ramp up gradually: 10% → 25% → 50% → 90% → 100%
         - Phase 4: Delete v1 deployment when confident
         - Full rollback at any phase: change weight back to 0% for v2
         - DEFINITION: A canary deployment releases a new version to a
           small slice of real users first — named after the canary birds
           miners carried underground as an early-warning system

         📖 KEY TERM — Canary Deployment: sends PARTIAL, REAL production
           traffic to the new version only — never 0% (that's
           mirror/shadow) and never one instant 100% switch (that's
           blue-green). The % that moves is a live VirtualService
           weight edit, never a redeploy.
         - With Istio the % lives in a VirtualService weight field, so
           "more traffic to v2" is a 2-second YAML edit — no re-deploy,
           no DNS change, no load-balancer surgery
         - Prerequisite: a DestinationRule defining subsets v1 and v2 that
           match the pods' "version" labels — no subsets, no split
         - Golden progression for anihpj: Mirror → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%,
           with a metrics gate between every step (see 14.5)

    14.2 Shadow / Mirror Traffic Testing
         - Mirror 100% of live traffic to v2 — but discard v2 responses
         - Users never see v2 responses, but v2 processes real production traffic
         - Use to: verify new jobpost-api handles production load before going live
         - Zero risk — users unaffected, v2 gets real-world testing
         - DEFINITION: Mirroring (shadowing) = the sidecar duplicates each
           request and sends the copy fire-and-forget; the mirror's reply
           is discarded and can never delay or corrupt the user's response
         - Envoy tags the copy: the Host header arrives at v2 as
           "jobpost-api-shadow", so v2's Django logs can separate
           mirrored traffic from live traffic

         🔧 UNDER THE HOOD: mirroring is one field on the SAME route
         Istio already compiled from the VirtualService, not a second
         component watching traffic. Envoy's router holds a
         request_mirror_policies entry for the route; on a match it
         clones the request, rewrites the clone's Host/:authority to
         jobpost-api-shadow, and dispatches it to the v2 cluster over
         its own connection — v1's reply to the real caller never
         waits on it.
         - ⚠️ Mirrored requests still execute for real: if v2 handles
           POST /api/jobs it INSERTs a real row into PostgreSQL — point
           v2 at a shadow database or mirror read-only endpoints only
         [MIRROR TRAFFIC YAML + FLOW DIAGRAM]

         [TRAFFIC MIRRORING — safe production testing for anihpj]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  spec:                                                 │
         │    http:                                               │
         │    - route:                                            │
         │      - destination:                                    │
         │          host: jobpost-api                             │
         │          subset: v1           # Real users get v1      │
         │        weight: 100                                     │
         │      mirror:                                           │
         │        host: jobpost-api                               │
         │        subset: v2             # v2 gets a silent copy  │
         │      mirrorPercentage:                                 │
         │        value: 100.0           # Copy 100% to v2        │
         │                                                        │
         │  ✅ Users: 100% served by v1 (no impact)               │
         │  ✅ v2: receives all real production requests silently  │
         │  ✅ Check v2 metrics for errors before any user sees it │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [MIRROR FLOW — one user request, two deliveries]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │   user ──▶ Envoy sidecar (in front of jobpost-api)             │
         │                │                                               │
         │       ┌────────┴─────────┐                                     │
         │       ▼ LIVE             ▼ COPY (fire-and-forget)              │
         │   v1 pod                 v2 pod                                │
         │   Host: jobpost-api      Host: jobpost-api-shadow              │
         │       │                      │                                 │
         │       ▼                      ▼                                 │
         │   response ──▶ USER      response ──▶ DISCARDED                │
         │                                                                │
         │   v2 slow or crashing? user never notices — v1 already replied │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    14.3 Blue-Green Deployments with Istio
         - Maintain two identical environments: blue (current) and green (new)
         - All traffic on blue; green is fully deployed but receiving 0%
         - Switch: change VirtualService to route 100% to green (instant!)
         - Rollback: change back to blue (instant!)
         - Difference from canary: no gradual ramp — instant switch
         - Istio advantage: the "switch" is a YAML change, not a DNS update
         - DEFINITION: Blue-green = two complete, identical stacks; only
           the router (here, a VirtualService) decides which one is live
         - Cost trade-off: green duplicates blue's full capacity while
           both run — a canary only adds a couple of v2 pods
         - ⚠️ Shared-state gotcha: blue and green usually share the same
           PostgreSQL — schema changes must stay compatible with BOTH
           versions until blue is finally retired
         - Keep blue warm for 24h after the flip: rollback then stays as
           instant as the cut-over was
         [BLUE-GREEN SWITCHING DIAGRAM: instant traffic cut-over]

         [BLUE-GREEN SWITCHING — instant cut-over, instant rollback]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  BEFORE THE FLIP                  AFTER THE FLIP               │
         │  ───────────────                  ──────────────               │
         │  VirtualService                   VirtualService               │
         │       │                                │                       │
         │       ├─ 100% ─▶ 🔵 v1 (blue)          ├─ 100% ─▶ 🟢 v2 (green)│
         │       └─   0% ─▶ 🟢 v2 (green:         └─   0% ─▶ 🔵 v1 (blue: │
         │                  deployed, idle)                  kept warm)   │
         │                                                                │
         │  Switch   = edit ONE line in the VS  → live in ~2 seconds      │
         │  Rollback = the same edit, reversed  → equally instant         │
         │  No DNS propagation, no pod restart, no LB re-pointing         │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [THE FLIP — the entire blue-green cut-over is one line of YAML]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                            │
         │  kind: VirtualService                                          │
         │  metadata:                                                     │
         │    name: jobpost-api-vs                                        │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                           │
         │  spec:                                                         │
         │    hosts:                                                      │
         │    - jobpost-api                                               │
         │    http:                                                       │
         │    - route:                                                    │
         │      - destination:                                            │
         │          host: jobpost-api                                     │
         │          subset: v1        # ← BLUE serving 100% of traffic    │
         │                                                                │
         │  # THE SWITCH — change that one line, then kubectl apply:      │
         │  #     subset: v2          # ← GREEN now serves 100%           │
         │  # THE ROLLBACK — the same edit, reversed:                     │
         │  #     subset: v1          # ← BLUE back, ~2 seconds, no drama │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    14.4  Deployment Strategy Decision Matrix — Which to Use When
         - DEFINITION: A decision matrix maps each release strategy to
           its risk, rollback speed and cost — choosing one becomes a
           lookup, not a debate
         - Why it matters: the ICA exam (and 2 A.M. on-call reality)
           hands you a scenario — "high-risk rewrite", "DB migration",
           "tiny patch" — and expects the matching strategy, every time
         - How to read it: risk = worst-case user impact mid-rollout;
           rollback = time to undo; cost = extra infrastructure kept
           running while the rollout is in flight

         [DECISION MATRIX — four strategies scored for anihpj]
         ┌────────────┬─────────┬──────────┬─────────┬────────────────────┐
         │ Strategy   │ Risk    │ Rollback │ Cost    │ Use at anihpj for  │
         ├────────────┼─────────┼──────────┼─────────┼────────────────────┤
         │ Canary     │ 🟡 Low  │ ~2s: v2  │ + a few │ jobpost-api v2:    │
         │ (weights)  │ 5% blast│ weight→0 │ v2 pods │ risky matching-    │
         │            │ radius  │          │         │ logic rewrite      │
         ├────────────┼─────────┼──────────┼─────────┼────────────────────┤
         │ Blue-Green │ 🟡 Low  │ ~2s: flip│ 2× full │ user-service:      │
         │ (VS flip)  │ all-or- │ VS back  │ stack   │ PostgreSQL schema  │
         │            │ nothing │          │ (blue + │ migration needing  │
         │            │         │          │ green)  │ an instant undo    │
         ├────────────┼─────────┼──────────┼─────────┼────────────────────┤
         │ Rolling    │ 🔴 High │ minutes: │ ~1×     │ location-service:  │
         │ (K8s only) │ no %    │ rolling  │ (surge  │ trivial stateless  │
         │            │ control │ restart  │ pods)   │ patch bump         │
         ├────────────┼─────────┼──────────┼─────────┼────────────────────┤
         │ Shadow /   │ 🟢 Zero │ n/a: rm  │ + v2    │ skills-service:    │
         │ Mirror     │ users   │ mirror   │ pods    │ prove the 8.1%-    │
         │            │ never   │ stanza   │         │ error fix under    │
         │            │ hit v2  │          │         │ real load, safely  │
         └────────────┴─────────┴──────────┴─────────┴────────────────────┘

         [DECISION FLOW — pick a strategy in four questions]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Q1  Must users be 100% shielded while v2 is tested?           │
         │        │ YES → SHADOW / MIRROR  (then come back to Q2)         │
         │        ▼ no                                                    │
         │  Q2  All-or-nothing change (DB schema / infra) + instant undo? │
         │        │ YES → BLUE-GREEN                                      │
         │        ▼ no                                                    │
         │  Q3  Risky code you want to watch under partial real load?     │
         │        │ YES → CANARY  5% → 25% → 50% → 100%                   │
         │        ▼ no                                                    │
         │  Q4  Boring, low-risk, stateless patch?                        │
         │          YES → plain Kubernetes ROLLING UPDATE                 │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    14.5  Deep Dive — Automated Canary: Metrics-Gated Promotion and Rollback
         - DEFINITION: A metrics-gated canary promotes (or rolls back) v2
           automatically, based on Prometheus numbers instead of a human
           staring at Grafana for five days
         - Why it matters: humans miss 3 A.M. error spikes; a controller
           checking every minute does not — and it rolls back in seconds,
           before the pager even fires
         - How it works: a loop queries Prometheus → compares v2 against
           the gates (and against v1's live baseline) → edits the
           VirtualService weights up on pass, to zero on fail
         - Set the gates BEFORE the rollout starts — deciding thresholds
           mid-incident is how bad deploys reach 100%

         🧠 ANALOGY. Think of the metrics-gated loop in 14.5 like a
         car's adaptive cruise control: it never asks the driver's
         permission every second, it just watches one gauge (here:
         v2's error rate and p99 latency) against a set limit, and
         brakes — drops v2's weight to 0 — the instant that gauge is
         crossed. A human can still grab the wheel, but the system
         never waits for one before reacting.

         [PROMOTION GATES — what jobpost-api v2 must prove at each step]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  GATE 1  ERROR RATE  v2 5xx ratio < 1%                         │
         │                      AND not > 2% above v1's live rate         │
         │  GATE 2  LATENCY     v2 p99 < 300ms                            │
         │                      AND not > 2× v1's p99 (baseline 234ms)    │
         │  GATE 3  SOAK TIME   24h clean at the current weight           │
         │                      before ramping to the next step           │
         │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────        │
         │  ALL gates pass → promote:  5% → 25% → 50% → 100%              │
         │  ANY gate fails → rollback: v2 weight → 0  (~2 seconds)        │
         │                                                                │
         │  # Gate query — v2 error ratio over the last 5 minutes:        │
         │  sum(rate(istio_requests_total{destination_service_name=       │
         │    "jobpost-api",destination_version="v2",                     │
         │    response_code=~"5.."}[5m]))                                 │
         │  / sum(rate(istio_requests_total{destination_service_name=     │
         │      "jobpost-api",destination_version="v2"}[5m]))             │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [INSTANT ROLLBACK — the one-liner to memorize]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  kubectl patch vs jobpost-api-vs -n anihpj --type='json' \     │
         │    -p='[{"op":"replace",                                       │
         │         "path":"/spec/http/0/route/1/weight","value":0}]'      │
         │                                                                │
         │  # route/1 = the v2 entry in the VS route list                 │
         │  # With v2 at weight 0, Envoy sends ALL traffic to v1 —        │
         │  # weights are relative proportions, so v1's number does       │
         │  # not need to be edited back to 100                           │
         │  # Propagation ~2s. Pods untouched. Users never notice.        │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [AUTOMATED CANARY LOOP — what a controller does every minute]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  T+0m : set v2 weight = 5, start the clock                     │
         │  T+1m : query Prometheus → all gates pass? ✅ keep watching    │
         │  ...                                                           │
         │  T+24h: 24h clean → weight 25 → re-gate → 50 → re-gate → 100   │
         │  ANY minute a gate fails:                                      │
         │    → v2 weight = 0        (automatic — no human in the loop)   │
         │    → alert #anihpj-oncall with the failing metric attached     │
         │    → rollout marked FAILED; fix v2, start again from MIRROR    │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Flagger (CNCF, Flux family): you declare a Canary custom
           resource holding these gates; Flagger then OWNS the
           VirtualService — it creates it, walks the weights up step by
           step, runs the Prometheus checks between steps, and flips the
           weight back to 0 on failure. One page of YAML replaces five
           days of dashboard-watching.
         - Argo Rollouts: swaps your Deployment for a Rollout CRD whose
           strategy.canary.trafficRouting.istio block points at your VS
           and DR; AnalysisTemplates run PromQL gates between steps and
           abort automatically on failure. Pairs naturally with Argo CD
           for GitOps-driven progressive delivery.


    14.6  Traffic Mirroring at Partial Percentages and Multi-Destination Mirrors
         - DEFINITION: mirrorPercentage is NOT locked to 100 — it accepts
           any float from 0.0 to 100.0, so anihpj can shadow only a
           slice of live traffic instead of the full firehose
         - Why it matters: mirroring at 100% doubles jobpost-api's real
           compute load on the mirror target; ramping the percentage
           (1% → 10% → 50% → 100%) gets a valid production sample while
           v2 is still small, cheap, and easy to kill if it falls over
         - How it works: mirrorPercentage is completely independent of
           the route's weight fields — v1 keeps serving 100% of real
           users the whole time, no matter what mirrorPercentage is set to
         - If mirrorPercentage is omitted entirely, Istio mirrors ALL
           traffic (100%) by default — always set it explicitly during
           a ramp so "no field" doesn't silently mean "full load"
         - Envoy generates separate stats for the mirrored destination,
           so v2's mirrored-traffic metrics land in Prometheus/Grafana
           under its own destination_version label — the same dashboards
           anihpj already uses for the weighted-canary gates in 14.5
         - HTTPRoute also supports a plural mirrors[] field
           (HTTPMirrorPolicy) that mirrors to MULTIPLE destinations at
           once, each with its own destination and percentage — e.g.
           mirror to the v2 canary AND a separate load-test sandbox from
           one rule

         [PARTIAL-PERCENTAGE MIRROR RAMP — shrinking the blast radius]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  http:                                                         │
         │  - route:                                                      │
         │    - destination: {host: jobpost-api, subset: v1}              │
         │      weight: 100                                               │
         │    mirror: {host: jobpost-api, subset: v2}                     │
         │    mirrorPercentage: {value: 1.0}    # STEP 1: 1% mirrored     │
         │    # ...gate clean 1h, then bump the value...                  │
         │    mirrorPercentage: {value: 10.0}   # STEP 2: 10% mirrored    │
         │    mirrorPercentage: {value: 50.0}   # STEP 3: 50% mirrored    │
         │    mirrorPercentage: {value: 100.0}  # STEP 4: full firehose   │
         │                                                                │
         │  v1 weight never changes — real users see ZERO difference      │
         │  across all four steps; only v2's mirrored load grows          │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [MULTI-DESTINATION MIRROR — the "mirrors" plural field]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  http:                                                         │
         │  - route:                                                      │
         │    - destination: {host: jobpost-api, subset: v1}              │
         │      weight: 100                                               │
         │    mirrors:                                                    │
         │    - destination: {host: jobpost-api, subset: v2}              │
         │      percentage: {value: 25.0}  # canary gets 1/4 of traffic   │
         │    - destination: {host: jobpost-api-loadtest}                 │
         │      percentage: {value: 100.0} # sandbox gets everything      │
         │                                                                │
         │  Each entry in mirrors[] is independent: different targets,    │
         │  different percentages, all from ONE HTTPRoute rule            │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    14.7  Istio Control-Plane Canary Upgrades vs Application Canary — Don't Confuse Them
         - DEFINITION: everything in 14.1-14.6 is APPLICATION canary — a
           VirtualService weight decides which version of jobpost-api a
           user's request reaches. Istio also has its own, completely
           separate CONTROL-PLANE canary: running two istiod versions
           side by side so a mesh upgrade can be tested before it
           touches every namespace
         - Why it matters: the ICA exam tests both, and they are graded
           independently — a scenario asking "how do you safely test a
           new Istio version before a mesh-wide upgrade" is answered
           with istioctl revisions, NOT VirtualService weights
         - How it works: istioctl install --set revision=canary installs
           a second, fully independent istiod (its own Deployment,
           Service and webhook, all labeled with the revision name)
           alongside the existing control plane — nothing mesh-wide
           changes yet
         - A namespace only picks up the canary control plane once it is
           labeled istio.io/rev=canary AND its pods are restarted so the
           sidecar injector re-runs — untouched namespaces stay on the
           stable revision the entire time
         - ⚠️ The legacy istio-injection=enabled label takes precedence
           over istio.io/rev for backward compatibility — it must be
           REMOVED (istio-injection-) when adding istio.io/rev, or the
           namespace silently stays on the stable control plane
         - Revision names can't contain "." — use 1-30-2, not 1.30.2
         - Production pattern: point namespaces at a stable TAG
           (istioctl tag set) instead of a raw revision, so promoting
           the whole fleet is one --overwrite command, not N relabels
         - Full coverage of the upgrade workflow, canary-then-promote
           cadence and istioctl x precheck lives in Chapter 17 — this
           entry exists only so 14's "canary" is never mistaken for 17's

         [TWO DIFFERENT THINGS THAT SHARE THE WORD "CANARY"]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                    APP CANARY (14.1-14.6)  CONTROL-PLANE       │
         │                                             CANARY (Ch 17)     │
         │  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────      │
         │  What splits     jobpost-api v1 vs v2       istiod stable vs   │
         │                                              istiod canary     │
         │  Lives in        VirtualService weight      istioctl revision  │
         │                  / mirror fields             + namespace label │
         │  Blast radius    % of USER requests          % of NAMESPACES   │
         │                                               on the new mesh  │
         │  Rollback        edit VS weight to 0          relabel ns back  │
         │                  (~2 seconds)                 to old revision  │
         │  Who cares       jobpost-api developers        mesh operators  │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [CONTROL-PLANE CANARY — installing and testing a new istiod]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  # 1. Install a second istiod next to the stable one:          │
         │  istioctl install --set revision=canary                        │
         │                                                                │
         │  # 2. Point ONE test namespace at it (never anihpj-prod yet):  │
         │  kubectl label namespace anihpj-staging \                      │
         │    istio-injection- istio.io/rev=canary                        │
         │  kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj-staging          │
         │                                                                │
         │  # 3. Watch anihpj-staging on the new control plane; clean?    │
         │  #    relabel more namespaces the same way, one at a time      │
         │                                                                │
         │  # 4. Rollback = relabel to the stable revision + restart —    │
         │  #    the OLD istiod never left, so this is instant            │
         │  kubectl label namespace anihpj-staging \                      │
         │    istio.io/rev=canary- istio.io/rev=stable                    │
         │  kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj-staging          │
         │                                                                │
         │  # Production pattern: a stable TAG so app teams never         │
         │  # relabel by hand — promote by moving the tag instead:        │
         │  istioctl tag set prod-stable --revision 1-29-1                │
         │  istioctl tag set prod-canary --revision 1-30-2                │
         │  istioctl tag set prod-stable --revision 1-30-2 --overwrite    │
         │  #  ^ moves EVERY ns labeled istio.io/rev=prod-stable onto     │
         │  #    1-30-2 with no relabeling at all                         │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — What Envoy Actually Does at Each Weight Shift
    14.5 already showed the PROMOTION GATES that decide WHEN jobpost-api v2
    is allowed to ramp. This is the layer underneath that decision: what
    literally happens inside Envoy the instant that YAML edit lands, and why
    "propagation ~2s" in 14.1's rollback box is a specific, provable number
    and not a hopeful guess.

    Every VirtualService edit follows the same path: the Kubernetes API
    server stores the new weight, istiod's controller (watching that object)
    recomputes jobpost-api's route configuration, and istiod pushes it to
    every subscribed Envoy over the SAME long-lived xDS gRPC stream those
    sidecars have held open since they started — no new connection, no
    restart, no drain. Envoy hot-swaps its in-memory route table (RDS) as
    soon as the push lands, and the NEXT request it receives — even one
    arriving on an already-open, kept-alive connection — is weighed against
    the new split. Nothing about a weight edit ever touches a running pod.

    ┌──────────┬──────────────┬─────────────────────────┬─────────────┐
    │ STAGE    │ WEIGHT v1/v2 │ ENVOY RDS, VIA xDS      │ IN-FLIGHT   │
    ├──────────┼──────────────┼─────────────────────────┼─────────────┤
    │ MIRROR   │ 100 / 0      │ v2 added as mirror only │ untouched   │
    │ 5%       │ 95 / 5       │ clusters [v1:95, v2:5]  │ unaffected  │
    │ 25%      │ 75 / 25      │ clusters [v1:75, v2:25] │ unaffected  │
    │ 50%      │ 50 / 50      │ clusters [v1:50, v2:50] │ unaffected  │
    │ 100%     │ 0 / 100      │ clusters [v1:0, v2:100] │ none on v1  │
    │ ROLLBACK │ any -> 0     │ v2 dropped from RDS     │ v2 finishes │
    └──────────┴──────────────┴─────────────────────────┴─────────────┘

    Rollback works by the exact same mechanism, run in reverse: patching
    v2's weight to 0 is one more RDS push, and Envoy simply stops selecting
    the v2 cluster for any NEW request. Requests already in-flight to v2 are
    NOT killed — they finish normally and return their response — which is
    the real reason 14.1's rollback box can promise "user impact: ZERO"
    instead of "user impact: minimal."

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
      ⚡ Rollback is a weight edit, never a redeploy — if you find yourself
         reaching for kubectl rollout undo on a canary, stop: the correct
         one-liner is the same kubectl patch vs from 14.1
      ⚡ mirrorPercentage and route weight are INDEPENDENT fields — check
         both before assuming "0% traffic" means v2 sees nothing at all
      ⚡ Never mirror a write endpoint at 100% without a shadow database —
         the copy is real, not simulated; a mirrored POST still INSERTs
      ⚡ Blue-green's instant switch is only as safe as its shared schema —
         confirm both versions tolerate the CURRENT PostgreSQL schema before
         flipping, not after
      ⚡ On a decision-matrix question, read "instant rollback needed" as
         blue-green and "watch it under partial load" as canary — the exam
         rarely uses either word directly
      ⚡ "Canary" in a question about istiod, revisions, or mesh upgrades is
         Chapter 17's domain, not this one — don't reach for VirtualService
         weight on an installation question

    COMMANDS CHEAT-CARD
    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
    │ COMMAND                                   │ WHAT IT DOES                 │
    ├───────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┤
    │ kubectl apply -f jobpost-api-v2.yaml      │ deploy v2 at replicas:0      │
    │   -n anihpj                               │ (Phase 1 — zero traffic yet) │
    │ kubectl get virtualservice jobpost-api-vs │ read the CURRENT weight /    │
    │   -n anihpj -o yaml                       │ mirror split                 │
    │ kubectl patch vs jobpost-api-vs -n anihpj │ edit ONE weight field —      │
    │   --type='json' -p='[...]'                │ ramp up or roll back         │
    │ istioctl proxy-config routes              │ confirm Envoy's live RDS     │
    │   deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj            │ route matches the VS         │
    │ istioctl analyze -n anihpj                │ catch a bad subset/weight    │
    │                                           │ before it ever applies       │
    │ kubectl delete deployment jobpost-api-v1  │ retire v1 once v2 is         │
    │   -n anihpj                               │ fully promoted (14.1)        │
    │ kubectl label ns anihpj-staging \         │ opt ONE namespace into a     │
    │   istio-injection- istio.io/rev=canary    │ CONTROL-PLANE canary (14.7)  │
    │ istioctl tag set prod-stable \            │ promote every ns on that     │
    │   --revision 1-30-2 --overwrite           │ tag at once (14.7)           │
    └───────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘

    🧪 PRACTICE DRILL (6 minutes) — Ramp jobpost-api from 10% to 50%, then roll it back
      1. kubectl get virtualservice jobpost-api-vs -n anihpj -o yaml —
         confirm the CURRENT split (should read v1:90 / v2:10)
      2. Patch the VirtualService so v1:50 / v2:50 — one weight edit,
         both destinations
      3. istioctl proxy-config routes deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj —
         confirm the sidecar's live route table already shows 50/50
      4. Time a rollback: patch v2 back to weight 0 and note how long it
         takes to see 0% in proxy-config routes again
      5. Re-run the same istioctl proxy-config routes check — confirm v1 is
         back to 100% and no pod was ever touched

    VISUAL SUMMARY — the whole chapter, end to end
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ 14.1  Canary: weight ramps mirror → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%,           │
    │       gated at every step — rollback is weight → 0                   │
    │   │                                                                  │
    │   ▼                                                                  │
    │ 14.2  Shadow/Mirror: mirror + mirrorPercentage copy live traffic to  │
    │       v2 with ZERO user impact — responses are discarded, not routed │
    │   │                                                                  │
    │   ▼                                                                  │
    │ 14.3  Blue-Green: the same weight field, used for an INSTANT         │
    │       all-or-nothing switch instead of a gradual ramp                │
    │   │                                                                  │
    │   ▼                                                                  │
    │ 14.4  Decision Matrix: risk x rollback x cost turns "which strategy" │
    │       into a 4-question lookup, not a judgment call                  │
    │   │                                                                  │
    │   ▼                                                                  │
    │ 14.5  Automated Canary: Prometheus gates replace a human watching    │
    │       Grafana — Flagger/Argo Rollouts own the weight edits           │
    │   │                                                                  │
    │   ▼                                                                  │
    │ 14.6  mirrorPercentage ramps independently of weight (1% → 100%),    │
    │       and mirrors[] can shadow MULTIPLE destinations at once         │
    │   │                                                                  │
    │   ▼                                                                  │
    │ 14.7  APPLICATION canary (VS weight, jobpost-api) is NOT the same    │
    │       thing as CONTROL-PLANE canary (istioctl revision, istiod)      │
    │   │                                                                  │
    │   ▼                                                                  │
    │ RESULT: jobpost-api v2 ships to 100% of anihpj with a rollback       │

    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    In prose: Chapter 14 starts from two fields you already know — weight
    and mirror — and spends seven sections turning them into disciplined
    release strategies: a gradual canary (14.1), a zero-risk shadow test
    (14.2), and an instant blue-green switch (14.3), each scored against the
    others in a single decision matrix (14.4). The back half goes deeper on
    the exact same primitives — a metrics-gated loop that promotes or rolls
    back jobpost-api v2 without a human watching a dashboard (14.5), a
    mirror that can be ramped or split across multiple destinations instead
    of firing at 100% (14.6) — before closing on the one distinction the ICA
    exam grades separately from everything else in this chapter: an
    application canary is a VirtualService weight decision, a control-plane
    canary is an istioctl revision decision, and the two are never the same
    question (14.7).

Chapter 15: Rate Limiting and Envoy Filters
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    [CHAPTER 15 ROADMAP]
         Chapter 15 of 14-16 (Part 8: Advanced Traffic Patterns) · Difficulty:
         🔴 Advanced · Extends Traffic Management (35%) — not its own graded
         ICA domain
         "What stops one caller from taking jobpost-api down — even after a
         perfectly safe rollout?"

    [WHY THIS MATTERS]
         By the time you reach Chapter 15, jobpost-api has survived Chapter
         14's canary rollout and is running v2 for 100% of real users, fully
         authenticated end-to-end since Chapter 12's mTLS lockdown. None of
         that protects it from a single caller who is technically welcome: a
         retry storm from search-service during a bad deploy, a scraper
         hammering /api/jobs/ every few milliseconds, or one batch job that
         forgot to add backoff. Rate limiting is the layer that catches
         exactly this — Envoy rejects the 101st request in a second before
         Django ever sees it, either per-pod (local) or mesh-wide against one
         shared counter (global). And some problems still won't fit any
         built-in CRD at all: a bespoke auth-token format, a one-off header
         rewrite, a legacy protocol quirk — which is why this chapter also
         covers EnvoyFilter and WasmPlugin, the two doors Istio leaves open
         for running your own code inside Envoy when VirtualService,
         AuthorizationPolicy, and Telemetry all fall short. Both doors are
         powerful and both carry real risk: EnvoyFilter edits Envoy's
         internal xDS config directly, and istio.io's own reference page
         warns it can destabilize the entire mesh if used carelessly.

    [LEARNING OBJECTIVES]
         ✅ Configure a local (per-pod) rate limit on jobpost-api using
            EnvoyFilter and Envoy's built-in token bucket
         ✅ Decide when a requirement ("1000 req/min per IP") demands GLOBAL
            rate limiting instead of LOCAL, and size the Redis-backed RLS
         ✅ Shape traffic by client type (e.g. a batch-job header) using
            fault-injection delay as a deliberate latency brake
         ✅ Compute sustained rate and burst ceiling from a token bucket's
            maxTokens / tokensPerFill / fillInterval
         ✅ Choose between WasmPlugin and a Lua EnvoyFilter to extend Envoy,
            and justify the choice by risk and blast radius
         ✅ Read and write an EnvoyFilter's applyTo/context/operation patch
            triple, including the two-patch pattern global rate limiting needs
         ✅ Predict which EnvoyFilter's patch wins when two collide on the
            same workload, and apply anihpj's governance checklist to avoid it

    [EXAM / ICA RELEVANCE]
         Chapter 15 has no dedicated ICA exam domain of its own — the
         blueprint has no line item called "rate limiting." Instead, these
         skills sit at the production edge of two domains you ARE graded on:
         Traffic Management (35%) expects you to shape and protect traffic
         beyond basic routing, and Installation/Upgrade/Configuration (20%)
         expects you to understand Istio's extensibility points and their
         operational risk. Expect questions that hand you a local_ratelimit
         or WasmPlugin YAML and ask you to spot a wrong field, compute a
         derived rate from fillInterval math, or decide which of two
         colliding EnvoyFilters wins — not questions that name "rate
         limiting" directly.

    [CHAPTER 15 SECTION MAP]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ CHAPTER 15 SECTION MAP — three groups, one throughline                       │
         │                                                                              │
         │ GROUP 1 — THE BEHAVIORS  (15.1-15.3): what you actually configure            │

         │   (maxTokens/fill/rate)      (two extension doors)      full CRD reference   │
