    Read top to bottom: 16.1-16.2 widen the mesh's membership (more
    clusters, one VM), 16.3-16.5 change what runs inside each member
    (sidecar-free where it counts, down to the HBONE wire format), 16.6
    turns that architectural option into a per-service decision, and
    16.7-16.9 give the resulting shape a name and a CLI to run it
    day-to-day.

    16.1 Multi-Cluster Istio — Spanning Kubernetes Clusters
         - Single mesh spanning multiple Kubernetes clusters
         - Control-plane models: Multi-Primary (each cluster runs its
           own istiod) and Primary-Remote (a primary's istiod also
           manages remote clusters with no control plane of their
           own) — each can be single- or multi-network; see 16.7
         - Use case: anihpj deployed across EU and US clusters with
           geographic routing — send EU users to EU cluster
         [MULTI-CLUSTER DIAGRAM: two clusters with mesh federation]

         [MULTI-CLUSTER ISTIO — anihpj EU + US deployment]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                                                                    │
         │   🌍 EU Users              🌎 US Users                             │
         │        │                        │                                  │
         │        ▼                        ▼                                  │
         │   [EU LoadBalancer]        [US LoadBalancer]                        │
         │        │                        │                                  │
         │   ┌────▼────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────┐   │
         │   │                   SINGLE ISTIO MESH                        │   │
         │   │                                                            │   │
         │   │  CLUSTER 1 (EU — Frankfurt)  │  CLUSTER 2 (US — Virginia) │   │
         │   │  ┌─────────────────────────┐ │  ┌────────────────────────┐│   │
         │   │  │ istiod (EU primary)     │ │  │ istiod (US replica)   ││   │
         │   │  │ jobpost-api:v1          │ │  │ jobpost-api:v1         ││   │
         │   │  │ user-service            │ │  │ user-service           ││   │
         │   │  │ skills-service          │ │  │ skills-service         ││   │
         │   │  └─────────────────────────┘ │  └────────────────────────┘│   │
         │   │           │    mTLS cross-cluster calls   │               │   │
         │   │           └──────────────────────────────┘               │   │
         │   │                                                            │   │
         │   │  VirtualService: locality-based failover                   │   │
         │   │  • EU users → EU cluster (low latency)                    │   │
         │   │  • EU cluster down → auto failover to US cluster          │   │
         │   │  • mTLS works ACROSS clusters seamlessly                  │   │
         │   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────-┘   │
         │                                                                    │
         │  DEPLOYMENT MODELS:                                                │
         │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
         │  │  Primary-Remote:  One istiod manages both clusters           │ │
         │  │  Multi-Primary:   Each cluster has own istiod (recommended)  │ │
         │  │  External CP:     istiod in a separate dedicated cluster     │ │
         │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - DEFINITION: EAST-WEST GATEWAY — a dedicated Istio gateway that
           carries service-to-service traffic BETWEEN clusters
           ("east-west"), unlike the ingress gateway which carries user
           traffic INTO the mesh ("north-south"). It exposes port 15443
           in tls AUTO_PASSTHROUGH mode and forwards mTLS connections
           without ever decrypting them
         📖 KEY TERM
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ EAST-WEST GATEWAY != the ingress gateway in ROLE, but IS     │
         │ the same Envoy gateway image under the hood -- only its      │
         │ Gateway resource differs: port 15443, tls AUTO_PASSTHROUGH,  │
         │ so it forwards mTLS bytes by SNI, never decrypting them.     │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Cross-cluster mTLS requirement: all clusters must share the
           SAME root CA → SPIFFE identities stay globally unique and a
           certificate minted in one cluster validates in the other
         → No shared root CA → cross-cluster handshakes fail → each
           cluster becomes an island that can only talk to itself
         - Service discovery across clusters: each istiod is given a
           "remote secret" (a kubeconfig) so it can read the OTHER
           cluster's API server and learn its endpoints

         🔧 UNDER THE HOOD: that remote secret isn't magic -- istiod
         points its normal Kubernetes informer at the OTHER cluster's
         API server via the borrowed kubeconfig, running the same
         List/Watch on Services and Endpoints it runs locally. Results
         merge into ONE internal registry alongside local endpoints,
         then push to every Envoy/ztunnel over standard xDS -- why EU
         and US pods appear side by side with no visible seam.

         [CROSS-CLUSTER PLUMBING — what multi-cluster really requires]
         ┌───────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
         │ REQUIREMENT               │ WHY IT EXISTS                    │
         ├───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Shared root CA            │ certs from either cluster        │
         │                           │ validate in the other → mTLS     │
         ├───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
         │ East-west gateway :15443  │ dedicated gateway carrying       │
         │ (tls AUTO_PASSTHROUGH)    │ service-to-service traffic       │
         │                           │ BETWEEN clusters, unopened       │
         ├───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Remote secrets            │ lets each istiod read the OTHER  │
         │ (istioctl create-remote-  │ cluster's API server to discover │
         │  secret)                  │ its services and endpoints       │
         ├───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
         │ topology.istio.io/network │ tells Istio which network each   │
         │ label per cluster         │ cluster is on → route via the    │
         │                           │ east-west gateway when crossing  │
         └───────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

         [LOCALITY FAILOVER — keep EU traffic in EU, fail over to US]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                          │
         │  kind: DestinationRule                                       │
         │  metadata:                                                   │
         │    name: jobpost-api-locality                                │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                         │
         │  spec:                                                       │
         │    host: jobpost-api                                         │
         │    trafficPolicy:                                            │
         │      loadBalancer:                                           │
         │        localityLbSetting:                                    │
         │          enabled: true            ← prefer local endpoints   │
         │          failover:                                           │
         │          - from: eu-central-1     ← EU cluster's region      │
         │            to: us-east-1          ← where EU traffic goes    │
         │      outlierDetection:            ← REQUIRED for failover!   │
         │        consecutive5xxErrors: 5    ← marks region unhealthy   │
         │        interval: 30s                                         │
         │        baseEjectionTime: 30s                                 │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    16.2 VM Workloads in the Mesh
         - Add non-Kubernetes VMs (legacy apps, databases) to the Istio mesh
         - VM gets a WorkloadEntry and certificate — treated like a Pod
         - anihpj use case: legacy PostgreSQL VM joins the mesh for mTLS
         - 🎯 ICA EXAM NOTE: this is the external → in-mesh direction of
           "Connecting In-Mesh Workloads to External Workloads and
           Services." The reverse direction (in-mesh → external, e.g.
           calling api.stripe.com) is ServiceEntry — see Ch8

         [VM IN THE MESH — legacy PostgreSQL VM joining anihpj mesh]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  BEFORE (VM outside mesh):                                         │
         │                                                                    │
         │  [skills-service Pod] ──plain TCP──▶ [PostgreSQL VM: 10.0.5.20]   │
         │  No mTLS. No metrics. No circuit breaker. Just raw database.      │
         │                                                                    │
         │  AFTER (VM inside mesh):                                           │
         │                                                                    │
         │  Step 1: Install Envoy proxy on the VM (istio-proxy binary)       │
         │  Step 2: Apply WorkloadEntry in Kubernetes:                        │
         │    apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                              │
         │    kind: WorkloadEntry                                             │
         │    metadata: {name: postgres-vm}                                  │
         │    spec:                                                           │
         │      address: 10.0.5.20          ← VM IP                         │
         │      labels: {app: postgres}                                      │
         │  Step 3: istiod issues certificate to VM's Envoy proxy            │
         │                                                                    │
         │  [skills-service Pod] ──mTLS──▶ [PostgreSQL VM: 10.0.5.20]        │
         │  ✅ Same mTLS as between pods                                      │
         │  ✅ Metrics visible in Grafana                                      │
         │  ✅ AuthorizationPolicy controls who can query the database        │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - DEFINITION: WORKLOADGROUP — the "Deployment template" for VMs:
           it declares the labels, network, and serviceAccount that every
           VM instance inherits. Think of it this way: WorkloadEntry is
           to a VM what a Pod is to a container; WorkloadGroup is the
           Deployment that stamps them out
         📖 KEY TERM
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ WORKLOADENTRY is a real Istio CRD (networking.istio.io) --   │
         │ not a native Kubernetes object. Without one, istiod has no   │
         │ record of the VM: no CSR gets validated, no SPIFFE SVID      │
         │ gets issued, and AuthorizationPolicy can't allow or deny it  │
         │ -- Postgres could be perfectly healthy and still be a        │
         │ complete blind spot to the mesh.                             │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - How the VM earns its identity: the VM's istio-proxy sends a
           CSR to istiod:15012 → istiod validates it against the
           WorkloadGroup → signs and returns a SPIFFE SVID certificate
         - A ServiceEntry (location: MESH_INTERNAL, resolution: STATIC)
           gives the VM a stable DNS name that anihpj pods can call —
           psql connection strings keep working, now over mTLS

         [VM ONBOARDING FLOW — WorkloadGroup → proxy → SVID → mTLS]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  1. Apply WorkloadGroup (template: labels, serviceAccount)   │
         │  2. Generate VM bootstrap files:                             │
         │       istioctl x workload entry configure ...                │
         │  3. Copy files to the VM, install + start istio-proxy        │
         │  4. VM proxy sends CSR ──▶ istiod:15012                      │
         │  5. istiod validates vs WorkloadGroup ──▶ signs SPIFFE SVID  │
         │  6. WorkloadEntry auto-registered (one per live VM)          │
         │  7. ServiceEntry (MESH_INTERNAL, STATIC) gives it a DNS name │
         │  ──▶ skills-service ══mTLS══▶ postgres VM, psql unchanged    │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    16.3 Istio Ambient Mesh — Sidecar-Free Mode
         - New Istio architecture (alpha in v1.18, beta in v1.22, GA
           since v1.24): no sidecar injection required!
         - Layer 4 (ztunnel): handles mTLS + basic routing without sidecar
         - Layer 7 (waypoint proxy): optional, per-namespace L7 features
         - Reduced overhead: no per-pod sidecar → less memory, faster startup
         - anihpj use case: ambient mode for lower-overhead deployments
         [AMBIENT vs SIDECAR ARCHITECTURE COMPARISON DIAGRAM]

         [SIDECAR vs AMBIENT MESH — architecture comparison]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
         │  SIDECAR MODE (classic Istio)    │  AMBIENT MODE (GA in 1.24)       │
         ├──────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
         │                                  │                                  │
         │  [Pod: jobpost-api]              │  [Pod: jobpost-api]              │
         │  ┌────────┐ ┌──────────┐         │  ┌────────────────────────┐      │
         │  │Django  │ │istio-proxy│         │  │Django (no sidecar!)   │      │
         │  │:8000   │ │(Envoy)   │         │  └────────────────────────┘      │
         │  └────────┘ └──────────┘         │          │                       │
         │  Sidecar in EVERY pod            │          ▼ (via iptables)        │
         │  • ~128Mi memory/pod overhead    │  [ztunnel DaemonSet on Node]     │
         │  • ~50ms pod startup overhead    │  • One per NODE (not per pod)    │
         │  • Full L4 + L7 features         │  • Handles L4: mTLS, auth        │
         │                                  │                                  │
         │                                  │  [Waypoint Proxy - per namespace]│
         │                                  │  • Optional, for L7 features     │
         │                                  │  • Shared across namespace        │
         │                                  │                                  │
         │  OVERHEAD:                        │  OVERHEAD:                       │
         │  7 anihpj services × 128Mi =      │  1 ztunnel/node (~50Mi) +        │
         │  ~900Mi extra memory             │  1 waypoint/namespace (~100Mi)   │
         │  = 9× more memory for mesh!      │  = 150Mi total! 6× less ✅       │
         └──────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

         [AMBIENT MODE ENABLEMENT for anihpj]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  # Install Istio with ambient mode:                                │
         │  istioctl install --set profile=ambient -y                         │
         │                                                                    │
         │  # Enable ambient for anihpj namespace (no istio-injection label!) │
         │  kubectl label namespace anihpj istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient    │
         │                                                                    │
         │  # Result: pods in anihpj get L4 mTLS via ztunnel automatically    │
         │  # No 2/2 containers — pods stay at 1/1 ← big difference!         │
         │                                                                    │
         │  # To enable L7 features (traffic management, retries, etc.):      │
         │  kubectl apply -f - <<EOF                                          │
         │  apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1                         │
         │  kind: Gateway                                                     │
         │  metadata:                                                         │
         │    name: anihpj-waypoint                                           │
         │    namespace: anihpj                                               │
         │    annotations:                                                    │
         │      istio.io/service-account: anihpj-waypoint                    │
         │  spec:                                                             │
         │    gatewayClassName: istio-waypoint                               │
         │  EOF                                                               │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    16.4  Ambient Mesh Architecture — How ztunnel and Waypoint Work Together
         - DEFINITION: AMBIENT MESH splits the sidecar's job into TWO
           independent layers — a mandatory Layer-4 "zero-trust secure
           overlay" (ztunnel) and an optional Layer-7 processing tier
           (waypoint proxy). You pay only for the features you use.
         - Why it matters: with sidecars, EVERY anihpj pod carries a full
           Envoy even if it only needs mTLS. Ambient gives the whole
           namespace mTLS for the cost of one small per-node agent.
         - How the two layers divide the work:
           • ztunnel — a Rust-based DaemonSet, ONE per node. It captures
             the traffic of every ambient pod on that node and provides
             mTLS, L4 authorization, and TCP telemetry. Always on.
           • waypoint proxy — an Envoy Deployment, typically one per
             namespace. Only created when you need L7: VirtualService
             routing, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, HTTP-level
             AuthorizationPolicy, and full RED metrics.
         → No waypoint = L4 only. Add a waypoint = full L7. Either way,
           application pods are never restarted or reconfigured.

         🧠 ANALOGY. Picture ztunnel and the waypoint proxy as a
         building's front door versus its front desk. EVERY visitor
         passes the front-door guard (ztunnel), who checks ID and logs
         who came and went — no exceptions, nothing to configure. Only
         a few floors bother staffing an actual front desk (waypoint)
         that also asks WHY you're visiting and can redirect you based
         on the answer. Low-traffic services like notification-service
         never need that second desk at all.

         [AMBIENT TWO-LAYER DESIGN — L4 overlay + optional L7 tier]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  LAYER 2 — WAYPOINT PROXY (optional, per namespace)    L7    │
         │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
         │  │ Envoy Deployment, runs as a normal pod in anihpj       │  │
         │  │ • VirtualService routing (canary weights, headers)     │  │
         │  │ • Retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, fault injection │  │
         │  │ • L7 AuthorizationPolicy (methods, paths, JWT claims)  │  │
         │  │ • Full HTTP telemetry (RED metrics, tracing)           │  │
         │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
         │                    ▲ used only if deployed                   │
         │  LAYER 1 — ZTUNNEL (always on, one per NODE)         L4 🔒    │
         │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
         │  │ Rust-based DaemonSet — shared by ALL pods on the node  │  │
         │  │ • mTLS with SPIFFE identity (same certs as sidecars)   │  │
         │  │ • L4 AuthorizationPolicy (identity / port allow-deny)  │  │
         │  │ • TCP metrics (bytes, connections, mTLS status)        │  │
         │  │ • ~50Mi per node — pods stay 1/1, zero pod overhead    │  │
         │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [AMBIENT TRAFFIC FLOW — jobpost-api calling skills-service]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  L4 PATH (no waypoint deployed):                             │
         │                                                              │
         │  [jobpost-api pod] ──▶ ztunnel(node A) ══mTLS/HBONE══▶       │
         │                        ztunnel(node B) ──▶ [skills-service]  │
         │  ✅ encrypted, identity-checked, TCP metrics collected        │
         │  ❌ no HTTP routing, no retries, no circuit breaking          │
         │                                                              │
         │  L7 PATH (waypoint deployed for anihpj):                     │
         │                                                              │
         │  [jobpost-api pod] ──▶ ztunnel ══▶ [waypoint proxy] ══▶      │
         │                        ztunnel ──▶ [skills-service pod]      │
         │  ✅ everything above PLUS VirtualService routing, retries,    │
         │     timeouts, circuit breaking, L7 authz, RED metrics        │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [AMBIENT ENABLEMENT CHEAT SHEET — the three commands to know]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  # 1. Install Istio with the ambient profile                 │
         │  istioctl install --set profile=ambient -y                   │
         │                                                              │
         │  # 2. Opt a namespace into ambient (L4 overlay, no sidecar)  │
         │  kubectl label namespace anihpj \                            │
         │      istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient                         │
         │                                                              │
         │  # 3. (Optional) add L7 — deploy a waypoint proxy            │
         │  istioctl waypoint apply -n anihpj --enroll-namespace        │
         │  # under the hood this creates a Gateway resource with       │
         │  #   gatewayClassName: istio-waypoint                        │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [SIDECAR → AMBIENT MIGRATION — six safe steps for anihpj]
         ┌────┬───────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┐
         │STEP│ ACTION                        │ RESULT                  │
         ├────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
         │ 1  │ istioctl install --set        │ ztunnel DaemonSet runs  │
         │    │   profile=ambient -y          │ on every node           │
         ├────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
         │ 2  │ On a TEST namespace: remove   │ next rollout: pods come │
         │    │ istio-injection label, add    │ up 1/1 — no sidecar     │
         │    │ istio.io/dataplane-mode=      │ container at all        │
         │    │ ambient                       │                         │
         ├────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
         │ 3  │ kubectl get pods → verify 1/1 │ mTLS still enforced —   │
         │    │ + Kiali still shows 🔒 edges   │ now provided by ztunnel │
         ├────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
         │ 4  │ Need L7? istioctl waypoint    │ VS routing, retries, CB │
         │    │ apply -n anihpj               │ return via the waypoint │
         ├────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
         │ 5  │ Repeat namespace by namespace │ sidecar + ambient       │
         │    │ — no big-bang cutover needed  │ coexist during rollout  │
         ├────┼───────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┤
         │ 6  │ Retire unused sidecar         │ clean, all-ambient mesh │
         │    │ injection config/webhooks     │                         │
         └────┴───────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────┘

    16.5  Deep Dive — HBONE: HTTP-Based Overlay Network Environment
         - DEFINITION: HBONE (HTTP-Based Overlay Network Environment)
           is ambient mesh's tunneling protocol — every pod-to-pod
           connection is wrapped in an HTTP/2 CONNECT tunnel between
           ztunnels, secured with mTLS, on dedicated port 15008
         - Why it matters: it replaces the per-pod iptables + sidecar
           interception model; the application's bytes ride inside the
           tunnel unchanged, so no app code or port changes are needed
         - How it works: the source ztunnel opens ONE mTLS connection to
           the destination ztunnel and multiplexes many application
           streams over it as HTTP/2 streams → fewer TCP handshakes,
           fewer TLS sessions to manage
         - Identity is preserved: the mTLS handshake uses the SPIFFE
           certificate of the SOURCE POD's service account (not the
           node!) — AuthorizationPolicy still sees
           cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api as the caller

         [HBONE PROTOCOL STACK — layers of an ambient connection]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
         │  │ Application data (HTTP / gRPC / psql wire bytes)       │  │
         │  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤  │
         │  │ HTTP/2 CONNECT tunnel (HBONE) — one stream per app     │  │
         │  │ connection, many streams multiplexed per peer          │  │
         │  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤  │
         │  │ mTLS — SPIFFE cert of the SOURCE POD's service account │  │
         │  ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤  │
         │  │ TCP → destination ztunnel, port 15008                  │  │
         │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
         │                                                              │
         │  KEY FACTS:                                                  │
         │  • 15008 = HBONE tunnel port (memorize alongside 15001,      │
         │    15006, 15020, 15021, 15090, 15443)                        │
         │  • Identity survives the tunnel: authz still evaluates the   │
         │    calling POD's SPIFFE ID, never the node's                 │
         │  • Waypoints speak HBONE too — same tunnel, extra L7 hop     │
         │  • Transparent to apps: no code change, no port change       │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [INTERCEPTION COMPARED — sidecar iptables vs ambient HBONE]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  SIDECAR MODE:                                               │
         │  app :8000 → pod iptables REDIRECT → localhost:15001         │
         │  → own Envoy sidecar → mTLS → peer sidecar :15006 → app      │
         │                                                              │
         │  AMBIENT MODE:                                               │
         │  app :8000 → node-level redirection → local ztunnel          │
         │  → HTTP/2 CONNECT over mTLS → peer ztunnel :15008 → app      │
         │                                                              │
         │  → Same zero-trust guarantees, none of the per-pod plumbing  │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    16.6  Sidecar vs Ambient — Decision Guide
         - There is no single "right" mode — decide per namespace using
           four questions: per-pod L7 needs, resource budget, upgrade
           blast radius, and maturity requirements. Both modes coexist
           inside one mesh, so mixed deployments are normal.
         - Rule of thumb for anihpj: latency-critical public services
           that rely on canary weights and circuit breakers (jobpost-api,
           skills-service) → sidecar, or ambient + waypoint; internal
           low-traffic services that only need mTLS + identity allow/deny
           (notification-service, location-service) → ambient L4 only
         → When in doubt, start new namespaces in ambient L4 and add a
           waypoint the day you actually need L7 — it is a one-command,
           zero-restart upgrade

         [DECISION TABLE — choose the data-plane mode per namespace]
         ┌───────────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────┐
         │ QUESTION          │ SIDECAR              │ AMBIENT          │
         ├───────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
         │ Per-pod L7 needs  │ Full L7 in every pod │ L7 only where a  │
         │ (VS, retries, CB, │ including per-pod    │ waypoint exists; │
         │  WASM/Lua, fault  │ EnvoyFilter / WASM   │ no EnvoyFilter   │
         │  injection)       │ customization        │ or WASM per pod  │
         ├───────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
         │ Resource budget   │ ~128Mi × every pod   │ ~50Mi per node + │
         │                   │ (7 anihpj svcs ≈     │ ~100Mi/waypoint  │
         │                   │ 900Mi just for mesh) │ (≈6× cheaper)    │
         ├───────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
         │ Upgrade blast     │ Proxy upgrade means  │ ztunnel upgraded │
         │ radius            │ restarting EVERY     │ per node — app   │
         │                   │ injected pod         │ pods never move  │
         ├───────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
         │ Current maturity  │ Battle-tested for    │ GA since 1.24 —  │
         │                   │ years; every Istio   │ newer, a few     │
         │                   │ feature supported    │ features lag     │
         └───────────────────┴──────────────────────┴──────────────────┘

         - The two questions above (L7 needs? enforce in-pod?) collapse
           into a real decision tree — walk any anihpj workload through
           it branch by branch and it lands on exactly one mode:

         [DECISION TREE — branch-by-branch, not just the table above]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │   SIDECAR vs AMBIENT — WHICH MODE FOR THIS WORKLOAD?                │
         │                                                                     │
         │   Q1  Need L7 traffic mgmt / L7 security per workload?              │
         │       (canary weights, retries, circuit breaking, fault             │
         │        injection, JWT or HTTP-method-level authz rules)             │
         │          │                                                          │
         │      ┌───┴───┐                                                      │
         │     YES      NO                                                     │
         │      │        └──▶ Q1b  Need mTLS + basic L4 identity               │
         │      │              allow/deny only (AuthorizationPolicy on         │
         │      │              source principal, no HTTP-level rules)?         │
         │      │                        │                                     │
         │      │                    ┌───┴───┐                                 │
         │      │                   YES     NO  → still AMBIENT L4-ONLY —      │
         │      │                    │            it is the mesh-wide default; │
         │      │                    │            mTLS is free, add a waypoint │
         │      │                    │            only once L7 is truly needed │
         │      │                    ▼                                         │
         │      │              AMBIENT L4-ONLY                                 │
         │      │              (ztunnel handles mTLS + L4 authz — no waypoint, │
         │      │               no sidecar, ~50Mi shared per node)             │
         │      ▼                                                              │
         │   Q2  Need that L7 policy enforced INSIDE the workload's own        │
         │       pod — custom EnvoyFilter/WASM, or per-request tracing         │
         │       spans emitted from the app's own proxy?                       │
         │          │                                                          │
         │      ┌───┴───┐                                                      │
         │     YES      NO                                                     │
         │      │        └──▶ AMBIENT + WAYPOINT                               │
         │      │             (L7 policy runs in a shared waypoint proxy;      │
         │      │              the app pod itself stays sidecar-free)          │
         │      ▼                                                              │
         │   SIDECAR MODE                                                      │
         │   (full L7 stack in every pod — VirtualService, DestinationRule,    │
         │    EnvoyFilter/WASM, and per-request tracing all run in-process)    │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - Running five real anihpj services through that same tree —
           notice jobpost-api and auth-service both land on sidecar for
           DIFFERENT reasons, while skills-service and user-service need
           the same L7 features but NEITHER needs them in-pod, so a
           waypoint is enough:

         [FIVE anihpj SERVICES WALKED THROUGH THE TREE]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ jobpost-api                                                              │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Q1 (L7 traffic mgmt/security needed?)                                    │
         │     → YES — canary weight-shifted rollouts (v2: 5%→25%→50%→100%)         │
         │       and a circuit breaker guarding calls to skills-service             │
         │ Q2 (enforce in-pod / own tracing?)                                       │
         │     → YES — rate-limiting WASM filter and Jaeger trace spans are         │
         │       emitted from jobpost-api's own proxy, not a shared one             │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ MODE → SIDECAR                                                           │
         │ WHY  → needs canary weights + circuit breaker + its own per-pod          │
         │        WASM/tracing → full in-pod L7 → sidecar mode                      │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ skills-service                                                           │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Q1 (L7 traffic mgmt/security needed?)                                    │
         │     → YES — outlier detection + retries fix the cold-cache/              │
         │       warm-cache load-balancing problem (Chapter 1.2, Problem 4)         │
         │ Q2 (enforce in-pod / own tracing?)                                       │
         │     → NO — the retry/outlier-detection policy is generic L7              │
         │       traffic management; no custom WASM or private tracing              │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ MODE → AMBIENT + WAYPOINT                                                │
         │ WHY  → needs L7 traffic policy but nothing that must run inside          │
         │        its own pod → a shared waypoint covers it, no sidecar cost        │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ auth-service                                                             │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Q1 (L7 traffic mgmt/security needed?)                                    │
         │     → YES — circuit breaker isolates auth-service the moment it          │
         │       starts returning 503s (Chapter 1.2, Problem 7)                     │
         │ Q2 (enforce in-pod / own tracing?)                                       │
         │     → YES — a per-pod WASM filter validates JWT claims before            │
         │       the request ever reaches Django                                    │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ MODE → SIDECAR                                                           │
         │ WHY  → circuit breaker + a custom in-pod WASM claims-check → the         │
         │        L7 policy must live with the workload → sidecar mode              │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ user-service                                                             │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Q1 (L7 traffic mgmt/security needed?)                                    │
         │     → YES — needs a retry + timeout policy so one slow response          │
         │       can't cascade into thread-pool exhaustion (Chapter 1.2, Problem 1) │
         │ Q2 (enforce in-pod / own tracing?)                                       │
         │     → NO — a shared retry/timeout policy is enough; user-service         │
         │       ships no per-pod EnvoyFilter/WASM of its own                       │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ MODE → AMBIENT + WAYPOINT                                                │
         │ WHY  → needs L7 resilience (retries/timeouts) but no in-pod              │
         │        customization → waypoint handles it, sidecar not required         │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ location-service                                                         │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Q1 (L7 traffic mgmt/security needed?)                                    │
         │     → NO — internal, low-traffic geo lookups; no canarying,              │
         │       no retries policy, no per-request L7 rules                         │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ MODE → AMBIENT L4-ONLY                                                   │
         │ WHY  → just needs mTLS + identity allow/deny between anihpj              │
         │        services → ztunnel alone is enough, no waypoint needed            │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    16.7  Multi-Cluster Deployment Models — The Four Topology Combinations
         - DEFINITION: Istio's multi-cluster topologies come from
           crossing TWO independent axes — the CONTROL-PLANE axis
           (Multi-Primary vs Primary-Remote, from 16.1) and the
           NETWORK axis (single-network vs multi-network) — which
           together give exactly four supported combinations
         - Control-plane axis: Multi-Primary = every cluster runs its
           OWN istiod and reads the other cluster's via a remote
           secret, so one control plane's outage only affects that
           cluster's workloads. Primary-Remote = only the primary
           cluster(s) run istiod; remote clusters carry NO
           control-plane pods at all — their sidecars/ztunnels are
           configured by the primary's istiod over the network
         - Network axis: single-network = every pod in every cluster
           can reach every other pod's IP directly (e.g. VPC-peered
           clusters) — no east-west gateway is deployed. Multi-network
           = pods CANNOT route to each other's IPs directly — an
           east-west gateway (16.1) is REQUIRED in every cluster so
           cross-cluster traffic has somewhere to land
         - Why it matters: picking the wrong combination for anihpj's
           real network topology is a day-one outage, not a tuning
           problem — if EU and US clusters sit in different VPCs with
           no peering, skipping the east-west gateway means
           cross-cluster calls never resolve, no matter how correct
           the DestinationRule locality config (16.1) is
         - anihpj reality: the EU (Frankfurt) and US (Virginia)
           clusters are in different cloud regions with no direct
           pod-to-pod routing between them → anihpj runs Multi-Primary
           + Multi-Network, the bottom row of the matrix below

         [MULTI-CLUSTER DEPLOYMENT MODEL MATRIX — all four combinations]
         ┌─────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┐
         │ MODEL / NETWORK             │ EAST-WEST GW?        │ WHO RUNS istiod                   │
         ├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Multi-Primary, single-net   │ No                   │ Every cluster (own CP)            │
         ├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Multi-Primary, multi-net    │ Yes, 1 per cluster   │ Every cluster (own CP)            │
         ├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Primary-Remote, single-net  │ No                   │ Primary cluster(s) only           │
         ├─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Primary-Remote, multi-net   │ Yes, 1 per cluster   │ Primary cluster(s) only           │
         └─────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┘

         - All four combinations still require the 16.1 baseline —
           shared root CA, bidirectional remote secrets via
           `istioctl create-remote-secret` — the matrix above only
           tracks what changes ON TOP of that baseline. The two
           multi-network rows additionally need the east-west gateway
           installed per cluster AND a `topology.istio.io/network`
           label so Istio knows which pods can reach each other direct

         [MULTI-PRIMARY / MULTI-NETWORK — anihpj's actual EU + US topology]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ MULTI-PRIMARY / MULTI-NETWORK - anihpj EU + US, no direct routing           │
         │                                                                             │
         │ CLUSTER 1 - EU                          CLUSTER 2 - US                      │
         │ istiod (own control plane)              istiod (own control plane)          │
         │ topology.istio.io/network=network1      topology.istio.io/network=network2  │
         │ east-west gateway :15443  <==mTLS==>    east-west gateway :15443            │
         │                                                                             │
         │ Pods can NOT reach the other cluster's Pod IPs directly (multi-network)     │
         │ -> every cross-cluster call transits the east-west gateway, SNI passthrough │
         │ -> remote secrets let each istiod discover the OTHER cluster's Services     │
         │ -> shared root CA -> SPIFFE identity from either cluster validates on both  │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    16.8  The WorkloadGroup CRD — Full Field Reference & Auto-Registration Lifecycle
         - DEFINITION: WorkloadGroup has exactly three spec fields —
           metadata (labels/annotations every generated WorkloadEntry
           inherits), template (a WorkloadEntry-shaped stencil:
           serviceAccount, network, ports — NEVER an address, since
           each live VM supplies its own), and probe (a readiness
           check, same shape as a Pod's) — see 16.2 for how
           WorkloadEntry/WorkloadGroup map to Pod/Deployment
         - Why it matters: without a WorkloadGroup, every new anihpj
           VM needs a hand-written WorkloadEntry. WITH one — plus
           auto-registration — a VM that boots with the right
           bootstrap files registers ITSELF, and one that dies gets
           cleaned up automatically. VMs start behaving like a
           self-healing fleet instead of static, hand-tracked hosts
         - How it works: WorkloadGroup is the template (think
           Deployment); istiod, with auto-registration enabled, stamps
           out one WorkloadEntry per live VM instance it sees a valid
           CSR from — the WorkloadEntry is the instance (think Pod)

         [WORKLOADGROUP — anihpj's postgres VM template, fully annotated]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1                                          │
         │ kind: WorkloadGroup                                                         │
         │ metadata:                                                                   │
         │   name: postgres-vm-group                                                   │
         │   namespace: anihpj                                                         │
         │ spec:                                                                       │
         │   metadata:                                                                 │
         │     labels: {app: postgres, version: v1}   <- every auto-WorkloadEntry      │
         │                                                inherits these labels        │
         │   template:                                                                 │
         │     serviceAccount: postgres-sa   <- identity every VM instance gets        │
         │     network: vm-network           <- must match the WorkloadEntry's network │
         │     ports: {postgresql: 5432}                                               │
         │   probe:                          <- readiness check, same idea as a Pod    │
         │     periodSeconds: 5                                                        │
         │     initialDelaySeconds: 5                                                  │
         │     tcpSocket: {port: 5432}       <- unhealthy VM is pulled from the pool   │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - The four bootstrap files are what turn a bare VM into a
           mesh member — `istioctl x workload entry configure`
           generates all four in one shot:

         [VM BOOTSTRAP FILES — generated by istioctl x workload entry configure]
         ┌────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ FILE           │ WHAT istioctl x workload entry configure PUTS IN IT      │
         ├────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ cluster.env    │ namespace, service account, network, ports the VM joins  │
         ├────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ istio-token    │ K8s token the VM's first CSR uses to prove it may join   │
         ├────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ mesh.yaml      │ ProxyConfig: discoveryAddress, health-check settings     │
         ├────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ root-cert.pem  │ root cert the VM uses to authenticate istiod itself      │
         └────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         - 🎯 ICA EXAM NOTE: auto-registration is an ALPHA feature,
           gated behind PILOT_ENABLE_WORKLOAD_ENTRY_AUTOREGISTRATION=
           true. Without that flag, WorkloadEntry stays a resource YOU
           create by hand (as shown in 16.2) — auto-registration only
           changes WHO creates the WorkloadEntry, never whether one is
           needed for a VM to be part of the mesh

         [VM AUTO-REGISTRATION LIFECYCLE — WorkloadGroup to self-healing fleet]
         ┌──────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ STEP │ ACTION                                    │ RESULT                               │
         ├──────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ 1    │ Install w/ PILOT_ENABLE_WORKLOAD_         │ istiod will auto-create a            │
         │      │ ENTRY_AUTOREGISTRATION=true (Alpha)       │ WorkloadEntry for any matching VM    │
         ├──────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ 2    │ Apply the WorkloadGroup template          │ defines what a valid VM instance     │
         │      │ (labels, serviceAccount, network, probe)  │ looks like                           │
         ├──────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ 3    │ istioctl x workload entry configure       │ generates cluster.env, istio-token,  │
         │      │ --autoregister -f group.yaml -o out/      │ mesh.yaml, root-cert.pem for the VM  │
         ├──────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ 4    │ Copy the 4 files to the VM; install       │ VM's istio-proxy boots with its      │
         │      │ and start istio-proxy                     │ bootstrap identity                   │
         ├──────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ 5    │ VM agent sends a CSR to istiod:15012      │ istiod validates it against the      │
         │      │ using the istio-token                     │ WorkloadGroup, signs a SPIFFE SVID   │
         ├──────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ 6    │ istiod auto-creates the WorkloadEntry     │ kubectl get workloadentry shows it,  │
         │      │ for the now-live VM                       │ health tracked via the probe         │
         ├──────┼───────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ 7    │ VM stops heartbeating past the            │ WorkloadEntry is marked unhealthy,   │
         │      │ health-check timeout                      │ then garbage-collected               │
         └──────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘

    16.9  The istioctl waypoint Command Family
         - DEFINITION: `istioctl waypoint` is the CLI front door for
           ambient mode's optional L7 tier (16.4) — five subcommands
           cover the whole lifecycle: apply (deploy), generate
           (preview YAML without applying), list (inventory +
           readiness), status (is-it-actually-in-use check), and
           delete (teardown)
         - Why it matters: a waypoint is "just" a Gateway API resource
           (gatewayClassName: istio-waypoint, per 16.3) underneath, but
           hand-writing that YAML for every namespace, service, and
           GitOps pipeline is exactly the toil istioctl waypoint
           exists to remove — apply for imperative use, generate for
           anything that goes through a PR review first
         - How it works — the five subcommands, in the order an
           anihpj platform team would actually use them:

         [ISTIOCTL WAYPOINT COMMAND FAMILY]
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
         │ COMMAND                                 │ WHAT IT DOES                     │
         ├─────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
         │ istioctl waypoint apply -n <ns>         │ creates/updates a waypoint GW    │
         │   [--enroll-namespace]                  │   + labels the namespace for you │
         ├─────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
         │ istioctl waypoint generate -n <ns>      │ prints the GW YAML, does NOT     │
         │   --for service|workload                │   apply it - safe for GitOps     │
         ├─────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
         │ istioctl waypoint list [-n <ns>|-A]     │ waypoints + PROGRAMMED status    │
         ├─────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
         │ istioctl waypoint status -n <ns>        │ is THIS workload/svc using a     │
         │   <name>                                │   waypoint right now? (live)     │
         ├─────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
         │ istioctl waypoint delete --all -n <ns>  │ removes waypoint(s) from a ns    │
         └─────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

         - Waypoints don't apply themselves to traffic automatically —
           a resource must be LABELED to say "route my traffic through
           this waypoint," and that label can be scoped as narrowly or
           as broadly as the anihpj use case needs:

         [WAYPOINT SCOPING — istio.io/use-waypoint at three levels + cross-ns]
         ┌────────────┬───────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┐
         │ SCOPE      │ LABEL                         │ anihpj EXAMPLE            │
         ├────────────┼───────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
         │ Namespace  │ istio.io/use-waypoint=<name>  │ ns anihpj (or pass        │
         │            │ on the Namespace              │ --enroll-namespace)       │
         ├────────────┼───────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
         │ Service    │ istio.io/use-waypoint=<name>  │ svc user-service ->       │
         │            │ on the Service                │ only that Service         │
         ├────────────┼───────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
         │ Pod        │ istio.io/use-waypoint=<name>  │ Pods matching a           │
         │            │ on the Pod(s)                 │ label selector            │
         ├────────────┼───────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
         │ Cross-ns   │ + istio.io/use-waypoint-      │ ServiceEntry routed       │
         │ (egress)   │ namespace=<ns>                │ via a shared waypoint     │
         └────────────┴───────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘

         - Worked anihpj example: `istioctl waypoint apply -n anihpj
           --enroll-namespace` gives every ambient pod in anihpj L7
           through one shared, namespace-wide waypoint. To carve
           user-service out onto its own dedicated waypoint instead —
           e.g. because it needs a heavier L7 AuthorizationPolicy that
           should not add latency to the rest of the namespace:
             kubectl label svc user-service -n anihpj \
               istio.io/use-waypoint=user-svc-waypoint
           user-service's traffic now takes the per-service waypoint
           while every other anihpj service keeps using the
           namespace-wide one — both coexist in the same mesh, the
           same way sidecar and ambient namespaces coexist (16.6)

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     CHAPTERS 14-16: DAILY WORK TAKEAWAYS (Advanced Patterns)
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    After these chapters, in your daily work you will:
      • Run a full canary: deploy v2 → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% over days
      • Rollback instantly: change weight to 0% — one YAML edit, no downtime
      • Use traffic mirroring to test v2 with REAL production traffic safely
      • Do blue-green deployments: instant 100% switch, instant rollback
      • Add local rate limiting per pod (EnvoyFilter) to protect Django
      • Set up global rate limiting (Redis-backed) per user/IP
      • Understand multi-cluster: EU + US clusters with locality failover
      • Add legacy VMs to the mesh via WorkloadEntry
      • Evaluate Ambient mesh: sidecar-free mode, 6x less memory overhead
      • Know when to use sidecar mode vs ambient mode

    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
     CHAPTERS 14-16: ICA EXAM TIPS & QUESTIONS (Advanced — extends Traffic 35% & Install 20%)
    ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    🎯 ICA EXAM FOCUS — Advanced Patterns is not its own domain; canary/
       blue-green (Ch14) is graded under Traffic Management's "Configuring
       Traffic Shifting," and ambient mode (16.3-16.6) is graded under
       Installation's "Sidecar or Ambient Mode" (see 4.11):
      • "Deploy new version gradually" = VirtualService weight-based canary
      • "Test v2 with real traffic safely" = VirtualService mirror
      • "Block excessive requests per pod" = EnvoyFilter local rate limiting
      • "Join a VM to the mesh" = WorkloadEntry
      • "Enable ambient / no sidecar" = istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient label
      • "Cross-cluster traffic" = east-west gateway :15443 + shared root CA

    Q1: How do you mirror 100% of production traffic to a v2 deployment?
    A1: In VirtualService, add mirror: {host: jobpost-api, subset: v2} with
        mirrorPercentage: {value: 100.0}. v1 handles all user responses; v2
        gets a silent copy for testing.

    Q2: What Istio resource registers a legacy VM in the service mesh?
    A2: WorkloadEntry — specifies the VM's IP address and labels so istiod can
        issue it a SPIFFE certificate and apply mesh policies.

    Q3: jobpost-api must reject anything above 100 requests/minute PER POD
        with HTTP 429, without deploying any extra service. What do you use?
    A3: An EnvoyFilter that inserts envoy.filters.http.local_ratelimit into
        HTTP_FILTER (INSERT_BEFORE envoy.filters.http.router) with
        token_bucket: {max_tokens: 100, tokens_per_fill: 100,
        fill_interval: 60s}. Local rate limiting is per-pod and in-memory —
        no Redis or external rate-limit service needed, unlike global.

    Q4: You mirrored production traffic to jobpost-api v2 for a week and
        Grafana shows v2's error rate matches v1. Promote v2 as a canary —
        what exactly changes in the VirtualService?
    A4: Delete the mirror:/mirrorPercentage: block and replace the single
        route with weighted destinations: subset v1 weight: 95, subset v2
        weight: 5, then raise v2 (25 → 50 → 100) while watching dashboards.
        Mirroring proved correctness silently; weights now shift REAL user
        responses gradually.

    Q5: During a blue-green cutover, v2 (green) starts throwing 8.1%
        errors. Roll back with zero downtime — what is the fastest fix?
    A5: Edit the VirtualService weights back to v1: 100 / v2: 0 (kubectl
        edit virtualservice jobpost-api -n anihpj, or re-apply the old
        YAML). xDS propagates in ~1-2 seconds and no pods restart — that
        instant, restart-free rollback is the whole point of blue-green
        behind Istio.

    Q6: EU users must be served by the EU cluster, failing over to the US
        cluster only when EU endpoints are unhealthy. What do you configure?
    A6: A DestinationRule on jobpost-api with trafficPolicy.loadBalancer.
        localityLbSetting: {enabled: true, failover: [{from: eu-central-1,
        to: us-east-1}]} PLUS an outlierDetection block (e.g.
        consecutive5xxErrors: 5). Locality failover only activates when
        outlier detection can mark the local endpoints unhealthy.

    Q7: Cross-cluster calls between the EU and US clusters fail their mTLS
        handshake. Name the two multi-cluster prerequisites you check first.
    A7: (1) Both clusters must share the SAME root CA — otherwise certs
        minted in one cluster do not validate in the other. (2) The
        east-west gateway must be deployed and exposing port 15443 in tls
        AUTO_PASSTHROUGH mode so cross-cluster mTLS can transit unopened.
        Then confirm remote secrets exist (istioctl create-remote-secret).

    Q8: Bring the legacy PostgreSQL VM at 10.0.5.20:5432 into the anihpj
        mesh so skills-service reaches it over mTLS. Outline the steps.
    A8: (1) Create a WorkloadGroup (labels app: postgres, serviceAccount:
        postgres-sa) and a WorkloadEntry with address: 10.0.5.20 using
        apiVersion networking.istio.io/v1. (2) Install istio-proxy on the
        VM; it sends a CSR to istiod:15012 and receives a SPIFFE SVID.
        (3) Add a ServiceEntry (location: MESH_INTERNAL, resolution:
        STATIC) so pods resolve the VM by name. psql traffic now rides
        mTLS and obeys AuthorizationPolicy.

    Q9: Enable sidecar-free Istio for the anihpj namespace and verify it
        worked. Which commands?
    A9: istioctl install --set profile=ambient -y, then kubectl label
        namespace anihpj istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient. Verify: kubectl
        get pods -n anihpj shows 1/1 (no istio-proxy container), the
        ztunnel DaemonSet is Running in istio-system, and Kiali still
        shows lock icons on edges. For L7 features add a waypoint:
        istioctl waypoint apply -n anihpj.

    Q10: One team runs 40 low-traffic internal services needing only mTLS
         and identity-based allow/deny; another team needs per-pod WASM
         filters plus canary weights on jobpost-api. Which data-plane mode
         fits each, and can they share a cluster?
    A10: The 40 internal services → ambient L4 only (ztunnel gives mTLS +
         L4 authz for ~50Mi per node instead of 40 × 128Mi of sidecars).
         The jobpost-api team → sidecar mode (per-pod WASM/EnvoyFilter is
         not available in ambient), or ambient + waypoint if plain canary
         weights suffice. Yes — sidecar and ambient namespaces coexist in
         the same mesh with working mTLS between them.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — ONE REQUEST, EU SIDECAR CLUSTER TO US AMBIENT CLUSTER
    16.5 walked through HBONE's protocol stack in isolation; here it is
    doing real work across BOTH boundaries anihpj actually has — a
    cluster boundary and a sidecar/ambient boundary — in one live
    request:

    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ SCENARIO — jobpost-api (EU cluster, sidecar mode) notifies                │
    │ notification-service (US cluster, ambient mode, L4-only) of a new post    │
    ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ HOP 1  jobpost-api's own Envoy SIDECAR intercepts the outbound call       │
    │        (iptables redirect → localhost:15001) — EU cluster, sidecar mode   │
    │ HOP 2  EU sidecar routes it to the EU EAST-WEST GATEWAY :15443            │
    │        (SNI → topology.istio.io/network=network2, mTLS untouched)         │
    │ HOP 3  EU gateway ══mTLS, AUTO_PASSTHROUGH══▶ US EAST-WEST GATEWAY :15443 │
    │        (neither gateway decrypts — they only route on SNI)                │
    │ HOP 4  US gateway hands off to the local ZTUNNEL on whichever node        │
    │        is running notification-service, over HBONE port 15008             │
    │ HOP 5  ZTUNNEL relays the still-encrypted stream straight to              │
    │        notification-service's pod on localhost — no sidecar, pod is 1/1   │
    ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ IDENTITY CHECK — one mTLS session, five hops, one SPIFFE identity:        │
    │ AuthorizationPolicy in the US cluster still evaluates the caller as       │
    │ cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api, exactly as if both services       │
    │ sat in the same cluster with sidecars on both ends. Neither the           │
    │ cluster boundary (Hop 3) nor the sidecar-to-ambient boundary              │
    │ (Hop 4-5) is visible to identity or policy — only to the proxies.         │
    └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    SPEED TIPS
      ⚡ Default new anihpj namespaces to ambient L4-only; add a waypoint
         (istioctl waypoint apply) only the day you need retries/canary/
         L7 authz — it's a zero-restart upgrade, not a rewrite
      ⚡ Cross-cluster mTLS handshake failing? Check the shared root CA
         FIRST, before touching gateway or network config — it's the
         single most common multi-cluster failure
      ⚡ istioctl create-remote-secret is NOT automatically bidirectional
         — Multi-Primary needs one secret per direction, so an EU-only
         secret leaves US istiod blind to EU services
      ⚡ Verify a VM's health with kubectl get workloadentry -n anihpj
         -o wide, not by pinging it — an unhealthy WorkloadEntry
         silently drops out of the pool with no user-facing error
      ⚡ Before declaring an ambient migration done, check BOTH kubectl
         get pods -n anihpj (1/1) AND istioctl waypoint list -A
         (PROGRAMMED) — either check alone can hide a half-finished
         rollout
      ⚡ Match topology.istio.io/network labels to your REAL VPC peering,
         not your cluster count — a single-network assumption on an
         actually multi-network topology is the exam's favorite trap

    [MULTI-CLUSTER / AMBIENT / VM COMMANDS CHEAT-CARD]
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ COMMAND                                        │ WHAT IT DOES                                 │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ istioctl create-remote-secret ...              │ lets istiod read the OTHER cluster's API     │
    │ istioctl install --set profile=ambient -y      │ installs ztunnel DaemonSet + ambient profile │
    │ kubectl label ns anihpj dataplane-mode=ambient │ opts a namespace into ambient L4, no sidecar │
    │ istioctl waypoint apply -n <ns>                │ deploys/updates a waypoint Gateway           │
    │ istioctl waypoint generate -n <ns>             │ prints waypoint YAML, doesn't apply (GitOps) │
    │ istioctl waypoint list [-n <ns>|-A]            │ waypoints + PROGRAMMED status                │
    │ istioctl waypoint status -n <ns> <name>        │ is this workload using it right now?         │
    │ istioctl waypoint delete --all -n <ns>         │ removes waypoint(s) from a namespace         │
    │ istioctl x workload entry configure            │ generates the 4 VM bootstrap files           │
    │ kubectl get workloadentry -n anihpj            │ lists VM instances + health                  │
    │ kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide             │ 1/1 = ambient, 2/2 = sidecar                 │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    🧪 PRACTICE DRILL (8 minutes) — flip notification-service to ambient without touching jobpost-api
      1. kubectl label pods -n anihpj -l app=notification-service istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient --overwrite
      2. kubectl rollout restart deployment/notification-service -n anihpj
      3. kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=notification-service -o wide → confirm READY is 1/1 (no istio-proxy container)
      4. kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=jobpost-api → confirm it is STILL 2/2, completely unaffected
      5. From any jobpost-api pod: curl -v http://notification-service:PORT/health and confirm success → mTLS now comes from ztunnel, zero app code changed

    [CHAPTER 16 VISUAL SUMMARY — from one cluster to whatever anihpj needs]
    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ STEP 1  SPAN CLUSTERS + ONBOARD THE VM (16.1-16.2)                    │
    │   anihpj crosses EU/US via an east-west gateway + one shared root CA; │
    │   the legacy Postgres VM joins via WorkloadEntry, same mTLS as a pod  │
    │                      │                                                │
    │                      ▼                                                │
    │ STEP 2  DROP THE SIDECAR WHERE IT ISN'T NEEDED (16.3-16.5)            │
    │   ztunnel gives every ambient pod mTLS for ~50Mi/node; a waypoint     │
    │   adds L7 only where a namespace needs it — both ride one HBONE       │
    │   tunnel on port 15008                                                │
    │                      │                                                │
    │                      ▼                                                │
    │ STEP 3  PICK THE RIGHT MODE PER SERVICE (16.6)                        │
    │   jobpost-api/auth-service → sidecar; skills-service/user-service →   │
    │   ambient+waypoint; location-service/notification-service → ambient   │
    │   L4-only — decided by two yes/no questions, not by habit             │
    │                      │                                                │
    │                      ▼                                                │
    │ STEP 4  FORMALIZE + OPERATE IT (16.7-16.9)                            │
    │   Multi-Primary/Multi-Network names anihpj's real EU/US topology;     │
    │   WorkloadGroup makes VM onboarding repeatable; istioctl waypoint     │
    │   apply/list/status/delete runs ambient day-2 like any other CRD      │
    └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    Chapter 16 took anihpj from a single-cluster, all-sidecar mesh to
    whatever topology production actually demands. It crossed the EU/US
    cluster boundary with an east-west gateway and a shared root CA,
    then folded a legacy VM into the same trust domain with a
    WorkloadEntry. It replaced the sidecar's all-or-nothing footprint
    with ambient mesh's two-layer split — ztunnel always on, a waypoint
    only where L7 is earned — and showed that both layers ride the same
    HBONE tunnel whether traffic stays in one cluster or crosses to
    another. The decision guide in 16.6 turned "sidecar or ambient" from
    a mesh-wide policy into a per-service, even per-pod, choice anihpj's
    real services actually need. And 16.7-16.9 gave that whole shape a
    name (Multi-Primary/Multi-Network), a template for repeatable VM
    onboarding (WorkloadGroup), and a CLI family (istioctl waypoint) to
    run it without hand-writing YAML. Nothing here replaces Chapters
    1-15's primitives — VirtualService, DestinationRule,
    AuthorizationPolicy, WorkloadEntry — it just proves they still work
    at the hardest edge cases the exam and production both throw at
    them.

    PART 9 INTRO
    Every Part before this one answered "how do I build the mesh?" —
    route traffic, observe it, secure it, then layer canaries and rate
    limits on top. Part 9 answers the question that matters at 3am on a

    the last Part before the Appendices, deliberately capstone-shaped:
    no new CRD is introduced — by the end of Chapter 17 you are not
    learning Istio anymore, you are OPERATING it, with the exam's own
    Configuration / Control Plane / Data Plane reflex (17.9-17.11).

    💡 anihpj THROUGHOUT: the same jobpost-api, user-service,
    skills-service, location-service, auth-service, search-service, and
    notification-service that have anchored every diagram since Part 1
    now sit behind a control plane that has to survive an Istio version
    bump, a resource crunch, and a real incident — without anyone
    re-learning Istio from scratch under pressure.

    🧠 ANALOGY: Parts 1-8 taught you to fly the plane — controls,
    instruments, the checklist. Part 9 IS the flight: swapping an engine
    mid-route without landing (canary/in-place upgrade), knowing how
    much cargo the plane can carry before it strains (performance
    tuning and istiod HA), and — when a warning light comes on —
    knowing in three seconds whether it's a cockpit-instrument lie
    (control plane), one failing engine (data plane), or a mis-set dial
    (configuration).

    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

    "The mesh is live — something just changed — now what?"

    WHY THIS CHAPTER MATTERS
    Every chapter before this one added something new to anihpj's mesh — a
    Gateway, a DestinationRule, a PeerAuthentication, a rate-limiting
    EnvoyFilter. Chapter 17 introduces no new CRD at all. By now jobpost-api,
    user-service, skills-service, location-service, notification-service,
    auth-service, and search-service already run behind a fully-configured
    mesh — the only open question is whether that mesh survives contact with
    reality: a version bump, a resource crunch, a page at 3am. This is the
    chapter where you stop LEARNING Istio and start OPERATING it — upgrading
    istiod without dropping a request, sizing sidecars before a capacity
    review becomes an incident, and keeping the control plane alive when a
    node disappears. It closes on the same reflex the ICA exam itself is built
    around: when anihpj breaks, is it the YAML (Configuration), the brain
    (Control Plane), or one misbehaving Envoy (Data Plane)? Get that three-way
    split right and every outage in this guide becomes a checklist instead of
    a guess.

    ✅ LEARNING OBJECTIVES — by the end of Chapter 17 you can:
      ✅ Execute a canary upgrade of Istio (old + new istiod side by side) and
        roll it back in minutes if anihpj's error rate spikes
      ✅ Explain why istioctl upgrade (in-place) is exam-testable but
        production-risky, and when a canary upgrade is mandatory instead
      ✅ Size istiod and sidecar resource requests/limits for a named pod
        count, and make istiod HA with 3 replicas plus a PodDisruptionBudget
      ✅ Run the golden debug sequence (analyze, proxy-status, proxy-config,
        logs, dashboards) against a live anihpj incident, in order, every time
      ✅ Classify any anihpj symptom into exactly one of Configuration, Control
        Plane, or Data Plane before reaching for a fix
      ✅ Collect a full diagnostic bundle with istioctl bug-report, and check
        upgrade compatibility with istioctl x precheck first
      ✅ Wire istioctl analyze into a CI/CD pipeline as a merge-blocking gate
        for anihpj's Istio manifests
